the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: - mr president, commissioner, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating mrs sanders-ten holte on the work she has done and the fruitful cooperation which has been established between parliament, the council and the commission in order to arrive at the text which you have just presented to us. i believe that this text will make a significant contribution to the strengthening of quality education in europe, which we are all striving for. i would like to stress, on behalf of my committee on employment and social affairs, the importance of improving the quality of school education and vocational training, the need to establish a system for the exchange of good practice and methodological tools, as an important contribution to social cohesion and the fight against unemployment. the integration into the labour market, the fight against the early withdrawal of young people from the school system, our capacity to provide lifelong learning and access to new technologies are objectives which quality education systems must integrate. i should like to stress two aspects of this qualitative assessment as envisaged in the common position. firstly, this process makes a clear distinction between administrative evaluation and the innovative procedure that we want, that we want to implement and in which, as has been said, all the actors must participate. the second aspect i would like to stress is that it has perhaps not been taken up as fully as we would have liked. we do not want to make this process of qualitative evaluation a factor of prioritization, classification or ranking of excellence among institutions. on the contrary, this form of assessment must enable each institution, however different it may be from the others in terms of the public it receives, the methods or means it uses, to respond to all the risks of academic failure, to increase the intrinsic quality of its teaching for each one, to accommodate all the audiences, from the weakest to the best students, by offering an education adapted to the reality of each student and allowing each one to position himself in a perspective of personal development.
- mr president, we are discussing today a draft recommendation to the member states on the qualitative assessment of education which could bring interesting innovations to the union's working methods. the project is already well advanced on the ground. as early as 1998, at a conference in prague involving 26 european countries, national education ministers agreed to set up a system of common indicators of their methods and results. the aim is first to establish common languages, then to compare results, and finally to exchange experiences, while leaving each state fully responsible for its own education system. we find this initiative interesting, both in its motives and in the method used. firstly, in the knowledge and information society, education is obviously a key not only to human development but also to economic competitiveness. we must therefore make sure that we make the best use of the limited resources at our disposal. it is surprising to see the wide disparities between the member states of the european union, as shown in particular by the first statistics published by eurostat last july. for example, if the european average of public expenditure per pupil in secondary education is 100, germany is 84.9 and france 131.6. the gap is therefore very substantial. and he does not always play the same way. that is why it is in our mutual interest to share our experiences. this interest is particularly evident in the case of france, whose very rigid educational system deserves to be much more subject to the demands of 'school consumers'. but precisely because of this rigidity, any reform is very difficult to carry out. the new cooperation on the evaluation of education systems could open the way to a new and interesting method. it represents an application of open coordination, which the lisbon council had already mentioned, and which could, if developed, constitute a break in european working methods. it is not a question of setting objectives with a view to compulsory harmonization. in any event, articles 149 and 150 do not give the community the power to do so. it is simply a question of discovering together the best practices, without setting quantified objectives a priori, while leaving each country free to draw its own conclusions. with this new method of coordination, we would not be faced with a centralised europe, but with a networked europe, organising exchanges between the various centres of power, namely the national ministries of education. this network coordination is more decentralized, more flexible and more liberal than the traditional harmonization directive. moreover, it can easily cross the union's borders to bring together 26 or more states instead of 15. for all these reasons, mr president, we see great promise in this new form of differentiated cooperation.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it is commonplace to say that heritage and its protection are the determining elements of european identity. it may be commonplace, but it's nevertheless true. heritage is one of the most visible and closest elements to the culture of our fellow citizens. it is part of their daily environment and their own identity. it reinforces the sense of belonging to the european union by identifying our common roots. the protection of heritage is therefore a vital necessity because of the damage it suffers from the effects of time, but also because of the new forms of aggression to which it is subject, such as air pollution, disorderly urbanisation, population pressure and, unfortunately, others. the european parliament has dealt with this matter very seriously, in particular in two resolutions adopted in 1982 and 1988, which constitute references for action to be taken in this field. it seems to me necessary today to take stock of the current state of this question, taking into account both the principle of subsidiarity and the evolution of the european union as a result of the increase in the number of member states. the purpose of the unesco convention is worth recalling. it is about preserving the heritage, not just putting it on a prestigious list. since the last selection of sites in december 2000, 690 sites have been inscribed on the world heritage list, 208 of which are located in the european union. of these 208, 192 are cultural, 11 natural and 5 mixed. the european union is high on the list, with almost a third of the sites, and this is easily explained by europe's important contribution to world civilization. however, in order to achieve a more balanced list in the distribution between the different categories of heritage, as well as between states, a global strategy has been defined by unesco, accompanied by an action plan for its implementation. i think it is desirable that parliament should recommend that member states with a large number of listed properties should limit their listing proposals in the future. it seems to me that they should help to make the world heritage list more representative and balanced, both in terms of geography and content. when this report was adopted by the committee on culture of our parliament, the two provisions on self-limitation were removed by a small majority. it seems to me, however, ladies and gentlemen, that these provisions should be reintroduced, and i have tabled two amendments to that effect on behalf of the ppe group. a second proposal put forward in this report is the establishment of a list at european level. indeed, unesco has a geographical vision of heritage, and in a geographical vision, there is a limitation in the idea of sites. for example, we classify a port, but we don't deal with ships. we'll file a suit against a steel plant, but we won't take care of the hardware. it seems to me that europe, the european union, should have a dynamic vision. it could intervene in the dynamics of heritage and, in this respect, a european list could make a breakthrough. it would make it possible to give greater value to sites whose importance goes beyond the national interest, without, however, encountering worldwide recognition. and this would help to bring europe closer to its citizens, making them aware of a common cultural heritage. heritage often needs restoration. the situation of heritage restorers in the member states should be the subject of a commission study in order to organise the restoration professions in order to guarantee the quality of this work. a quality restoration requires adequate financial resources, and the need for economic management must not be at the expense of the quality of the work. finally, it would be desirable for the european commission, in collaboration with the council of europe and unesco, to study the viability of a legal and fiscal arrangement facilitating forms of patronage relating to the conservation of cultural and natural heritage. this aspect of the matter could be introduced into the discussions on the harmonization of european taxation. the protection of heritage is a subject which requires constant vigilance on our part. we have a responsibility to pass this heritage on to future generations. the young people of europe must be able to identify with it in order to build their future and to better perceive their european identity. when we feel european, is it not more by reference to cultural elements than to economic and social data? i would like to conclude by quoting a phrase which you all know to be from one of the great founders of the european union: 'if i had to do it all over again, i would start with culture'. it's a phrase that could have been uttered by haydn composing in london, by vinci painting in amboise, or by byron expiring in missolonghi. it is the feeling, the happiness, that we feel when each of us, on our travels through the european union, marvels at the treasures we encounter and feels the pride of having become, thanks to the existence of the european union, a modest owner of them, and also the guardian of their sustainability.
- mr president, the report by mrs de veyrac is aimed in particular at broadening the concept of heritage and the criteria for selecting national heritage. the uen group will vote on this report. no one can deny the need to extend this concept to elements that are not only monumental, natural or furniture. it is clear that a large amount of ethnographic data can be collected and protected as world heritage. the importance of musical heritage and oral literature can be emphasized, for which work of collection, analysis and protection is still to be carried out in many countries. this heritage, which is not part of the traditional concept, which often refers only to monuments or sites, is often present in the daily lives of the inhabitants of this planet. it is this presence and permanence, in culture and everyday life, which should determine the very notion of heritage, as mrs prets has also mentioned. i would like to stress, for example, particularly here in strasbourg, the attachment of our fellow citizens to their national currencies and their willingness to regard them as a heritage dimension. the german magazine focus-money recently published a poll showing that 70 percent of germans are attached to the deutschmark and want to keep it. this is an average figure, as the figure rises to 80% in eastern germany. the french ministry of finance, which is responsible for implementing the disappearance of the franc, recently published on its website a very interesting survey on the attachment of the french to their currency. this is only a diagnosis of the contrary, because, of course, they were not asked about the franc but about the euro. the response was no less harsh. only 26% of french people trust this artificial currency. it is not superfluous for me to mention some of these realities, since they do not seem to have been taken into account or to have any bearing on this parliament. in britain, which has decided to protect the national currency, the pound sterling, only 14% of young people aged 18 to 24 want to abandon the pound. the fact that some 45% of danes said yes to the euro would make the recent danish referendum look like a plebiscite in favour of the single currency. europeans are attached to their currencies as they are to their values, their nations, their natural sites, their languages and their cathedrals. it is therefore appropriate to protect national currencies as part of the world heritage. that is the meaning of the amendment which i tabled on behalf of my group and which i propose you support.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. it is astonishing how good reports can be produced when the commission's base is totally inadequate. the rapporteur proposes to interview companies which have not benefited from any support programmes. as a medium-sized entrepreneur, i interviewed a large number of my colleagues. the almost unanimous opinion is that small businesses are losing sight of the european investment fund and, in particular, of the various components of the amsterdam special action programme asap on smes and employment, because there are a large number of individual subprogrammes, with different responsibilities. for example, the regular sme guarantee facility, the growth and jobs initiative, the growth and environment initiative, the eif technology facility etf, the eif start-up programme, new sub-programmes on innovation, e-europe, e-learning etc. which have been part of the eif-etf since lisbon. how are they related to each other and where do i, as an entrepreneur, have to put my project ideas? the same problem is faced by the european parliament, on the other hand, when it wants to assess the overall development of the asap, because there is no coherent presentation of this in the accounts of the eib and the eif. the general theme of sme support is sometimes discussed in its entirety, and the individual components of the asap are sometimes presented in different contexts. the political orientation of the asap is also a matter for consideration. the growth and environment initiative has not received any more funds. it also aims at a completely outdated form of environmental protection. the rest, growth and employment, etf etc, have been continuously increased, but are concentrated in a few high-tech sectors, mainly innovation, communications and genetic engineering. in many cases these smes are not served directly, but are served through intermediaries, usually traditional venture capital and investment funds, which receive loans and guarantees from the eib and where smes must be represented. so nobody really knows which smes are being supported for which projects and how many jobs are being created, except the eib. the eib therefore does not use concrete figures in its estimates of the employment effects of these programmes, but uses a simple macroeconomic model. the results of this will be known in five to ten years. the commission has also proposed that the asap should be extended to cover the whole of the european union, including the countries of central and eastern europe, the former soviet union and the former soviet union. the eib's homepage, which lists the funds to which the eib has granted loans and guarantees, supports this view.
- mr president, europe usually has difficulty in assessing the impact of public policies; this is not the case in this report. i therefore find the estimate of the programme's effects on net job creation interesting. moreover, since the agreement of the social affairs council of 20 december on the statute of the european company, the legal and administrative horizon of smes has been clarified. this is essential, as smes represent 99.8% of all enterprises and employ 66% of the european workforce. however, the concept of smes continues to cover a catch-all category that includes a wide variety of structures and situations. the vast majority of these are enterprises with a maximum of 10 employees. it is regrettable that their specific features are not recognised and that they do not benefit from special measures. unlike the committee on industry, which mentions this in its opinion, the committee on employment and social affairs does not mention such recognition. similarly, the aid scheme should not be reserved for large smes using or producing advanced technologies. the traditional sector should be able to benefit fully from this. i am thinking in particular of the craft sector, which provides jobs, know-how and innovation. in this context, i support the start-up helpdesk programme for small smes. i am more sceptical, however, about encouraging member states to change their tax laws. the creation of a single european structure for venture capital funds operating alongside national structures is envisaged. this may complicate administrative procedures for small smes, which may not have the means to undertake them.
in writing. - the commission's recommendation aims to harmonise the rights of creditors in the event of the winding-up of credit institutions throughout the union. however, nowhere are the rights of employees of the credit institutions concerned specified. certain national laws do recognize employees as creditors. but at best they are assured only of the payment of their due wages. however, they are not compensated for the loss of their jobs, i.e. their future wages, whereas creditors are guaranteed the repayment of their debts, i.e. their capital, the source of their future income. employees have no responsibility for the failures of a bank or credit institution because they have no say in the decisions taken. they are the ones who should be compensated first for the loss of their jobs. we voted against this recommendation which is concerned only with capitalist creditors, not with the employees who run the credit institutions.
in writing. - while we have nothing against 'european cooperation in the field of quality assessment of school education', everyone knows that the quality of education depends on the resources made available to public schools. to ensure quality education, there must be sufficient schools, classes with a limited number of pupils, and a large number of teachers, professors, technical and administrative staff at all levels of education, starting with primary schools. in all european countries, it is at the primary school level that a differentiation is established which causes children from the working class districts to fall behind in their education, often irreversibly. the first step towards european harmonization should be the obligation to align with the countries with the highest educational resources. but even in these countries, the tendency is to cut back on the funds for education and, more generally, for public services, in favour of other budgetary expenditures, the main one being the aid and subsidies granted to capitalist enterprises, that is to say, to their owners. in the absence of an increase in the resources available for education in all the countries of the european union, and in particular where these resources are the weakest, the european recommendation on the quality of education will remain a wishful thinking.
in writing. - the defence and promotion of our heritage in each state is fundamental in that it guarantees our identities and our particularities, while respecting differences. this heritage, whether cultural, architectural, economic or natural, comes from our past: defending it is not a rearguard battle, but preparing for our future. thus, as ernest renan wrote: "the only men of progress are those whose starting point is a profound respect for the past". we must therefore draw on the wealth of our past, our heritage, our roots, our traditions, even the oldest, to prepare our life for tomorrow. we must not forget that the european union is a global community of nations, and that it is not just a european union. but to do this we must respect all the diversity of our heritage, all our differences, and only the principle of subsidiarity can make this possible. this principle will enable us to preserve, develop and pass on our heritage, culture and traditions. to eliminate one or to reduce it to a mere shell (such as hunting, rural life or gastronomy) is to cut the chain of transmission of our wealth and our ways of life, it is to cause a cultural impoverishment that, in the end, will only result in creating a mold in which everyone will have to sink to live in an insipid society, but more malleable, and controllable by the "leaders and rulers". we can't accept that. so, in this perspective of defending, maintaining and promoting our heritage, we must safeguard our architecture, support our crafts, preserve and enhance our landscapes but, and i stress this point, without putting them in jeopardy, and without excluding the cultural traditions and customs that are practiced there. we must also ensure the right to diversity and help maintain all these values, because the countryside has a right to exist in this ultra-urban society. in the light of this report, it is therefore important to defend the heritage of third countries and the union, but it is equally important and fundamental to defend the heritage of our countries and regions. we therefore welcome all the announcements concerning the inclusion of this heritage in the various training projects for the protection and restoration of this heritage. the same applies to aid and support for craft activities, a sector which is very much a creator of jobs, provided that it is not stifled by unrealistic and cumbersome regulations, as has been done for market traders. however, we will make a reservation on european regulation which, under the guise of protecting the environment (a term which is too exclusive), will only erase local traditions and customs which are an integral part of the culture of our lands, which is the opposite of the aim of this report, which we support but on which we will abstain for this reason.
in writing. - as opponents of the market economy, we do not take a position on the alleged simplification of the european market. we therefore abstain on the report. as regards the social legislation and social security, we are in favour of simplifying it to the extent that it is most favourable to workers. as regards vat, we are in favour of simplification by abolishing vat and all taxes on consumption, which are particularly unfair because they affect the lowest income groups, and replacing them with a substantial increase in the tax on capitalist enterprises and a highly progressive tax on all forms of capital income.
in writing. - the heaton-harris report confuses two issues. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft budget for the financial year. the rapporteur, however, criticises the ecb for preventing the action of olaf (european anti-fraud office). it is reported that 'the ecb has stated that it will not allow the office for the fight against fraud (olaf) to carry out internal investigations', that 'in its first report to parliament, the council and the commission, the olaf monitoring committee requested that actions be brought before the european court of justice against community institutions which had not implemented regulation no 1073/99 by the end of 1999' and 'that the commission has initiated proceedings before the european court of justice against the decision of 7 october 1999 of the european central bank concerning the non-application of regulation no 1073/99 of the parliament and of the council'. we consider all this to be very serious and we support the passage in the report which 'deplores the obvious contradiction between this public commitment by the ecb to establish close cooperation with olaf and the decision by the ecb itself to prevent olaf from carrying out internal investigations pending the judgment of the european court of justice'. for that reason, we shall vote for the heaton-harris report.
mr president, the question of frontier workers, which we are discussing today, is a pressing problem in the european union, which has still not found a satisfactory solution. madam commissioner, mr president, this situation does not allow those who live and work on the margins of the various countries of the union to really experience the concept of european integration that we advocate and of which, however, they should be the first beneficiaries. we are accustomed in this house to raise the question of the free movement of persons, and therefore of workers. and yet, on this issue, date, two schools can be distinguished. one is that it wants to overturn the whole system and all the foundations that have made and make the common fisheries policy. the other wishes, without seriously calling into question its foundations, to clarify, modify and improve the system so that the fisheries sector can continue to develop while, of course, respecting and preserving the fishery resources. it is well known that the european fisheries sector is facing the same problems as most other fisheries industries in the world today, and not just on our continent or in our waters. overfishing, which reduces stocks, catches and income, is the main threat to the future of the resources and the fishing industry itself. increased competition, which is linked to the globalisation of the fisheries market, is an additional challenge. the competitiveness of the fishing industry will depend on the ability of the sector to adapt to the constraints imposed by both the state of resources and commercial demand. the common fisheries policy is the management tool the union has adopted to manage fisheries and aquaculture. this policy was designed to manage a common resource and to respect the obligations laid down in the first european treaties. the report thus reflects the views expressed on the four aspects of the common fisheries policy: conservation and management of resources, structural policy, market organization and relations with third countries. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment mr president, the european union's fisheries policy is a vast subject. i am addressing this from the perspective of globalisation and the specific problem of guinea-bissau. as for us, the green group, i would like to remind you that we are in favour of fishing practices which respect natural balances, of the development of small-scale and artisanal fishing - which creates jobs - and of selective fishing which is attentive to the stocks available. it is not only a question of achieving satisfactory economic development for enterprises, but also of preserving the social aspect. we are not in favour of subsidies which encourage over-industrialised fishing, fishing which takes everything without discrimination, even if it means wasting species and damaging food security and biodiversity, fishing which allows for the excessive increase in fleets, etc. we therefore believe that uncontrolled market forces are one of the main reasons for this overinvestment and that these issues must be taken into account in the forthcoming wto negotiations on trade liberalization. we therefore ask the commission to submit appropriate proposals to the other wto members, both on the question of the orientation of the subsidized sectors and on the social side. in addition, we are generally not very favourable to bilateral fisheries agreements between the european union and third countries, which are often small and whose budgets are sometimes of the same order of magnitude as those of the subsidies provided. we must, as far as possible, remain at an integrated level. however, in the case of guinea-bissau, we accept the allocation of the reserve which has been set at eur 6.5 million, as it is devoted to supporting local fisheries, infrastructure and control activities, and a detailed report on the use of these funds will be submitted to parliament.

in writing. - the report by jonas sjöstedt of the gue/ngl on the protection of natural habitats in europe seems to us to be particularly important, especially for france. this is one of the countries where the implementation of the habitats directive, which is more than eight years old, and the birds directive, which is more than 20 years old, as well as the establishment of the natura 2000 network, has been the most delayed, to the point of being seriously called into question. however, as time passes and the more (semi-) natural environments are destroyed, the more difficult it will be to conserve or restore ecosystems in their diversity and richness. far from being "marginal", the maintenance and enrichment of biodiversity (and thus of the diversity of ecosystems) is a major political issue, as it has global implications for our living conditions (including climate change). the aim is not to create local 'reserves' where species would be protected as in a museum, but to integrate these concerns into the overall policy of the community and the member states. the implementation of the habitats and wild birds directives must now be rapid, widespread and effective.
in writing. - i fully agree with the habitats directive and its objectives of protecting the outstanding and endangered natural heritage of the countries of the union. this heritage and its biological and genetic diversity are the most precious assets of the planet and we must ensure that they are protected, reproduced and passed on to future generations. however, i voted against the sjöstedt report for two main reasons. firstly, it introduces an unacceptable blackmailing of the european funds allocated to our countries by making them conditional, by article 11, on compliance with the habitat directive as it stands. if it had simply been a question of ensuring that european funds do not finance projects which destroy these remarkable ecosystems, i would have accepted it and voted for it, but it is unacceptable and unprecedented that one union policy is made conditional on respect for another and that environmental conditionality is, for example, made conditional on social conditionality. secondly, the resolution does not specify the concept of 'disturbance' and its legal aspect, the deliberate blurring of which may lead to the reopening of a dogfight before the courts, leading to bans on popular and traditional hunting where the birds directive and the subsidiary law of the states allow them. it is precisely because the union deliberately maintains this ambiguity that countries have difficulty publishing their 'nature 2000' lists and applying calmly and without resistance from their own farmers the 'habitat' directive, whose noble aims are universally recognized.
in writing. - this report and its amendments deal with financial support for guinea-bissau in the fisheries sector. we voted for them, and we did so out of solidarity with the people, and in particular the fishermen of this country, but with many reservations. firstly, because the aim of fisheries agreements between the european union and third countries is - as is explicitly stated in some other reports - to save the union's fisheries resources and, as a consequence, to increase catches in the seas of other countries. secondly, because we do not know how this aid will be used and where it will be used. unfortunately, too much of this aid is often just a de facto rebate to european companies investing in these countries. on the other hand, these aids are often also misused by local leaders. despite all this, the money that is supposed to help the local population will still be used less badly there than the money given here to the big employers who are laying off workers.
in writing. - the committee on development welcomes the fact that the growth rate of bangladesh's export sector is three times the growth rate of bangladesh's domestic production. but exports are almost exclusively by large, mostly western, companies based in the country. while it is true that these companies are enriching themselves by exploiting the underpaid workers of this country, including its children, this does not help bangladesh to get out of underdevelopment, nor does it help its working population to get out of poverty. the report calls for "the efficiency and competitiveness of the private sector" in world markets. this clearly indicates who it is in his interest to eliminate "infrastructure bubbles", including "transport and energy infrastructure", make the "financial system efficient", or ensure "a transparent and accountable institutional environment", a euphemism for standing up against what in the corruption environment bothers western investors. in these circumstances, the proposal to release european funds is essentially aimed at making up for the failures of the bangladeshi state and at having the european institutions bear the infrastructure costs of the large trusts to enable them to make the most of one of the poorest populations on the planet.
in writing. - since rapid police intervention, like war, is the continuation of politics by other means, and since we have no more confidence in the policy of the european union than in that of the member states, we are against any form of military or police intervention by the european union, wherever it may be. the report gives the example of the balkans. but an 'independent' european police force would be no better than one under the auspices of the un, that is to say the united states. at most, it would strengthen the position of the large european industrial groups in the region, which are looking to the market for the reconstruction of what nato bombers have destroyed. as for the wish that "the rapid reaction mechanism will not be geographically limited", he predicts acts of bribery on behalf of former colonial powers in africa and elsewhere, as france did to protect dictators whose people did not want them, or as britain is doing now in sierra leone. we therefore voted against the creation of the rapid reaction mechanism, as we will vote against any budget devoted to it.
in writing. - by deciding to create the nucleus of a european army, the nice summit opened a new chapter in the history of the eu. for twenty years it has tried to win popular support by claiming to be building a social europe. faced with failure, and following the balkan war, she has just changed her shoulder gun. it now openly admits that its aim is a europe-power which will 'defend its interests everywhere in the world'. it is openly showing its imperialist character. it will do so in conjunction with the united states within the framework of nato. in the future, by coordinating its diplomatic and military forces, the eu will try to optimise what its member states have done individually over the past century. all this is done in the name of "keeping" or "enforcing" peace and "humanitarian operations". both inside and outside the us-dominated nato, the eu is trying to "sell" us its project in the name of "europe's autonomy" vis-à-vis the us. we do not need a euro-militarism: we are as radically opposed to this european army as we were to that of nato. the first consequence will be a drastic increase in the military budget, which will inevitably go hand in hand with increased militaristic propaganda. it will shift scientific and technological research to the military sector. it will transfer an increased share of the state budget to the companies in the sector, with the aim of creating a european military industry (eads, dassault, bae) capable of beating the united states. workers have nothing to gain and everything to lose from this "new" imperialist aim of the eu.
in writing. - this report is mainly concerned with general considerations, but does not propose any concrete decisions. the commission is also proposing to extend the right to health care benefits to the dependent family members of frontier workers or to retired frontier workers and their families. we supported this request but abstained on the report. all workers in the union should enjoy the same social protection, aligned in each of its components (social security, pensions, family allowances) on the practices of the country where they are most favourable to workers. in the meantime, to improve the situation of frontier workers, they and their families should be able to choose, in each of these areas, between the country of residence and the country of work, according to the situation which is most favourable to them.
in writing. - if the directives on the conservation of natural habitats, the disposal of pcbs and pcts and the protection of waters against nitrate pollution are only insufficiently applied in the member states, this does not in any way mean that these directives are bad and need to be changed, as some in this house are trying to make us believe. these directives are in line with the aspirations of european citizens, who are demanding greater consideration for their environment and are calling for the european institutions to act as arbiters. the numerous complaints and petitions registered by the committee on petitions concerning breaches of the environment and these directives bear witness to these expectations. in fact, if these directives are only partially applied, it is because the member states did not assess their consequences when they were adopted. they had not taken into account the financial cost and the changes, sometimes fundamental, which these directives imply for their policies. this applies to both the habitats and nitrates directives, both of which call for a review of agricultural and land use policies which pollute and destroy natural environments. the aim of the habitats directive is to protect a european network of biologically important natural habitats in the long term and to protect it from future development, in order to avoid conflicts of use and the degradation of the habitats concerned. these objectives have been very poorly presented in the member states, leading to sometimes very serious conflicts between the owners and users of the areas concerned. however, where genuine consultation has been established, the results have been quick, with the habitats directive providing the means to support respectful management of the heritage by providing sufficient compensation. this habitat directive is absolutely innovative in the field of land use planning and nature protection, since it reconciles the management of outstanding natural areas and their uses for a better use of the territory. in this sense, the european union must do everything possible to support the implementation of this directive. it must not, under any circumstances, give way to certain categorical interests which would undermine the very spirit of the directive. the commission, as guardian of the treaties, must, on the one hand, show its firmness towards the member states in order to ensure that they apply these directives and, on the other hand, stand firm against attempts to amend these directives before they have been able to show their full relevance, particularly in the fields of water pollution by nitrates and the protection and development of remarkable natural areas. for these reasons, the green group supports the reports presented in general, and in particular the sjöstedt report, which will contribute to a better application of the habitats directive. we abstained because the last-minute attempts to distort the report by weakening the habitats directive and calling for its amendment do not seem to us to be in keeping with the directives we are voting for.
in writing. - we are in favour of helping young farmers who have lost money so that they can cope with the considerable expense of setting up a farm, with the acquisition of the farm and the purchase of equipment. we have therefore voted for this report despite our reservations, because there is no guarantee that much, if not all, of this aid will not go to the children of rich farmers and that once again the poorest will be left behind. we denounce in advance the misappropriation of these funds for the benefit of the children of wealthy farm owners.
in writing. - it is clear that the situation of young farmers is a serious problem in the european union and that they have no real prospects, despite the support given to them at european and national level. that is why i think this report is so important and why i am glad that we voted for it. the economic situation, especially for young people, is poor and sometimes very bad. there is a real lack of prospects for young farmers, and a significant decrease in the number of farmers in general, with an ageing of those who remain. what can the union do? the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, as an opinion committee, did not want to stress aspects which fall within the competence of the other committees. we have therefore focused on issues relating to the education, training and information sectors, and to social and cultural life. we see that young farmers are facing problems, often due to inadequate education and training. even agenda 2000 neglects these fundamental aspects, which are not in the report. as regards the education and vocational training of young farmers, it is necessary for the union, in the framework of the socrates and leonardo programmes, to promote the strengthening of the education and training of young farmers in order to raise their qualifications to the required level. it is necessary to provide training in computer science. internet access must become a reality and young farmers must be aware of integrated production management and marketing systems in order to manage their farms properly. desertification can be combated by maintaining public services in rural areas (schools, post offices, transport), and social life can be maintained by grouping communes together, for example, or by providing mobile services. if the conditions are met for a new boom in agricultural activity, young people from the urban world, who are aware of nature and concerned about a better quality of life, will be able to move to the countryside, while rural young people will no longer renounce the farms left by their parents.
in writing. - the parliamentary reports on which we have to give our opinion cover various aspects of the common fisheries policy, including the management and conservation of fisheries resources, structural policy, the union's external relations on fisheries, market organisation, surveillance and control. the priorities expressed by the commission are: better coherence between the different objectives of the cfp, in particular between conservation of resources, economic efficiency and employment in areas dependent on fisheries; better account being taken of the economic dimension of fisheries; better integration of environmental and fisheries policies; improvement of management tools, including the integration of multiannual tools; a more transparent decision-making process and the maintenance of the external dimension of the cfp. of course, we can support all these points in principle. however, i think it is necessary to stress the following points, the importance of which the commission does not seem to have sufficiently emphasised. while it is true that the determination of tacs must be based mainly on objective scientific evidence, it is essential that dialogue with the professionals be institutionalised and strengthened. fishermen's representatives must be involved in the work of the scientists upstream, in order to build confidence and facilitate informed and more easily acceptable decisions. this guidance will be even more necessary when preparing multiannual guidelines. it is imperative that inspection and sanction systems be harmonised across the different fishing zones, in order to avoid distortions between member states. the system of controls by the community countries over third-country fleets operating in community waters must be strengthened. finally, while maintaining the tac and quota system at the heart of the cfp, we wish to reaffirm our commitment to respect for the principle of relative stability and our opposition to the privatisation of quotas.
in writing. - in 2003, the blue europe with its common fisheries policy will be modified. the year 2001 marks the end of one of the fisheries management instruments, the ipa iv or fisheries guidance programme. there are two years left, until 31 december 2002, to consider and decide on a common policy which, according to the european commission's inventory, raises 18 questions, ranging from free or restricted access to territorial waters, to the control or management of the market in fishery and aquaculture products, to international fisheries agreements, scientific research on fish stocks or the specific features of the mediterranean. this review, if not this revision, of the cfp is taking place in a context with many aspects. first, the resources are not infinite. fish stocks are endangered or in difficulty, from hake, cod, sardines and tuna. there is a waste. more than 15% of the world's fisheries are discarded each year, particularly in the eu, under the pretext of avoiding falling prices or enforcing prohibitions, while countries such as norway value these fisheries above the permitted standards. that's 20 million tons out of 122 million worldwide. international and regional organisations, from the fao to the general fisheries council for the mediterranean, and the north-west atlantic institutions, are also concerned with fisheries control, with the participation of the ec. europe has also concluded 25 bilateral fisheries agreements with angola, the seychelles, madagascar and others, and is trying to reach a difficult agreement with morocco, which is currently in disarray. and above all, there is now a globalisation of the market, with the problem of cheap imports. in essence, the re-writing of the cfp, with its often too many and obscure regulations, must reconcile conflicting objectives: protecting fish stocks, according to a precautionary principle, but also preserving coastal economies and societies sometimes dependent on fishing for employment: this is the case in the channel. the cfp must also be clear, but differentiated enough to take account of regional specificities, from the north sea to the mediterranean and even, as the italians want, in the adriatic or other subregional 'seas'. above all, we must reconcile the extreme openness of the european market, which accounts for 60% of its consumption, with the need to protect our fishermen, who are closing the japanese, american or korean markets. to deal with this diversity of problems, the european commission has used a good method by consulting widely with fisheries, environmental or producer organisations. (intervention by the commission under article 137 of the regulation)
in writing. - the fact that the armies of the major powers have known for at least ten years about the harmfulness of depleted uranium munitions, including to those who use them, only proves that the staffs are as contemptuous of their own soldiers as they are of the civilian population and the enemy army. there is reason to be indignant at the consequences of the use of these weapons for nato soldiers. there is even more reason to be outraged at the consequences for the civilian population, for those who died from depleted uranium weapons as well as those who died under conventional bombs. but what about the hypocritical astonishment of the representatives of all these political groups who participated in the decision to bomb serbia and kosovo, after having supported, for the most part, the gulf war? they have left their staffs free to do whatever they want and now, in the face of public reaction, they seem to be concerned about the consequences of their decision by trying to avoid their own responsibility. we voted for the amendment by the etuc calling for a 'ban on the manufacture, testing, use and sale of depleted uranium weapons', even though we knew that an unjust war would not become a 'clean war'. we voted against the compromise resolution in protest both against the use of depleted uranium weapons, against the wars in which they have been used, and against the hypocrisy of the parties who have supported those wars.
in writing. - public opinion is particularly concerned about the link between depleted uranium used in munitions and public health. the effects of these weapons on military personnel, civilians, and the environment are still unknown. moreover, even depleted uranium (20% less radioactive than natural uranium) is still a nuclear waste whose use is dangerous. there may be a link between the cases of leukemia detected in soldiers who served in the balkans and the use of such weapons by nato. even if the definitive evidence is not clearly established, if scientists do not agree with each other, there is more than mere suspicion today as shown by the results of various investigations. so anxiety is justified and should not be taken lightly. until there is definitive evidence, we must apply the precautionary principle and a moratorium on the use of these weapons. this is the least we can do now, pending a complete ban if the studies confirm the danger. nato must be fully transparent about the use of these weapons and more generally about the conduct of its operations and the european commission must launch an independent scientific inquiry of its own. we owe this demand for truth and transparency to all those who are suffering or currently living in distress. at a time when international law is evolving towards the duty of intervention justified by humanitarian objectives and the defence of human rights, our armed forces cannot put at risk the civilian populations we wish to protect.
in writing. - is the discovery of the dangers of depleted uranium weapons really a surprise? we all know that these weapons, used by nato in the gulf war (1991), in bosnia (1994-95) and in kosovo (1999), have had serious consequences for the civilian populations first bombed, for their environment, for the military, whether they belong to nato, the iraqi, bosnian, serb or kosovar armed forces. for a long time, military and political authorities have been content to belittle those who have expressed concern. and it took american soldiers, then french, to mobilize before the scandal finally broke, after the suspicious death of an italian. there is no such thing as a "clean" war. the implicit admission of the former belligerent forces should help to shed light on the responsibilities of governments and warlords, first and foremost those of the former secretary-general of nato, j. solana. we must demand a ban on the manufacture, testing, use and sale of depleted uranium weapons. we are in favour of signing an international treaty. and in the meantime, we demand a programme of medical surveillance of soldiers who have participated in operations in the balkans, of members of humanitarian organisations who have worked on the ground and of the populations of the affected areas.
- mr president, our group voted in favour of the resolution on communist korea. of course, we strongly deplore the actions of the communist dictatorship in north korea since 1950. the contempt for the human person which has been fostered in it is only the fruit of the unbridled materialism on which communism in particular, and revolutionary ideology in general, is based. our group wishes that north korea will soon be returned to genuine freedom, a prerequisite for peace. we are pleased that the two koreas have been enjoying improved relations for some time. this peace effort is a great hope for thousands of families separated for half a century. we must, as far as we can, encourage this change. nevertheless, we cannot but deplore the desire expressed in the resolution to entrust the european union with the task of managing relations with communist korea instead of the member states. it should be remembered that diplomacy is one of the royal prerogatives of any sovereign state. each state is free to establish diplomatic relations with any other state. each nation must be able to retain the freedom to pursue the foreign policy of its choice, the policy which is most suited to its political and economic interests. i very much doubt that our community institutions, which are all inflated with large, poorly digested principles, have the maturity necessary for such realism.
the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. first of all, i would like to thank you for the strong support which i believe this house and the honourable members have given to active action by the european union at the forthcoming commission meeting in geneva. i also thank you for the many concrete points of view that have been raised in the debate. let me comment on some of them. first of all, it concerns russia and more specifically chechnya. the honourable member is right; i did not mention russia but i did mention chechnya. i would just like to emphasize that the council considers that the situation in chechnya remains serious. perhaps it cannot be described as as acute as in previous years but it is our assessment that we should follow up the resolution presented and adopted last year because of the serious situation in chechnya. we have therefore by no means forgotten this important question. several speakers raised the situation in china. i would like to firmly reject the allegations that the union is trying to hide behind other countries when it comes to combating human rights violations in china. at the same time, it is important that when we do something about the mr situation in china, we actually get a large enough group of countries in the un commission on human rights to succeed. there are problems here, as several members have pointed out in their speeches. right now, we're in a dialogue with china. there will be an opportunity here next month to have a discussion with the chinese about the union's view of the situation. but we also need to have further discussions with the new administration in the united states, because the united states is traditionally the author of this resolution and has been. i can therefore assure the honourable members that the situation in china will continue to receive the union's attention. the honourable member is raising the question of the death penalty, which is extremely important. of course, the union must reject the death penalty wherever it exists - including, of course, the united states. i am particularly grateful to mr van hecke and others for addressing the human rights situation in africa and can only regret that i did not do so myself in my opening speech. it is not just a matter of human rights concerns, but we all know that in many african countries the problems have a greater dignity than that. it is not only human rights that are the problem. this should not, of course, prevent us from paying attention to the problems that exist. i can assure the honourable member that we on the union side will take very carefully into account what has been said in this debate, particularly with regard to africa. finally, a few words on the situation in burma/myanmar. the union is preparing a proposal on the situation in burma/myanmar to be presented to the meeting of the mr commission again this year. it can only be seen as one element in an overall strategy to address the human rights situation in burma/myanmar. for example, we have been responsible for many years on the swedish side for a resolution in the un general assembly on the situation in burma/myanmar, and the union as a whole is actively involved in the discussions in the international labour organization (ilo) on the fact that burma still has forced labour. there are a number of measures which the union strongly supports. i therefore thank you for all the concrete comments and promise to take them into account in the council's further deliberations ahead of the important meeting of the mr commission in geneva later this year.

- it is a great pleasure to welcome prime minister persson. mr president-in-office of the council, i would like to say how pleased we are to welcome you for the first time in this house for the beginning of the swedish presidency, to which we wish every success. without further ado, i would like to give you the floor.
the council. madam president, president of the commission and members of the european parliament! in the last decade alone, europe has changed in an unprecedented way. the cold war has been replaced by cooperation. technological progress has exploded and our economies have become closely interwoven in a global market. the threat to democracy and peace can no longer be simply identified as totalitarian regimes on the other side of the iron curtain. today, instead, the threat to democracy is growing from within the mature democracies themselves. this is evident from the declining confidence in the elected representatives, the decline in voter turnout, the success of populist parties and the radicalisation of far-right movements. few of the great challenges facing europe can be solved by individual nations alone. and we're too dependent on each other. the need for cooperation has never been greater. at the same time, i would venture to say that the prospects for cooperation have also never been more promising. the swedish presidency of the european union is entering an important phase, during a period of great change and challenge in europe. the union is facing its biggest enlargement to date. having agreed on the economic and institutional framework for this historic event, the real negotiations are now under way. the union has adopted a programme of new forms of cooperation to become the most dynamic and competitive economy in the world. we have full employment as a strategic goal. within the framework of economic and monetary union, the important introduction of banknotes and coins is about to take place. the issues of concern to the citizens are increasingly in focus. the union today is an association of active welfare states. today, there is a growing awareness that welfare is not a brake on development, but that welfare and development are mutually reinforcing. sweden is now taking over the presidency for the first time. we shall act in the interests of the union as a whole, be responsible for openness and continuity and promote the development of europe. we also want to consolidate the progress achieved. it is an honour for me as swedish prime minister to present our work programme to you. i will listen to your views and comments with the greatest interest. on the union's comprehensive agenda, we will prioritise three areas: enlargement, employment and the environment. there are three broad policy areas, each of which is crucial to shaping the future of europe's citizens. i shall start with the question of enlargement. no issue is more crucial to the future of the eu and to the development of europe than welcoming new members to the union. it is about our ability to consolidate the foundations of peace and freedom, democracy and prosperity in europe. we are in the process of completing the historic event which will put an end to the division of europe into east and west. it is with humility, pride and strong will that the swedish government wishes to contribute to this work, this historic development. the french presidency successfully concluded the intergovernmental conference aimed at preparing the union's institutions to function well in an enlarged union. an economic framework was already defined in berlin in the spring of 1999. in nice it was made clear that the next intergovernmental conference should not constitute an obstacle or a condition to enlargement. much work remains to be done, but the opportunity exists to welcome new member states after the end of 2002. in the first half of 2001, the enlargement process will enter a phase of concrete negotiations in many areas. sweden's objective is to try to pave the way for a political breakthrough in the negotiations. the principle of differentiation will be a cornerstone of this work. each candidate country will be judged on its own merits, and all will be given the opportunity to catch up. the candidate countries have made considerable progress. however, a breakthrough will require the candidate countries to continue vigorously implementing reforms to meet the conditions for membership and the member states to contribute constructively to the progress of the negotiations. the commission must facilitate the process. we must all work together to ensure that enlargement can take place with strong support among the citizens of the union. the swedish presidency will seize the opportunities to move forward more quickly with the best prepared candidate countries. the european council in gothenburg in june 2001 will assess progress in the enlargement process and provide the necessary guidelines for its successful completion. the eu's relationship with turkey as a candidate country will continue to receive attention. the adoption of the partnership with turkey and the submission of the national adaptation plan by turkey will be key instruments in this respect. much work remains to be done, but the opportunity now exists to welcome new member states after the end of 2002. i hope that the candidate countries will be able to participate in the elections to the european parliament in 2004. another priority is employment. today, unemployment is falling in the eu countries and more people are finding work. but we must not take it for granted. there are still 14 million people in the eu without work. unemployment is a gigantic waste of economic resources and, what is worse, of human knowledge and ambition. nothing is more important for the development and freedom of the individual than having a job and a livelihood. nothing is more important to democracy and equality than work for all. a union which does not take unemployment seriously can never be the union of citizens we all want to see. the ambition to make the eu an employment union has sometimes been described in the debate as just a pipe dream, but something new has happened here. the lisbon european council last march set a new strategic objective for the union. within 10 years, the eu will have the most competitive and knowledge-intensive economy in the world. at the same time, it was agreed that full employment should be a fundamental objective of the union's economic and social policy. i regard this as a great success and as extremely important milestones in the development of the union. today's europe is better equipped than it has been for a very long time to extend the possibility of work to all those who want and are able to work. the outlook for the european economy remains good. the public finances are strong. prices are stable. reforms of product and capital markets are under way across europe. the path to full employment lies through continued economic reforms, enhanced social protection and enhanced welfare. it also covers investment in education and research, new technologies and entrepreneurship, environmental investment and gender equality. the european council in stockholm on 23 and 24 march will be the first in a series of summits in the spring designed to push forward the objectives set in lisbon. we in stockholm should openly and self-critically assess the progress made. the work is being carried forward by community law where appropriate, but mainly by the new open method of coordination. as the presidency, we are committed not to undermine the lisbon strategy by adding too many new issues. we don't need any new processes either. the stockholm meeting should instead identify certain priority areas. we're in the midst of a rapidly accelerating evolution where growth is driven more and more by brain power and less and less by muscle power. at the same time, mobility is increasing. human capital will become the main competitive factor for firms, and education will become the main competitive factor for workers. health care, schools, care, education and other welfare services become competitive assets for countries and localities. the swedish welfare model has always been based on the idea that equality and justice are productive in themselves, that development is stronger if everyone is given the opportunity to contribute to it and everyone shares its fruits. today, developments show that nations with high employment rates and a well-educated population, which have managed to spread technological progress, and which have a fair distribution and a well-covered welfare system are also the countries at the forefront of development in the new technological sectors. nations that do not harness the skills and creativity of all their citizens will lose competitiveness. to this must be added the expected demographic development of europe. low birth rates and a rising proportion of older people threaten to increase the support burden for people of working age significantly from around 2010 onwards. demographic change must be addressed on a broad political front. a comprehensive review of pension systems and health and elderly care systems will be required. measures to increase participation in the labour market will be required. the importance of improved conditions for families with children, gender equality and lifelong learning should be clearly highlighted. as more people are employed, working conditions are also becoming more and more of a focus. the aim is to agree on a definition of quality of work and its importance for growth and employment. in addition, we should emphasize in stockholm the importance of new technologies by further developing the eeurope action plan and paying greater attention to the role of biotechnology in innovation and growth. i would also like to stress the vital importance of the successful development of economic and monetary union for the stability and the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. i think that your work has contributed considerably to the understanding of a very technical and very complex proposal by this house, and one which is certainly not easy to translate into language that is accessible to the ordinary citizen. in this respect i think it has been very successful. the amendment we are proposing to the regulation currently in force has two objectives: firstly, to promote the harmonization of the regulatory system in the field of civil aviation safety by extending it to the harmonization of the operational requirements of aircraft; secondly, to establish the procedures which will enable the community to manage the variants and exceptions which the member states are obliged to adopt from time to time for operational needs. as regards technical requirements, the report deals mainly with two aspects. in accordance with the jaa standards, from which the requirements are derived, the commission proposal does not contain any prescriptions on flight and duty times and rest periods. this is a very controversial issue and the reality is that, through the jaa, no agreement has been reached on this. the commission naturally hopes that the social partners representing operators and crew, whom mr simpson has urged to conclude a voluntary agreement on safety systems relating to flight and duty times and rest periods, will succeed. if they are not able to reach an agreement between now and may, then we will have to consider whether we should not act. in any event, among the amendments concerned, the commission accepts the spirit of amendments nos 12, 13 and 17, but with a different wording. as regards amendment no 1, the commission shares parliament's wish to regulate safety of flight and duty times and rest periods, but it would prefer that this objective not be pursued solely with the specific proposal we are debating today. there are other possibilities, such as the amendment of the regulation following the adoption of this proposal. i would also like to add that any proposal the commission makes in the future must ensure the high level of security we all want. so if the commission were to use the voluntary agreement between the social partners - to which i have just referred - to make a proposal, it would amend the agreement where appropriate to achieve the high level of safety required. with this reservation, i repeat, the commission accepts the spirit of amendment no 1. the commission has also adopted a number of amendments on the requirements for cabin crew. while this proposal addresses the operational requirements for cabin crew, the training requirements and the certification of professional competence are the subject of a separate and complementary commission proposal. care must be taken to maintain the conformity and compatibility of the two texts. amendments nos 9 and 10 can be accepted unchanged, but the wording of amendments nos 6, 7, 8 and 11 will have to be changed, which we now accept in principle only, as do amendments nos 12, 13 and 17, by amending their wording. finally, the amendments on technical requirements, namely amendments nos 4, 5 and 16, are acceptable, although the final text of amendment no 4 will reflect the solution to the problem in question found by the council. as regards the procedures for the approval of variants and temporary derogations, the commission does not accept amendments nos 2, 14 and 15. the consultations referred to in the amendments are already an institutional obligation of the commission. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft regulation. finally, as regards amendment no 18, the two issues covered by it concern the health of passengers rather than the operational safety of flights. as already mentioned in the communication on the protection of air passengers, the commission intends to set up expert groups to examine the risks to the health of passengers, including those due to cosmic radiation, in order to be able to identify these risks and propose the necessary measures. as regards the specific issue of arterial thrombosis - which has been raised by some of you - the commission has written to airlines asking them to provide passengers with information on the risks, the predisposing factors and what they can do to minimise those risks, in particular with regard to the problem of thrombosis and health problems in general. the commission considers that such information would be a very valid precaution and that, within the framework of strengthening passenger rights, it would be very appropriate.

september. we must therefore be politically cautious and gradual and selective. it will have to be gradual, that is to say, you cannot put extra prices on the road until the rail is able to pass it in writing. - while everyone agrees that the considerable number of road accidents in the various european member states is to be condemned, the edd group cannot entirely agree with mr hedkvist petersen's report on the means to be used to achieve this. the solution cannot be more europe, more money and more repression. this cocktail, already implemented on different scales in several countries, has proved ineffective. on the other hand, a better match between concrete measures and national specificities seems to be the way to go if we want real positive results. the car, with all its features, is more a matter of training, behaviour and culture. how can we then seek solutions which are harmonized at european level? we regard mr hekvist petersen's report as a denial of the very subsidiarity which we are trying to preserve, not in a dogmatic way, but in order to be as effective as possible, respecting the differences of each individual, and to the greatest benefit of our peoples. what about implementing the real solutions, the ones that require significant investment? the real challenges of a smart road safety policy are: reform of training (e.g. learning to drive at school age, or emergency braking at driving school), systematisation of active and passive safety elements from low-end vehicles by means of tax incentives for car manufacturers, or the modification of infrastructures by completely eliminating "black spots". so of course, this is certainly more difficult than the repressive whole of putting a radar in a car that is unmarked, at the bottom of a three-lane highway that is totally clear!

- ladies and gentlemen, the french initiative under discussion today once again demonstrates the need to clarify all the measures relating to freedom of movement which raise the problem of the opening of frontiers. all statistics show that migration flows have not decreased and will even increase in the coming years. the question of the free movement of residents of third countries in the schengen area will therefore be raised with even greater urgency. the european citizens expect a comprehensive, clear and coherent migration policy. the key element of the french initiative is the amendment of article 18 of the schengen agreement. the holder of a long-stay visa must not have fewer rights than the holder of a short-stay visa. the aim is to facilitate the free movement of migrants who have returned legally, regardless of their visa status. it is now necessary to know that a third country national can only transit through the territory of another member state to go to the country which issued him with his long-stay visa. then he will not be able to move around the schengen area until he has obtained his residence permit. that's where the stick hurts. in the light of the principle of free movement, the third-country national holding a long-stay visa is the one who is in the most unfavourable position, even if he has had to wait for several months or even years to obtain his visa. the french text also ignores the problem of family reunification, which arises in particular when union citizens marry third-country nationals. so why not treat long-stay visa holders as already resident, so that they can enjoy the same rights of movement? the legal basis on which the proposal is based could have been, as our rapporteur has also pointed out, considered differently and covered all the aspects mentioned in these provisions. in conclusion, it seems appropriate to reject an imprecise and incomplete initiative in a sensitive area such as community immigration policy. in order to respect and fully ensure the legislative power of the community, it is urgent to adopt a code on freedom of movement, immigration and asylum. the rejection of a fortress europe can only be achieved by a real relaxation of visa policy, which is repressive, does not reduce the flow of migration but, on the contrary, makes the networks of smugglers prosper.
commission. – mr president, on behalf of the commission, i should like to offer my congratulations on the thorough and exhaustive work of the rapporteur, mr deprez. the commission supports the objective pursued by the french initiative to facilitate freedom of movement within the schengen area for holders with long-stay visas prior to the issue of a residence document with equivalent status to a visa. however, the commission cannot support the selected legal basis, which has obvious implications for the content of the actual instrument. the commission accordingly shares your rapporteur's position. it considers that the proper legal basis for this regulation is article 62(3) of the ec treaty, "measures setting out the conditions under which nationals of third countries shall have the freedom to travel within the territory of the member states during a period of no more than three months". for the sake of consistency with that legal basis, the commission also agrees with your rapporteur on the need to amend article 21 of the convention for the implementation of the schengen agreement, which regulates the movement of foreigners, rather than article 18. the latter article merely specifies that long-stay visas are issued on a national basis and sets the conditions for transit by holders of long-stay visas. the only further point that the commission might add to those made by the rapporteur is this: it regards the amendments to the common consular instruction as going far enough. it is also necessary to amend the common manual so that border police can be informed of the new status of the long-stay visa. finally, the commission can confirm its intention of shortly presenting an overall proposal for legislation as regards the right to travel in the schengen area to avoid fragmentary action that would not be conducive to transparency and clarity in the public mind or certainty as to the law.

in writing. - by proposing that long-stay visas pending a residence permit should offer the same freedom of movement as residence permits, the deprez report improves on the french initiative which proposed that these long-stay visas should have the same value as short-stay visas in terms of movement. when france reintroduced tourist visas in 1986 under the pretext of fighting terrorism, the european parliament asked it to abandon them, saying that this was 'discrimination against citizens of non-community countries'. today, this discrimination is made commonplace by the schengen convention and the communitization of migration policies. visa applications are refused by consular services in a total lack of transparency, and the motivation is rarely mandatory. the european consulates simply refer to the 'migration risk' or to the schengen information system. in addition to the mass of refusals recorded, there are countless cases of non-oral purposes. the scarcity of visas causes a lot of traffic in the consulates. this permanent humiliation of the citizens of the peoples of the south has no other purpose than to close the frontiers to them and has no other effect than to feed the clandestine channels. the deprez report rightly concludes that there is no transparency and no democratic control in the field of visas and movement in europe. that is why i shall vote in favour of it. submission of reports to committees - authorization to draw up own-initiative reports - enhanced hughes/hughes procedure - membership of parliament - statements entered in the register - transmission of texts adopted at this part-session - calendar of next part-sessions: see minutes.
