- my colleagues, i must now give you some information. on 26 january the president of the court of first instance of the european communities issued an order suspending the implementation of the european parliament's decision of 23 october 2000 taking note of the notification by the french government to us that mr jean-marie le pen's mandate had expired. the order states that mr le pen must be reinstated in parliament and i am naturally responsible for immediately implementing what is a court decision. i also asked our committee on legal affairs and the internal market for an opinion on the action that the european parliament should take on this matter. i am already observing a new element. the president of the court of first instance confers on the european parliament a power of assessment in respect of a decree terminating the mandate of a member of the european parliament. if this decision were confirmed on the merits, the le pen case law would thus have helped to give the competence of the european institutions precedence over that of national governments.

the formation of a region of shared prosperity through the progressive establishment of free trade, and finally a better mutual understanding between peoples and the emergence of a civil society. mr president, of these three objectives, only the establishment of a free trade area can be considered to have been the subject of a start to effective implementation. however, as i was pleased to hear commissioner barnier say earlier, liberalization alone in a context of deep inequality cannot guarantee economic development or the integration of deeply disrupted societies. it is also a free trade area under european conditions. only one figure can prove this today. overall budgetary transfers from the european union to the mediterranean countries amount to €1 billion per year, while those resulting from the trade deficit of the mediterranean countries with the union amount to €34 billion per year. in other words, the budgetary effort of the european union vis-à-vis the mediterranean countries represents less than one-third of the benefits that the free trade area brings to europe. as regards the creation of an area of peace and stability, the union does not carry much political weight, despite the strong demand for europe from the countries of the south. the areas of conflict are numerous and risk jeopardising the barcelona process as a whole. as regards the emergence of an active civil society, it can be seen that the meda programmes mainly reached people who had links and contacts in europe, or who were very close to governments. civil society, in fact, has been little involved. finally, decentralised cooperation programmes, which were supposed to allow civil society actors from both sides of the mediterranean to meet to develop projects, have been frozen since 1995. the results are therefore very modest, the frustrations very strong, the marseille conference was experienced by many as a semi-failure. the overall vision of the euro-mediterranean partnership, which was launched in barcelona in 1995, has now been replaced by negotiations, i would say, without any real political will. in my report i try to make a number of proposals to overcome this situation. i will now present the six main axes. firstly, i think that the free trade area must be seen in a genuine strategic perspective. we must lay the foundations with our mediterranean partners for an associated common market which can be integrated positively into the european economic context, taking into account the endogenous parameters of the development of the south. the idea of a free trade project geared towards the eventual establishment of a genuine common market incorporating all goods must be defended. secondly, migration must be placed at the heart of development today. there will be no real partnership between the two shores of the mediterranean until the organized movement of people is on the agenda. that is why, in my view, migration will be an essential element in our relations with these countries in the years to come. we need a common management of migration flows, including the fight against illegal immigration and the mafia. we must also move towards temporary migration, as the international labour organisation is now proposing, without this giving the right to permanent residence. i also think that a specific travel visa for partnership actors should be granted. immigration must also be used to promote the development of the countries of origin. immigrants contribute to the development of their home countries. i know that the european union, i know that the commission is making a great effort in this direction. i invite him to go much further by funding the micro-projects of immigrants. and i propose, in this spirit, to set up a migration observatory, the purpose of which would be to study migration flows with a view to making proposals to the union. the strengthening of the association of the euro-mediterranean states which so wishes must also be encouraged. i would like to take up a proposal which i find extremely interesting from commissioner patten. the commissioner said he wanted certain regional projects to be accessible to a variable number of member states and mediterranean partners directly concerned, in configurations which could differ from one project to another. i support this approach because i believe it introduces real, and really strong, relations between the countries of the northern and southern mediterranean that want to go further together. and of course - fourth point - the management of the meda programme must also be reformed. the commission tends to be critical of its mediterranean partners. however, it is clear that, while some partner countries may have encountered difficulties, in particular due to poor infrastructure, the under-consumption of meda funds is mainly due to the commission's inability to manage these funds and to rely on actors capable of implementing them. the defence of human rights must also be more than a statement of principle. the aim is indeed to help build the rule of law in the southern mediterranean countries, and not just to create economic systems that fit into the structural adjustment programmes proposed. sixth, it is necessary to commit substantial financial resources. the blockage of the middle east peace process makes any subregional, economic, social and/or cultural dynamics difficult. i think the commission should be aware of this. in conclusion, i would say that the organized movement of people, co-development and decentralized cooperation are the main lines which structure my report today, and which, in my opinion, should be those of the commission. the council. mr president, i would like to thank you for your reply. ladies and gentlemen of the house, mediterranean cooperation has been the subject of a critical and constructive examination in today's debate and in the two reports which have been presented. i welcome this debate. i have listened carefully to the views expressed and have noted that the criticisms made on several points are justified. i believe that dialogue with the partner countries is of paramount importance. the real potential of the barcelona process can only be realised if all participants feel a real sense of ownership and therefore responsibility for the different parts of the process. let me briefly comment on some of the interesting contributions made in the debate. the honourable member beazley raises the question of whether the enlargement process and mediterranean cooperation are coordinated processes. the obvious answer from the presidency is yes; they will be coordinated. like mr esteve, we do not see any contradiction between enlargement on the one hand and mediterranean cooperation on the other. we must be able to work with full force in both these areas. i am pleased that several members, in particular mr carlotti and mr martin, are raising the importance of association agreements between the eu and partner countries. we see these agreements as necessary building blocks for note that the association agreement with egypt was initialled a few days ago. we hope that under the swedish presidency we will be able to hold a first association council with jordan. the association negotiations with algeria, syria and lebanon are also progressing well. we therefore believe that these association agreements are not only of great importance in terms of trade and economic integration but also an important political platform. they form the basis for a regular, in-depth and broad political dialogue. in the debate today, there has been a fair amount of criticism of the fortunately been able to play a leading role for a long time. examples include the so-called euro-islam project and the so-called stockholm conclusions of 1998, which provide guidelines for further work in a wide range of areas within this dialogue. mrs napoletano raised the extremely important issue of judicial cooperation. the swedish presidency would like to promote cooperation in this area. we will be organizing a high-level meeting and a seminar. both are intended to contribute to the commission's new regional programmes in the field of justice and home affairs. an important part of this complex of issues is the issue of migration, which several members have touched on in today's debate. i think it's important to look at these migration issues in a holistic way. we must take into account the social, economic and cultural aspects of the situation. mr president, i would like to thank you. the phase we are now entering must be directed towards implementing what has already been agreed by all those involved in the barcelona process. i think it was mr obiols who spoke about the lack of symbolic concreteness. the honourable member carlotti was on the same subject. i now believe that the eu, together with its mediterranean partners, must ensure that the aims and commitments of the barcelona declaration are 'put into action', because, like all other activities, the barcelona process will not be judged by what it promises but by what it delivers.
commission. – mr president, it gives me very great pleasure to participate in this debate on the mediterranean today. i am particularly grateful to the two rapporteurs, mrs muscardini and mr naïr, for the excellent work that they have done in preparing their two reports. it has been an extremely good debate. it is personally rather a disappointment that many of those who were able to find time in their busy diaries to take part in the debate were not able to find time to hear very much of the debate or even to wait until the end to hear the responses. it is, i guess, a sort of discourtesy on my part to reply to people who ask serious questions but who are not able to stay to hear the response, so i will not do that. i will just respond to people who have been able to stay until the end, which in fact gives the debate some meaning. the mediterranean is our near abroad, on our southern flank, so it should enjoy a very special place in our external relations. the objectives agreed at barcelona remain fundamentally valid and they are increasingly relevant: working together for peace and stability, creating shared prosperity through establishing free trade, providing the economic and financial assistance to meet the challenges which that implies, and helping to improve mutual understanding and tolerance among peoples of different cultures and different traditions. as the house will know, i had long believed that the time had come to see how we could improve the delivery of the barcelona objectives. we therefore worked very hard on a commission communication on reinvigorating the barcelona process, which in turn provided the main input for the euro-mediterranean foreign ministers’ meeting in marseilles last november where our ideas were overwhelmingly endorsed. that document was on the table, that document was the principle agenda for that meeting. i should like now to give you my assessment of where we stand and where we should go from here. with the permission of the house, i will address points arising from both reports in this context rather than dealing with each report separately. first, let me look at the political situation in the region, which we are going to debate in a few moments’ time. both reports note the considerable significance of the middle east peace process for european union policy in the mediterranean. i note the calls in both reports for the european union to play a more active role in the peace process. let us not underestimate our contribution. we are, for example, and it is not an unreasonable point to make, the major donor to the palestinian authority. last year eur 155.6 million was earmarked from the community budget, which included eur 90 million for a special cash facility that i made available at the end of the year to help preserve the institutional framework of the palestinian authority, which we have helped to create and fund. i would like, without reservation, to thank the house – to thank this part of the budgetary authority – and also to thank the council for their assistance in ensuring that we could make that cash facility available before christmas. as events have sadly proved, it is going to be all too necessary. at the meeting in marseilles, ministers decided, rightly in my view, not to seek agreement on the proposed charter for peace and stability. this was clearly not the right moment. nevertheless, in substance a good deal of progress had been made towards agreement on this instrument. we should make sure that we can capitalise on that progress when the time is right, so that it becomes a genuinely meaningful document, reflecting the european union’s active commitment to maintaining regional peace and stability. in the meantime – and here i also echo comments made in both the reports that we are considering – we should not wait for the charter to be in force to make more efforts to promote respect for human rights and democratic freedoms in the region. our communication is unequivocal on this subject. the european union should use all appropriate fora to press for progress on these issues. the meda democracy programme should continue to be used to fund positive actions and meda allocations themselves should be more dependent on adequate progress. i very much welcome parliament’s backing on this and i hope that the council will also react positively. economic and financial matters are, of course, at the heart of the partnership though they are not, as several speakers pointed out, anything like the whole of that partnership. in marseilles there was a high level of consensus on our proposals for reinvigorating it and i would like to highlight the following: we must speed up the negotiation, signature and ratification of the association agreements. i am happy to confirm that we are achieving considerable progress on this. on friday last week we managed, at last, to initial the agreement with egypt and we are encouraged by the progress we are making with algeria, with lebanon and with syria. i want to see negotiations with algeria, lebanon and syria pursued vigorously this year, however the ratification process in the member states is lamentably slow. the agreement with jordan was signed three years ago, but it is still not in force. help from the european parliament in this respect would be most welcome. i do hope that, as well as making speeches in the chamber, honourable members will get on to their own parliaments and governments to ensure that when we reach agreement on one of these associations agreements it can be ratified rapidly. there are two states which still have not ratified the jordan agreement – no names, as they say, no pack drill – but i very much hope that belgian and french meps – i hope i have not given the game away – will get on to their parliaments to press for ratification as soon as possible. in due course we also need to tackle the issue of agricultural trade. the credibility of our partnership lies in being able to deal with sensitive matters like that and we need to have a genuine discussion. we must develop south-south trade and cooperation, including on a subregional basis. we want all countries signing an association agreement with us to conclude free-trade agreements among themselves within five years. this is the only manner to prepare our already agreed objective of an overall european-union-mediterranean free-trade area by 2010. the development of subregional trade needs to be accompanied by greater subregional cooperation. trading opportunities will not be used unless the infrastructure is there. we must introduce accumulation of origin for all partners establishing free trade between themselves and adopting the harmonised protocol on rules of origin. we must harmonise measures relating to the single market. we want a timetable to be in place by next year for priority sectors – such as rules of origin, customs, norms and standards, and intellectual property protection – for implementation starting in 2004, both between the partners and the union and among the partners themselves. all this, together with the support we give to our partners under meda, will increase the attractiveness of the region to investors. a decompartmentalised and open market with a sound and predictable legal and administrative environment is the best way to ensure that the very low levels of local, european and world-wide investment will increase. both reports rightly pay much attention to the need to improve meda, which one or two of the speakers who are still present in the chamber mentioned during their remarks. indeed, meda has an excellent record on commitments but is much less good on payments. last year the record on commitments was maintained: the provisional figures show that eur 879 million or 98% of available commitments were executed and the record on payments improved to eur 335 million or 95% of available appropriations. i am happy to say that the control of the overhang of payments required to execute the commitments has begun to improve. as an average over the last five years, we have now paid 30% of existing commitments, compared to 26% one year ago, but there is still a long way to go. we are in the process of implementing two reforms, the revised meda regulation and the internal commission reform. taken together, i am confident that they will bring about serious improvements in the years to come. mr honourable friend, mr beazley, who i am delighted to say is still in his place, spoke about that and asked a specific question about cyprus and malta and their participation in regional programmes. i am delighted to answer “yes” – in the affirmative. it is a positive “yes” rather than negative or equivocal “yes”. i note the opinion that the amount made available for the period 2000 to 2006 is insufficient. i was not surprised to see that mentioned in the report. it is certainly true that the eur 5.35 billion agreed by the council – i give away no secrets – is less than the commission had proposed. nevertheless, together with eib lending, this means that nearly eur 13 billion will be available over that period, which is not an insignificant amount of money. the important thing now is to see that this money is used effectively in terms both of the quality of our actions in relation to the policy objectives and of actual payments on the ground. the commission has proposed that, for the future, meda allocation should be more closely linked to the association process and the implementation of economic reforms. i make no apology for this and i am glad to note support for this line in one of the reports. i have noted the calls to increase the numbers of commission staff available to work on this sector. i recognise that the staff concerned are extremely hard pressed, but any decisions will have to be taken in the context of the evolution of commission staffing levels overall and here again i would be delighted for concrete help from parliament. we will also be working this year on a programme to take account of the social effects of economic transition. this will promote education and training, the enhancement of the role of women and social security systems as well as actions on health. i was not surprised that both reports called for increased support for civil society. i fully agree with these. the question is how best to go about it. i fear that financing micro-projects is not the answer. these are not cost-effective and they are wasteful of staff resources. decentralised cooperation is to be welcomed, but not in the sense of relaunching the old mediterranean decentralised cooperation programmes. however worthy their objectives, they were seriously criticised by the court of auditors and indeed they were seriously criticised by this parliament. rather we need to explain more clearly to civil society – whether ngos, local authorities or other groups – that our programmes are open to their participation and they only need to organise themselves to respond to our calls for proposals. good examples of this already exist in our sectoral , in writing. - the two reports of the conciliation committee on the development of the community railways and on licensing of railway undertakings welcome the fact that a compromise has been reached on the full opening of the sector to the private sector for freight by 2008. this compromise opens the way for new proposals for the liberalisation, i.e. privatisation, of other rail transport, i.e. passenger transport. the recent tragic accidents in england and the increase in incidents on privatised networks, as in germany, are, however, a further indication of the harmful effects of privatising this public service. and when we claim to solve the social problem of transporting goods mainly by road by opening up the railway to private companies, it is at least an imposture. for years, rail services have been closed across europe to promote the interests of private companies in all forms of road transport. with road networks now on the verge of collapse, some private capital is turning to rail to make new profits, aided by the european institutions and national governments alike. neither the users nor the general population should expect anything good from the privatisation of public services. the same is true for workers in this sector, who denounce and fight liberalization-privatization and its ravages on employment and working conditions. we are of course in full solidarity with these workers and their trade union organizations when they denounce these evils. that is why we voted against both reports.
in writing. - i would like to warmly congratulate the rapporteur on the work he has done. his report on the barcelona process is very comprehensive, so i will simply stress a few points that are close to my heart. i would first like to recall that the commission's communication 'a new impetus for the barcelona process' had a twofold objective: to take stock of the barcelona process and to formulate recommendations in the run-up to the ministerial conference in marseille (november 2000). if we're being honest, the balance sheet is weak. of the three strands of the euro-mediterranean partnership, the political, cultural, social and human, and economic and financial strands, only the latter has been implemented. and then again! the imbalance in this area is glaring. we ask our partners to open up their markets in the sectors where we are most competitive. on the other hand, when it comes to agricultural products, the european union's frivolity leads to the maintenance of barriers that penalize these countries. as the rapporteur says, we want to see the implementation of a 'european lez'. this is a very bad attitude and it is irresponsible. let us stop with the hypocrisy and let us stop wishing for the establishment of a common prosperity zone! it is time to denounce loudly the lack of importance that europe attaches to this partnership, as busy as it is with its enlargement to the east. this is a miscalculation. europe has everything to gain from the sustainable economic and social development and political stability of this region on the other side of the mediterranean, europe's inland sea. it is now urgent to give a new lease of life to this euro-mediterranean partnership. the rapporteur proposes several ways forward. i suggest that we start by intervening more voluntarily in the political arena. the new international situation is perhaps an opportunity we must seize. the european union has a role to play in the middle east peace process. resolving the conflict in the middle east is a key element in the establishment of peace and stability in the region. this means the right to security for israel and for all other states in the region, as well as the recognition of the legitimate right of the palestinian people to live in a viable and internationally recognized state. in the same spirit, the euro-mediterranean charter for peace and stability must be adopted as soon as possible. the european union must also invest more in financial and human resources, and promote interregional cooperation and the involvement of civil society. i would like to conclude on an optimistic note by expressing my satisfaction at the willingness of the swedish presidency to undertake a serious reflection on the barcelona process, in line with what the french presidency has begun. it remains to be hoped that it will soon be put into practice. that is why i voted in favour of the sami naïr report.
in writing. - the nair report on europe's mediterranean policy is more than ambiguous. it does not provide a framework for cooperation between europe and the mediterranean countries. the report also calls for the establishment of a european union-wide network of information centres for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. firstly, the report is part of the commission's approach to free trade and economic liberalisation in the mediterranean countries. article 21 is very clear in this respect: 'promote the liberalisation of the economic systems of the mediterranean partner countries and the implementation of the structural reforms necessary for competition in more open markets'. the report addresses the central issue of debt only in terms of 'reconversion', whereas european governments should be required to cancel it. on migrants, the naïr report is restrictive in its talk of flow management and criminalization of immigrants. borders have never stopped men and women. to consider them illegal immigrants is to play into the hands of the mafia and the smugglers. it takes the will to open up borders. finally, while the rapporteur recognizes the right of the palestinians to a state, his legitimate demands are not mentioned: the release of all political prisoners, the right of return for refugees. for these reasons i did not vote for this report.
in writing. - we voted the resolution on colombia to denounce the plan put in place by the united states, a plan which, under the pretext of combating drug trafficking, involves the forced displacement of populations, mostly peasants, for the greatest benefit of the large landowners. the main purpose of this military intervention is to facilitate the exploitation of colombia's resources by the major capitalist groups. we are against the us military intervention in colombia, just as we are against the british intervention in sierra leone and the direct or indirect french intervention in rwanda, the congo and zaire. we are also against the plans to privatise large sectors of the colombian economy and measures to reduce the purchasing power of the population, such as the reduction of pensions. from this point of view, we know that the aid granted by the european union and the imf is primarily concerned with creating favourable conditions for investment by the bourgeoisie of the imperialist powers. that said, we are against any repression and displacement of the population, and that is the meaning of our vote.
in writing. - the us plan for colombia was decided in a totally undemocratic way, without any consultation of the various social and political actors, and without the approval of the colombian congress. it only proposes an extremely dangerous solution, a genuine plan of military intervention under the guise of combating drug trafficking, criminalising small producers, destroying their crops by fumigations dangerous to man and the environment, condemning them to leave the land they exploit. the committee on development and cooperation, in proposing a resolution to support the peace process in colombia, breaks with the murderous logic of the colombia plan. we can only support proposals for land reform, support for the peace process, in connection with the neighbouring countries. the resources allocated by the european union will then have to be controlled to ensure that they are not used for law enforcement purposes. but only a condemnation of the paramilitary groups and the establishment of a dialogue with the farc and the eln can constitute a first step towards peace. the fight against drug trafficking and the real drug traffickers requires radical measures: a real and effective fight against the laundering of the money thus raised, the introduction of a tobin tax on capital movements which would make it possible, by redistributing it, to satisfy the needs of all citizens.

the rapporteur. - i thank you, mr president, for giving me the floor on this second reading of a report which is very important for the future of railways in europe and for the achievement of the railway europe. the last few months, under the presidency of commissioner de palacio, have undoubtedly been decisive for the future of rail transport in europe. as a result of the conciliation on the swoboda/jarzembowsky reports, the opening up, or the liberalisation, whatever you want to call it, of networks is now a reality. the many technical incompatibilities between them have yet to be overcome, and this is not, of course, the easiest of all, since these networks have been built with strong national specificities, both technical and industrial. the purpose of this draft directive is precisely to ensure the technical and procedural interoperability of border crossings between the 15 different european networks. today, the situation is very complex. there are about 15 signalling systems, five or six voltages, different gauges, different track gauges, different procedures, different railway cultures, disjointed information systems between different railway companies, all of which compromise the smooth running of the railway. and while the road was easy to open, because the break in continuity was immediately removed, the railway still encounters all these technical obstacles. it so happens that in 1996 a first directive was adopted, which was easier to implement because it concerned a new network, the high-speed rail network, and which now shows us the methodological way forward. in this respect, it was therefore decided to develop technical specifications for interoperability for each rail subsystem in consultation with railway undertakings, infrastructure managers and industry. each of these subsystems is subject to a specification which will then be defined for the components by means of hardware certification. we have a very considerable amount of work to do and we have chosen to adopt the procedure which was inspired by high speed, that is to say a gradual procedure. the work will take so much time that it is important to make improvements immediately where they are easily achievable and at a lower cost/benefit ratio. this is the heart of the method: to choose and evaluate the cost and benefits of any given interoperability advance and to prioritize it and make it a priority rather than a choice to implement it later. naturally, the main areas for progress are the exchange of information, procedures, telematics and all the procedures for crossing borders, and we shall see later, gradually, through a process of convergence, how to tackle the problem of roads, gauges and equipment. i think, ladies and gentlemen, that i have to thank all the members who have been involved in this report, because we have done a great deal of work on the first reading. 46 amendments were tabled and voted by parliament. of these 46 amendments - and i must pay tribute to the council and the commission this time - 33 were accepted as they stood and it can be said that it is a legislative process with broad consensus which is now, or should be, completed at the time of the vote. the council and the commission have accepted many amendments and have allowed parliament to make a clear change in the consultation of users and staff, to involve the applicant countries in these discussions from the outset, and also to make a clear change in the derogations, because some countries, rightly, had concerns about derogations. the council also made very important contributions to safety and to access for people with reduced mobility to future equipment. in short, i believe that we are now arriving at a text which is quite solid, which can be implemented fairly quickly, which is based on the experience of high speed and which has been nourished by exemplary collaboration between the various parliamentary groups in the committee on transport - and i would like to pay tribute to all my colleagues in the various groups - but also between the commission, the council and parliament, and i personally welcome the fact that such an ambitious dossier has been concluded so quickly, which is now really setting the railway europe in motion. the commissioner will have to answer two other crucial questions: the question of pricing, which is still the big question of the road/rail modal switchover today, and the question of financing the infrastructure - the intermodal platforms, for example - which is necessary if we are to make real progress in this area.
mr president, commissioner de palacio, ladies and gentlemen, while i am particularly sympathetic to the rubber-bicycle industry, i am pleased that we have achieved a good result, not least as a result of the hard work of mr savary. it is clear that the competitiveness of railways needs to be improved, and this is particularly important in congested central europe. europe needs a long-term rail - mr president, today's discussion of an oral question on the follow-up to the nice european council, even though the draft treaty has not yet been signed and the next igc is due to be held only in 2004, shows that some are impatient to relaunch a round of negotiations. for them, and for the commission in particular - as its president has just said - it should finally be the great european constitutional process which the nice council refused to accept, a process which should be promptly guided by a european convention inspired by the one which prepared last year the charter of fundamental rights. but haste, even agitation, should not replace thought. the idea of a european constitution is a reference to the idea of a european state which our peoples do not want. the nice council, it should be noted, did not include this idea among the objectives of the future igc. the future europe will need, not a future state with its constitution, but a network of nations that respects national democracies and is formalized by a fundamental treaty. in the meantime, we must think about the method of the future debate. let us say that the convention which drew up the charter of fundamental rights was a failure because it constantly mixed up the powers, confused the responsibilities and, in the end, produced a text which may have pleased the ears of the supranationalists, but which was unacceptable to all the members of the union. yes, in future the igcs will have to be prepared differently, but certainly not by means of weightless conventions which would lead us to new dead ends. the next igc must first be organized in and around national parliaments, under their responsibility. in the second stage, the future igc should negotiate only credible proposals, i.e. those supported by at least one quarter of the union's national parliaments following a vote by their plenary assemblies. this would ensure that we do not drift and remain firmly anchored in national democracies.

- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this is an oral question to the commission. a few months ago, at the european council in lisbon, our president, mrs fontaine, expressed concern, and i quote her: 'about the devastating effects on social cohesion' of certain mergers or restructurings. it asked the heads of state or government, and i quote it again, 'to take the necessary measures to regulate them in a balanced way, to assess their social impact and to take the necessary accompanying social measures'. in doing so, mrs fontaine was focusing on a major problem: how to reconcile the necessary flexibility of companies with the essential security of workers? since lisbon, mr president, the restructuring has been even more intense. we are now talking about over 300 mergers a year. every day brings its share of worries for employees, whether in the sectors of what is curiously beginning to be called the old economy, that is to say the main part of the economy, or in the sector of new information technologies. the nice summit has sent very positive signals in this respect. the unblocking, after 30 years, of the european company statute and its 'worker involvement' component, as well as the adoption of the social agenda, have demonstrated the importance which the european council attaches to improving the situation of workers in the union. the request we are making to the commission today, through this unanimous oral question from the committee on employment and social affairs, is to make clear that it is relying on this new political will to make a real difference in its proposals. we have therefore the honour to ask the commission for specific commitments. first of all, we want better forecasting of the social consequences of restructuring. how do you intend to use, for example, the new industrial relations observatory, which will be operated by the dublin foundation and to whose creation this great house of parliament was so attached? we want you to undertake a re-reading of the existing social directives, in the light both of the review of their implementation and of the new challenges posed by their restructuring. wherever necessary, we ask you to propose the necessary revisions, in particular to monitor more rigorously the implementation of the rights of workers to information and consultation, to take measures to punish the absence of consultation and to anticipate, as far as possible, the information of the social partners in the restructuring process. we would appreciate it if the commission proposed a revision of the current directive on european works councils now, not in 2002 as has been announced, since the text of the directive itself provides for a revision in a few years' time, and the time has come. we also ask you to revise the directive on collective redundancies to introduce the necessary mechanisms to prevent the breach of the obligation to inform workers. finally, we want - and we know that mrs diamantopoulou is not totally opposed to this idea - the 'totally' being inspired by a cautious courtesy, because i am more certain than that - that the internal procedures of competition policy within the commission be amended to take account of the social aspects. would it not be appropriate that when a company applies to brussels for a merger authorization, the commission ensures that the minimum information and consultation of workers, as provided for by community legislation, has been complied with? these are our demands, commissioners, which are symbolic for public opinion, justified for workers and, let me say, economically useful, because how can a knowledge-based economy be managed without the involvement of workers? the debate on this oral question was unanimous in my committee, as was the unanimous vote on the motion for a resolution which is on the table today. i should point out that another proposal has been tabled by the liberal group. as we share the views of our liberal friends who voted for the first resolution and, above all, for the question of my committee, we believe that there has been a malfunction, a lack of information on the part of our liberal friends. we have worked in complete agreement, including with the liberals. commissioners, we look forward to your answers.
mr president, faced with the gigantic mergers and industrial restructurings which result in thousands of job losses, many workers, citizens of the union, have found europe powerless, if not complicit, in the name of the laws of free competition. it is high time that measures were taken to protect employees. there is an intolerable contradiction between the priority given to employment by the council and the commission and the massive redundancies by large companies which, at the same time, are making fabulous profits. michelin, moulinex, danone and alsthom are not groups in difficulty. they are competitive: they make more than comfortable profits but they are eliminating thousands of jobs. the danone example is instructive: 3,000 job cuts in europe, 1,700 in france. in 2000, the company's european plants made a net profit of eur 795 million, 17% more than in 1999. we cannot but react to the waltz of mergers that leaves women and men unemployed and plunges whole families into disarray. the european citizenship we so often refer to in this society will remain purely rhetorical as long as workers are not really informed and consulted on the choices that determine their future, that of their region and their country. how can we accept that groups which receive public financial aid in the name of employment development benefit from it without respecting the commitments they have made? in this case, the aid should be reimbursed to the community, which bears the burden of the social consequences of the choice of financial profitability over employment. i do not think that the problem can be reduced to employability and adaptability, or to dealing with the social consequences alone, as the commissioner has done. that is why i have supported the proposals in the resolution and the amendments which clarify and strengthen certain aspects. it will take even more to meet the democratic demands of the citizen employees. i think that the development of rights must go as far as the possibility of suspending planned redundancies, of stopping the merger processes in progress. any merger agreement must include social clauses. sanctions should also be introduced for failure to comply with the consultation guidelines. at a time when there is much talk about european identity and the meaning of its construction, a text which specifies certain rights of employees in relation to financial objectives seems to me to be the minimum to give the union some credibility. i shall therefore vote in favour of the resolution, which i hope will be enriched by a number of amendments.
in writing. - in justifying european aid, the rapporteurs emphasize the difficult economic situation in cambodia and laos and the implementation of the vital demining programmes after years of conflict in that region, while taking care not to stress the heavy responsibility of the imperialist powers, including france and the united states, on these two points. if this were simply a disinterested european aid, paid in reparation for years of plunder and destruction of these two countries, and without any return, it would have our support. but this so-called aid is only a thin screen to conceal the aims which are, however, revealed in a single sentence: to stop the decline in the european community's exports to this region of the world, that is to say, in short, to allow the predators of the large european companies to continue and, as far as possible, to extend what remains a policy of plundering this region of the world. we therefore abstained on these reports.
in writing. - the united kingdom had obtained a derogation from the application of the regulation on the limitation of working time and night work for adolescents. today the commission and this report propose to abolish this derogation. it would have been a good thing if the united kingdom had introduced rules that would have given young people greater protection at work. but in reality, the perfect agreement between the conservatives and labour, the liberals and the socialists, on the end of this derogation period is based on the fact that, according to the report itself, 'the existing derogations are otherwise sufficient to provide the necessary flexibility' and that this 'will therefore not have a negative effect on the employment opportunities of young people'. this is a demonstration of the fact that not only can the said regulation of the european institutions be circumvented, but that, even if it is applied, it does not protect adolescents from the profit-hungry bosses. we voted against this report.
in writing. - unfortunately, the situation of young british workers may not be greatly improved by the adoption of this resolution. the scandal of the english exception (the united kingdom did not comply with the whole of the directive on the restriction of child and adolescent labour) does not mean that the directive no longer meets the needs of young workers. on the contrary, this debate should have been an opportunity to amend it in order to remove all the exceptions which it contains and which deprive it of any real effectiveness. there is no justification for allowing 14- or even 13-year-olds to work in any capacity (article 4 (2) (c)), in addition to their school duties (article 8 (1) (b) and during their holidays (article 8 (1) (c)). nor is there any justification for derogations allowing young people under 18 to work more than 40 hours a week, more than 8 hours a day (article 8 (5)), or even at night (article 9 (2)). there is no reason why there should be no limitation on domestic service in a private household or on work in family businesses (article 2 (2)). there is no point in denouncing child labour in asia or africa if we do not protect young people from economic exploitation and work harmful to their health, safety and development and if we do not provide them with qualified training independent of employers.
in writing. - i welcome very much the report by mr gilles savary on the interoperability of the rail system, which approves the council's common position without amending it. this common position incorporates 33 of the 46 amendments at first reading. i agree with the rapporteur that the future of the european transport system is bound to depend on the revitalization of the railway sector. as has often been pointed out, investment in rail networks within the union is still very much a matter of national policy. it is clear that these national differences represent a significant obstacle to the development of rail transport in europe, despite the many advantages of this low-polluting mode of transport. at the same time, the completion of the internal market has led to a considerable increase in flows within the european union. the main beneficiaries of this increase were the road transport sector, particularly in the transport of goods. the causes of the railway's decline are many. this is partly due to the fact that it is organised along national lines. there is no internal market for rail services at community level. in addition, networks have not always adapted very well to the new ways of organising economic activity and urbanisation, nor to the changes in traffic flows that these have brought about. that said, it is clear that the future of the european transport system is dependent on the rapid revitalization of the railway sector. i am in favour of this because i am convinced that rail has a central role to play in solving the mobility problems facing the european union. european citizens suffer daily from pollution, congestion and the risk of accidents resulting from an excessive reliance on the road, a reliance that has only worsened over the last thirty years. the objective of sustainable mobility is thus closely linked to the revitalization of railways. i am also pleased that the european parliament has succeeded in imposing amendments which aim to take better account of important social standards, such as professional qualifications and health and safety at work. the council also took account of certain sensitive points. this is the case for the protection of the existing railway system, the adoption of a system of derogations or specific cases, such as the situation of certain countries isolated from the rest of the community or the difference in track gauge. the council's common position is also realistic, setting out a progressive work programme and taking account of the problems posed by enlargement in the railway sector. for all these reasons i voted in favour of the savary report.
in writing. - we vote in favour of this report because it is important to promote the interoperability of the transeuropean rail network. the road transport network is currently saturated and needs to be revitalized. the commission has also taken steps to increase rail transport to reduce road congestion. however, behind the rapporteur's laudable objectives on the revitalisation of the railway sector, there is the specter of liberalisation, because this report also aims to contribute to the opening of the markets for transport services and capital goods and to the promotion of the competitiveness of the railway sector as a whole. we have serious reservations on this point, because we have always been opposed to liberalization.
in writing. - if we really want to create an alternative to 'all road transport', it is essential to harmonize rail transport infrastructures in europe. i can only follow the rapporteur on this. moreover, it seems to me that the inclusion of social standards, professional qualifications and hygiene, safety and working conditions in the process of building a transeuropean rail network is the least that can be done. however, i will be extremely vigilant to ensure that harmonization is based on the best existing social acquis, and not at the expense of users and employees in this sector. but a dangerous unspoken question remains: in what framework should the interoperability of networks be achieved? in the case of public services coordinated at european level, guaranteeing quality jobs and security, or in that of a market sacrificed to competition and profit? the recent adoption by the parliament and the council of the three directives of the railway package suggests that europe is looking to the future of transeuropean rail transport from the second perspective.
in writing. - in addition to the oil tankers, which are bad news, other types of merchant ships are in a deplorable state. the consequences may not be as dramatic as those of oil tankers, but they are even more tragic when you consider that in ten years 146 oil tankers have sunk and 780 crew members have lost their lives. in voting on this report we voted for concrete measures to improve the safety of bulk carriers and their crews. but we would like to stress the antinomy between security concerns and those relating to what the report calls 'risks of distortion of competition for european ports and terminals'. the attempt to save the profits of the shipowners and the contractors inevitably sacrifices safety. it is good to give the captain the opportunity to object to loading or unloading operations which he considers to be dangerous to his crew and ship. but it would be hypocritical to ignore that the laws of competition and the market (including the labour market) imposed by shipowners and contractors are such that the theoretical ability of a captain to oppose them is not worth the means at the disposal of the shipping capitalists to impose dangerous, and sometimes deadly, conditions of navigation and work on board ships.
in writing. - in 10 years, nearly 150 bulk carriers have sunk, causing the deaths of 800 people. this is the tragic record of an industry left to the laws of competition and the market. i agree with the rapporteur that the physical condition of the ships and the incompetence of the crews are the main factors in these shipwrecks. the first thing to be done is to control the ships and the crews and their working and living conditions on board. that is why i support all binding measures to strengthen safety standards, port state controls and the accountability of loading and unloading terminals and captains. it is still necessary to provide the personal and financial means to enforce the legislation in the member states, in particular by increasing the number of inspectors. in addition, combating impunity and complacency in maritime transport also means holding shipowners and ship-owners accountable by giving them the means to take legal and financial action where appropriate. i shall vote for all the proposals along these lines.
in writing. - i agree with the rapporteur that the european commission's proposals are welcome and help to improve the community's policy on maritime safety. recent disasters have raised serious public concern. it is therefore up to us to take voluntary measures which will be in contrast to the laissez-faire policy which has prevailed until recent years, both at european and global level. i would also like to welcome the progress we have made in this area under the french presidency. i am of course referring to the adoption of the package of measures better known as the erika package. to return to the report before us today, i would remind you that we have discussed two proposals: a proposal for a regulation on the setting up of a regulatory committee called the 'maritime safety committee', which implies an amendment to the regulations in force, and a proposal for a directive amending the existing directives to include the 'maritime safety committee'. in practical terms, this means that the committee will replace the current committees responsible for safety at sea; the committee will be a single committee whose purpose is to facilitate the implementation of amendments made by member states to existing international conventions in this field. the european union already has a stockpile of 12 directives and three regulations aimed at ensuring stricter enforcement of regulations in the areas of ship safety, protection against pollution from ships, seafarers' training and qualification criteria and working conditions on board. at the same time, the establishment of this new committee is expected to enhance the effectiveness of the maritime security policy implemented by the european union. while the european commission's proposals were satisfactory overall, the provisions for the involvement of the european parliament were not acceptable. that is why amendments were tabled to preserve the rights of parliament to participate in the regulatory procedure. in voting for this report, i therefore joined the voluntary approach taken at european level to make maritime transport safer.
in writing. - the proposal by the rapporteur, mr bakopoulos, to set up a 'committee on maritime safety and the prevention of pollution from ships', which would replace the existing committees, is a further step towards renationalising the community's maritime safety policy, but also an additional asset for improving the control of community and international enforcement. but the recent shipwrecks of the erika and the ivoli sun have shown us that the best resolutions are useless unless we give ourselves the means to implement them and to have them implemented. the member states must therefore be required to apply the legislation in force, in particular that which regulates protection against pollution, the control of the training and qualifications of seafarers and the working conditions on board. to this end, efforts must be made not only to increase the number and quality of controls and controllers but also to ensure that all actors - ship owners, charterers, carriers and classification societies - are held financially accountable. to put an end to impunity and complacency in shipping, i voted for this report.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after much thought on the question of the copyright directive and harmonization which first involves a list of exceptions, i think we have simply agreed to remain confused in order to have time to think about this question. the confusion is due to the fact that there are three interests in this directive: that of authors and creators, that of consumers, who are also users, and that of producers and managers. producers and managers are trying to find their place between the two, and i feel that the directive is there with its list of exceptions, to which the legal affairs committee has just added one - which raises many problems - concerning broadcasting. i feel like we're giving the consumer a chance. but what's he gonna eat? i ask you what we will be consuming, in a short time, if we do not protect and defend creation. that's the question we can ask ourselves. it so happens that, apart from my mandate as a member of parliament, i am both an author of books and a user of libraries and research facilities. in both cases, however, we need a certain amount of protection, as well as security, not insecurity, in order to produce. if i take the consumer's point of view, i am surprised that our parliament, which defends the europe of markets, is ultimately extremely bad at defending the production of that market, because, with this list of exceptions, we refuse to pay for the goods, we want the goods to be free. you'll admit it is amazing. nor is there any question of the production conditions of these commodities; but to produce commodities, you need creators, you need authors. when you have no more creators or authors, i don't know what you will sell, i don't know what you will consume, but in any case the europe of markets will not do well. that's it for the markets. now, if we go into the details of the directive, we find that if we say, for example, 'the archive has existed for a while, for an hour,' it means that things that have been shown on television are archives. when you're a bit of a historian, you're a little surprised to hear about the archives in this way. how are we going to make, if archives are this, if private copying is multiple, how are we going to make culture, which is cultural diversity, not just heritage, museums, not just a list that we find in places that are actually archives and museography, but so that it is living creation? to do this, we must - whether we like it or not - help creation. and to help creation, we must support copyright, not criticize and attack it. that is what my group will be seeking to defend in the vote tomorrow.
mr president, the report before us on copyright and the information society, the so-called information society, is an example of the growing perversity of a community system whose only real driving force is the completion of a market from which no product, no good, no service can be exempted. while the damage caused by this system is obvious, because harmonization protects less than the previous protections provided by the states, and therefore this damage is obvious - i will not give an example - it is now the whole of cultural services that the commission and the council are proposing to convert into commodities, as mrs fraisse has just said quite well. under the pretext of this information society, which the financial markets themselves are relativising - a lot of water has flowed under the bridge of this information society over the last three years - it is the whole of european creation, all creators combined, that this directive and the common position which the legal affairs committee proposes us to adopt want to bring under the rules of international trade of the world trade organisation in particular, renamed for the occasion wipo. it is a paradox that the institutions of this european union are becoming, in essence, the complacent footstool of an unrestrained and unconscious globalisation. that is why i believe that many of us in this house will try to prevent this acceleration of a process which is emptying the very idea of europe of all content and meaning. i hope we will reject the amendments tabled by the legal affairs committee because they break with the tradition of this parliament, which has hitherto defended the diversity of european cultural production and the special, indeed exceptional, role of creators, writers and artists in european civilization. the information society is a decoy, used complacently here to try to confiscate the oldest and most beautiful of properties, intellectual property.
- mr president, i too, of course, would like to congratulate the rapporteur first of all on his willingness to achieve a balance on a text which has been under discussion for almost three years. the adapt existing legislation to new technologies while respecting the international treaties adopted in 1996. there is a legal vacuum regarding copyright protection in the digital age. the internet is a great tool, but it must not be a zone of lawlessness. the cultural and economic issues are important and, with the internet growing at an impressive rate, a legal framework must be found in europe, as the united states already adopted one two years ago. there is therefore urgency, especially as this directive is a decisive element in the fight against piracy (a fight which is particularly close to my heart) and as piracy is a real scourge of the information society, which is all the more evident in the digital environment as copies are and remain of an equivalent quality to the original. private copying is a recognized consumer right. it is only right that those entitled should receive fair compensation in return, all in a balanced way. for copying to remain truly private, the legislator must express himself in a sufficiently restrictive way and there must be no ambiguity in the wording of the definition. i am therefore in favour of a narrow definition of private copying. in order to protect works against illegal copying, rightholders must be able to use technical safeguards. that is why we must fight against the so-called 'hackers' by sanctioning the way in which they offer the public the means of overcoming these safeguards, thus encouraging the piracy of protected works. this new and ever-changing environment raises many questions and concerns. the directive must strike a balance between the interests of consumers and those of rightholders. it tries to answer these questions, imperfectly and as quickly as possible. the adaptation of this directive, in two years' time, will enable us to identify its shortcomings and weaknesses in the face of the dramatic development of the information society.

- doc. a5-0024/2001 by mr swoboda, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, on the proposal for a council regulation on assistance to turkey in the context of the pre-accession strategy, and in particular the establishment of an accession partnership (com (2000) 0502 - c5-0468/2000 - 2000/0205 (cns))
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. i would like to begin by thanking mr swoboda very warmly for his report and also thank parliament as a whole for an extremely constructive and responsible debate which i believe sent a very positive but also a very clear and distinct signal to turkey. i think we can see at the end of this debate that the consensus on the question of turkish policy has grown considerably. we agree that the current situation of human rights, protection of minorities, the quality of democracy and the rule of law in turkey does not correspond to our expectations. unfortunately, that hasn't changed. there is no point in sugarcoating this statement or concealing any of the facts. it is precisely because this is so, because the situation is so unsatisfactory, that we are talking about it and about the political options we have to change it. that brings me to my second point. we also agree that it is in the interest of the whole of europe, and particularly the european union, not just turkey, to have turkey as a stable and reliable partner for the long term. i am sure that everyone in this house will agree with me when i say that the long-term stability of a state is only guaranteed if that state is founded on the values we share together, such as democracy, the rule of law and the protection of minorities. thirdly, i think we also agree that the prospect of membership of the european union has proved to be the central, the most important accelerator of reform, at least so far in the whole history of our enlargements. if you look at the countries of central and eastern europe, with the enormous pace of reform they have put forward and the enormous successes, they have done so only because they see the prospect of membership. the question now is: can we do the same with turkey? in helsinki we said yes, we should try. we have now reached a point where the strategy agreed in helsinki is becoming operational, where we can actually implement it. it is therefore pointless to discuss today whether the strategy adopted in helsinki has changed the realities in turkey or not. she didn't have it! i would never say that it has changed it, but the instruments of this strategy are not there yet. that is why we cannot say that it has not had any results. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the accession partnership sets out our expectations for turkey. it is a matter of the european parliament's right to decide on the basis of the treaty on european union. as soon as this document is formally adopted - it is not yet formally adopted, as parliament's opinion is still pending - we shall await turkey's reply immediately afterwards. this document will be the most important in european-turkish relations, perhaps in recent decades. what i know so far about this leads me to say that we may be on the verge of the most far-reaching political reform in the history of modern turkey. this does not mean that we can know today whether everything turkey will say in its reply is in full accordance with what we expect from it. in this respect, mr swoboda is quite right when he says that the ball is now in turkey's court. it is now up to the community to decide how, at what pace and with what quality it will work to meet the conditions for opening negotiations on membership of the european union. i would therefore like to emphasize what has been said by several speakers. turkey is an important country. turkey is even of particular strategic importance. but this does not mean that the european union can change its internal character because of turkey's strategic importance. she can't and she won't! it is perfectly right that turkey wants to join the eu, not the european union of turkey, and that therefore the conditions of accession which we have set for all apply, and they apply unchanged and without restriction to turkey as well. turkey will only be able to join if these conditions of accession are met in full and in detail. i do not know, and no one knows, whether the strategy we adopted in helsinki, which is supported by parliament, will have the desired effect. but we have reached the point for the first time where turkey must present us with a binding programme and say what it will do to change the situation. it will give us the opportunity to influence this programme because it is a jointly agreed programme, because we are co-financing it, because we have the possibility to influence and monitor it. that is why i think we have really taken a significant step forward. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. first of all, all those who say that it would be logical in itself to include the pre-accession funds for turkey, malta and cyprus in budget line 7 because they are clearly pre-accession funds are absolutely right. the commission wants that too. i must say clearly, however, that this does not change the resources available, because we would simply reduce the corresponding budget line 4 and increase it by 7. malta, cyprus and turkey are not doing well, because they want more money. they don't want us to change the budget line, they want more money. but we have not, because the programmes are laid down in the financial perspective adopted in berlin. there are no budgetary residues here either - a member of the house asked the question - no, we have no budgetary residues in the pre-accession instruments. they're completely draining. only the sapard instrument is running a little late. this is due to the regulation of this instrument, but the funds programmed for 2000 will be fully depleted in the course of 2001. but we don't have any household waste there. we could therefore only satisfy the wish - shared by many here - of the rapporteur to increase preaccession aid for turkey, malta and cyprus to make the ispa and sapard instruments available by providing additional budgetary resources, money which the commission does not have. this must be discussed with the council; the commission has already taken a number of decisions on the basis of the information it has received from the member states. mrs stenzel has quite rightly pointed out that there is of course a difference between the candidate countries in eastern and central europe and turkey, malta and cyprus, because the candidate countries in eastern and central europe not only have to adapt to the acquis, but also have to face the challenge of system transformation. that is the political justification for the situation we are in. let me conclude by saying that in my view, we did make a difference in turkey in 2000. you as politicians know as well as i do that the beginning of a political movement is not first measured in real change, whether in prisons, whether in the ngos, whether in schools or wherever, but the beginning of a political movement is first measured in the way a society discusses, what it discusses and what long-term goals it sets for itself. here in turkey we can see very clearly a massive movement within the year 2000. i believe that the european union's response is to support such a political movement and to provide the instruments we need now so that concrete results can be seen in practice. let me say one last thing: we will not measure the success of our pre-accession strategy towards turkey by what is promised; we will not therefore be measuring it by what is written in the editorials of turkish newspapers, but we will be measuring the success of this strategy by what is actually changing for the people of turkey, whose situation in the present circumstances is deplorable, regrettable, and in any case in need of change. they are measured by real changes in structures and real changes in people's living conditions. when we see these changes, it's time to talk about the next step, but not today. i am glad to see such broad agreement on this issue in this parliament today. i think it would be very helpful for turkey to realise that the council, parliament and the commission have a very firm common position on this issue, at least in principle. firmness in this matter will the council. mr president, i would like to thank you for your reply. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i would like to begin by agreeing fully with the thanks which commissioner verheugen has addressed to swoboda for the excellent report on turkey's accession support which has been discussed here in the house. i am convinced that your report, mr swoboda, will be an important contribution to the difficult debate in which we are all so deeply involved, namely how best to bring turkey closer to the union. i asked to speak on behalf of the council to answer the question put to the presidency by mr sacrédeus on religious freedom and tolerance in turkey. let me just say that we in the council of ministers consider these matters to be of the utmost importance. we are obviously building our discussion with turkey on religious freedom on the basis of the basic copenhagen criteria and on what we find in the partnership with turkey on the fulfilment of the requirements of respect for minority rights. sacrédeus raises the important question of how to stimulate dialogue between the different religions in turkey and in general. we see this as an important element, not only in the partnership with turkey but also in euro-mediterranean cooperation in general. the swedish presidency has tried to build on some of its own experience. the so-called euro-islam project and the conferences against intolerance recently held in stockholm, of which sacrédeus is certainly aware, are examples. we have tried to build on the experience there and to bring some of these ideas into cooperation with turkey in order to emphasize the importance of respect for religious freedom. the sacrédeus also raises the important question of the trial of a turkish priest. the council is monitoring this matter very closely. we know the next court date is february 22nd. we in the council will be watching very closely what happens then and will react in any way we see fit.

- the agenda calls for the joint debate on: - the report (a5-0034/2001) by mr bullmann, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the spring 2001 european council: the lisbon process - the way forward; - the commission statement: synthesis report on progress since lisbon and future actions; and - the report (a5-0020/2001) by mr gasòliba i böhm, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the impact of liberalisation and the process of economic reforms on economic growth in the european union.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, what is the way forward after lisbon? i would like to answer the question as to the substance, our responsibilities and the method. firstly, i believe that the european union's strategy for sustainable growth, full employment and greater social cohesion cannot be considered as already set. the lisbon process has great virtues, very ambitious and well-founded objectives, it reflects a global and open approach to coordination and a clear awareness of the challenge posed by the information revolution. however, significant biases remain. the current framework of monetary, budgetary and financial policies promotes fiscal and social competition; the capacity to conduct public policy remains limited at national level and is severely hampered at european level. i would say that it is a negative integration in the tinbergen sense, not a fully positive integration. these biases are reflected in the current problem of indicators. these are comparable national indicators, which is useful; but there are no european indicators to help us to identify europe in the world economy and to apply common policies. nor is there any examination of the impact of the choices made by one or more of the countries on the others. why are we criticizing ireland? for its anti-cooperative social dumping policy or for its growth-friendly public spending policy? i understand that mr bullmann is saying that growth is here, but that we must not rest on our laurels. in this respect, it is particularly disturbing that the council and the commission do not assess the social and economic impact of the large integrated financial market and the launch of the euro. that is why we must not regard lisbon as a given, but as a beginning; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the future of the european union. there is a good amendment by mr goebbels and mr bullmann on this point. secondly, the european parliament must be able to make clear choices. in my view, the two reports, which were voted unanimously in committee, follow contradictory logics. i agree with the bullmann report, which calls for public investment and social legislation. i cannot, however, support the gasòliba i böhm report. it is all about deregulation and flexibility. i would also point out that if the objective of the internal market is not achieved for essential services such as energy and transport, it is not because of deregulation, but because of the lack of common infrastructure and public regulations. i also want to express a negative opinion on the continuing reduction of social charges, which is always advocated, which takes away the responsibility of companies and creates poor workers. thirdly - and this will be my last point - we must actually help all european social and civic actors to participate in the choice of economic and social policies. but people don't know these coordinates. they have no idea what it is. so we have to ask ourselves about our responsibilities. in this connection, let me remind you that this parliament voted in december 1996, following a report i had presented, a resolution in which it stated its intention to set up an annual european parliament conference on the basic choices of economic and social policy, preceded by an interactive debate between the various national authorities and by a public consultation with civil society actors. i think we could take this proposal back, to win the citizens' attention.
