in writing. - as in the first two readings in the european parliament, on 11 february 1999 and 12 april 2000, i have today refused to approve the draft directive on the voluntary release of genetically modified organisms, as it now emerges from the work of the council-european parliament "conciliation committee". apart from the strategic reason i already explained in the main debate (we risk being misled if we accept the introduction of an authorization procedure and tomorrow the moratorium is lifted without further guarantees), the current text still seems to us, on the substance, very unsatisfactory. some progress is being made, for example on the timetable for eliminating antibiotic resistance markers. but there are also some disturbing shadows. firstly, there is nothing on the liability and possible insurance obligations of the distributors of gmos. the commission has only vaguely promised to "make proposals", but it will certainly not be on the obligation to take out insurance, which it does not want (nor do the gmo producers). the commission has also been very active in the fight against fraud, and has been very active in the fight against fraud. the national safeguard clause in article 23 is not strong enough, because a member state may be required to grant a marketing authorization which would be valid throughout the community. finally, among the sad provisions, there are those concerning public information: sites of cultivation of gm plants for commercial purposes will have to be notified to the competent authorities and "communicated to the public in a manner deemed appropriate by the latter". in other words, there will be no obligation to provide information in a frank and transparent manner. this method of minimising information is reminiscent of the one already used by the commission in the early 1990s, when the mad cow epidemic was developing. the european authorities are definitely repeat offenders.
in writing. - in voting against this report, we have voted neither against agricultural research nor against the scientists who are carrying out research in this field. but the results of this research are inevitably used by the agro-food trusts, and they reinforce their dominance over agriculture, because farmers will have to go through these trusts more and more often to get the seeds, etc. we have no confidence in the agri-food trusts, whose action is motivated exclusively by the pursuit of maximum profit, even at the expense of consumer health and ecological balances. but nothing in the proposal for a directive suggests that the dissemination of gmos, and especially their marketing, will be subject to draconian controls, leading to a total ban if this is in the interest of society, even if it directly conflicts with the interests of the agri-food trusts. the fact that the agri-food trusts have continued to sell animal flour despite the fact that it was proven to be harmful and the laxity, if not the complicity, of the european states and institutions in this respect, is already a serious warning and will no doubt pay dearly in the future. we therefore voted against this report.
in writing. - we shall vote against the report by mr david bowe on behalf of the conciliation committee, because the objectives of the revision of directive 90/220 on the deliberate release of gmos have not been achieved; the european parliament should have been able to agree on all the problems raised and to ensure that all the measures to guarantee the precautionary principle were implemented simultaneously. although progress has been made compared with the old directive (exclusion of pharmaceutical products and renewal of authorizations), we cannot accept a directive which does not guarantee traceability, labelling or producer responsibility. how can we envisage the dissemination of gmos without the formal responsibility of the industrialists, without a directive regulating the problem of traceability and labelling of gmos? the commission announces its intention to table draft directives, but when will they be adopted? what will they contain ? we cannot vote on dissemination without these guarantees. we must not forget the consequences of the bse crisis, the precautionary principle, the principles of food safety and the risks of transmission to other crops, not to mention the impact on human health. in any case, five member states have already announced their willingness to maintain a strict moratorium on any new marketing of gmos, even if the revision of the directive were to be approved, and i congratulate them on this. this draft directive is more dangerous in its omissions than in its content. the european parliament, however, placed great emphasis during the conciliation procedure on clear labelling and traceability rules for gmos, which are essential for consumers who can only decide whether to buy products containing gmos if they are appropriately labelled. this is a fool's market. it is more important that the precautionary principle prevails over the commercial interests of certain multinationals and that only the protection of european consumers is taken into account.
in writing. - the new directive on the deliberate release of gmos was intended to 'include all direct or indirect ecological aspects'. it is clear that the result is far from the stated ambitions and that the irritating topics have been eliminated. the question of environmental liability covering damage caused by gmos is thus postponed, as is the consideration of the potential long-term cumulative effects of the interaction of several gmos. in other words, the dissemination of gmos in agriculture is allowed without knowing what the real risks are and without knowing who will be legally responsible for the damage caused! the uncertainties acknowledged by the drafters of the directive once again show that it is essential to impose a moratorium on the production of gmos for reasons of ecology and public health. the directive, by merely setting an imperfect framework for their dissemination, is contrary to the requirement of a moratorium, and that is the first reason why i am voting against the report. moreover, the social and democratic implications of the expansion of gmos are well known: this expansion further strengthens the dominance of agro-industry over producers and consumers. the directive favours the large industrialists here, and that is the second reason why i am voting against the report.
in writing. - we are obviously for the right of authors, artists, composers, performers, writers, journalists, etc., to live properly from their work. that is why we support their demands for copyright protection. but those who use copyright to hide their own interests are often the big companies that publish records, books, cd-roms, the media and the internet, which take their profits precisely from the authors and at the expense of consumers, who are often kept out of culture, if only because of the cost of books, cds, etc. for these big companies, copyright is just their own right to make the most profit at the expense of the authors and the public, and of organizations like lending libraries that try to make available to the public works that otherwise would never be available to the public. the text seeks to reconcile the interests of the information capitalists with those of authors as well as the public, so we abstained on many amendments, while voting for those which really protect the interests of authors and the rights of the public.
in writing. - on the occasion of the vote on the boselli report, i want to make it clear that with this report and the great debate it has provoked, the question of the cultural future of europe, which is very closely linked to the means granted to creators, is being raised. the cultural world and the creative world were right, and they were very energetically mobilized. i have met many of their representatives, i have read their papers and i think, like many in this house, that they are very much right. of course, it is in everyone's interest that the works be widely disseminated, especially through the new means of communication. but this must not lead to savage looting! hence the absolute need to properly manage the process and in particular to maintain a truly private status for private copying. after today's vote, the battle is still far from being won. this is one more reason to continue the citizens' struggle for a europe that is not just a cold and heartless economic and financial 'monster'.
in writing. - the protection of copyright and related rights, which are a factor in creation, is in itself a difficult problem. it is increasingly acute in the new society, which is also falsely called the information society. the new technologies, of which the internet is the symbol, seem to allow total freedom which favours the consumer but prevents the creator and the industry from deriving full benefit from works and reproductions. this is why it is difficult to reconcile triangular interests between consumers, industries and beneficiaries. how can we protect the profit of the so-called cultural industry without ending the free "copyright" of all the works we encounter while wandering the paths of the internet? for the industry which makes profits from the so-called information technology, with its bloated mouth, the brussels proposal for a directive on copyright is a good compromise. for authors and composers, this compromise weakens copyright protection. the broadcasters' archives, works consulted by libraries or media libraries, ephemeral reproductions, etc., would be excluded from the scope of protection. the authors legitimately claim fair compensation for the losses suffered as a result of the exceptions. they believe that the compromise between the interests involved must be made by contract. these exceptions to protection would, in fact, be expropriations for which there should be compensation.
in writing. - once is not customary, we agree with a proposal for a directive from the commission. it is not that we welcome any intervention on its part - you know how we feel about european construction as a whole and this institution in particular - but we must recognize that, for once, the commission has made efforts: prior consultation of users and industrialists, cost-benefit study, efforts at economic and technical realism - this is an approach that is only too rarely found in the multitude of cases we are dealing with here. we shall not, however, follow the rapporteur, who is not known for sure whether he is making as much demagogy as possible or whether he is being paid by our competitors to sink european manufacturers. at this point, he might as well ask motorists to stop breathing so as not to emit more co2 into the atmosphere. so yes to cleaner motorcycles, yes to new test protocols more in line with the real use of vehicles, yes to the timetable that the manufacturers have considered realistic. but not to unrealistic emission standards, not to additional devices which are not required for other modes of transport, not, in short, to mr lange's amendments.
in writing. - the title of this report itself is suspicious, because generally speaking, when we talk about employment incentives, we are talking about giving subsidies, rebates or tax advantages to employers under the pretext of creating jobs - which they do not create. of course, the text is not very explicit on this point and the intentions in the text are wrapped up in general considerations, some of which are relevant, notably the lack of equality between men and women in employment. but good intentions in words do not make a policy, or more precisely, they can mask a policy which does not solve the problem of unemployment at all. the solution to this problem would require binding measures against those who hold the keys to the problem, i.e. the large industrial and financial groups. but to expect this from the european institutions is to ask the impossible. that is why we voted against this report.
in writing. - the report we voted on today concerns a commission proposal to implement community employment incentive measures (emi). the purpose of this proposal is to implement the provisions of article 129 of the treaty establishing the community (legal basis for the necessary expenditure on employment) and to develop the activities highlighted by the lisbon european council in the framework of the european employment strategy. the aim is to promote cooperation between member states and to support their action in the field of employment. these measures will be financed from the community budget at the rate of eur 55 million for the period 2001-2005 (i.e. eur 10 million per year, with an initial amount of eur 15 million in 2001). the measures mainly concern the development, programming, monitoring, follow-up and evaluation of the european employment strategy, with a focus on the long-term perspective. the following activities are particularly important: (1) analysis and evaluation of employment trends, general policy conditions, evaluation of policy options and impact of community policies; 2. evaluation of the national action plans; (3) collection and exchange of national experience, as defined in the annual employment guidelines for member states; (4) technical and scientific actions necessary for the development of common indicators, the improvement and complementarity of statistics, the benchmarking of performance and the exchange of information on best practice. apart from the implementation of these various measures, it is important that the commission takes account of statistical data, studies and actions from international organisations such as the oecd or the international labour organisation. it is also essential to promote the widest possible dissemination of the results of the actions undertaken. parliament also recommended that the commission ensure that all the activities envisaged are consistent with and complementary to other community programmes and initiatives. the activities envisaged will also be open to the participation of the eea countries and the ceecs candidates in accordance with the arrangements, including financial arrangements, to be agreed with these countries. i also call for our mediterranean partners to be involved. the european parliament expects the commission to present an interim report and a final report by 31 december 2003 and 31 december 2006 respectively. with all of us thinking of the preparations for the extraordinary council on employment to be held in stockholm next march, i voted with conviction for these new measures in favour of employment!
in writing. - the european parliament's proposal for a decision on community incentive measures in the field of employment is in line with the logic of the luxembourg compromise (1997), which introduced a process of evaluation and comparison of 'good practice' in the member states. in this context, amendments aimed at better informing european citizens, acting in cooperation with the social partners and local or regional authorities, or those aimed at raising awareness of the situation of women and equal opportunities in the workplace through studies on the causes of interruption of work, parental leave and parttime work are positive, and i will vote for them. but we are opposed to a method which aims to subordinate employment and social rights in general to the broad economic policy guidelines (gepgs) and stability plans. we reject the logic of the four luxembourg pillars (employment integration, entrepreneurship, adaptation of enterprises, equal opportunities), which serve as criteria for evaluating member states and support the construction of a european labour market subject to the liberal economy. as a result, i abstained.
in writing. - i voted against the swoboda report, which calls for eu financial aid to turkey (nearly €200 million a year) to be classified under heading 7 of the financial perspective, 'pre-accession aid', where it would join the aid granted to the candidate countries of central and eastern europe, and soon to cyprus and malta. this new classification seems to me inappropriate, because although the helsinki council of 13 december 1999 did indeed recognise turkey's status as a candidate for accession (which i contest), it was specified that negotiations would not be opened with that country as long as it did not meet the copenhagen criteria, in particular those relating to democracy and respect for human rights. but turkey is not satisfied with that today, and everyone in europe recognizes that. in these circumstances, even for her supporters, she is only a kind of virtual candidate, not an actual and actual candidate. why should it be granted a financial status which does not correspond to its real status? our concern is heightened by the rather provocative attitude of this country following the recent recognition of the armenian genocide by the french national assembly. not only did turkey not admit its fault (although old enough in theory not to tarnish the current regime), but it denied the evidence, and even took unjustifiable retaliatory measures against french companies. these pressures, this constant blackmail, are not acceptable from a country which wants to be admitted to the european club. we therefore do not see why the swoboda report is proposing that we take a measure today which will reinforce these erroneous provisions.
in writing. - we are in favour of turkey receiving, like the other applicant countries, financial instruments and assistance commensurate with its size and needs. this is particularly the case for the restructuring of agriculture, the development of rural areas and the protection of the environment. any discriminatory treatment in this respect would not punish the officials of the turkish authoritarian regime, but the workers of that country. on the contrary, it would in no way strengthen the conditions for the struggle to enforce the respect of basic democratic rights. the best way for the european union to force the turkish government to keep its 'commitments', a way which is devoid of hypocrisy and which does not serve as a pretext for new liberal pressures - which only serve european free trade - would be to support and support the democratic opposition. because the initiatives of human rights activists, trade unionists and politicians can, if given the means, mobilize public opinion to stop a regime that murders kurds, makes political prisoners disappear, represses the movements of prisoners, tortures democrats or leaves öcalan languishing in the corridors of death.
the rapporteur. - mr president, the exercise to which i was invited was extremely informative and, i must say, a real pleasure. i had to deal with three constraints: the doubts or questions of my colleagues on the committee on economic and monetary affairs; the commission's proposal for a regulation on the european investment bank (eib) is based on the following three elements: i would like to thank my colleagues in the committee on economic and monetary affairs in particular for the relevance of the questions they asked me to put to the european investment bank. i would like to thank these civil society volunteers for their expertise in overseeing a bank which, after all, accounts for 5% of fixed capital formation in the european union, making it the major investor in the european union. finally, without any flagrancy, i must thank the president of the european investment bank and his colleagues for the kindness and goodwill, indeed the warmth, with which they were willing to talk to me, to take these criticisms into account, to respond to them, sometimes convincing me that they were right, sometimes accepting them and sketching out with me the answers to be given. we have therefore reached a report which is almost unanimous. you have seen that the amendments deal with details, which i will deal with in the last two minutes of my speech. the general consensus was on proposals for inflation which are at least as much aimed at the other bodies of the european union, or even at the states, as at the european investment bank. we fully agree with the european investment bank and we give it credit for the priorities it has set itself and for the pillars on which its policy is based. however, we want to stress that things are changing. europe is opening up to the east. it is taking on more and more responsibilities for the balkans, which are not yet in the accession process. in addition, europe has signed up to the kyoto agreement, which requires it to reduce its output of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases by an average of 8% by 2010. in other words, this international agreement becomes binding in 7 years. in addition, europe has set itself the objective, from lisbon, of becoming a world power of excellence based on knowledge and new technologies. finally, europe has given priority to the development of smes. it is not through a europe incorporated with big mega-city champions, but rather by relying on smes, that europe aims to achieve this state of excellence. three new objectives, therefore, including in the light of the 1999 report which we are formally examining today. but of course, in doing so we are looking at all the eib's guidelines: accession, kyoto, the development of smes towards excellence. it is in the light of these three objectives, which were perhaps not so clear when the eib adopted its priorities and drafted its 1999 report, that we wanted to call on the european union bodies and the eib itself to change its policy. the first paragraphs of the report before you are absolutely unanimous and are essentially aimed at extending or facilitating loans in these three directions. to say simply a few words about what we do not agree on: the official importance of ngos in the preparation of the decisions of the european investment bank, the affirmation of the kyoto objective as truly predominant and, finally, the modalities of the eib's prudential supervision. on these three points i leave it to the judgment of the house.

- mr president, when the committee on employment and social affairs decided to put this question to the council, it wanted to focus on two specific points, which are also interrelated: the free movement of third-country nationals, following the decisions of the tampere european council, on the one hand, and the legal basis envisaged in this respect, on the other. at that time, our question was of course also linked to the preparatory work for the nice summit, since we were hoping for elements promoting social policy and free movement. since then, and particularly in the period preceding the european council mentioned above, the committee on employment and social affairs has had the opportunity to examine the question of free movement more generally. this more general approach has been useful to us, because before extending free movement to third country nationals, we must of course ensure that it works properly for union citizens. we have had to note with concern that regulation 1408/71 was becoming increasingly inadequate and that its modernisation and simplification were being postponed from month to month. this is a serious situation, because freedom of movement is one of the fundamental principles of the european union. it is the one that allows citizens of the union to move, settle and work without hindrance. this is why regulation 1408/71 - which was designed to coordinate national social security systems - is one of the cornerstones of the people's europe and any obstacle or delay affecting its modernisation is serious. so let me take these three elements one by one. let us first go back to the text of our question. firstly, as regards the extension of regulation 1408/71 to third country nationals, what are we to conclude? it is clear that the council's action to date does not always reflect, or rather still does not reflect - the nuance is not the same - the political will of the european council in tampere on 15 and 16 october 1999 to create in the union, i quote the council acts, 'an area of freedom, security and justice, an area in which the legal status of third-country nationals legally residing in a member state should be closer to that of nationals of the member states'. i would remind you that parliament had already made such a statement in october 1998, since the commission's proposal had been adopted by parliament without amendments. in other words, the commission took the initiative, parliament supported the proposal by a clear vote and the european council, at the highest level, in tampere, legitimised this approach a year later; but the council has not yet adopted a common position in 2001 to enable us to continue the procedure. what is the reason for this unacceptable delay and for this denial of the political will of the heads of state and government when, for once, the three institutions are in perfect agreement, which is not always the case? it seems that the council's position is different from that of the european parliament and the commission on the question of the legal basis of this text. but let me put this legal controversy in terms that are accessible to the general public. what is the council's intention in opposing this legal basis? it wants to exclude (you will tell us that it could) the european parliament from the codecision procedure. that's the problem. come on, no more shaking your head! you're not giving us a vote. this is not just a matter of the european parliament's role. it is a direct political and civic issue. the extension of regulation 1408/71 to third country nationals is a matter of such great sensitivity that the citizens of the union must be fully involved in it through the european parliament, which represents them. the committee on social affairs and employment cannot therefore accept the reference to other legal bases than those provided for in the commission's proposal and would like to recall that regulation 1408/71 can only be amended by the codecision procedure. mr president-in-office of the council, what we are disputing in the council's proceedings is in fact the same thing, whether it is community citizens or citizens of third countries. in both cases it is the slowness of the council's work that is holding back the development of free movement. the council cannot shirk its responsibilities. it must implement the decisions of the european council, it must implement them in full transparency to public opinion and in full respect for democratic rules and the role of our parliament. if we do not do this, mr president, we shall undoubtedly have to see the members of the european parliament react vigorously - with the support of public opinion, we have no doubt - against the continuation of these obstacles to free movement. i would add that my protest is not, of course, directed at the swedish presidency as such, but at the council. i think that the swedish presidency, in its tradition, could make a great contribution to solving this problem. finally, i would like to conclude on one last question, which concerns the immediate future of the union, namely enlargement. the committee on employment we share parliament's concern about religious freedom in that country. it is true that the living conditions of the majority of the chinese population seem to have improved during the past twenty you have referred. we are not just talking about the catholic and protestant churches, but also about any other kind of belief. i'll make some references to falun gong later. other issues raised with fundamental element in the improvement of individual rights. this field of human rights is one of the preferred topics of our work, where i believe we can improve our relations. now, dialogue is only congratulating the government on its commitment to respect for human rights and freedom of the media, noted that there were still problems in some areas, in particular restrictions on the activity of political parties and judicial practices. and also at that time the troika expressed its concern at the concessions being made to certain groups which advocated intolerance. in the absence of a democratic counterweight, the influence of such groups can certainly increase. what is the commission doing to improve the situation in the field of human rights? the commission is ready to support measures to improve the good governance of public affairs in pakistan, which will benefit everyone.

- doc. b5-0009/2001 by mr von wogau and mrs suominen and mrs doyle, on behalf of the group of the european people's party (christian democrats) and european democrats, to the commission, on the stability situation in ireland and france.
commission. - madam president, i would like to thank mr von wogau for raising an issue which i think deserves debate. i am not saying that the commission has not taken the necessary steps to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. starting from the end: why do our decisions not affect the transfer of resources at all? because we are talking about economic policy coordination. we are not talking about regional policy, competition, taxation or any of those other things. i would like to make an opening remark so that we all know or will know what the model is that we have agreed to in the maastricht treaty. according to the treaty, the coordination of economic policies is based on an instrument which is adopted annually by the european councils in june, on the proposal of the ministers for economic affairs and finance, and which is called the 'great economic policy guidelines'. that is the basic document of our economic policy coordination, which you know well, because you have had occasion to discuss it more than once in the committee on economic and monetary affairs. the document contains general decisions and specific decisions by the member states, containing specific recommendations which - i should like to stress this - are unanimously adopted by the european council, as well as, of course, the views of each of the member states which sign them. it is true that, alongside the broad economic policy guidelines and in order to maintain a proper balance between fiscal policy and monetary policy, the stability pact is being put into effect. hence, sometimes we may get the impression that - as in the case of ireland - there is some contradiction between actions which may be difficult to understand, according to the fulfilment of the criteria of the stability pact. firstly - and i think this is important - from the point of view of the stability pact, ireland has had and continues to have a lax, comfortable compliance with the stability pact and the behaviour of the irish authorities deserves all the praise possible for the smooth functioning of public finances and the progress of their structural reforms. it is true that the irish economy has continued to grow very strongly in the year 2000, but it is also true - and this is where we come to the first point you have raised - that the irish economy is in a state of overheating. is global warming an important issue from the point of view of global balances? i am not concerned at all with whether each of the specific measures is correct or not. it is the responsibility of the member states, and there is nothing to object to. we are talking about general global positions. the problem of the overheating of the irish economy is not a new one. this is a theme that dates back to 1998 and was already reflected in the broad economic policy guidelines. it was also reflected in 1999 and has been reflected in 2000. in 2000 it was said - i am referring to a decision adopted by the european council, proposed by the ministers for economic affairs and applicable in each member state - that the use of budgetary policy must ensure economic stability, given the extent of overheating in the economy and the 2001 budget must be managed with this objective in mind. what is the content of the 2001 budget, shall we say? i think this can help us to clarify two questions: what is the commission's concern in the first place, and the member states' concern in the second place. i would like to give two figures for the 2001 budget: the current expenditure voted in the budget represents an increase of 1.06% in irish gross domestic product; the tax reduction represents 0.57%. the total demand boost, as a result of these two factors, is therefore 1.6% of irish gross domestic product. there is another fact that i find interesting about what we were talking about in the broad economic policy guidelines. the message is: 'seek or maintain a balanced budgetary policy and, if possible, have a somewhat more restrictive budgetary policy, which compensates for the difficulties that ireland may have as a result of a monetary policy, defined for the euro area, which is, of course, more expansionary for irish conditions. if we look, for example, at what the impact is, in terms of primary impact on the cyclically adjusted surplus, which are the figures we normally use to see the behaviour of economies, we see that, whereas in the year 2000 the figure was a budgetary boost of 0.4 points of gdp, in the year 2001 it is 0.9 points of gdp. this matter is, incidentally, being discussed between the irish government and the commission. he considers that the figures we have calculated have an increase of 0.3 additional points. we can arrive at somewhat different figures with the figures they give us - this is a subject under discussion at eurostat. that is why we have referred to 0.5 in the recommendation, which in fact admits this situation. third, an important issue in the behavior of economies is how supply works in relation to demand and whether demand growth is very fast in relation to existing supply. we measure this technically with what's called the potential output gap, the potential for production, which is how much more demand grows than supply. in 2000 the potential output gap was 4.5%, meaning that ireland demanded 4.5% more than it produced. in 2001 this figure rises to 5.4%. so we are talking about a very expansionary budgetary policy, when the commitment the irish government had accepted in the broad economic policy guidelines was a budgetary policy which, in principle, should be more restrictive to compensate for the other problems. we come to the second point raised by the honourable member which i find particularly interesting: the irish economy is relatively small and its impact on the monetary area is minimal. that argument is correct and could lead us to conclude - as many economists do - that if we had no other kinds of commitments, why act on ireland if it does not affect monetary policy? i think that in connection with this argument we must ask ourselves a double question. firstly, can we treat the member states of the european union unequally? can some states do what they think is appropriate and others not, depending on whether they are larger or smaller? secondly, we could discuss whether this is the model to be applied in the future, but in any case it is not the model we are applying today, in accordance with the legislation in force. it is therefore absolutely essential, at least for the commission - if we are to maintain our role as guardian of the treaties - to apply the treaties as they exist. the commission then did what it considered to be its duty, namely to send a recommendation to the council of ministers under article 99 (4). i have stressed very strongly that when i say recommendation, i do not mean sanctions. i understand that, in media terms, it is much more attractive to talk about sanctions. when we talk about recommendations we are pointing out to the irish government that the budgetary policy they have defined is inconsistent with what they agreed and has additional problems of overheating their economy. we evaluated the recommendation in the explanatory statement, saying: 'we consider that overheating to be 0.5%'. we can discuss it. it's a number that depends on the methodologies we use. it is obviously up to the irish government to do what it deems appropriate thereafter. the commission's position was submitted to the council of ministers, which adopted it by consensus. this is the situation we are in at the moment and, like you, i think it should be given the importance it deserves, because, while it is an important milestone in the implementation of our model of economic policy coordination, we should not try to draw conclusions which are something the commission has certainly never intended.

- madam president, i would first like to thank you for setting an example by chairing this closing session, so to speak, of our session. i now come to our debate and welcome the opportunity to express - madam president, the recommendation adopted by the council of finance ministers last monday, which nails ireland to the pillar because of a supposedly too expansionary national budget, seems to us to be completely disproportionate, to the point that one has to ask why it was issued. disproportionate, because ireland seems to be a rather good pupil of the european class and its inflation, which is quite low in absolute terms, is not likely to upset the balance of the whole area. in these circumstances, why should we demand restrictive measures which may be harmful to this country? the explanation must be sought in the analysis of the new single currency system, where flexible adjustments through exchange rate fluctuations are replaced by the rigidity of the single currency, supplemented by disciplinary procedures. market adjustments are therefore replaced by administrative and centralised adjustments. but is it assured that the new administrative procedure is intended to produce a better result than the market one? we don't think he did. the most certain outcome is the imposition on the individual members of an economic policy which is not optimal for all. this rigidity can lead to disadvantages which in the long run will overshadow the supposed advantages of the single currency. one question, however, remains unsolved to this day. is this compulsory unified policy determined by the big countries for their own benefit and to the detriment of the small ones? or could it one day turn against the great countries themselves? i don't have a ready answer to that question. ireland might well think today that it is in the first scenario, that of a small country sacrificed to the interests of the heavyweights. but the question is more complicated because, behind the condemnation of ireland, we also see that more important targets are being targeted, perhaps france being the first of these. the challenge is to reduce or even toughen the multilateral surveillance provided for in article 99 of the treaty, so that it can be applied to other states in the future. the process of coercion is therefore far from complete. disciplinary europe strikes small states first, but it may strike everyone tomorrow.
madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, it is a strange matter that we are here today, because when i hear mr wurtz and the commissioner, i have the impression that they are fighting the same battle. both of them tell us: "you don't have the right to grow, but you have the right to spend". you have no right to grow up. this is a state, ireland, which has an impressive budget surplus, extremely limited debt, a very high growth rate and inflation, which is admittedly too high, notably for exogenous reasons, but which therefore respects the essence of what we said should be respected in the stability pact, and you say: 'it is not good to grow even though you respect the criteria'. mr wurtz says: "you must have the right to spend". i would point out to you, mr wurtz, that this is not the case in ireland. ireland doesn't spend much. it's growing fast because it's not spending too much. we are told that france is the only country to which we can give a small sign, a small rebuke, but in reality we accept it. i have to say that france is not keeping its commitments. france had committed itself to reducing public spending and to a movement of tax relief. that imbalance is broken. we see that the movement towards deficit reduction is declining in france, while growth is taking hold. we see that france retains the highest level of public expenditure of all the euro area countries. we see that france finances, from its national budget, expenditure on wage costs which would logically fall within the scope of the market economy. all this is not satisfactory, but you say nothing, because france, like germany, like italy, like other countries, is too big a piece for you. i am concerned, then, because to have a real policy mix, commissioner - commission. - madam president, i would like to thank all the speakers for their views. i have tried to make some points clear in my initial speech, but i have a feeling that i have not succeeded. first of all, we are not judging ireland in comparison to anyone else. we are judging ireland in terms of its own commitments, accepted in the broad economic policy guidelines. secondly, we are not making a decision that falls out of the sky, that was not planned. the council recommendation of 1998 already spoke of the need for a stricter fiscal policy for ireland; the 1999 recommendation recalls that, despite the efforts made, it is insufficient, and in 2000, when it is said that irish budgetary policy, accepted by ireland, must be more restrictive, the result is a clear expansionary budget by ireland. when i talk about expansionary budget, i'm talking about global numbers: more spending on health care, more spending on tax cuts. that sounds great. it is something that corresponds to a national policy decision. my concern as the commissioner responsible for economic and monetary affairs is the overall position of the irish budget. but this is not just my concern, it is the concern of the central bank of ireland, which i think is quite aware of the position of its economy and clearly understands that the current budget is providing a substantial pro-cyclical stimulus to the economy. that is the situation and those are the facts we judge. from there, we can talk about what we do or don't do. my duty as the commissioner responsible for these matters is to implement the broad economic policy guidelines, which are more binding than the stability pact. the stability and growth pact - to satisfy mrs torres marques - is a decision which is the result of a community regulation. the broad economic policy guidelines are the model which we agreed to introduce in the maastricht treaty. and what we've done is we've applied that model strictly, as intended. it is clear that - contrary to what some people think - this is not a commission position - it is a position of the commission and the council - and we have not based our proposal on anything other than the assessment of this point itself. so let no one think that there are problems of another nature or for any other reason, whether small or large. we are talking about consistency with the model we had proposed in the past. some reference has been made to more understanding. i think we have had the understanding since 1998, but it is clear that in this situation, at some point decisions have to be made. the commission's lack of diplomacy has been cited. i can assure you that none of the leaks that have appeared in the press have come from my services in the commission. of course, you might think that the best in the class is punished. i said we don't sanction. we are highlighting through a recommendation an incorrect behaviour with regard to the economic policy guidelines. and this is not inconsistent with good behavior in terms of growth and inflation. we could talk about a lot more details. mr bradbourn argued that not enough data had been given. i am prepared to appear before the committee on economic and monetary affairs when they see fit to comment in more detail on all the data we were discussing. article 99 (4) - which is one of its concerns - is applied in accordance with the provisions of the existing legislation. there has been some discussion as to whether the sanction against ireland is justified or not. in my opinion, it is. if i wasn't, i wouldn't have made this proposal. and it's founded despite ireland's small impact on the overall european economy. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we can talk about other issues that have come up as well. the problems relating to ireland's contribution to european growth, the specific problems, the evolution of inflation, etc. i think all these technical issues can be discussed. it is true that nominal inflation in ireland has fallen over the last two months. however, when we talk about the irish economy warming up, we are talking about underlying inflationary pressures, the workings of underlying inflation, rising wages, rising house prices and many other elements that are fundamental to making a correct assessment of what is happening in ireland. is our approach a misrepresentation? we are now entering a difficult subject, because the treaty of nice must be ratified and because this is an element which will affect other models. i would ask you whether you think that this kind of political assessment absolves the commission of its duty to apply the treaties as they stand. i think the commission has acted quite prudently, having repeatedly urged the irish government to change the course of events. the commission has presented the matter to the euro group and the economic and financial affairs council. this was not approved by accident. it has been discussed in the special group of the economic and financial committee after analysing each of the arguments put forward by the irish administration. and yet, as i said earlier, the decision was taken on a proposal from the commission and - let us say - by consensus of the council of ministers. in my view, the commission has done what it should have done. i would like to stress once again the value of recommendation. i am not talking about a sanction, but a recommendation, and i think we can only draw one conclusion from this council decision on a proposal from the commission, which is its content: the application of a rule in the treaty to solve a number of specific problems arising in the model of economic policy coordination that we have established, which in the future, of course, could change, but which is the one in force today.

commission. – madam president, i totally agree with the sentiment that mr harbour expressed in his excellent report last year, together with three other honourable members who were rapporteurs on associated reports. the reform should proceed as quickly as possible in order to avoid the demoralisation and destabilisation of the staff of the european public service. i agree with that even more strongly now than i did then. in any reform process there is an unavoidable gap between original design and effective implementation. it is in the interest of everyone who wants progressive change, and the stronger institutions which that change will bring, to try to make that gap as narrow as possible. nevertheless we first have to undertake full and thorough consultation and negotiation as a matter of courtesy to our staff but also to encourage the sense of ownership of reform which is essential to success. the four and a half months that we have set aside for those negotiations and consultation allow us to work quickly but thoroughly. secondly those decisions which are the responsibility of the commission can be taken quite quickly after the end of that four and a half months, taking into account the result of those consultations and negotiations. we can then embark upon the changes probably by the end of this year. others, however, must be submitted as formal legal proposals to this house and to the council. that will, everybody anticipates, involve a year of negotiations on the detail of amendments to the staff regulations and the pay and pensions package, which will take nearly the whole of 2002. these delays are regrettable but obviously we want to ensure that we go through the full and effective system of democratic scrutiny both by the council and this house. that is understood amongst the staff. it also means, of course, that the two-year rollover of the present system of pay and pensions will provide stability and security for all the institutions, which would not have been the case if the council and parliament had not agreed to our proposal on that. hopefully, therefore, if the legislation rhythm is not subject to delay, we could year, or even twice a year, to their home country. that was one thing when there were six member states with contiguous boundaries and railway systems connecting them. that has changed somewhat. into line with modern travel realities. i hope that custom will also be emulated.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, among the most sought-after fish species in the world are those defined as 'highly migratory', including the most commercially important tuna and orca species (swordfish, marlin, sailfish). large stocks of these species are being caught. in 1997, 3.5 million tonnes of highly migratory species were caught in the atlantic, pacific and indian oceans. the european union was actively involved in the fishery for these species in oceans around the world, with vessels flying the flags of different member states accounting for over 400,000 tonnes in 1997, with japan also competing. several regional fisheries organisations have been set up to regulate the catching of these species: the international commission for the conservation of atlantic tunas, iccat, the inter-american tropical tuna commission, the citt covering the eastern tropical pacific, the indian ocean tuna commission, the iotc. the european union is a member of icfta and the iotc and has applied to the ittc. these international organisations adopt recommendations concerning, in particular, technical measures relating to minimum size and weight, fishing prohibition periods and/or zones, restrictions on certain types of gear or fishing practices, and capacity limits for certain fleets. at present, these measures are scattered over a number of regulations. the commission's proposal is aimed, quite rightly, at bringing together all the technical measures relating to large-scale migration in a single regulation. some of them have been in force for many years, others, all of them recent, were adopted only last autumn, and we took this into account in our report. the simplest way is to assess the effectiveness of these measures, and is to consider the status of the stocks for which it aims to improve conservation. in the atlantic, many, if not all, tuna and halibut stocks are in poor condition. for example, according to the 2000 report of the ices standing committee on research and statistics, the biomass of fresh bigeye tuna has deteriorated rapidly over the past five years and the current level of fishing cannot be maintained and is expected to continue to decline. of the main stocks, only the striped belly ray is considered not to be overfished. in short, the management of these highly migratory species in the atlantic is more characterised by failures than by successes, and as the leading fishing power in the region, the european union must accept its share of responsibility. each of the oceans faces identical problems, which is not surprising given the high mobility of tuna and tuna-like fish, but also of the fleets that exploit them. so there is an excessive fishing effort and the catching of small fish in particular must be controlled. one remedy for over-exertion is to keep a register of vessels. this is a first step. it's fresh. it has not proved effective and does not allow for a drastic reduction in the catches of certain species of bluefin tuna. as regards the capture of small fish, the increasingly widespread practice of fishing with rotating trawls and fish aggregating devices, rather than fishing in pursuit of free-swimming flocks of tuna, has led to a high exploitation of juveniles. iccat has shown that a minimum landing size can be imposed, but this is only a convenience, still not effective. the commission has also proposed that the fishing fleet be reduced to a minimum. the position of the citt, which provides for the conservation of certain species on board, is interesting. this could be effective, but it is not sufficient for fishing areas other than the eastern pacific. these areas do not have large seine observers. finally, as regards flags of convenience, if no effort is made to eliminate these vessels, all the other measures proposed will be rendered null and void. in conclusion, i would like to draw your attention to two points: firstly, the special attention that must be paid to reducing by-catches, other than juveniles, which are often the result of long-line fishing and rotating nets. cicta is on it. other organisations should do the same. the last problem is that of allowing certain countries, which do not currently have quotas, to fish in their exclusive economic zone, the eez. this seems normal, but it would be logical if the european union then agreed to reduce its catch shares, something it has refused to do so far. it would be reasonable for the union to adopt a more flexible stance on this issue.

their ills. today, we don't make peace by making war. the iron curtain and the berlin wall were broken down by international information and the resulting need for freedom. instead of continuing to in writing. - pursuant to article 62-2 tec, the council submitted to the european parliament, for consultation, a proposal for a regulation which was difficult to draw up, establishing the list of third countries whose nationals will be subject to the visa requirement when entering the european union, as well as the list of countries exempt from this requirement for visas of less than three months. at the border of the two, there was the difficult case of romania: it should in principle be included in the second list as a candidate country with which accession negotiations are open, but a more restrictive attitude unfortunately seems necessary, since this country feeds many countries in europe with illegal immigration. the council has found a rather elegant solution: it agrees to include romania in the list of countries whose nationals are exempt from the visa requirement, but the proposal for a regulation, in its article 8, provides that this provision will only enter into force when this country has indicated 'the commitments it is prepared to undertake in the field of illegal immigration and irregular residence, including the repatriation of persons residing illegally'. that seems to me to be the most important condition. the european parliament, in the amendments it has just voted, has removed it, not out of any particular affection for romania, which we could have understood, but in the spirit of free movement without control that is so often its characteristic. in the same spirit, a few other amendments were voted on, of lesser importance, but which i cannot accept either. in these circumstances, i refused to vote for the european parliament's report, while supporting the original position of the council.
in writing. - i have just voted in favour of this first amending budget of the european union for 2001, which provides in particular for additional expenditure of eur 971 million to deal with the consequences of mad cow disease. but i would like to stress that this figure, which was drawn up by the commission in january, seems to have been completely overtaken by the development of events. since last monday in particular, we have been in a paradoxical situation: the european union cannot, or does not want to, finance additional aid to french farmers, and leaves france to manage on its own by allowing it to distribute exceptional national aid. it is at the moment when the crisis hits hardest, and when european solidarity is most needed, that the union collapses without glory. i am certainly the first to say that we must not increase the overall european budget, which is already costing us a lot, and that we must respect the financial perspective for 2000-06 agreed at the berlin council in 1999. but that does not mean that nothing can be done: for the time being, the financial perspective still leaves us a margin of eur 506 million for the agricultural headings for 2001, which is no reason to let it lie dormant in the short and medium term, even if the agricultural appropriations planned are fully spent. there is another solution, rather than increasing the overall budget of the union: to shift to the agricultural part of the budget the expenditure entered under the heading of the structural funds - which have never been fully used up in recent years, and which in any case do not always meet such urgent needs (putting aside, of course, aid to the applicant countries). moreover, this would not be a diversion, since the structural funds also have a priority mission to maintain activity throughout the territories, which would be the case if they helped to combat the devastating consequences of bse. the tragedy we're living through would justify this unusual operation. in the longer term, it is becoming clear to everyone that the european agricultural policy, which may have had the merit of helping to develop our agriculture in the 1960s, is now producing such perverse effects - subsidiarity, bureaucracy, cost inflation, intensification dangerous to health, etc. - that a profound reform becomes inevitable. as we have been saying for years, much stricter rules than those currently in force will be needed to protect nature and health, but without adding to the burden on the taxpayer: it is the consumer who should logically pay the difference by buying the product at its true price, or at a price closer to the truth. at the same time, if we want to preserve our food independence, we will have to impose on imports, on the one hand, the same safety rules, of course, and on the other hand, in certain cases, levies to preserve production in the countries of europe.

- doc. a5-0040/2001 by mr hatzidakis, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the communication from the commission on the report of the standing working party on the safety of the transport of radioactive materials in the european union (com (98) 0155 - c4-0034/1999 - 1998/2083)
- mr president, commissioner, once again the european parliament has missed the opportunity to speak the truth on nuclear energy. once again, the debate on the safety of dangerous goods is being avoided, as if nuclear energy in europe were the preserve of experts and nuclear democrats and that debate necessarily meant passion and controversy. i tried to have this debate as first rapporteur at the public hearing on 21 january 2000, but the all-powerful nuclear lobby pulled the strings again. if mr maurice's first report was never presented in the previous parliament, the report we are debating could have been a breakthrough, but it will not be. the resolution adopted in the committee on transport, with the full support of the committee on industry, shows nothing of public concern about these highly sensitive matters of the transport of radioactive materials, whereas my initial report was perfectly in line with the changing sentiments of the european people on these matters. this theatrical move - and this is one of them - is a way of exposing the subtle game of agreements between the major political groups, manipulated by the pro-nuclear lobby. so despite the work we have done, the draft resolution presented runs counter to the original proposals and, as a member of parliament, i cannot accept that it should be included in a resolution: silence can be treated as a criminal offence. while i had managed to secure a number of compromises with colleagues who had worked on this issue and tabled amendments, on the eve of the vote in the regional committee, this work flew apart as the major groups refused to vote on our compromises. the report before you summarizes the essential questions on the transport of radioactive materials, transparency, safety and, above all, the means of reducing them. the report adopted by the chairman of the committee on transport is nothing but an ode to the nuclear industry. the influence of the nuclear lobby in the development of this amendment is shown by the identical word-for-word amendments tabled by both the conservatives and the socialists and by the lobby's thanks to the members who played the game. the transport of radioactive materials is not a matter for the nuclear industry, and we greens are wrong in our debate: let us stop the hypocrisy! while much of the radioactive waste is small packages destined for laboratories and medicine, it is not the most dangerous. the transport of radioactive waste is the most dangerous because of its radioactivity. to say otherwise is manipulation. the question of the packaging of these radioactive packages is therefore not provocative, since the whole policy of safety in the transport of radioactive materials is based on the packaging, which is guaranteed to be resistant to any attack. we know that many radioactive substances, including some of the most toxic ones, such as plutonium, are on european roads. is it a crime of lese majeste to want to remove these rolling bombs ? my report attempted to answer these questions and raised the crucial question of the origin of the transport of radioactive materials. this is where the question of the nuclear industry comes in, and particularly the question of the reprocessing of nuclear waste, since it is the reprocessing in the hague and sellafield plants that causes the most radioactive transport. without reprocessing, no more transport of radioactive waste. this is the simplest solution, and it is possible because we know that reprocessing is an economic and ecological aberration in the present state of knowledge. the latest upsurge in the transport of highly radioactive materials concerns waste from nuclear power stations fed by mox, which is being stored in the hague illegally. this means, mr president, that they were also transported illegally. it is useless to try to shorten the debate, as this report attempts to do. however, it can be improved by voting for the amendments i have just tabled.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we were not supposed to discuss the need for nuclear power, but the sworn opponents of nuclear power turned the report around. the greens do not want to understand the undeniable environmental benefits of nuclear power. what a paradox! it is clear that the greens' position on nuclear power is based on the ideology of 1968 and that they continue to refuse to have an honest debate on nuclear power. their position seems to be preconceived and not affected by the facts. the first version of the report was used as a stepping stone to oppose nuclear power. the commission's action plan, which contains many sensible initiatives, is a significant point, but it is not mentioned in the report. fortunately, the changes made to the committee have brought the matter back to the heart, rather than one-sided. the transport of radioactive materials shall comply with the rules of the international atomic energy agency. the commission has consulted a working group of experts from the member states - not politicians. the working party considers that the revised rules provide significant additional protection, although they were not considered to be inadequate in the past. the risks are kept low, and strict rules have prevented accidents for nearly half a century. this is despite the irresponsible efforts of some - but not all - opponents of nuclear power to sabotage transportation by, for example, dismantling railway tracks. the question arises as to who is responsible and who is endangering the safety of the citizens. i encourage everyone to stick to the facts. the commission's remark that the public should be informed of how good the situation is after all is therefore more than justified. nuclear power is a necessary energy solution because it promotes prosperity and cleanliness. if the french nuclear power plants were to be shut down now, there would be a rush to find candles in this hall.
- mr president, i think the general approach of mr schwaiger's report is positive. it is part of the commission's leadership's major efforts to redefine our trade policy and put trade at the service of sustainable development. that said, i have four observations to make. the first is that, while the initiation of a new round of negotiations on a broad agenda remains a good objective more than ever, the mandates given by the council cannot be said to be satisfactory as they stand. this time it is not about negotiating trade concessions in return for environmental or social clauses, but rather about negotiating trade differently so that it better respects societal models and public regulatory requirements. in this respect, the negotiations provided for in the incorporated agenda are a test, which brings me to my second point. the agricultural line is not without ambiguities. there is certainly an awareness that trade in agricultural products must be compatible with food self-sufficiency, public health and land use, but we suffer from a handicap, namely the postponement of the reform of the common agricultural policy beyond 2006. the report speaks of the survival of the model, whereas it is more a question of the need to change the model. as far as trade is concerned, while the reduction of export subsidies is essential, we say no to alignment on world prices because it is a major factor in productivity. thirdly, the services line is not ready. we are talking about gradually increased liberalization. it's a one-sided goal. the commission also says that trade policy is not an end in itself, but that it must help to support the social model. but in our social model, there are services of general interest, and in developing countries, these services of general interest are to be built. i therefore say yes to the development of trade which is compatible with the promotion of services of general interest or which promotes it. the union wants to exclude certain sectors such as education and culture from free trade. it's too little. we must work from the perspective of global public goods. it would be great if the directorate could produce a communication on the complementarity and compatibility of free trade and services of general interest. i would like to raise one last point which concerns a major problem of governance. we need to work with civil society and developing countries and compare our views. the commission's management is doing it, but the member states are not doing it and parliament is behind schedule. the responsibility for this effort lies with all of us. this is a crucial step in the successful organization of world trade.
mr president, mr schwaiger's report on the negotiations at the world trade organisation on the so-called 'incorporated agenda' raises three questions which i hope our debate will answer. firstly, is it not dangerous to negotiate separately on the embodied agenda? the negotiations on agriculture, services and certain aspects of intellectual property, which are referred to as the 'incorporated agenda', were certainly already scheduled by the uruguay round and are therefore considered to be legally unaffected by the failure of the general negotiations in seattle. they seem to be tacitly agreeing that the discussions should continue separately. but is that reasonable? because all subjects are, in fact, interdependent. the european union's previous position, it seems to me, has always been that there should be only global negotiations. shouldn't the failure of seattle lead to a rethinking of the whole negotiating process? secondly, the motion for a resolution before us calls on the commission, in paragraph 1 of the motion, to conduct the negotiations on this incorporated agenda on the basis of the guidelines given by the council before seattle. but is the situation the same ? public opinion has changed a great deal in the regulation of international trade. the failure of seattle was a first indication of this, but the trend has accelerated since then, particularly under the pressure of a few agricultural tragedies. it is true that the 1999 negotiating mandate already took into account the need for multifunctional agriculture and an agricultural policy that integrates non-commercial concerns. but at the same time it stressed the urgent need to continue on the path of trade liberalization. is it still compatible ? do we not need further reflection on this? for example, i am struck by the fact that among the new concerns to be taken into account, product safety, environmental protection, food quality, animal welfare are always mentioned, and rightly so, but never food independence. but food independence is absolutely essential. it is closely linked to all the other objectives, which are considered desirable. we have seen the opposite with the dependence on vegetable protein which was unfortunately accepted at blair house and which has led us to overuse of animal flours. in the light of these events, does it not appear that blair house should be renegotiated? thirdly, how will the future negotiations be monitored by the council and the parliaments concerned ? in some of the preliminary drafts of the treaty of nice this point was clarified, either by a new wording of article 133 or by a new protocol which stated very precisely how the council would guide the commission during the wto negotiations so that it would not deviate from the common position. but all these fine features were removed from the final version. the absence of any provisions on parliamentary control is also striking. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we believe that this is the essential condition for the interests of the citizens to be well defended.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a regulation on the organization of the market in sugar. in its explanatory memorandum the commission stresses that the cmo has duly fulfilled many of its objectives and rightly proposes a status quo, but limited to two years and accompanied by adjustments which contradict the commission's assessment in the first place. it also proposes to carry out, in record time, various in-depth studies in order to propose a thorough reform within two years. in view of this attitude, the council was right to opt for a renewal of the cmo for five years. the project is being submitted to us at a time when the agricultural sector is facing one of the most serious crises it has ever faced. but is that reason enough to reform a cmo which, in the commission's own opinion, has met its objectives? i don't think he did. that is why it seems reasonable to me to let this com operate on the present basis for a period of five years. that is the proposal your rapporteur proposes you adopt today. firstly, i would like to remind you that, in the various contacts i had during the preparation of my report, there was a fairly consistent criticism of the excessive community sugar price. in order to understand the reasons for this situation, i think it is necessary to recall that the common organization of the sugar market is an atypical organization in more than one respect. the market organization is based on a system of production quotas. this leads to strict control of the volumes produced. this self-regulation between production, import and export is complemented by the fact that the producers bear the bulk of the costs of this com. the budget of the european union shall finance only sugar exports corresponding to preferential imports granted to developing countries benefiting from the sugar protocol annexed to the cotonou convention. the cost of this com to the eu's finances is therefore particularly low in view of the importance of the sugar beet sector. it is true that this situation has a specific internal price. throughout the debate which preceded this report, various speakers did not fail to stress the artificial nature of the community price in relation to the world price. this criticism, which has been widely reported in various reports and media, also deserves some comment. first, it is necessary to weigh any reference to a world price which cannot be considered as representative of the transactions actually carried out. on the other hand, the objectivity which our parliament must show in this matter leads us to conclude that the community price has been falling steadily in real terms for the last fifteen years or so. in addition, 75 per cent of sugar is consumed as processed products. these sweet products have a price which changes independently of the price of sugar. i note, moreover, that these products are not more expensive in the european union than in other countries. second observation: several studies mention the absence of competition in the sugar sector within the european union. competition is one of the issues which will be the subject of a thorough study by the commission's departments in the next two years. i think that we must now make a statement. competition between sugar manufacturers does exist, since intracommunity trade is larger than the commission indicates. they cover more than 30% of sugar as such and 26% in the form of processed products. finally, a final comment: the consequences for the community market and for the acp countries of the decision adopted by the council 15 days ago on the initiative for the least developed countries. we have just discussed this, and this initiative is also part of the european union's intention to launch the round of multilateral negotiations, on which our parliament will be voting tomorrow. on the substance, i think that this initiative will have important consequences for the acp countries which have not been clearly assessed by the commission. this is why both the studies which the commission intends to carry out as part of a reform of the sugar cmo and the evaluation which it is to carry out in 2005 on the transitional phase of the ldc initiative are fundamental. it must take account of the concerns of the acp countries, which have traditionally been exporters to the european union. i would like to take this five-minute opportunity to make a few remarks which i thought were important before you give your opinion on the substance tomorrow. in conclusion, i would like to thank the commissioner for his contribution and hope that he will be able to elaborate a little this evening on his views on the parliament's draft, all the officials of the parliament's secretariat for the valuable help they have given in the drafting of this report, and all the colleagues who have been very active in this project. mr president, the proposal for a directive on the establishment of a european temporary protection system in the event of a massive influx of displaced persons from third countries replaces proposals for joint action on the same subject which we discussed in 1997, but which were not implemented because of the, in my view, justified reluctance of several member states. unfortunately, today's proposal, although relaxed in some respects, still has a number of important criticisms. the first is that the institution of this temporary protection is in fact the creation of a second status, parallel to that of refugee, of beneficiary of political asylum recognized by the 1951 geneva convention, but much broader than it. the beneficiaries of this new scheme would not only be those who meet the very specific criteria for political asylum, but also broad categories of third-country nationals who have had to leave their country of origin for various reasons. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the commission proposal, although limited in theory to protections of a maximum of two years, risks creating situations which will have everything to last, since the exit is not provided for otherwise than by the voluntary departure of the persons concerned. in this respect, the commission's proposal seems to us to be seriously incomplete. second major criticism: although the agreement of the states is required for the physical distribution of the protected persons - and this is an improvement on the previous version - the current text still seems to be a discharge for the member states. to avoid this inconvenience, the basic decision taken by the council to trigger the temporary protection regime should have been taken unanimously. but the commission's proposal only provides for qualified majority voting, which in our view was not legally necessary and which, in substance, seems completely inadequate in such a serious matter.
- mr. president, how do we best track all the unwanted ones? what additional barriers should be added to the schengen fortress to protect against external threats? that is the effect that certain
