mr president, i rise to speak on the initiative of the french republic on the mutual recognition of decisions to expel third-country nationals, which aims to prevent the free movement, the uncontrolled movement within the union, of foreigners who have been subject to an expulsion order. it is therefore very timely in a time of increasing pressure from illegal immigration and we regret that, as if by chance, the european parliament intends to reject it. the french initiative is aimed at establishing a kind of mutual application of certain judicial decisions, that is to say a new form of cooperation whose principle deserves more attention. when a member state has taken a decision to expel a third-country national who constitutes a threat to public policy or who is staying illegally, another member state, according to the plan, in whose territory the foreigner is staying, could execute the expulsion measure ex officio, subject, of course, to legal remedies. despite the advantages of this proposal, the committee responsible for this matter in the european parliament rejects it for two reasons which do not seem convincing to me. first, article 63 (3) (b) of the ec treaty does not constitute a relevant legal basis. this is incorrect, as this article is specifically concerned with cooperation measures for the repatriation of illegal aliens. this is the case here, since mutual recognition is indeed a measure in this category. secondly, we are told, once again, that the french initiative is too repressive and that a comprehensive european immigration policy should be put in place first. this is obviously a delaying tactic, because the authors were careful not to use the same argument when we were discussing the temporary protection of foreigners from third countries. the french republic's initiative on the mutual recognition of expulsion decisions is therefore entirely to be welcomed.
mr president, the initiative of france and sweden on cooperation between national agencies in the fields of juvenile delinquency, crime and drugs follows on from the tampere summit. this european strategy is based on the principle that union intervention necessarily adds value to the policies of the member states. but today we are faced with a patchwork of programmes and a veritable stack of measures without coherence. in the field of justice and home affairs alone, we are now being offered a sixth programme, hippocrates. it is legitimate to ask whether increasing the number of such programmes increases the effectiveness of the fight against crime, especially since these programmes have paltry budgets. what are we going to do with the million euros allocated annually to this programme? besides, hippocrates is not clear. the community budget would be limited to 70% of the total cost of the project. given that the commission's partners may be universities, administrations, ngos, how will the remaining 30% be financed? the definition of the proposed forms of prevention and of organized crime is also not very clear. there are also very anecdotal measures, such as the annual european crime prevention award in article 3. we create, we implement, without any reservations as to the relevance and effectiveness of the measures. it is time to take stock, rather than risking the burning of steps which are so necessary in building effective cooperation between national prevention policies.

in writing. - i supported the draft council directive aimed at harmonising the penalties to be imposed on carriers who bring illegal immigrants into the territory of the member states. contrary to what some speakers have claimed during the debate, this is not about making the carriers play the role of border police, since it is obvious that they do not have the means to verify the authenticity of the residence and travel documents of the people being transported. in reality, the draft law only provides for sanctions in the case of illegal immigrants who are completely undocumented, which is obviously something a carrier should not be able to ignore. in line with its usual strategy, the european parliament started by voting amendments which completely destroy the balance of the project. in particular, it exempted carriers from any sanction where the illegal traveller applies for asylum immediately after arriving in the territory of the state of destination. this derogation is not acceptable, as it is well known that the majority of asylum applications are unfounded and are only used to buy time. in the strictest sense, it would have been possible to imagine that the fines imposed on the carriers would be reimbursed if the traveller did indeed obtain asylum. but it is difficult to do more without encouraging an inflation in asylum applications for convenience. once the text had been so unbalanced, the european parliament rejected it, expressing its displeasure at the fact that the states were presenting such 'repressive' texts, using the right of initiative which they still provisionally had in this area. on the contrary, we felt that the draft council directive was worth pursuing, since the european parliament fortunately has only an advisory role in this matter.

in writing. - in a world where borders are opening up, the flow of refugees is not about to dry up. those who welcome the progress of globalisation but who wish to add a social dimension to its economic component must not forget that the movement of goods also involves the movement of people. the arrival on 19 january of a group of 910 kurdish refugees on french shores is a good example of the growing importance of organized crime in illegal immigration. but above all, this massive influx of refugees raises the question of the right to seek asylum on european soil today. it highlights the existence, within our own borders, of a genuine human trafficking which, according to some experts, now rivals that of drugs, a trafficking which can only be discouraged by establishing genuine legal access routes for immigration. the organization of legal channels of immigration in europe would help to reduce significantly the pressure on the right of asylum, which is the only one that really exists, together with family reunification for persecuted persons in their country of origin, because the right to seek asylum is, under the geneva convention (1951), a fundamental and inalienable individual right that must be strengthened and protected from any political consideration. strengthened, because refugees are not only subject to state persecution; because often it's not just individuals that are targeted, but entire families! commission - my dear colleague, the age of 23 only counts for training, because we had to set ages. fifa offered them to us. the training is scheduled between the ages of 12 and 23 and there is payment of training costs in the event of transfer until the age of 23. the training is considered to be completed from the age of 23. as regards the duration of contracts and the possibility of breaking them, we have always said from the outset that pacta sunt servanda: if adults conclude a contract, it is not to be broken but to be observed, and there are also the rules of sport. if clubs start buying players left and right during the championship, well, they're upsetting the balance of the championship. and if, during a championship, players leave their team, rightly or wrongly, it is not only a personal matter for them, but they also destabilize the team. all these sport-specific considerations have led us to provide for measures to ensure the stability of contracts. so, regardless of age, you can't get out of a contract during the league season and you can't get out of a contract outside of that season if the contract is extended, unless for very specific reasons, like an injured player or a change in the system in the team. it will be up to the court, the arbitration tribunal, to decide who is right. if, for no specific reason, you break your contract during the first two years, there are sports penalties. we tried to limit these sports sanctions as much as possible, because at the beginning, the sports authorities talked about one year, even two years, of sports sanctions, which would have completely destroyed the career of the professional player. that's why we agreed to a four-month sports ban, which can be extended to six months in the case of a repeat offender or someone who has already done this little game several times. it is therefore to ensure the stability of the teams and the championship that we have agreed to such measures, to be introduced not by the commission but by the national, european and international federations. i should also like to say that we did not want sports sanctions to be imposed only on players, because it is often clubs that sell their players for purely commercial reasons, not for sporting reasons. well, there will also be sporting sanctions against clubs, and there will be sanctions against agents who encourage players to leave their clubs at the expense of contract stability.

- mr president, the debate on the future of the union decided at the nice council must avoid a major pitfall: confining itself to the circle of specialists in european affairs, among whom i include members of the union's institutions, which risks once again locking it up in a language and topics coded for insiders and ultimately widening the gap between europe and its peoples. to renew this closed circuit a little, some federalists propose a solution of pure facade: a convention inspired by the one that has already prepared the charter of fundamental rights, composed of creatures in the majority docile and headed, for more security, by a steering group or a drafting group that would lead the debate where the institutions want it to go: towards more federalism. that would be a very dangerous method. it should be borne in mind that the previous convention produced a charter text which was unacceptable and binding on all the member states and that the differences had to be covered up by the proclamation of a non-binding text. if a future convention were to work with the same methods in a weightless state, it would produce in 2004 an ultra-federalist text unacceptable to all or some of the members. that would be disastrous for europe. but neither should there be a debate in which confusion and disorder prevail. we must both stay close to the people, keep up with them and keep orderly in order to remain productive. that is why, mr president, we believe that there is only one viable solution: to organise the debate around the national parliaments and under their responsibility.

in writing. - it is the responsibility of the european union to regulate emissions from combustion plants. the wind knows no borders and emissions from large combustion plants cross all member states and the candidate countries. the main problem is to be able to set ambitious emission limit values, which protect the health of all citizens, while knowing the possibilities of the various installations and power stations. the introduction of too high ceilings would undermine the efforts to improve the situation. i voted in favour of the amendments which would substantially improve the council's common position, but i voted against all the provisions which are considered unrealistic today. although i am in favour of reducing emissions, we must be pragmatic and not impose criteria which the industry cannot meet at the moment. the credibility of the european parliament depends on the realistic objectives which its members are called upon to vote for.
in writing. - in the commission communication to the council and parliament of 29 november 2000 on the prevention of crime in the european union, the terms 'crime', 'delinquency', 'violence' and 'inquisition' are treated as equivalent. that is extremely dangerous logic. it is no wonder that the proposal to create a european prevention network is based on the public authorities or the judiciary, but also the private sector, in conjunction with europol, olaf or the european monitoring centre for drugs ... the creation of this network for the exchange of information, which is intended to be a pilot project, with priority given to youth crime, urban crime and drug-related crime, in addition to the risk of the creation of european files, can only contribute to the criminalization of a youth already often victim of security policies carried out under the guise of combating the feeling of insecurity. and as far as prevention is concerned, no concrete proposals are made, except for the award of a european crime prevention prize! at a time when european employment policies are more often condemning young people to unemployment or precarious employment, when entire city districts are places of economic and social exclusion, a real prevention policy should be established with social workers and public services. for all these reasons, i voted against this report.
in writing. - the full resolution of the very serious cases of fraud identified in 1999 is both a test of credibility for the european commission and an efficiency test for olaf. the commission will have to convince us - and the european citizens - that it is willing to see its declarations put into effect in the fight against corruption and fraud. our group supports the request of the committee on budgetary control for greater operational independence of olaf and its director in relation to the european commission in the field of investigations. similarly, in order to be able to fulfil its monitoring task, the european parliament should have access, without particular difficulty, to olaf reports when requested. we are, however, strongly opposed to the federalist demand for the rapid appointment of a european prosecutor, as called for in mr bösch's report, even though the most seasoned supporters of a federal system acknowledge in small committees and in secret that it would be wiser to wait here for a good ten years. in the field of community fraud and legal matters, it would be preferable and much more sensible to have recourse to eurojust, an intergovernmental cooperation structure under the council, which is made up of three officials for each of the 15 member states of the union, namely: one judge, one representative of the public prosecutor's office (procureur) and one police commissioner. this option would also be much more respectful of national wishes. if we also take note of the very serious cases of fraud that were discovered in 1999 and which need to be clarified, we can only be surprised here by the "double standard" of a unilateral approach that highlights only certain cases (such as fléchard i, which attempts to destabilise certain high-ranking french officials and highlight, with a real therapeutic zeal, ireland and france, or fléchard ii, in which german, italian and belgian companies are now involved). mr president, to prevent conflicts, we must know their causes, whether they are economic interests, social rebellion, inequality, dictatorship, repression, the struggle for power or access to natural resources. conversely, the escalation of conflict in the countries of the south is hampering their development prospects. the cycle is vicious. the prevention of conflict cannot therefore be separated from a policy of sustainable development, aimed at a better distribution of wealth and the establishment of genuine democracy at world level. i hear and approve of the speeches, including those in this parliament, which advocate dialogue, the participation of civil society, access to education and health for all, the rational use of resources and regional cooperation. the structural costs of tensions must be tackled upstream. but what are these declarations worth, accompanied by paltry and shrinking budgets, when european states sell arms to warring countries or support the oil and mining industries in their over-exploitation of the wealth of the south at the expense of human rights and life. as long as development concerns do not override financial interests, as long as european states see external conflicts as a means of enriching themselves, conflict prevention will remain a pipe dream.

the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. foot and mouth disease is a terrible disease. it's enormously contagious and it's deadly. it also causes great economic damage and great suffering. it is therefore not surprising that this issue is engaging members of parliament now that an outbreak has been detected within the union for the first time in many years. on 20 february this year, outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease were reported in the united kingdom. at the meeting of the council of agriculture ministers on 26 february, the united kingdom informed the council of the situation in the country and of the measures taken to prevent the spread of the infection. as is well known in this field, the council has left it to the commission to decide, after consulting veterinarians from the member states, on measures which are normally implemented by the member states. the commission has accordingly adopted a decision introducing certain protection measures to prevent the spread of the disease. the decision prohibits the export from the united kingdom of live animals, of species susceptible to foot-and-mouth disease and of milk, meat and other animal products derived from these species. on 6 march this year, the commission took further decisions to ban all transport of animals of species susceptible to foot-and-mouth disease throughout the union and to ban markets and assembly places for animals of species susceptible to the disease throughout the union. derogations from this decision are granted for transport directly to a slaughterhouse. at an extraordinary meeting yesterday, the standing veterinary committee was informed that an outbreak had also been detected in northwestern france. measures similar to those previously introduced in the united kingdom have now been introduced there. the question will of course be taken up at the next meeting of the council of agriculture ministers early next week. the eu veterinary committee will hold its next meeting on 20 march, when the situation in the uk and france and possible further action will be discussed again. the council regrets the situation in the united kingdom and france and is closely monitoring developments in close contact with the commission, while member states are taking various preventive measures. the council has full confidence in the measures taken in the united kingdom and france and in the way these two countries have dealt with the problems. an outbreak of such a contagious and serious disease as foot-and-mouth disease is always extremely painful for all who are affected. however, it is particularly difficult when the outbreak affects an already severely tested professional group, consisting of breeders, milk and meat producers and, to a large extent, small farmers.
commission. – mr president, i am glad of this opportunity to up-date parliament on the latest developments in the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in the united kingdom and now also in france. you will recall that the first outbreak in the uk was confirmed in the evening of 20 february. the commission adopted a safeguard decision the following day, 21 february. this measure imposed a ban on the export of certain live animals – cattle, sheep and goats – from the uk and restrictions on the export of meat, meat products, milk and milk products and certain animal products. since then further measures have been introduced to ban movements of livestock throughout the european union. this measure is precautionary and aimed at reducing any potential for the spread of the disease to a minimum. it must also be viewed in the context of the continued increase in cases in the united kingdom. any expectation that the crisis would end quickly have been disappointed. clearly we need to be very concerned at the progress of the outbreak. three factors in particular are disturbing. first, the continuing uncertainty over whether the incidence in the uk will peak, second, the discovery of a case in france which ends our hopes that the outbreak might be confined to the uk and third, the restrictions imposed by third countries, on imports of community products, many totally unjustified. i would now like to look at each of these three concerns, beginning with the incidence in the uk. it is clearly disappointing that expectations that the incidence of the disease would shortly peak have not been realised. the veterinary experts remain of the view that the restrictions on animal movements will, in time, limit the potential spread of the disease. this highlights the continued need for vigilance in the uk and for the strictest possible implementation of the measures already in place. since the initial decision to ban exports of certain meat and meat products, dairy products and so on, there has been a ban on movements of livestock both in the uk and in other member states. while these restrictions are naturally unpopular, they are a small price to pay compared to the consequences of not quickly eradicating this disease. i would hope that this greater good is not lost sight of in the present crisis. so, turning to france, i am sure that everybody shares the commission's concern at the discovery of the first case of the disease on the european mainland. as you are no doubt aware, a case of foot-and-mouth disease was confirmed yesterday in north-west france in the mayenne region. it was detected in a cattle farm under restrictions imposed preventatively more than a week prior to the confirmation of the outbreak. the cattle farm is next to a farm to which incubating sheep had been imported from the united kingdom on 16 february, a few days before the uk outbreak was known about. the sheep from the uk had been destroyed on 1 march as a preventive measure in accordance with the relevant commission decision. the slaughter and destruction of all 114 cattle in the outbreak confirmed yesterday started yesterday evening and this operation is still on-going. this discovery dashes our hopes that the disease could be confined to the uk. however, we can take considerable comfort from the very decisive action taken by the french authorities to isolate and destroy livestock potentially exposed to contaminated animals imported from the uk. the early action to restrict movements of livestock in france should also have reduced the potential spread of the disease. these measures, wrongly viewed as excessive by some, have proved to be very prudent. nonetheless, there is a risk of further outbreaks and the situation will have to be very closely monitored. the standing veterinary committee took the decision late yesterday evening to ban exports of susceptible animals from france and also to impose restrictions on the movement of animals and certain products from the mayenne department and the adjoining department of orne. clearly, any further outbreaks would require additional restrictions on the regions concerned, but the prompt action taken by the french authorities will hopefully ensure that there will be no need for more draconian measures. turning to third countries. the commission is deeply disappointed that the very decisive action taken to tackle the current outbreak has not received the recognition it deserves. instead of being reassured by this action, third countries have, in many cases, responded with both excessive and, in my view, unnecessary restrictions. the commission is consulting urgently with the third countries concerned to establish the basis and rationale for the restrictions. we shall, of course, be explaining the measures already in place, which make such restrictions unnecessary, and we shall make full use of our bilateral contacts and our wto trade arrangements to have these restrictions lifted. i have already been in contact with the us secretary of agriculture this afternoon regarding the measures imposed by the united states. i was reassured by the secretary that these measures will be reviewed urgently. we have agreed that our respective veterinary services should cooperate urgently on finding solutions. we agreed to remain in close contact until a solution is found and i am convinced of her goodwill in that regard. as an example of the approach followed by the commission, i would point to the community approach towards argentina. beef imports have been permitted from argentina despite its regional problems with foot-and-mouth disease. this was, of course, subject to very strict controls. the beef had to be from bse-free regions, deboned and matured, to eliminate the risk of transmission of the disease. it was only following the further recent outbreaks, the introduction of vaccination and the self-imposed ban on exports to the united states and canada that the commission felt compelled to ban imports of beef from argentina. the commission remains nonetheless committed to a regionalisation approach in which exports can be allowed to resume in safe conditions. on a more general level, i would once more like to defend the firm action taken by the commission in dealing with the current outbreak. it is an essential and very necessary reaction to a highly infectious disease, with potentially huge economic and trade consequences for the entire european union. this approach continues to enjoy the strong support of the member states in the standing veterinary committee and in the agriculture council. i firmly believe that the veterinary authorities, the member states and the commission have been working together very closely and effectively. the approach is also supported by eu farmers, who are very conscious of the grave threat to their livelihood from this disease. there is still a consensus that vaccination should be a last resort, to be introduced only in the circumstances i outlined before, namely as a preventive step to stop the further spread of the disease pending eradication measures. i would like to conclude in writing. - the report we are discussing today concerns the role of the member states and the european union in the icann system. it should be noted that icann (internet corporation for assigned names and numbers) was created in october 1998 in order to counter the us hegemony in the management of the internet, including dns (domain name systems) and the allocation of internet protocol address spaces. icann is governed by a 19-member board of directors whose directors and external members are selected on the basis of geographical balance. icann also has four advisory committees, including the gac (governments committee), in which the european commission and the member states participate. in view of these factors, it is clear that the european union must take steps to play a leading role in the international management of the internet and to strengthen the neutrality of icann through a strong presence of the european union, in collaboration with the united states and other governments, through the advisory committee of governments. it is also important that the icann board be geographically representative. its representatives should be elected and africa must now be part of it so that all continents are represented. i would stress that the governance structure and the legal framework in which icann operates must be based on transparency, neutrality and independence. this implies that the budgetary and financing system of this organisation is based on criteria of clarity. only then can icann be assured of its viability. the union should ensure that icann respects the protocols of wipo (world intellectual property organization) and cooperates with it in its role as negotiator and protector of rights. i welcome the rapporteur's reminder of the importance of tackling the digital divide and of providing the widest possible access to the internet. when we talk about the development of new telecommunications networks, we cannot ignore this essential objective!
in writing. - the resolution which the european parliament has just adopted, following the purvis report on the future of the biotechnology sector, seems to us to be too lenient, and often even regional, international or global level. addressing the issue of affordability of medicines should never exclude the focus on prevention efforts, nor negatively affect the debate on research and development. all these areas are complementary and we will continue to address them in a complementary, comprehensive manner, not allowing one to be played off against the other. we strongly support the international commitment to tier pricing as the most efficient way in the short term to increase affordability of medicines. the community will support, through its technical and development assistance programmes, the reinforcement of pharmaceutical policies and global production capacities in developing countries as a medium-term means of increasing affordability. we would insist on keeping the debate on a broader level, including targeted action in favour of those millions who suffer and die from malaria and tuberculosis, and who, like those infected by hiv or living with aids, simply cannot afford to pay for medicines. as you know, treatment for malaria and tuberculosis – however problematic – exists. it costs between usd 10 to 25 to treat a malaria patient and usd 11 to treat a patient suffering from tuberculosis. hiv/aids involves medicines which are priced way above the potential of the poorest and most vulnerable. finally, i would urge parliament not to lose sight of the need for the development of an aids and malaria vaccine. the crisis will continue to prevail and become even worse if prevention efforts are not sustained. it will take some time before vaccines are developed and available. however, we are on the right track and we urgently need to make progress.

- mr president, commissioner, 6,000 years of human history, 10,000 wars, and mankind has always encouraged the production of weapons. a certain consciousness seems to be emerging in humanity. biological weapons were banned in 1972, chemical weapons in 1993, and land mines in 1997. nuclear proliferation is relatively under control, even though we have been in a bad phase since the nuclear non-proliferation treaty was signed in 1968 and came into force in 1970. but in today's world, the weapons that kill the most are small arms. an estimated half a billion of them are scattered over the face of the planet. they kill 200,000 people a year - 20 times as many as land mines - and more than half of the victims are in africa. it is therefore no mystery that the secretary-general of the united nations, who is now a great african, has put on the agenda of the united nations general assembly, which will meet in new york in july, the discussion of a convention to try to limit this dangerous and terrible flow. the idea would be to identify weapons, to enable them to be tracked and kept on record, to encourage all states to tighten controls and their internal legislation on exports and re-exports, to organise the prosecution and punishment of trafficking brokers and, finally, to finance and promote national programmes for the collection and destruction of weapons. with such a project, the european union, which three years ago adopted a moratorium on arms sales at the suggestion of the united kingdom, would be proud to have an effective common policy and to play its full part. i would like to welcome the fact that six political groups were able to table a motion for a resolution which is an excellent compromise and which is well received. i will say no more, it must be supported, it is entirely in line with our code of conduct, in good relation to what has already been decided within the organization for security and cooperation (osce) and entirely in line with the prospects of the next united nations convention. i shall ask for two oral amendments, mr president, which i know are generally accepted. the first in the recitals, i will say the place at that time, to add a visa to the declaration - willingness to move forward alongside parliament. the commission has the political initiative, but we are asking it today to use it and formally submit a proposal to amend regulation 1408/71 to add a simple paragraph on the situation of assistants. the council must then take its responsibilities, whether or not to keep our assistants and ourselves in a situation of legal and social insecurity. - mr president, the amendment to the cosmetics directive has given rise to a lively debate on the question of animal testing. the text seems to have abandoned the idea of banning the marketing of new cosmetics tested on animals. it prefers to limit itself to a ban on animal testing of cosmetics within the european union. of course, no one is in favor of animal experimentation. however, in this case, realism and consistency are required. animal testing represents only a very small part of cosmetic testing and is, moreover, destined to disappear within ten years, thanks to the research undertaken by laboratories to replace it with new forms of experimentation. but as things stand, there are no sufficiently reliable alternative methods. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of animals used for experimental purposes is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. is there not at least an unfortunate collision on our agenda? in addition, the immediate ban on animal testing could lead laboratories to conduct their experiments on humans, who are forced by poverty to accept anything to survive. then it won't be pictures of red-eyed rabbits that you can pity, but pictures of third world women disfigured by allergies. as usual, it is the poorest who will suffer from our legislative whims. the question is not whether we are for animal welfare or not, but whether animal welfare is more important than the welfare of the poor. finally, if we impede the activities of our industries too much, they will move their activities outside the european union in order to face foreign competition, and in particular american competition, since animal testing will not be banned there. thousands of workers are at risk of losing their jobs? yes, and again, it's the more modest who will pay the bill! is this, ladies and gentlemen, the social europe you are so eagerly awaiting?
commission. – mr president, on behalf of the commission i would like to thank mrs roth-behrendt and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy for their support and also for the discussion today. the commission is well aware that the debate on animal testing is a very difficult and sensitive one. it has raised, and is raising, a great deal of concern among the public as many of you have mentioned here today. the issue is linked to many policy areas, all of which have to be taken into account including public health, consumer protection as well as the need for us to comply with our international obligations. i have therefore worked in constant and close cooperation with my colleagues david byrne and pascal lamy, responsible for health and consumer protection and trade issues respectively. i would like to congratulate mrs roth-behrendt and the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy for the many suggestions made in their report which aim to improve health and consumer protection not least by providing consumers with more relevant information. the commission welcomes, in particular, your proposal for amendments relating to some categories of products such as products for children and intimate hygiene products. you propose the improvement of safety requirements of these products as well as the extension of the requirement of requirements allowing consumers who are sensitive to certain ingredients to avoid products which contain them. on the issue of animal testing, the commission understands and shares the objective of highest possible level of safety in all products which they use. this proposal has the advantage of achieving these objectives by providing legally and practically enforceable measures without giving rise to possible trade disputes. by contrast, a marketing ban would give rise to serious difficulties according to the commission's trade and legal experts. it would have a significant impact on trade community is bound to ensure compliance with its international obligations. such a unilateral measure would run contrary to the eu's current policy in the wto to seek the inclusion of animal welfare issues in the discussions for the next round. only a coordinated approach at international level can improve animal welfare on a wider scale. in the meantime, the commission will continue its efforts to bring about the elimination of animal testing both at home and internationally. i am convinced that further work in close cooperation in this very difficult and sensitive issue will finally lead to a balanced solution offering genuine benefits to animal welfare while safeguarding consumer health. the commission can, in principle, accept amendments nos 1 (first part), 2, 4, 5, 7 (second part), 9, in writing. - the reports on the first guidelines for the 2002 budget of the european institutions appear to us to be incomplete or obscure on three key points. agriculture and rural development the mad cow crisis will lead to new and heavy agricultural expenditure, even though the financial perspective adopted in 1999 is not, quite rightly, intended to be revised. how can we reconcile these two requirements? according to the reports, we should try to find the money by means of internal restructuring of heading 1 (agriculture), which seems impossible to us in view of the commitments made. we want, as we have already said in our recent debate on the revision of the 2001 budget, that a wider contribution from heading 2 (structural actions) be considered. the enlargement. the budgetary guidelines for 2002 appear to be too discreet on the cost of enlargement. the consequences for agriculture or the structural funds are not yet determined, but will come in due course. the financial implications for the functioning of the european institutions, on the other hand, must be assessed today. they should be part of a multiannual plan for capacity building, which would start in 2002. the treaty of nice. political announcements are made here and there that the treaty of nice should be ratified by all by the end of 2001. the protocol on the ecsc, as annexed to the treaty, is due to apply in july 2002. we are sceptical about the timetable, but since this commitment seems to have been made, at least an estimate of the cost of the new provisions of the treaty should be included in the budgetary guidelines for 2002. but we don't see them. however, the expenditure involved will not be negligible, whether it concerns (amongst others) the unified statute of the european parliament, the financing of the so-called 'european political parties' from the community budget, or the administrative expenditure related to the rapid action force, under article 28-2 of the eu treaty, from the same budget. as usual, we will have to get the member states to ratify the new provisions, the cost of which we are careful not to disclose.
in writing. - we voted against the budgetary guidelines proposed in this report and in subsequent reports. it is a budget entirely geared to satisfying financial groups, industrial and agricultural lobbies and, incidentally, to financing the foreign policy that european big business considers useful to its interests. each of the member states is reducing the redistributive part of its budget by sacrificing public services, hospitals, education, transport and drastically reducing social spending to serve as a profit-pump for large companies. the european union budget, under the guise of subsidiarity, pushes this trend even further by reducing social spending to insignificance. this is one of the expressions of its refusal to work towards the equalization of social protection and benefits and wages throughout the union from above. since the financing of the states and that of the union are intimately linked, we reiterate our opposition to all forms of budgetary revenue which mainly affect the working classes, such as taxes on consumption (vat, etc.), and to all expenditure in favour of large enterprises and the rich class (grants, subsidies, tax gifts).
in writing. - during the discussion on the budgetary guidelines for 2002, we heard some welcoming the low cost to the european budget of operations to introduce the single currency. this seems to us to be a somewhat cynical remark, because a relatively high burden will be borne by small traders, who will derive little benefit from it and who will not be helped by anyone. many other small businesses are in the same situation. on the contrary, large companies operating at european level will benefit, directly or indirectly, from the changeover to the euro and thus be able to absorb the costs of reorganisation and the investments it entails. but how will the others do? this particular aspect - but there are many others along the same lines - shows how this operation was designed from the outset to solve some of the big problems, but not the small ones. this is why we believe it is urgent that the union - or the member states by delegation - should provide direct financial assistance, at least to small traders. it is not right that the states and the european institutions take costly decisions and then burden others with the burden. finally, the physical changeover to the euro, in the form of coins and banknotes, risks being hampered by those who decided it.

that of a financial year - confined within a specific scope. we can grant discharge, we can postpone it, we can never refuse it definitively, or else the chain of balances would have to be interrupted. finally, discharge is not intended to replicate the act of authorizing the budget. it is not an act of expediency, but an act which sanctions irregularity and which may sanction the lack of management excellence. it is a framework that we must stick to if we are to avoid the repetition of psychodramas. i am personally very pleased about all this. i would like to make three observations on what has happened to us this year. firstly, i see that there is a serious problem, namely the imbalance between the responsibilities of the commission and those of the member states in relation to discharge. 80% of the appropriations remain to be spent by the member states and we give the commission discharge. i think that is why we have difficulty in demanding, with sufficient efficiency, the improvement of a positive declaration of assurance. we're punishing someone who's only partially responsible for what's happening to him. i would like to see the eurosceptics here and there accept, before they punish the commission, more extensive controls at home on how expenditure is implemented in the member states. the second observation - - mr president, mr commissioner, the matter of foot-and-mouth disease, which concerns us, comes at the right time. it comes at the right time for opening up to the east and at the right time for the wto negotiations. firstly, opening up to the east, because of course we have to reduce our agricultural expenditure because the annual agricultural budgetary cake will have to be cut into 21 shares instead of 15 and, therefore, everyone's share will be reduced, unless we reduce the number of farmers. the wto negotiations are next, since we must make room on our market for products from the southern hemisphere, for products from the cairns group - we have already done so for wine, for fruit and vegetables - but there are also new zealand and australia, which happen to be sheep producers! how, then, can we reduce agricultural expenditure in western europe and at the same time make room for products from the south on our market? simply by reducing the number of our farmers and the number of heads in our herds! how do we reduce our farmers and our livestock? simply by making a common case of foot and mouth disease, amplified by the media operation apocalypse now, by making a spectacle, with logs, scavengers, mechanical shovels, bulldozers, sanitary cords, military men, mountains of burning sheep, cattle, pigs. for months, fao has been warning about foot-and-mouth disease in anatolia, korea, japan, even south africa, greece last year. the world's flashing lights are red, and the european union is not moving! foot-and-mouth disease is coming, and it's coming, as if by accident, to britain, where the largest herd in europe is. we should vaccinate. what are we gonna do? - mr president, commissioner, on the occasion of this debate on foot-and-mouth disease, i would first of all like to express my deep solidarity with all the actors in the livestock sector, who are already severely affected by the bse crisis which has upset the markets, and in particular with all the cattle farmers who, for the vast majority of them, work well, with rigor, according to practices which respect both the environment and the animals they rear, and who are now being hit hard by this new crisis which is plunging them into disarray. i would like to draw a clear distinction between, on the one hand, the measures to be taken as a matter of urgency to deal with the current epidemic in a situation which is very difficult to control because vaccination has been suspended in the union since 1991, and, on the other hand, the measures to be taken subsequently, once the current epidemic has been brought under control, to prevent such a catastrophe from happening again. what will it take ? first, we must begin by thinking deeply about the changes in livestock farming which have made such epidemics possible. we have to be very careful not to allow the european parliament to be the one to decide on the future of the community. we have been right to push for an extreme concentration of slaughterhouses which, by causing the closure of nearby slaughterhouses, has encouraged the concentration of farms and systematised the transport of animals over long distances. the international rules imposed by the international office for diseases of animals, which, as they stand, seem absurd and outdated, must then be scrapped. at present, a live animal vaccinated against foot-and-mouth disease in the territory of a country deprives that country of its status as a foot-and-mouth disease-free country and therefore prohibits its export. who can see that this arbitrary rule is outrageously in favor of the united states? bilateral trade transactions will also have to be dealt with, each country being free to negotiate with russia, japan or others the terms on which exports can be made. we will also have to regionalise. there is no reason why any member state, let alone the european union as a whole, should be regarded as a homogeneous whole in this area. there is no reason why a case of foot-and-mouth disease in brittany should affect alsace, nor why a country with a thousand outbreaks like britain and a country with two like france should be subjected to the same treatment. the commission has also been asked to make a statement on the situation in the community. should not at least the vaccination of rare animals, breeding animals and, why not, dairy herds be allowed? to achieve this, it is essential to encourage research and development on vaccine markers which can distinguish a vaccinated animal from an infected animal. finally, the necessary means must be found to encourage holdings, and in particular small and medium-sized holdings, which give birth and fatten on the same site and thus reduce the risks of spreading the disease, since the integration of birth, rearing and finishing on the same holding is an essential factor in prevention. this role must be fully recognised in the framework of the common policy. first, mainstreaming and rights to difference, the second, family and disability, since the disabled person, whether an infant or an elderly person, is always someone's child or relative and it is in guidelines that we have formulated a number of proposals. the first is, of course, the implementation of the year 2003, which must be the european year of disabled people, as was said in nice. commission. – mr president, may i thank you once again for giving me the floor to reply to some of the comments made by members. mr von wogau said, if i understood him correctly, that the communication which has been referred to by members of parliament, and which i myself mentioned, is a source of law. i cannot see it that way. the source of law is the treaty. the treaty is clear. the commission is the guardian of the treaty and universally recognised as such. it issued the communication in 1997 in order to clear up certain misunderstandings in connection with the relevant articles of the treaty. it did not do so without reason. i shall refer to two particular instances. firstly in 1991 the united kingdom tried to use golden shares to oppose the acquisition of certain british companies which had been privatised by public entities, public companies, of other member states. at the time, in 1991, this was known as the "lilley doctrine". the commission took energetic action. the united kingdom changed its policy. the second instance is a more recent one. at international level my colleague, mr lamy, had to oppose an analogous american initiative which was taken against certain public european companies in the telecom area. so in both these instances one sees that the commission has taken action against the attempts, whether by a member state, or in the case of the united states by a third country, to block investments by companies, whether private or public from other member states, in privatised companies of the home state. to return to the main point at issue, the commission has done no more than interpret the relevant articles of the treaty – basically articles 56 and 43. that is what is laid down in the interpretative communication. so it cannot be said, as mr katiforis said earlier tonight, that the commission is constructing its own framework of rules. once again and for the last time, i will say that the commission has been entrusted with the duty to act as guardian of the treaty. in the years running up to 1997 there was uncertainty about the way articles 43 and 56 ought to be interpreted. that is the reason for the interpretative communication. the final instance that decides on what is right or wrong, what is legal and illegal, is the court of justice. naturally the commission does not, in the end, decide what the legal situation is. that is the responsibility of the court of justice. but before the matter can be considered by the court of justice somebody has to bring the case to the attention of the court. that is what the commission has done. this commissioner has played a certain role in this and has taken a number of member states to court for making use of the golden share. so i must reject the reproach made against the commission that it has arrogated unto itself certain competences that it should not have, that it is framing its own system of rules. no, the commission is merely interpreting and stating what the law is. that is the reason why it has taken some member states to court. hopefully we will soon see what the court of justice has to say. i was asked if i would issue a directive. there is no need for a directive. we have a treaty. the commission interprets the treaty and the court of justice decides. so we do not need a directive. having said all that, the commission is due to have a debate on this whole issue shortly. after that has taken place perhaps i can further inform parliament, but at this moment i see no reason to change the opinion that i have just given.

mr president, what is the situation regarding aid to developing countries, particularly those which are called less developed? this has been noted in the past. the mandate of the third united nations conference covers, in particular, official development assistance, debt and trade. in this context, we must not ignore the fact that the commitments made in the previous decade have not been fulfilled. it has often been said, but it must be repeated, that the decline in official development aid flows is unacceptable. they have thus declined by almost half over the decade to just 0.05% of donor gnp, well short of the un target of 0.7%. in europe, only the nordic countries are meeting this commitment. in addition, the share of this official development assistance devoted to economic infrastructure and the production sector has decreased. what future for these countries if they cannot reach a level of development that allows them to make truly independent choices? the reasons for the results obtained are not to be sought further. the mere mention of the drop in life expectancy to 51 years gives the scale of the disaster. behind the reports of experts are men and women who live in extreme poverty: 614 million people, one tenth of the world's population, live on less than $2 a day. worse still, the least developed countries are sinking into a vicious cycle of economic decline, social tensions, and violence that reinforce each other, as unctad notes. thus, the share of manufacturing in their gdp has not increased, and in some cases has even decreased. ldcs often remain dependent on the export of only one or two commodities. however, production capacity has been reduced in some countries. the preparatory committee for the third conference even notes that, in many cases, the industries created to supply the internal market have been eliminated by the increasingly fierce competition from imports which accompanies trade liberalization. the third united nations conference must not be another big event and i believe that the european union, as the host of the summit in a way, should help to ensure that this does not happen. europe's political authority is gained in its ability to cope with a globalist economy that is devouring everything, and which is governed only by the laws of trade and money. the effectiveness of its development policy is measured by concrete actions and there are avenues which urgently need to be explored: debt cancellation; the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: contribute to the decisive development of human capacities through effective public training services; the commission has also proposed that the i believe that development is not just about organising trade relations... at check-in is an important one for airlines. by notifying the passenger, the passenger secures a higher level of compensation than the normal one. we must avoid excessive bureaucracy. i think the airlines' requirement for pre-flight notification is reasonable. the clarity of the regulation is limited by the fact that the clauses of the montreal convention to which it refers are not found in the regulation. the simplicity of legislation should be the starting point, and that is not quite possible at the moment. the regulation is, however, a leap forward in substance and it is to be welcomed that the outdated warsaw pact is being abandoned. but even modern law cannot guarantee the success of a busy traveler's day. you know what i mean: breakfast in rome, lunch in paris, dinner in helsinki, luggage in moscow.
mr president, in the context of the british rail accidents which have shown the price paid by society to satisfy the profit-hunger of railway companies, the european institutions are considering authorizing the states to grant aid to improve infrastructure. the european union, which claims to oppose national state aids which might distort competition within europe, is preparing in the proposed report to rely on its own proposals in order to continue the policy of privatising public services. thus railway companies, which have received the revenue from the lines granted to them without bothering to make the minimum expenditure to maintain and renew the railway equipment, are not only absolved but will be entitled to receive additional subsidies to meet the investment obligations which should be theirs. we reiterate our opposition to the privatisation of public services and to the introduction of any idea of profitability for services essential to the whole population. the management of the railways in accordance with the law of private profit is as disastrous for the economy as a whole as it is for the railway sector.
the rapporteur. - mr president, it is urgently necessary, in order to enable a harvest to be made after 15 august 2001 and in the difficult conditions of the bse crisis, that you, commissioner, have proposed an amendment to the council regulation establishing a support scheme for producers of certain arable crops. this measure, which is one of your seven emergency points, would allow the re-cultivation of certain land that is currently fallow - for plants such as clover. the decision to amend the regulation as a matter of urgency should be seen by farmers as a sign of hope. europe does not abandon them and does not want to make them bear the brunt of a situation in which they are very often the victims. urgency or not, this decision is in line with the white paper on food safety, which included in its proposals the integration of problems linked to the production of animal feed. the proposal also addresses the problem of the production of vegetable proteins, which are necessary for the proper feeding of cattle. this production is in deficit in europe, partly as a result of the blair house agreements. the programmed freezing of land has led to the abandonment of arable land even as livestock were fed animal protein, some of it derived from the meal of dead bodies. in order to restore a healthier diet for the whole herd, as if to get out of the mad cow crisis, a change in the freezing regime of land which can be used for fodder crops seems to be essential. your proposal, commissioner, is certainly in the right direction, but it is a marginal amendment to the whole of the regulation you are proposing. it is merely symbolic, but we as parliamentarians can go further and give it a starting point for reflection leading to a revision of agenda 2000 in the long term. the spirit of the proposed measures is, firstly, to move from freezing land to a measure to expand the areas planted with solely organic farming. the effect of such a measure would be to revalue some of the frozen land by means of crops such as: beans, feverfew, lentils, chickpeas, lupine, vesces, alfalfa, fenugreek, mellilot, clover, white clover, and i forget. this would have a positive effect in reviving a more natural breeding because it is linked to the production of fodder. the effect would also be beneficial for the environment, since we now know that in this area, the jackfruit tree is often harmful. instead of encouraging the cultivation of protein and oilseeds as mass products and encouraging grazing via surface or quantity premiums, this treatment will allow the partial lifting of the land freeze in favour of fodder legumes, which are not suitable for human consumption. it is in the direction of a reorientation of the cap towards quality and extensiveness, which we all want. the question is whether this reorientation should be limited to a boost to organic farming alone, based on ec regulation no 2092/1991, or whether it is possible to go further. in the latter case, conventional agriculture must eventually be allowed to benefit from the same possibilities, if it agrees to limit itself to planting only fodder crops on its frozen land. the compulsory complementarity of cereal crops with leguminous and fodder crops for the purpose of obtaining subsidies can thus contribute to the establishment of ecological sites and contribute to soil improvement. this commitment, linked to a logic of good agricultural practice, would make it possible to restore a good crop rotation, as is the case in organic farming. however, if we limit ourselves to lifting the freeze on land for this organic farming alone, we are only taking cosmetic action. the commission has made this proposal too restrictive by proposing that jackfruit be returned to the jackfruit crop. it is not out of admiration for organic farmers but because it does not want to corner the wto agreements by taking a measure favourable to all farmers in the european union. however, in view of the food security crisis, under the terms of the wto agreements, a change in the rules by the states does not constitute a breach of its agreements, as the economic and social committee points out. moreover, if it is a question of the health of consumers and the survival of farmers, we must have the courage to review these famous agreements. mr bush, jr., is not so much a man about the kyoto protocol on climate change! the main thing today is to take a first decision quickly, so that farmers can start sowing this year. it would have been better if all conventional farming could have planted protein crops by 15 august 2001, but the commission does not accept this. the committee on agriculture and rural development as a whole has therefore proposed a compromise for you, commissioner, for the year 2001: it does not only concern organic farming, but also any farm which is implementing an agri-environmental programme. the measure could then be extended to the conventional sector from 2002. this one-off proposal should be only a first step towards a more comprehensive reform of the common agricultural policy.
mr president, in view of the extremely minimalist nature of the draft regulation, the merit of mrs auroi's report is that it actually opens up a way of starting, albeit in a very modest way, to reduce our enormous deficit in oilseed proteins. while most farms are mixed, the commission proposes to limit the possibility of growing fodder legumes on less than 10% of their pdo to 100% organic farms alone, i.e. just 2% of the cultivated area in the union. mrs auroi proposes to extend this possibility to conventional farms, particularly livestock farms, and she is right. but even with this revision, the proposal is clearly not up to the task we have to solve. our oil-protein deficit, which has increased considerably as a result of the blair house constraints, was over 35 million tonnes even before the ban on animal meal for monogastric animals. we must now add an additional 300 000 tonnes of imports per month. only an ambitious protein plan will raise the bar and meet the demand for traceability from our consumers. in this respect, i am appalled by the spirit of renunciation shown by the commission in its communication of 16 march, where short-sighted free trade is substituted for policy. i shall come back to that in the debate tomorrow.

(applause) i would like to thank
president of the federal republic of germany. the commission has already made a number of proposals. i thank you very much, madam president, for inviting me to speak to this house today about my thoughts on the future shape of europe. europe is becoming more and more concrete, more and more tangible to its citizens, because it is affecting them more and more directly. in 271 days, citizens in 12 european countries will have a single currency in their wallets. we travel freely in europe, from the north cape to gibraltar. but do we feel european at all? i feel as a great european journalist, the italian luigi barzini, once said, "... that despite the undeniable great diversity and difference, we are all basically people of one kind"... we have a rich store of common traditions, as winston churchill pointed out in his famous speech in zurich in september 1946. for him, the common european heritage consisted of christian faith and christian ethics, culture, the arts, philosophy and science, from antiquity to modern times. we all know of recent examples of the existence of common european interests. does not globalisation, at the latest, force us europeans to realise that the diversity of our cultural wealth is not a toy or a victim of the global standardization by global media powers, that the challenge to our values posed by fundamentalists and ethnic cleansing in europe requires a common response from us, that the market must not be unfettered but must be socially and ecologically constrained? we are witnessing today the attraction of the european union to many countries. there are certainly practical reasons for this, and it is true that the european union is increasing the benefits of all its members. but it is more than just a community of interest. europe is a certain idea of human existence, of people living together. that is why we are constantly striving to balance the freedom of the individual with his responsibility to society and the community. the greatest visionaries of the 1950s could not have dreamed of the concrete shape european unification would take, how many fields it would cover. the success of joint action should encourage us to set ourselves new goals. but we must be critical of ourselves and say that, in addition to the broad support of many citizens, there is also scepticism, distrust and even rejection of the european project. it is important to me that the doubts and criticisms are not so much directed against individual steps and their effects. most people are aware of the importance of living together in peace after centuries of conflict, of the extent to which we have succeeded in increasing our prosperity together, of the advantages that the single market offers our businesses, of the extent to which we can do research better in european cooperation, of the progress that is being made in being able to settle in other european countries without major difficulties, and of the fact that more and more qualifications are being recognised throughout europe. the concerns of the people of europe are about the question of how the difficult unification process is organized and how little influence they seem to have on it. many citizens rightly ask: who is actually driving the train of european unification? what are the speed limits on this train? what traffic rules? how and where are the lines drawn? which cars are to be coupled or disconnected? so, where's the trip going? these are not academic questions. these are the questions that the sovereign, the people, are asking in all the countries of europe. there can be no doubt that the sovereign in each of our european democracies, the people, is the one who has the right to decide all these questions. i sometimes hear that a democratic process in the traditional sense is not possible in europe because there is no unified european nation state. the european parliament has been a key player in the process of european integration, and it has been a key player in the process of european integration. but that should not prevent us from strengthening the principles of democracy at european level. (applause from the centre) democracy, properly understood, is nothing else than the creation of common rules and procedures by people who want to act together for a specific purpose. it is not at all contradictory that these people have very different interests and that they want to preserve these differences. that is what europe is all about. we want to pursue certain objectives and interests together, while preserving the diversity of european countries and nations, which is the basis and enriching characteristic of the european union. that is not going to change and should not change in the future. we must therefore answer the questions: how can we organise the european union in such a way that citizens feel more at home in it? what must we do to ensure that the decisions of the european union are given greater legitimacy at european level? what is the organizational framework? the answer to that, i am convinced, can only be that we need a european constitution. (applause from the centre) the european constitution is not the cornerstone of the european edifice, it must become its foundation. the european constitution should stipulate that europe is not becoming a centralised superstate but that we are building a 'federation of nation states'. i am aware that the terms 'constitution' and 'federation' may seem suspicious to some in europe. but is it not often just a matter of terminology? i am confident that we will be able to agree more easily on the substance of what is meant than on these terms. but then we have to discuss content, not debate terms. (applause from the centre) the european constitution must be the result of a broad debate in all countries. there are sceptical and critical voices in the debate. there are many serious objections which i take seriously, even where i myself disagree. i would like to speak to some of them today and explain to you how i see a european constitution and the way to achieve it. every further step in the process of unification, says a common argument against a constitution, is another step towards a european 'superstate' and the abolition of the nation-states. but those who, like me, are in favour of a federation of nation states want the opposite! if we want the european union to be a federation of nation states, we must improve the democratic legitimacy of joint action and at the same time guarantee the national states the powers they want and should retain. the new powers can only be transferred to europe if all the members of the federation agree to it in a transparent and democratically controlled procedure. preserving what has been, preventing what is undesirable and remaining open to new ideas - this is the basis of a constitution for a federation of nation states. that's what i'd like to talk to you about. no one wants to abolish the nation states and their sovereignty. on the contrary, we will need them for a long time to come, in all their diversity, as the guarantors of europe's diversity. the european parliament has been asked to give its opinion on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. but if you look closely, you will see that the idea of federation is supported for quite different reasons. the state systems of our european countries have grown historically, or, to put it another way: they are different but equal democratic responses to certain historical developments. and it is precisely because european development is not and should not be moving towards a single state that we must find a principle of governance which corresponds to this will, which respects our different traditions and is at the same time up to date. this ordering principle is the federation.

- mr president, over the years the deficit in protein crops in the union has swelled to 35 million tonnes in 2000. the bse crisis and the ban on animal meal have increased this by 300,000 tonnes per month in recent months. in view of this, what does the commission propose? well, she suggests that we do not take any specific initiative and go and buy the protein we lack from the highest bidder, the world's great supermarket of agricultural surpluses. i see at least three reasons for refusing this resignation, this spirit of abandonment. the first is that it is a food security issue. for such an important product, it is vital to strive for self-sufficiency. the second is the environmental benefits of oilseed protein crops: biodiversity, crop rotation, nitrogen balance. the third is the need to meet consumer demand for more traceability and visibility. the means are there: support for biofuels, the safety net for oilseeds, supplementary aid for protein crops, the intensification of public research efforts and agri-environmental aid for farms which include fodder legumes in the rotation. it is in these voluntary and responsible directions, mr president, that i would like to see the commission go, instead of simply invoking very short-term commercial considerations to limit itself to recommending the import of american or argentinian soybean meal.

in writing. - the piecyk report by the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism approves the agreement, in conciliation between the european parliament and the council, on the criteria to be applied to maritime ports, inland ports and intermodal terminals in order for them to be eligible for funding under the transeuropean transport networks (tens). we can agree with the rapporteur that the development of the necessary infrastructure for port facilities should be pursued at european level. the use of european public funds for the development of public facilities with the aim of improving the planning of the territory, rebalancing transport modes and combating pollution is undoubtedly a priority. but public funding must be used for public facilities and public services. the ambiguity facing the european union, which is reflected in this report, is precisely the question of the future status of port facilities, whether public or private. on the one hand, the council is promoting the transeuropean networks, and on the other hand it is preparing privatizations in these sectors, such as the directive presented on 14 february on the opening up of port services to competition. at no time does europe think in terms of the needs of its people and societies, but only in terms of openness and competition.
in writing. - the small war of amendments between parliament and the council sheds light on the knots of contradictions that bind them together, both in their pretension to fight against the laundering of dirty money without daring to touch the secrecy of business. to combat effectively the laundering of drug money or illegal trafficking would require the abolition of banking secrecy, of business secrecy, not just its limited and confidential collection, and not just before the courts. but that would be to expose to the public that there are a multitude of ways of accumulating and using capital which, while legal, are nevertheless criminal in the basic interests of society. it would be unacceptable for those who defend the profit and the right of those who benefit to use it as they wish. let them not be surprised at their own impotence in the face of those who push the logic of profit to the point of criminality. we do not want to endorse, by our vote, the ineffectiveness of the measures imposed, nor the laundering of capital, which is legal, but acquired at the cost of exploitation and used to the detriment of society.
in writing. - the directive on the fight against money laundering is a step in the right direction and responds, at least in part, to the aspirations of citizens' movements and to the proposals put forward by the judges most concerned by this issue. unfortunately, apart from one amendment (2) extending the obligations of the directive to accountants and another (27) which refers to olaf and a possible european prosecutor, the lehne report tries to reduce the scope of the directive. he himself said: "the right to privacy must not be infringed, even in the fight against money laundering". this argument is accompanied by absurd pretexts ("too complicated obligations") or loopholes which leave it to the professional bodies to establish "the necessary rules" themselves. we are in favour of full transparency in capital transactions. we recognize the absolute necessity of preserving the right of defence but in no case should this allow impunity for anyone involved in criminal acts. that is why we are voting against some absolutely outrageous amendments which are such obstacles to a vigorous fight against money laundering.
in writing. - the subject of our concern today is of paramount importance for the future of our democracies. the fight against money laundering can no longer be the business of one state alone. it is therefore necessary that cooperation between member states be organised to be effective. the definition of money laundering needs to be broadened, as the restriction on drug trafficking is no longer relevant. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the environment. the association of the legal professions with the anti-money laundering system has become an absolute necessity, otherwise the european system for preventing and combating money laundering would be ineffective. however, lawyers in particular cannot accept that the professional secrecy, and therefore the relationship of trust established with their clients, is compromised. the amendments concerning them are therefore inadmissible. the court of justice has also held that the principle of professional secrecy is not incompatible with the principle of the protection of legitimate expectations. it is incompatible with the declaration of suspicion, or worse, the declaration of possible suspicion. moreover, restricting professional secrecy is tantamount to restricting the fundamental rights of citizens. the lawyer is an assistant to the court, not an assistant to the police.
in writing. - we voted for the recommendation for the sole reason that it advocates some common sense measures, such as, for example, 'the encouraging definition of authorized raw materials'. but even if the council and the commission were to accept the amendments - they are rejecting and delaying them for the moment - this would not absolve the leadership of the european institutions of the major responsibility they have taken for the spread of bse by refusing to take precautionary measures as soon as the threat posed by this epidemic became tangible. this is not even negligence or carelessness, but deliberate choices, under pressure from the agro-food lobbies. this is yet another tragic demonstration of the fact that the aim cannot be to protect the profits of capitalist groups and at the same time to defend effectively the interests of the majority of the population.
