in writing. - as i said yesterday, mrs auroi's report shows the right way forward, even if the proposals it contains cannot, of course, meet our needs for vegetable protein in such a context. when i read the commission's report on vegetable protein in the context of the ban on meat and bone meal, i was shocked by the contempt in which the authors seem to hold their fellow citizens! firstly, consumer contempt: this position ignores the clear, strong and growing consumer demand for traceability and visibility of the origin of products. we are simply being told to continue buying the protein we lack from the highest bidder in the world's great supermarket of agricultural surpluses. and it doesn 't matter if they contain gmos ! the commission's resignation is an insult to european farmers, as if they were incapable of producing the vegetable protein we need on our soil! the commission's proposed measure under the seven-point plan (to allow the production of fodder legumes in organic farms) is a welcome one, but it is not at all up to the challenge. between organic and the massive import of genetically modified soybeans, there is room for creativity among european farmers. it seems that the commission is looking for technical, regulatory and budgetary reasons for not taking action. it's a "non-plan" protein that she presents to us. the commission is using an accounting logic which is not even economically relevant: just because soybean prices are currently low does not mean they will always be low; a future upturn in the course is certain. in writing. - the european parliament's resolution on foot-and-mouth disease deserves to be approved, particularly because it takes some distance from the policy of culling, which may be useful at times but does not seem to be very effective in a case like that of great britain. people are wondering, and they're right. the resolution we have just voted is therefore rightly directed towards authorising emergency vaccination, either in a given region affected by foot-and-mouth disease, in a buffer region or in the case of particular animal species. beyond these emergency measures, we must ask why foot-and-mouth disease, which was well known in our countryside in the past and which, for the most part, does not kill animals (let alone humans), is now producing such a national tragedy. the answer is twofold. first, the disease is spreading faster than before because agriculture has become ultra-productive, so it is parcelled out, specialised, fragmented. each animal may spend different periods of its life in different places in the national territory, or even in europe. transport is multiplied, the link with the responsible farmer is broken, traceability becomes random. it is therefore important to us to restore a more stable stockfarming system, where those responsible are known and where animals are not treated as inert commodities. this is part of the agricultural reform we are proposing in the coming years. secondly, the mass slaughter seems to be motivated by economic reasons that are not always transparent. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's health and safety standards are maintained. the commission has also taken a number of measures to ensure that the health and safety standards of the community's health and safety authorities are maintained. i think that financial reasoning is absurd. why can't we export by providing vaccination certificates? why, then, must everything be made dependent on exports, which contributes to agricultural productivity and entails the need for subsidies which cost the taxpayer dearly, all in order to destabilize agriculture in less developed countries? this system is going crazy, and it will be appropriate to raise the bar in the coming years.
in writing. - with mad cow disease, agribusiness has created a new, deadly human disease, and we still don't know how to cure it. foot-and-mouth disease is an ancient disease that does not affect humans and that most animals have been able to recover from. but agribusiness - with the evolution of the global livestock and meat market - has given it an international epidemic dimension that it did not have before. the market also imposes its health requirements, with dramatic consequences. the use of the vaccine was banned on purely economic grounds, the economic being reduced to commercial regulations and an otherwise questionable estimate of the financial costs. hundreds of thousands of healthy animals (or animals that could be cured) are being slaughtered in the name of a simple accounting calculation of profitability. the desperation of farmers whose livestock is being destroyed is countered by the policy makers' own trading rules. the most basic respect for life, the protection of local economies and the maintenance of a social fabric living in rural areas, the living and working conditions of farmers have not been taken into account in the definition of health policies in the face of the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic. the merchant order and its laws of bronze remain. an order from which it is high time to break free.
in writing. - we cannot accept the conclusions of the stockholm european council because, as i said in the debate, they present a jumble of all subjects, without hierarchy, giving the impression of a sprawling europe that is concerned with everything, without distinguishing between the big and the small issues, and without distinguishing between the national and the european level. this situation is detrimental to the union as a whole, since the european council, which is becoming increasingly important in the institutional balance, should present particularly clear conclusions. the necessary corrections imply a reform of the preparation of the councils, but also, more profoundly, a clarification and a relaxation of european powers, which should be the issues at stake at the next intergovernmental conference. in our view, rational and orderly council conclusions should have three parts: a first part would be devoted to some strategic questions of paramount importance, which the council would have actually discussed, and on which it would have actually taken decisions. a second part would give instructions to the various councils of ministers for implementation. a third part, which should be the most substantial, could set out some of the guidelines which the heads of state or government intend to follow in their respective countries, particularly as regards economic and social management - the one which was on the stockholm agenda. these guidelines would not be binding and would tolerate the expression of opposing views. they would thus express their willingness to develop informal, free and open coordination, respectful of national democratic choices. when we read the stockholm conclusions, we see that we are far from that. our proposal is in fact a fundamental reform of the treaty, which means that many powers will be returned to the member states.
in writing. - the stockholm european council welcomed the achievements of the european union and announced that its 'strategic objective' remains 'to become the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world'. the working classes certainly have nothing to congratulate themselves on. to say that "unemployment is at its lowest level since 1991" is at the same time an unintentional way of acknowledging that it remains as high as it was ten years ago, when it was already catastrophic. the balance sheet of the decade also shows the spread of low-paid precarious work throughout europe and the decline in the share of wages in total income. only large companies, their owners and shareholders, can boast of exceptional profits, but this result has been achieved at the expense of the world of work, as well as public services and social benefits. as for the future, the policy promised is the continuation of the policy pursued. some of the expressions even indicate a worsening of the situation, particularly in the case of longer working hours and attacks on pensions. we refuse to give a quitus for the future to the european institutions which are entirely at the service of industrial and financial groups.
- the stockholm summit was a "routine summit" for the public and the media. if it had not been for the announcement of the joint franco-german decision not to set a deadline for the full liberalisation of energy markets in order to better control all its consequences and effects, it would certainly not have been mentioned in the newspapers and on television. it was nevertheless an important summit on economic and social issues, in line with the lisbon summit, with the reaffirmation of the need to work towards a european society of full employment, with quality jobs. these guidelines were, moreover, met the next day with the sudden announcement of layoff plans at danone and marks and spencer. no consultation, not even for any real economic reasons. this veritable 'dictatorship' of the stock market and 'this unbridled hunt for profits' organised at the expense of employees, who are the main creators of wealth, has shown those who were still ignorant of the deep gap between the sometimes lax speeches of politicians and the realities experienced by employees on the ground. so, if we are not to see the death of the 'european social model' today, we cannot remain unresponsive and i personally called on the highest european and french authorities on 31 march to propose measures to stop this infernal spiral! i now expect, as do many in this house, precise and relevant answers. if this were not the case, there would be no need to organise employment and social summits in the future. in the meantime, i support francis wurtz's proposal to create within our european parliament an ad hoc structure, a subcommittee or an observatory to monitor and analyse these adjustment strategies of the major economic groups based solely on staff reductions. a forthcoming european summit should be held in 2001 to deal with this vital issue for the balance and future of europe. it is in this spirit that i voted today for the joint resolution tabled by the left.
- an additional summit to serve private interests. in stockholm, the fate of macedonia will be settled in a few minutes. the farmers will have to content themselves with european 'solidarity' in dealing with foot-and-mouth disease and will have to abandon the return to the vaccination programme, which was abolished several years ago to save money. this time, it's the financial services that are the big winners. by 2003, a single market in real estate securities will allow a few profiteers to speculate on stocks and bonds. in the most complete opacity, financial transactions are thus encouraged and will turn, even more quickly, into the hands of a few industrialists, playing, in the process, with the fate of millions of employees. we are calling for the abolition of banking secrecy at european level, for the opening of account books and for transparency in all transactions. this would be an effective way of combating money laundering and controlling the financial resources of those companies which, like danone and marks and spencer, persist in laying off workers while making record profits. finally, private operators have obtained confirmation of the liberalisation of public utilities such as jute, postal services, electricity and gas. the current social mobilizations call for a different kind of summit: that of the convergence of struggles to impose a quality european public service that meets the basic needs of the population.

- the next item is the report (a5-0123/2001) by mr zimeray, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the request for waiver of mr peter sichrovsky's immunity.
the rapporteur. mr president, the case of mr sichrovsky is probably the most delicate we have had to deal with in this mandate, for reasons not only of procedure but also, and above all, of substance. i would like to take this opportunity to recall the principles which guided us in the drafting of this report and which are - as we have seen in the debate we have just had - essential principles in this parliament. the first principle we must have in mind is that we should, as far as possible, disregard any political opinion when we are dealing with a report requesting the waiver of immunity, and also that we should refrain as far as possible, and this is not always easy, from judging or prejudicing the member in question. the second principle is that we must act in accordance with the law, respecting not only the law of the member state but also what becomes parliamentary law, both in terms of the substantive rules and the formal rules, which imposes on us an absolute duty of consistency with our previous decisions. it is also necessary, and this is an intangible principle, to stick to the qualification for which the parliamentarian is being prosecuted. this is a point which is particularly important in the case of mr sichrovsky, and i shall come back to it in a moment. finally, when there is doubt, that doubt must always be to the advantage of the person who is accused, the member of parliament whose immunity is being sought. so in mr sichrovsky's case, as in all cases, i think it is important to remember the principle of immunity and its purpose. immunity is not a privilege granted to one or another member of parliament. it's for protection. not protection of the individual, but protection of the institution through the individual. i must say that the case of mr sichrovsky, like the others we are about to see, is part of a context marked by a great fluidity of information, which explains why we have more and more cases of defamation and press offences, but also by a democracy of opinion into which we have entered, by the criminalization of life and in particular of public life, and i take this opportunity to recall that there are also civil laws to obtain reparation for the damage we consider ourselves to have suffered, and in particular when it comes to damage caused by the press or defamation, and i believe that we must take this opportunity to recall that immunity is not impunity, it is immunity in a suspended criminal proceeding, which in no way makes the prosecution of civil proceedings by the parliamentary mandate in any case. in the case of mr sichrovsky, i should remind you that he was prosecuted for saying that the president of the jewish community in vienna was an idiot, aggressive, angry, incredibly greedy, hateful, professional jew who would use his dead parents to appear on television. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. i refuse to consider this hypothesis for the simple reason that he is not being prosecuted for that offence, and in those circumstances i believe we must refrain from substituting a prosecutor for the one for which he was prosecuted. the detailed analysis of the file, the detailed examination of the file that we were able to make in the legal affairs committee during several meetings - since it is a file that has been returned three or four times before the legal affairs committee - has shown that these words, however vivid they may have been, however excessive, however odious they may have seemed, these words were made in a political context and in response to criticisms of mr sikrovsky himself and criticisms of his political affiliation because of his religious affiliation. his political position because of his religious affiliation. the legal committee therefore considered, as we had done in similar cases, particularly with regard to portuguese parliamentarians, that there was a link, however tenuous, between his expression and his political position and his political opinion. so this link, of course, does not concern all the speeches made, but i think we must consider that all the speeches form a whole, and that therefore the benefit of immunity must be granted to mr sichrovsky.
- for information, i will simply point out to our colleagues that, on this point, rule 6 of our rules of procedure provides as follows: 'without prejudice to the provisions of rule 122, a member whose immunity is being waived may not take part in the debate.' i'm just saying this so we all know what he's up to. i appreciate your understanding. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 11 a.m.

- mr president, in order to protect the euro against counterfeiting, we are discussing a series of technical measures tonight which, interesting as they are, do not exhaust the subject. in fact, they are even avoiding a fundamental political problem which the european parliament does not seem to be prepared to raise. so i'll take care of it. the risk of counterfeiting, when the euro is introduced, will be very high, in particular because of the decision to launch an entirely new currency ex nihilo, which will make citizens lose all their references. in fact, maybe it was meant to be. having lost their bearings, they are more likely to accept counterfeit euros as genuine. the consequences of this confusion will be aggravated by the high value of some denominations of 100, 200, 500 euros. but who is going to take this huge risk? the weakest, the most fragile, the least informed, small traders, micro-enterprises who may end up with worthless counterfeit notes that they have accepted by mistake. this situation is intolerable. it is all the more intolerable because they are the ones who will be asked, without any financial compensation, to bear the often very heavy adaptation costs of the changeover to the euro. it is therefore unacceptable to continue as we are doing today to pretend that these burdens do not exist and to accept implicitly that they are distributed among the weaker ones. we call on the european and national authorities to assume their responsibilities. we ask that they give the citizens a guarantee that the counterfeit notes which have been handed over to them by mistake will be refunded, at least for a transitional period. or, for that matter, we should give out free counterfeit detectors to small businesses. some people will say: but we don't have the money for that. i say to them: you should have thought of that before. now we must either take responsibility or - after all, why not - postpone the physical exchange of coins and notes until 1 january next year, which would be desirable for many other reasons anyway.

in writing. - we voted against the report on public access to parliament, council and commission documents because, under that false title, the aim is not so much to extend the possibilities of access as to regulate it, and thus to give the institutions the right to restrict public access. the institutions concerned retain the right to declare documents as 'confidential' in fields as diverse as 'defence and military affairs, international relations, economic, financial or monetary policy, and public security', as well as 'documents relating to judicial proceedings, inspections, investigations or financial audits'. that is, secrecy can be decreed about just about anything. public access to documents of the european institutions even seems to be a step backwards compared with certain national practices. in this area, as in many others, the minimum would be to align oneself with the least anti-democratic and most transparent practices. but in reality there is no reason why any document of the european institutions should be hidden from the public. we are in favour of full publicity of every document, agreement, treaty, as well as of elements of every intervention now hidden, of every secret negotiation, of every lobbying, which has led parliament, the council or the european commission to take a decision or issue a directive.
in writing. - this report raises some questions. first, the legal basis, with the combination of articles 37 (on the organisation of agricultural markets) and 152 (on plant health and veterinary measures). article 152 (1) (2) states that 'community action, which complements national policies, shall be directed towards improving public health'. harmonisation is excluded here. the second is the added value of the union: in the absence of any harmonisation of health policy, the fight against rabies has produced very good results in europe, for example by lifting quarantine measures in sweden and great britain. finally, there is the question of the financial implications of the proposed regulation for pet owners: a tattoo carried out by a veterinarian costs about 150 francs, whereas the installation of the chip will cost between 400 and 500 francs. the tattooing technique has been tested in france in the field of health and veterinary medicine and has the advantage of being immediately readable, making the search for the owner of the animal easy and quick and requiring no reading device. the proposal involves the standardization of transponders (iso 11784) and of readers for these same chips (iso 11785). in any event, the person responsible for the animal should not be responsible for the means of reading the chip during checks. at the end of the eight-year transitional period, the two methods of identification (tattooing and transponder) must coexist. the choice of the owner to opt for one or the other method of identification should remain the rule. as for those who advocate the widespread use of the transponder under the guise of animal welfare, we believe that this is a different debate. for all these reasons, we are opposed to the text.
in writing. - the swoboda report on the conclusion of the stabilisation and association agreement between the european union and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia is far from satisfactory. in the present situation, europe should exert all its economic and political weight, particularly in order to ensure that a negotiating round between the various protagonists is really initiated. the european union could work to amend the constitution to recognise the albanians as a constituent people of the republic and to facilitate the acquisition of macedonian nationality. the albanian language should be recognized as an official language of macedonia, from primary school to university, and in the administration. greater internal autonomy could be granted to the albanian-majority regions. the albanian population should also be able to have better access to public jobs where they are so far underrepresented. if nothing is done, the tensions between the communities may in the short term worsen. furthermore, criminalizing one in comparison to the other as "terrorists" only makes matters worse. rather than follow this policy, as the report suggests, parliament should encourage the macedonian government to negotiate with the parties representing the albanians to find constitutional solutions that will bring lasting peace to macedonia. for these reasons we shall not vote in favour of this report.

in writing. - one of the lessons i learned from yesterday's debate on the protection of the euro against counterfeiting is that the european union and the various governments involved are making a big mistake in their approach to the single currency. at the moment, they do not provide citizens with a financial guarantee against the risk of counterfeit euro banknotes, or financial assistance for adaptation measures, as if this were a routine operation of replacing one set of banknotes by another. that is not the case at all. we are facing a very exceptional and rather risky operation, both of replacing all the coins and notes and of altering all the landmarks simultaneously. to cope with this exceptional operation, to ensure the safety of the citizens and to provide them with the help they need, exceptional means must be put in place, with the corresponding budgets, of course. it is true that these budgets would probably be very high. they would not facilitate the fulfilment of the maastricht criteria for government deficits. this is a paradox of this operation that we must accept. to remedy this, one might first consider subtracting the budgets for the changeover to the euro from the calculation of the 3% deficit. of course, it would be a formal operation. the only problem is to find the money, at a time when economic growth is slowing down in europe and tax revenues are bound to fall. many ideas could be put forward in this connection, including the idea of lifting a 'special introduction of the euro' tax on the profits of large companies, since they will be the main beneficiaries of the single currency. in any case, i stand by my conclusion: it is dishonest and irresponsible to act as we are doing today, trying to shift the cost of the changeover to the euro onto the heads of hundreds of thousands of 'little people' who can do nothing about it.

in writing. - mrs cederschiöld's report rightly points out the magnitude of the risks of counterfeiting the euro "as soon as this currency starts to circulate in the form of banknotes and coins" and thus enters the race for the "most counterfeited currency on the planet", and this even though "internal borders have been abolished to the free movement of offenders throughout the territory of the european union". we must now face the consequences, deliberately minimized when it was a question of promoting them, of the political decisions taken in favour of the introduction of the euro, which are now proving to be formidable for the daily lives of our fellow citizens. we all know that the euro did not have to become a circulation currency. there was no financial logic to it. this decision is purely political, and is the result of a desire to eliminate national currencies altogether. if, as we advocated, the euro had been chosen not as a single currency but as a common currency overlapping national currencies for a number of uses which could evolve according to the real needs of society, as a complementary currency and not as a substitute currency, this huge counterfeiting problem would not arise today. the rapporteur is rightly concerned about the authenticity checks which will obviously have to be carried out by banking institutions. but i am surprised and shocked that nothing is being proposed to help the future victims of the counterfeiters of the euro. it is up to those who made the political choice of putting the euro into circulation, that is to say the choice of the maximum trauma inflicted on our populations, with the sudden and radical loss of the standard by which they set the various orders of magnitude in their daily lives, to assume full responsibility for the consequences of their decision. in writing. - the resolution on nuclear safety presented to the european parliament 15 years after chernobyl underlines the seriousness of this major accident and its consequences for health and the environment. it is careful not to endorse the replacement of nuclear energy in ukraine ("russian and old") by nuclear energy ("western and modern"). it advocates a sustainable policy, including energy savings and the use of renewable energy sources. it questioned the reliability of the 'risk model' used by the official bodies. all things that go in the right direction. however, to this day, european authorities have not really learned from the disaster. the resolution itself merely recommends the closure of 'at-risk' nuclear power stations. the causes of the accident are not primarily technological. chernobyl reveals first and foremost what happens when a nuclear power goes into crisis - a social crisis, not a technical one. the accident is not specifically "russian", it is universal and exposes one of the great lies of the nuclear apostles. nuclear-powered states act as if our societies could manage for centuries an energy with immeasurable risks and never go through a crisis. the lessons of the past century and the present world disorder are enough to show how irresponsible this assumption is.
in writing. - we shall vote against the katiforis report, which we reject in every respect. we particularly object to its insistence on promoting wage policies which are 'compatible with the maintenance of wage moderation'. we believe, on the contrary, that the growth which has been restored is fragile and that it is likely to be broken in its momentum by the application of such recommendations. instead, we should ensure that wages throughout europe grow at the same rate as gdp per capita. we are also opposed to the social-liberal policy of lowering taxes: the resources released by the surplus growth would be much better spent on increasing social budgets and fighting poverty brought about by long years of triumphant economic liberalism. we recommend that these 'structural changes to increase flexibility' which the report says it approves, be opposed. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat unemployment. we believe, on the contrary, that a european social policy should be established, based in particular on the introduction of a minimum wage system and collective agreements.
in writing. - our vote against this report is not an expression of opposition to the development of the internet or to any technical progress whatsoever. but, behind general considerations, several paragraphs point to the announcement of subsidies to private companies in this sector. this is suggested in particular by the expression of support for 'research projects carried out in partnership with the private sector'. we are opposed to any direct or indirect subsidy which is intended to use public money to generate private profit, and we voted against this report.
in writing. - the own-initiative report we discussed today is intended to encourage the european commission to 'give high priority to an eu research initiative on the second generation internet (and related electronic communications) in the context of the 6th research framework programme'. as rapporteur on the subject, i had to intervene. and i would like to stress that the european commission's proposal for the new cprd has taken this requirement into account, since the second priority, among the 7+1 priorities, is devoted to technologies for the information society. it was clear that such a promising sector was well placed in this multiannual programme. i generally agree with the demands of this report, although i regret that they are a little too liberal. the rapporteur often forgets that these new technologies must first and foremost be at the service of the citizen. it is rightly said that eu and member state resources should be allocated to pre-competitive projects in order to ensure an assertive eu presence in the development of future generations of the internet and new communication infrastructures globally and to strengthen the union's role in the management of the internet. i would remind you that at the march 2001 part-session parliament voted in favour of the carraro report, which stressed the role of the member states and the european union in the icann system (a private, non-profit-making company that manages several key internet systems) and advocated opening up the system to developing countries. i welcome the fact that the harbour report takes up both of these points. like mr harbour, i support the strategy to promote the 'centres of excellence' mentioned in the commission's proposals for a european research area, even though, as i said, this concept needs to be clarified. the idea that one of these centres deals with electronic communications seems to me to be a good one, but we are not there yet! the rapid establishment of a transeuropean research network with very high speed (100 gigabits per second) is of course a prerequisite for the achievement of a competitive, dynamic and knowledge-based economy as defined in lisbon. i take this opportunity to emphasize that broadband internet should be available to all sections of the population. i would have liked to have seen this reflected in my report for an opinion on universal service and new telecommunications networks. unfortunately, my amendments to that effect were rejected largely on the initiative of mr harbour!

- the next item is the report (a5-0162/2001) by mr maaten, on behalf of the parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee, on the joint proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the member states relating to the manufacture, presentation and sale of tobacco products (c5-0086/2001 - 1999/0244 (cod)).
- mr president, the commission's recommendations to the member states are imbued with the union's usual dogmas, with priority given to reducing public debt. the first thing to do is to reduce public and social expenditure. the report by mr von wogau is part of the same process. there is a complacency, which i find rather disconcerting, in the face of the deterioration of the economy and a refusal to think about the conditions to be met to be part of sustainable development. the stated ambition is to comply with the stability programme. objective 1 for the european central bank: price instability. the european central bank still refuses to lower interest rates because it is obsessed with the dangers of inflation, which is always possible, and the head of the bundesbank recently reminded us that the european central bank is not responsible for growth or employment. the ambition of a more competitive and dynamic european union is mentioned, a laudable objective, but proposals for the means to achieve this remain the domain of dogma: adapting pension schemes to take account of budgetary constraints, using the possibilities of reducing expenditure in all areas, which means, in the public mind, creating the most favourable conditions for investment in the labour market. and of course, the eternal icing on the cake, liberalizing the sectors that are not yet liberalized. nothing on the general interest service obligation at community level. in short, we continue to follow the same recipes, the consequences of which we know, that is the anti-inflationary credo, the priority of priorities. the report does not hesitate to highlight the progress made in reducing unemployment in some member states, while stressing the need to continue reforming labour markets. it would be useful to assess the nature of the new jobs created, which are often precarious. how can we expect to achieve employment results if we are perfectly ignorant of the strategy of these large european groups, which are largely profitable but which, with their eyes fixed on financial criteria, are laying off many of their employees in the name of competition? the credibility of the european social model is at stake, and there is much hesitation to take the necessary measures to protect employees. there is no mention of the social policy which is essential to consolidating growth. nothing about corporate social responsibility. once again, the economic policy thus presented is not in keeping with the ambition of sustainable development, which would presuppose a dynamic of public investment, a market organization with strong industrial ambitions. there are capitals. there is an urgent need to regulate the reality of the financial market. that is why my group is returning to the economic policies of the union in this report with the proposal to introduce a tax on speculative movements in order to control them, to reduce their volatility and above all to raise resources to be invested in the social and environmental fields. this report, and the situation in the union in general, once again show that the political, economic and social choices of the union would benefit from being prepared in the context of a genuine democratic procedure, which would be established in each country, after broad consultation of european civil society.
- ladies and gentlemen, this report by the committee on economic and monetary affairs will not go down in the annals of this house as a symbol of clarity or relevance, both in form and in substance. let's just get to the form. in article 5 you speak of 'the political priority of improving the quality and sustainability of public finances'. is there a public finances which is not sustainable because it is ephemeral? in article 10 of your resolution you stress - and i quote - 'the importance of public investment which should be targeted in the light of strategic objectives' - which is correct - 'but which could not replace private and priority investment'. what contradictory jargon to displease no one and privilege nothing at all ! in the background, you are showing your attachment to the social market economy, which is dear to the cdu. it's not the french design. why should it be adopted, given the rather poor performance of the german economy over the last 40 years? why, for example, should france abandon an industrial policy which has made it, in its strategic sectors, the first power in europe, and this without a monetary artifice such as the deutsche mark, overvalued by 15% at the time of the creation of the euro, or east germany, which was worth 350 billion dollars when it was worth 100 billion at most at the time of reunification, and this without drowning in the "all-european" in the way that eventually happened to the company aerospatiale - one of the former world leaders in aeronautics and space - absorbed by the company matra, although twice as small as it, these two companies having itself disappeared into the eads group. it is a great success indeed for france, which has gone from being a large majority to being in the minority! the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. what is the point of this report which contains no specific criticism of any country in the euro zone, which says nothing about the de facto devaluation of the european currency, whose collapse is still a cause for concern?
- mr president, in his report on the broad economic policy guidelines for 2001, mr von wogau advocates the idea that next year, after the introduction of euro coins and banknotes, the 12 countries participating in the single currency will form a higher area of integration which they will call the domestic market. this domestic market should be managed in accordance with the principles of the social market economy which, as stated in the explanatory memorandum, were successfully applied by germany after the war. i believe that it is indeed a common concern of the countries of europe to seek to reconcile social justice and the market. but it is good that everyone is free to follow the path most suited to his character with mutual coordination, but without using the brussels instrument to impose this or that single formula. i think there is also a big misunderstanding of the concept of the domestic market. this expression may suggest that european economies are managed by a single political authority. but that is not the case today, and the maastricht treaty does not provide for that in the future. in the maastricht model, the single currency managed by the european central bank coexists with a plurality of national political authorities. if there are those who think otherwise, they had better make that clear to the people before the end of the year and organise the necessary referendums.

- mr president, it is not enough to link the word 'social' to the word 'market' as you do, to make your economy better. the working people, the working majority of the population, do not judge by your words but by the difficulties of their own existence and they see clearly that what you call the 'social market economy' condemns 15 million women and men to unemployment in a european union which is one of the richest regions on the planet. your social market economy is the generalization of precariousness, the increase in the number of workers paid 4,000 or 5,000 francs a month, even here in france, and much less in other european countries, while shareholders, who do nothing, share among themselves the dividends of the huge profits of the companies. so this market economy that you glorify in your report is a stupid, unjust, inhuman economy. it works by accumulating wealth in the hands of a small minority and worsening the living conditions of the majority. you dare to say that competition is an important safeguard against abuse of power. but it is by invoking competitiveness, competition, that the boards of directors of large companies such as danone, michelin, alsthom, péchiney, marks & spencer and many others can commit this particularly abject abuse of power which consists in throwing some of their workers out on the streets, closing down entire factories and sometimes condemning an entire city to desertification, simply to ensure their shareholders additional dividends. you claim to want to fill, and i quote, 'the democratic deficit of european economic policy', but the first step in filling that deficit would be to deprive the big business of its divine right to dispose of the existence of all those whose work enriches it, starting with the prohibition of collective redundancies and by obliging it to take from the profits, from the dividends accumulated by the shareholders, enough to safeguard all the jobs threatened.

in writing. - the text we discussed and voted on calls on the member states to encourage the mobility of persons in training, traineeships, voluntary work and teachers and trainers who are in another member state, whether under a european programme or not. the european parliament has, of course, welcomed such a proposal. however, he felt that amendments were necessary to improve the quality of the text and, most importantly, and this is extremely important to me, to extend the scope of the proposal to include researchers. amendments to this effect were tabled and adopted at first reading. unfortunately, the european commission has rejected the proposals concerning researchers for legal reasons. as rapporteur for the sixth framework programme for research and development, i can only deplore this. i hope that the conference on the mobility of researchers and scientists, which is being held under the belgian presidency, will make progress in this area. the construction of a european research area implies that researchers and scientists from all geographical horizons can work together to advance research in the interests of all citizens. it is therefore essential to tackle the various obstacles that hinder their mobility. since this has not been possible under this proposal, another solution will have to be found. i am committed to working towards that. i would also like to welcome, like the rapporteur, the sustained efforts of the french presidency to produce the most ambitious common proposal possible, with which everyone could agree. the amendments adopted thus cover essential aspects of mobility and are intended to improve or remove administrative, financial or social difficulties. as regards practical measures to be taken by the member states, it is proposed, for example, linguistic and cultural initiatives to prepare future travellers for their future way of life, improved access to information on mobility and its practical difficulties, financial support in the form of grants, allowances or loans. citizens of candidate countries and those of third countries legally resident in the european union will also be able to benefit from the provisions of the recommendation. i am satisfied that the emphasis is being placed on the need to recognise qualifications of all kinds acquired in another member state. all too often member states show reluctance and create intolerable difficulties in an area of free movement of persons, thus preventing mobile people from making use of their experience! as mr evans also points out, since the first reading in parliament, the council has adopted a mobility action plan - a 'toolbox' of 40 measures - which complements the recommendation. the commission has therefore tabled amendments at second reading to take account of this development. i sincerely hope that these measures will be put into practice very soon!
- mr president, by imposing standards for the recycling of waste electrical and electronic equipment, the european parliament is making a major contribution to the 'greening' of this industry. in the end, the environment won the battle, with the proponents of an innovative industry in electrical and electronic products opposing traditional manufacturers who were working hard to delay the deadline for taking charge of the recycling of this waste. while the rapporteur is to be congratulated for choosing the clean products route, it is to be regretted that the commission has not dealt with electrical and electronic waste and the accompanying chemical substances at the same time. the report also calls for the commission to take a more active role in the fight against fraud and for the commission to be able to take a more active role in the fight against fraud. despite this discordant note, the great innovation of this report will be the individual responsibility of producers, where each one becomes financially responsible for his product, both for products already on the market and for future products. environmental considerations are gaining ground in this report and are evidence of a growing political awareness of the danger of industrial waste, especially electrical and electronic waste, proliferating. in the end, this forced passage will be a win-win for everyone: the manufacturers, the consumers and the environment. the florenz report on waste electrical and electronic equipment has therefore benefited from significant environmental guarantees which prove that european industry must be designed, for citizens and politicians, with an eco-culture in mind.
in writing. - if there had been only declarations of good intentions assuring the need for the wide spread of new technologies, especially in the educational system, we could have voted for this report, although good intentions do not yet provide the means for a policy. but behind these statements, several paragraphs indicate the intention to "provide technical and financial support to enterprises". we have abstained on this report because we do not want to endorse subsidies to private companies, even if they are hidden.
in writing. - the competence for education lies with the states. we reject all attempts to circumvent this fact. the questioning of this division of powers goes hand in hand with a further increase in liberal-commercial options in educational matters. the reports thus clearly encourage reflection in this direction, with a particular focus on the shift from 'content' to 'competence'. the aim is to challenge qualifications linked to diplomas in favour of 'flexible' skills assessments, for which companies are solely responsible. all this is part of the logic of the liberal counter-reforms undertaken in various countries. in the same way, "lifelong learning" is combined, in this perspective, with a drastic reduction in initial training and the role of public training institutions (in favour of "virtual", distance and, increasingly, commercial education). information and communication technologies (icts) must, on the contrary, strengthen the right to a common and public education for all, of a high standard and of good quality. the financial investment in this area does not make sense if it is accompanied by a very significant relative reduction in all budgets devoted to education over the past 15 years. consequently, we cannot vote for them.
in writing. - the debate on the guidelines for economic policies in 2001 has been marked by the greatest uncertainty, which is not surprising, after all, since the aim of the exercise is almost impossible to achieve: it is, in fact, a question of determining at european level common economic guidelines, even though the countries have different needs. this uncertainty is amplified by the european central bank's quarter-point cut in the key rate on 10 may. even though on 2 may, before the economic and monetary affairs committee of our parliament, the vice-president of the ecb, christian noyer, had expressed optimism about price stability in the euro area, even though the president of the ecb, wim duisenberg, has just presented a report which is also confident about the growth prospects, even though all these elements together suggested a stable rate, the ecb, by lowering rates, has just in a way refuted the reasoning it had the day before. the first effects of this operation will have been a fall in the euro - one more - and a mechanical recovery of the stock markets, without any significant benefit for growth being foreseen. the ecb lives in a series of permanent paradoxes, from which it is not about to emerge. it is impossible to take any measure which is not inappropriate to the situation of at least some of the member states. for example, our colleague mr blokland has just told us that the last fall in interest rates was met with perplexity in the netherlands, where inflation has just reached a level unmatched for twenty years, and where everyone thinks that, on the contrary, rates should have been raised. the same is true in other countries in the region. in these circumstances, any action by the ecb highlights divergences, which are immediately interpreted by international operators as 'hypotheses on the viability of a unified monetary policy', without general unification of all the other variables. the euro makes us feel that we are constantly on the verge of a crisis of confidence.
in writing. - we voted against this report on the broad guidelines of the economic policies of the member states and the community because these guidelines are entirely subordinated to the interests and wishes of the big business to the detriment of the workers. even with amendments such as those expressing environmental concerns or the one proposing "the introduction of a tobin-type tax on capital movements", the text remains a glorification of pro-employer, anti-worker policies pursued by the states and an endorsement of the current functioning of the economy. we abstained on this last amendment so as not to confuse our votes with those of the most ardent supporters of the capitalist order who voted against because they do not accept even such a ridiculous tax on capital as the tobin tax. but the claim that this tax 'controls' the movements of speculative capital or 'reduces the volatility of financial markets' is a lie. the avalanche of job cuts in some of the largest companies in the european union shows that it is not just the speculative use of big capital that is harmful to the working classes and to society, but capital itself and the economic system, which is driven by profit and capitalist enrichment. what the workers need are measures to protect them from the greed of the employers, not symbolic gestures which, moreover, justify the capitalist operation of the economy.
in writing. - we'll vote against this new liberal anthem. the 'structural reform' of the labour market which he advocates means an increased precariousness of employment contracts. this is indeed the policy followed throughout europe, and far from wanting to 'continue and accelerate' it, we want to bring it to an end. we would not be against the creation of 'general conditions favourable to investment' if they did not mean even more profits, whereas it is the consumption of employees that sustainably supports investment. as for pensions, we will always be in the forefront of the rejection of these so-called 'reforms', which in reality mean opening up to private insurance. we are also resolutely opposed to the liberalization of electricity and gas and, on the contrary, in favour of the creation of a large european public service. we also vote against this report because it is written in a hypocritical and undemocratic jargon and because it is characterized by an 'economy of ignorance'. after the british railways and the californian electricity, how can we forget that privatization is not synonymous with efficiency?
- the next item is the report (a5-0150/2001) by mrs stihler, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the proposal for a council recommendation on the consumption of alcohol by children and adolescents (com (2000) 736 - c5-0020/2001 - 2001/0801 (cns)).
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, as a representative of a wine-growing region, i shall support the text put to our vote without any difficulty. yes, alcoholism among youths is a scourge that must be combated, and this text well emphasizes the role that families, educators, producers and distributors have to play in this regard. this document will be a real recommendation of wisdom for the member states, and i appreciate that it is not binding but that it seeks to hold people to account. it should be stressed, however, that wine, consumed in moderation at meals, has been an integral part of our culture, our way of life and our social life since the dawn of our civilization. learning how to use it, as well as its moderate use, is a family activity. and this natural product, as diverse and varied as the soils that support the vine, has a beneficial influence on the health and the smile of the peoples of the mediterranean culture, as we have reminded you in the amendment we have tabled.
- mr president, we have just voted on the maaten report on tobacco, which contains excellent measures. now, with alcohol, we are in exactly the same situation, that is, we are faced with at least the same number of deaths, and not just from road accidents, which we seem to focus on, but also from cirrhosis, stomach cancer, esophageal cancer, not to mention the various social problems. as with tobacco, we know that smoking a cigarette is no more dangerous than drinking a glass of wine. but as with tobacco, we also know that alcohol use and addiction start in youth, especially because of the example set by adults and the positive image conveyed by advertising. we should in fact adopt the same type of measures for alcohol as for tobacco, and in this respect the commission report, if it is good, goes much less far, perhaps because the alcohol lobbies are even more powerful than the tobacco lobbies, or perhaps because of our cultural habits. in fact, we should have a labelling requirement on all alcoholic beverages, occupying 30% of the surface, stating that alcohol kills, that alcohol is dangerous to health. we should ban advertising, even disguised advertising, for alcohol. we should prohibit the sponsorship of any activity, particularly sporting activities, by the manufacturers of alcoholic beverages. there is no moral value in this, but, as with tobacco, it is not the repression of consumers that will bear fruit but prevention. so any temptation to drink among young people must be addressed now.
commission. – mr president, combating alcohol-related harm is a public health priority in many member states and also at eu level. this is clearly reflected in the draft of the future public health action programme where inappropriate use of alcohol is mentioned as one of the key health determinants to be tackled. over the last couple of years, there has been growing evidence that alcohol consumption by young people and the corresponding health and social problems have increased alarmingly. this is why the commission took the initiative to address the problems caused by the drinking of alcohol by young people in the form of a council recommendation which is a valid instrument foreseen under the public health article of the treaty, namely article 152. the broad discussions which we held during the last three years with the member states, experts and stakeholders clearly show that the drinking behaviour of young people is increasingly similar throughout the european union and mr president, the main concrete observation that i, the elected representative of the atlantic regions, have to make in this debate is that 18 months after the sinking of the erika, the many victims of this terrible tsunami are still struggling with a very slow, very complex and very unfair system of compensation. of the 1200 claims lodged, only 200 were dealt with by fipol. the amounts requested and justified are systematically and arbitrarily reduced. the slow pace of the procedures is putting at risk the financial equilibrium of many coastal enterprises, including shellfish, aquaculture, fishing and tourism. fipol functions as a mechanism for the self-limitation of the liability of oil companies, which thus exempt themselves from a significant part of the coverage of the damage they have caused. it is clearer why the united states has stayed away from this system; the commission has not been able to obtain through it the payment by exxon of the entire damage caused by the exxon valdez disaster, i.e. 50 billion francs. the damage from the erika is certainly more modest. they are currently valued at chf 5 billion, but fipol will cap its compensation at chf 1.2 billion, not a penny more, because fipol compensation corresponds to the sums held by the fund, not to the amount of damage suffered by the victims. the state and local authorities are therefore obliged to make a contribution, which means that the taxpayer bears part of the responsibility of the polluters. it is this very serious anomaly that we must urgently eliminate. we are moving towards this with the erika i package which we are examining tonight at second reading and we approve, for our part, the reinforcements proposed by the rapporteurs on the responsibility of ship certification companies. but when our assembly examines the erika ii package, we will have to ensure that a genuine system of clear, fair and dissuasive liability is also established for the essential shipowner/charterer relationship.

- the next item is the statements by the council and the commission on the situation in the middle east. i now give the floor to mrs lindh, the president-in-office of the council.
the council. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has handled this matter. the situation in the middle east is now worsening. there's growing distrust between the parties. violence is claiming more victims every day. for the palestinians, a normal life has not been possible for a long time, and conditions are getting worse. the eu condemns the escalation of violence in gaza and the west bank: israeli incursions and tank fire in palestinian-controlled areas, cross-roads firing, killing of selected individuals. on these occasions, innocent civilians have been killed, including many children. the economic situation is also difficult. the palestinian authority is in deep financial crisis since the israeli transfers stopped and normal economic activities in the areas stopped. in practice, the authority relies on financial contributions from arab donors and the eu. israel is also suffering from the economic downturn caused by the crisis, although to a lesser extent than palestinian society. the daily life of the israelis is also becoming more difficult. violence in the form of mortar fire, car bombs, and suicide attacks is increasingly affecting israel as well. israeli civilians and children are being killed. prime minister sharon was elected on a promise to increase security. instead, the level of confrontation has been raised, the military effort has been increased and readiness has been shown both to enter palestinian-controlled territory and to attack syrian targets in lebanon. the security situation has simply deteriorated. there is no long-term military solution. the battles will be neither won nor lost. the only solution to the conflict is through negotiation. that is why the peace process must continue. the presidency and the eu are in close contact with the parties and we call on them to continue the peace negotiations, building on the results of previous negotiations, aiming at a final status solution on the basis of international law, including un resolutions 242 and 338. a crucial difficulty is the fundamental lack of trust between the parties. both sides misjudge the other side as solely responsible for the violence and the stalled peace process. no one dares to show any signs of conciliation or flexibility, for fear that it will be seen as weakness. a diplomatic initiative is needed to break the deadlock. the stockholm european council instructed the high representative, javier solana, to report to the gothenburg summit in june, together with the commission, on how the eu could promote peace efforts. at the gymnich meeting in nyköping on 5 may, javier solana reported on the progress of this work. the eu welcomes and supports the mitchell commission report and proposals, as well as the egyptian-jordanian peace initiative, which is based on agreements in which israel participated. both proposals call on the parties to conclude ceasefire agreements immediately, to confirm their willingness to respect the agreements reached and to aim at resuming negotiations. confidence-building measures are a prerequisite for the success of the negotiations. one of the most critical issues for the peace process is israeli settlement policy. both the egyptian-jordanian initiative and the mitchell report call for a total cessation of all settlement activity. the mitchell report also suggests that the israelis should consider withdrawing from controversial and vulnerable settlements. we believe that settlement policy is contrary to international law and constitutes a serious obstacle to peace. the eu has called on israel to start withdrawing settlements. we also support the mitchell report's suggestion that the israelis should stop using live ammunition against demonstrators. the confidence-building measures also include israel's reimbursement of taxes owed to the palestinian authority. a negotiated solution, or a step towards such a solution, must be aimed at the establishment of a democratic, viable and peaceful palestinian state. the eu has defined its positions on this issue in the berlin declaration of march 1999 and the new york declaration of 12 september 2000. it remains the task of the eu, in cooperation with other interested countries and actors, to assist the palestinians in the building of such a democratic and peaceful palestinian state. a lasting peace in the region is not possible without peace agreements also between israel and syria and between israel and lebanon. significant progress has been made in the negotiations between israel and syria. it is now up to us to complete these and to find a solution based on the principles of international law which i have mentioned earlier. the israeli withdrawal from southern lebanon last may was an important precondition for a future peace agreement. in the period until the conclusion of the peace agreements, it is important for all parties to avoid incidents and other actions that could lead to a continuation of the violence. the eu will actively contribute to the continuation of the peace process, in cooperation with other states concerned, and through the high representative javier solana, the special envoy miguel moratinos and the commission. the middle east is the cradle of human civilization. it is an area of rare cultural richness and religious significance that is now increasingly associated with the long-running conflict that the region is sinking deeper and deeper into. the end of the current conflict is a prerequisite for a positive development in the region. the swedish presidency, together with the other eu partners, will do everything in our power to contribute to this.
commission. – madam president, i obviously very much regret that the situation in the middle east which has been well described by the minister has not improved since my last intervention in the house on this subject. the violence continues, killings on both sides, including of children, also continue unabated, property is being destroyed, particularly arable land and shelters in refugee camps, and settlements in west bank and gaza are still expanding. the european union is regularly urged to play a stronger part in the middle east. the core principles of our position are that peace must be built on international law, on the relevant un resolutions including un security council resolutions 242 and 338 and on the formula 'land for peace'. we, that is all the european union institutions, should clearly restate these principles in all our contacts with the parties to this bitter dispute. the european union continues to support any efforts to find a peaceful solution to the conflict. we support, as the minister said, the egyptian-jordanian initiative as well as the recommendations of the commendable mitchell commission of inquiry, including the settlement freeze and the swift and decisive cessation of violence and terrorism. there has been too much bloodshed and fighting. violence must stop. on the israeli side there is no justification for the disproportionate use of force against civilians and the destruction of property. on the palestinian side, the palestinian authority must do everything in its power to stop attacks on israeli civilians. this includes preventing incitements for such attacks, and the palestinian authority must naturally control its security services effectively. we cannot condemn violence on one side but not the other. the mitchell commission seemed to me to point a sensible way, the only way, to ending the blame game, stopping the killing and the maiming and getting back to talking. talks have to resume, and the parties must honour their international obligations. in the case of israel, these obligations range from complying with international humanitarian law, that covers respect for human rights, as stated by the european union at the human rights commission meeting in geneva, and also settlements. it goes on to bilateral obligations regarding the palestinian authority, for example the transfer of tax revenues, and it also includes obligations under the ec-israel association agreement. in the case of the palestinian authority, we need to see the implementation of long-overdue reforms both in financial and political terms including democratic transparency, fighting against corruption and strengthening the rule of law. i would like to refer to two concrete and practical points today about which i am regularly asked by parliament: the effect of the economic blockade on the palestinian authority and the policy of settlements. there has been some improvement recently concerning the movement of goods and people within and out of gaza. for example, a number of businessmen have received permits, but economic activities in the palestinian territories remain severely restricted. the palestinian authority is still facing financial and institutional collapse. the international donor meeting in stockholm on 11 april was a good step forward in bringing a solution to the palestinian authority's budgetary crisis. we particularly appreciate the commitments made by arab countries. following the stockholm meeting, the commission is discussing with the palestinian authority the basis for our future assistance. this includes measures intended to enhance financial management and complete the process of institutional reform. some of these measures, in particular those referring to institutional reform, constitute a clear confirmation of commitments announced in the past by the palestinian authority. we have noted the steps taken by the palestinian authority to adopt an austerity budget. the palestinian authority is also working on other welcome reforms related to financial management, such as the consolidation of revenues. the international monetary fund is monitoring this process, and our intention on the basis of this austerity budget is to make monthly payments of eur 10 million during the next six months once we can get the agreement we all want, but i repeat what i said earlier and what the minister said, what is important is to end the blockade and resume the payment of revenues. let me turn now to israel's settlement policy. the european union's position on settlements is clear. all settlement activities in gaza, the west bank, including east jerusalem, and on the golan heights are illegal, under international law, and constitute a major obstacle to peace. this includes the natural growth of settlements, a violation of international law that cannot be allowed to continue unabated. i am often asked, particularly in view of the failure of our efforts to resolve the issue, what this means for the working of our association agreement with israel and in particular for the question of rules of origin which is covered by the agreement. it follows from what i have said that the west bank, gaza and the golan heights fall outside the territorial scope of the agreement. this is not a new point i am making, it is not some political gesture. let me make that point crystal clear. this point has already been made in the commission's communication in 1998 on the same issue. the communication made it clear that preferential access to community markets for exports originating in israeli settlements in the west bank and gaza strip and in east jerusalem and the golan heights, and i quote, "contravenes agreed rules of origin since these territories do not form part of the state of israel under public international law". therefore the communication indicated that, and i quote again, "preferential access to community markets for exports originating in the west bank and gaza strip as originating in israel under the ec-israel interim trade agreement is a violation of the latter, given that it does not apply to these territories." the european union must uphold the rule of law. that was a point recently made very seriously in a similar case by the court of first instance which has stated that the existence of political tensions, and i quote, "does not exonerate the commission as guardian of the treaty and of the agreements concluded under it from ensuring the correct implementation by a third country of the obligation it has contracted to fulfil under an agreement concluded with the community". the position is absolutely clear. if, i stress the word if, israel wants to declare goods coming from the settlements as being of israeli origin, eu customs authorities would not be able to share this interpretation. (applause) customs is a community competence and the implementation of this common policy is delegated to member states, but the role of the commission is to ensure coherence and to avoid divergent interpretations by different member states. a number of member states have queried israeli origin certificates over recent months, and replies are now being received by member states' customs authorities. our responsibility in the commission today is to avoid uncoordinated action. this is why i have suggested that customs authorities discuss the replies received urgently and any action they may be contemplating at the next meeting of the customs code committee on 31 may. so what are the technical steps that will be taken now? this issue will be signalled at the eu-israel association committee on 21 may. the item is on the agenda agreed with israel and, as i have just mentioned, there will be a full discussion by member states' customs experts at the end of may on how to interpret israeli replies and the common line on how to respond. in the light of the conclusions reached at this occasion, this would be discussed in the customs cooperation committee between the european union and israel which would normally take place in july. i wish to stress that our decision will be entirely based on the law and its technical application case by case. we can do no more but we should do no less. as the court judgment to which i referred argued, the commission is the guardian of the treaty and of the agreements concluded under it. we cannot, nor should we seek to, resile from the duty. i return to where i began: like others we wish to see an end to the violence. we want to see a return to negotiation and we stand ready to help with the delicate and demanding work of building an enduring peace. there is no other way.

- madam president, the most surprising thing about our debate is our surprise, because israel's expansionist policy is the inevitable and predictable result of the growing imbalance in the region, an imbalance for which we bear a very large share of responsibility. firstly, because most of our states - with the notable exception of france - have not ceased since 1967 to give the impression to the state of israel - an increasingly self-confident and dominant state - that it can violate international law and un resolutions with impunity. in fact, we have followed washington here and elsewhere and we continue to turn a blind eye to the theocratic drift of this religious state whose governments are controlled by fanatical parties and minorities who have nothing to envy to the other religious fanaticisms in the region. for these reasons, we should consider sanctions against israel. but there is another serious imbalance where our responsibility is engaged, and that is the imbalance of forces. we must consider - i do not hesitate to say this - providing the arab side with sufficient force, including sufficient nuclear force, so that israel does not think that everything is permissible. that was the policy my country had embarked on in the 1970s when it gave iraq nuclear weapons. we destroyed it. so we will continue with our policy of imbalance and what is happening today is only the unfortunate but inevitable result of our collective blindness and cowardice.
- madam president, the european union is expected in the middle east. it is already there, much more so than in the past, thanks to the commitment of its high representative. now she must take an even more active part in it. gone are the days when she could just sit on the balcony of her mediterranean home and watch the drama unfold. an active part, because, as history has shown, in politics as in war, only passivity is infamous. to be useful, our action must be completely impartial and this is the first difficulty of the exercise, because each side first expects us to take sides against our opponent in the name of that old adage that the enemy of my enemy is my friend, but the friend of my enemy is my enemy. to help break the vicious circle of blood and revenge, here and elsewhere, we have no right to be anyone's enemy. so what do we do ? i believe very sincerely that no one will make peace in the middle east unless both sides are resolved and unless the various proposals put forward here right now by my colleagues and by the council and the commission are taken into account. if, as we must continue to hope, the will for peace exists, and only if it exists, we must also support the idea of deploying an international body of observers, in which europe could and should take part. i would like to stress this point after my friend salafranca and our colleague mrs napoletano to our colleagues in the knesset here, because i know that israel remains deeply hostile to this idea today. to appease the passions in the face of a tragedy as grave as the one that continues to engulf the holy land in blood, we will need impartial observers on the ground, able to prevent, by their actions and their testimonies, the incidents from degenerating into a new general conflagration, which will certainly increase when a real armistice is implemented, and which i, together with my colleagues, continue to hope will finally be established.
