commission. – i just want to try to answer three questions that were put during the debate by honourable members and i hope i can do so in a way which is moderately satisfactory. first of all, mrs van der laan asked about the rules of origin, and if there are points which i do not cover in what i am going to say, i will take them up in correspondence with the honourable member. what i would like to do is rehearse exactly what has happened so far. the issue of rules of origin was raised in the commission communication to the council and the european parliament to which i referred earlier. the general affairs council at the end of june 1998 took note of our communication and asked the commission to resolve these issues on a technical level. a great deal has happened since then. technical contacts at different levels with israel took place immediately after the communication. on 16 december 1999 the commission informed coreper on the outcome of these meetings. in early 2000 concrete information on specific imports from israeli settlements was supplied to the commission. on the basis of this information, at the customs code committee meeting on 6 april last year, the commission reminded member states of their obligation in this respect, namely to apply the provisions of article 32 of the protocol on customs of the association agreement to consignments for which information had been received that they originated in the settlements. after this meeting member states returned around 2000 eur1 certificates to israel for verification. in some cases, goods were only released for free circulation in the european union subject to the payment of a guarantee against liability for customs duties. replies to the letters of verification are coming in as the ten month deadline for israel's reply is expiring. all along there has been a notice to importers which was first published in the community official journal of 8 november 1997 warning exporters of doubts regarding eur1 certificates from israel. the notice is still in force, although of course references to the orange juice case, which honourable members will recall, no longer apply. that is all the information that i have at hand on the history of rules of origin. i am determined, as i said earlier, to conduct this issue by the agreement and entirely according to the law. mr lagendijk asked what we would be saying to the israeli side next week at our meeting on 21 may and he said that what we sought, or should seek, in the middle east was a balanced approach. i do not think, and i do not think he thinks either, that means we should search for some point on the political agenda where neither side will disagree with us. that is not what is meant by a balanced approach. i happen to think that the mitchell commission report was an extremely balanced and sensible document. the mitchell commission – and i hope we will do much the same – in my judgment supports those who are still committed to working for peace on both sides of the argument. that is a sensible, balanced approach. as for what we will say on 21 may, we can discuss human rights under the essential elements clause of our agreement, we will certainly discuss for the first time this summer rules of origin – that is already on the agenda – but i want to be scrupulous in sticking to the letter and the spirit of our agreement. to go beyond that would risk putting us on a very slippery slope indeed. so as far as i am concerned we stick to the letter of the agreement and do not go beyond it with any other political gestures. mr belder asked about the remarks of our colleague and friend the dutch foreign minister about the palestinian authority in particular and the importance of ensuring that it operates in a more transparent and democratic way. i have to say that what our colleague mr van aartsen said during his visit to the middle east was not just wholly in line with our views on the development of democracy in the palestinian territories, but an extremely eloquent and effective exposition of our view, as one would expect from him. even in these less than perfect circumstances we need to press the palestinian authority to be more open, to be more transparent, to be more pluralistic, to protect people's civil liberties and human rights and to become increasingly democratic. that is, i think, what the minister was saying and he has our total support.

- mr president, madam president-in-office of the council, commissioner, i believe we are at a pivotal moment in transatlantic relations. first, there is the legacy of the clinton era. apart from the serious trade disputes, the emblematic banana conflict, the one about hormonal beef, the one about gmos and about ten others, which are under consideration or have already been examined within the framework of the wto, apart from that, washington had already accumulated, in recent years, signs of unilateralism, the stigma of the superpower complex. opposition to the anti-personnel mine ban treaty, opposition to the charter of the rights of the child, opposition to the creation of an international criminal court which may one day have to try an american citizen, political disengagement and financial blackmail against the united nations, economic blockade, even military operation in violation of international law, the echelon affair, plan colombia, and so on. in addition, there has been little dialogue with our partners on the other side of the atlantic on civilization-related choices which are shocking to europeans, such as the death penalty or the denial of universal access to aids medicines. it is clear, however, that the first decisions of the bush administration are more serious than anything we have seen before. it was already worrying enough to hear the new president's security adviser, mrs condoleezza rice, illustrate her view of the new division of labour between americans and europeans for peacekeeping in the balkans, stressing with as much insight as elegance, and i quote her: 'that it is not the job of the igs to take children to kindergarten'. but the question of the kyoto protocol and the promotion of the missile shield is frankly irresponsible not only towards europe but towards the whole of humanity. in the face of this escalation, are we doomed to protest for form and finally compose for realism? i don't think he did. a europe open to dialogue, but firm in its commitment to the principles of a civilized and responsible international community, will find allies in public opinion on the five continents and even in the united states congress, as well as in many states themselves. the commissioner is of course not trying to develop any anti-americanism or aggressive rhetoric against a partner which is indispensable in today's world, but at least to assert a clear political will in a united front of the fifteen on objectives which can meet the expectations not only of europeans but of all those around the world who are striving to free themselves from the unipolar order which is increasingly enclosing them.
mr. president, heavy clouds are gathering over the atlantic and they're heavy with storm. i am not just thinking of the violence that is fuelling american society and whose rate of executions is just one symptom among many. in reality, this society, founded on genocide and whose values are constantly yielding to the law of the jungle called "liberalism", can only live in violence, and that, in the end, does not concern us. what we are concerned with is the american policy of doing what it wants anywhere in the world and of breaking all international rules, including those it imposes on others. we are thinking of the kyoto accords. we must not forget washington's refusal to sign the nuclear test ban treaty, which the united states considers to be valid for all states except its own, and so many other agreements which show that washington wants to bind the states of the whole world without being bound by anything concerning itself. let us also consider the scandalous echelon dossier, which shows that big brother, that is to say the big brother, does not he, intends to monitor the entire planet but does not accept the slightest right to look, as evidenced by the insulting and scandalous reception recently received by our commission of inquiry on this network which has brought its imperial power to its zenith. the worst thing is that we are like a rabbit, fascinated by the boa or the snake that will bite it, and that we follow this imperial policy, my last hope being that france resists this general flattening of the universe.
- mr president, i think that our debate on the state of the transatlantic dialogue is quite timely. i do not need to remind you how crucial this dialogue is in the perspective of cooperation between equal partners, between the united states of america and the european union. this dialogue is a way of addressing our differences, of settling some of our old trade disputes - i am thinking in particular of the banana case, which we finally settled a few weeks ago. i would like to emphasize the issue of european defence, which seems to me to be of the utmost importance, particularly as we are dealing with a new american administration which has already announced its plans for defence. obviously, the bush administration is much more suspicious of the esdp than the clinton administration, but that does not surprise me: it took the union several years to explain its objectives, to devise its means and to convince its american ally that european defence could be developed alongside nato. we must now preserve at all costs the achievements of the transatlantic dialogue. the concept of an ally should not be one-sided. it seems to me that if the union has been completely transparent in its presentation of the cfsp and then the esdp to the united states, it should also be made clear that the united states must consult its allies on any major project, and the missile shield project is one of them. as regards european defence policy itself, we must say forcefully, as we have always done, what we want and not systematically link every european defence question to nato's reaction. the union has always emphasised the complementarity of european action with that of the alliance, particularly with regard to the petersberg missions. this is not about competition or disengagement, but about union.

in writing. - the only reason we voted for this regulation is to avoid a vote against it being in the favour of those who are opposed even to this minimum aid to the poor countries. the commission has already made a number of proposals. to claim, for example, that this aid is being used to 'contribute to world food security' and 'respond to food emergencies', when hundreds of millions of people in the world are in emergency or even extreme distress, mainly because of past plunder by european powers represented here in parliament, is to try to give oneself a good conscience, at a good price.
in writing. - although this proposal is a simple statement of position which does not provide for how to impose its recommendations, we voted in favour because racism, xenophobia and anti-semitism are among the worst forms of barbarism that grow in the soil of present-day society. our vote is also an expression of our solidarity with all those who are fighting on this ground, as well as with those who are victims of this scourge, particularly in the territory of the european union which has the sad privilege of having given birth to its most abject forms and which is still affected by it today.
in writing. - the proposal for a recommendation on the position of the european union at the world conference against racism, xenophobia, anti-semitism and intolerance contains several positive points. but europe cannot 'fall into complacency'. indeed, 50 years after the holocaust, member countries actively participated in the genocide in rwanda... and many european minorities such as the roma are now persecuted. centuries of slavery and colonization have weighed heavily on the history of the member countries. however, the pressure and dependence of many countries continues and immigration policies are worrying. we have already had occasion to speak on the subject. the criminalisation of immigrants is a real scandal against people fleeing political or economic oppression. if we want to actively combat racism and xenophobia, we must respect the right to asylum, develop a policy of regularizing all undocumented people in europe, and grant the right to vote to third-country nationals in all elections. these are some of the measures that can be taken to combat racism and xenophobia effectively. finally, in order to meet the needs of the citizens, it is important that the european union should decide to cancel the debt and impose the tobin tax.
in writing. - the european parliament, in its resolution on police, justice and the movement of persons, which it has just voted on, calls once again for a complete 'communitarisation' of immigration policy and all related policies, such as asylum and temporary protection. we are also obliged to reiterate once again that, while european coordination is obviously indispensable, it must be up to each people to make the final, sovereign and decisive decision as to who may remain on its territory. the treaty of amsterdam had already transferred these matters to a community framework, removing them from the national parliaments, but with two essential exceptions to the usual procedures: the commission must share the initiative for texts with the member states for a transitional period limited to five years after the entry into force of amsterdam (i.e. until 1 may 2004); the council takes decisions not by qualified majority but by unanimity for at least five years, which allows each people to retain a temporary sovereign power. the european parliament's resolution adopted today attacks these two exceptions most vehemently: it denies the member states any right to propose texts, on the pretext that they would be exercising this power in an unorderly manner; the commission is also proposing that qualified majority voting be introduced more widely (or fully? this is not clear), a wish which would be largely fulfilled by the treaty of nice if it were to be ratified. our position is the opposite: if majority voting were to take place on immigration issues, the power would be taken away from the people and given to uncontrollable 'lobbies', unless it is to a member country better placed than others in the decision-making procedures. for the sake of europe, it is appropriate to leave these powers, both of proposal and decision, within the sovereign competence of each nation. in particular, direct decision-making power should be given to national parliaments.
in writing. - the draft resolution itself acknowledges that 'the member states and the council have failed to give substance to a common policy on asylum and immigration'. as for national policies, instead of being relaxed, they are becoming more restrictive. in the european union, capital and goods have long been free to move. but not men. it is the admission that this european union was not made for men, but for capital and those who own it. we have of course voted against this motion for a resolution. we reiterate our demand for complete freedom of establishment and movement for all those who live and work in a country of the european union and for the same political, legal and social rights as community citizens.
in writing. - the abolition of frontiers and the completion of the single market on 1 january 1993 have highlighted the existence of a market of more than 370 million consumers, for which it was necessary to provide for accompanying rules to guarantee a number of rights. the directive 92/59/eec on general product safety (gpsd) was developed with this in mind. although the overall approach of the 1992 directive has proved satisfactory, not all of its objectives have been achieved due to a lack of clarity or shortcomings in some of its provisions. the proposal is interesting in general, but several very important amendments, which were adopted by parliament at first reading, in particular with regard to the security of services, the precautionary principle, product surveillance and the european product safety network, were not taken up. the committee responsible has therefore rightly decided to put them forward again. the common position, however, takes up the parliament's amendments on charity shops in a recital which states that, in the context of charitable activities, it may prove impossible to provide information on the origin of a product and the possible risks it presents. the council also introduced a number of innovations compared with the commission's initial proposal, in particular: amendment of the definitions of 'product' and 'safe product' to clarify the scope of the directive, in particular as regards services; introduction, also for the sake of clarity, of additional definitions concerning 'serious risk' and 'withdrawal'; introduction of a three-stage procedure, with recourse to the regulatory committee, for the development of european standards; addition of provisions to promote a more voluntary role for producers and distributors. these proposals are in the right direction. product safety must be taken into account in the adoption of the rules governing the internal market. this is a key condition for regaining consumer confidence, which has been somewhat shaken by the various scandals that have recently surfaced. this is essential for the proper functioning of the internal market. the amendment of this directive is therefore a step in the right direction!
in writing. - although the commission's proposals aim to strengthen port state control through increased inspections and more stringent procedures, we are wondering what political will remains in governments to end the oil spills 16 months after the erika sinking. the legislation must be applied by all member states, including belgium, portugal, france, ireland and the netherlands. the commission has also been asked to provide the necessary resources for monitoring, which means in practice the hiring of additional inspectors and the extension of the powers and areas of control, particularly with regard to compliance with social standards and the living and working conditions of the crew. the fact that the largest possible number of vessels - oil tankers, bulk carriers and passenger ships - are equipped with vdrs is a positive point but should not exempt states from carrying out the necessary checks. the need to establish as soon as possible a body of european inspectors and coastguards with adequate financial, human and material resources will also be necessary. the council's proposals on the blacklist flags are still too timid. much stronger commitments must be made with regard to flags of convenience, particularly those belonging to member states such as those belonging to the kerguelen islands, wallis and futuna. we must demand that they be abolished and that all vessels which do not comply with these rules be prohibited from sailing in community waters.
in writing. - eighteen months after the sinking of the erika, is it necessary to recall the distress, the suffering, the anger of the people of our atlantic coast so badly affected in its maritime and tourist activities? we must remember the slow and inadequate compensation which, in many cases, is still delayed. in this house, the day after this tragic accident, i proposed the following policy lines: - the polluter-cleaner principle: will we leave the responsibility for cleaning up our coastlines to the communities, to the citizens, who are the victims? - the polluter pays principle: to emphasise the responsibility of shipowners and charterers in this type of disaster. - full and prompt compensation for the victims. - maintaining the community fleet and shipyards at an acceptable level, instead of allowing fleets to develop in our seas, in our ports, over which we have no control, flags of convenience with no traceability possible. - strengthening community legislation allowing for the inspection and certification of vessels operating in community waters, and banning dangerous vessels. after 18 months, what about the measures requested? the texts which parliament is voting on today are welcome and go in the right direction: in the watts report we see the strengthening of port state controls, the rigour of inspections and procedures; we support the rapporteur's requests for the use of travel data recorders. in the ortuondo report we see legislation on ship certification companies becoming more demanding, and we welcome that. we are also following with interest the progress of the erika ii package, which we are looking forward to. but we are still far from the necessary measures concerning compensation for victims, the polluter-cleaner principle, the rebalancing of maritime traffic between the various ports of the community, and the encouragement of the maintenance and development of our merchant fleets. these measures are becoming more urgent as a result of the overcrowding of european ports, particularly in the english channel and the north sea.
in writing. - we are voting today, at second reading, on the ortuondo larrea report on classification societies. some amendments go in the right direction by proposing a strict prohibition on the administration from engaging approved organisations if they have an economic interest in the management or ownership of ships, or by reaffirming the need for consistency between the european standard and the imo. other measures to reduce financial responsibilities do not seem acceptable to us. they are intended only to enforce the rules of competition between states, irrespective of the extent of the consequences due to errors or negligence on the part of the approved body. the responsibility must be full and complete, and the court or tribunal must judge and decide freely according to the reality of each disaster. as is often the case, this report proposes improvements in transparency or harmonisation, but limits the actual scope by not allowing sufficient financial sanctions.
in writing. -(de) this package on increasing safety in maritime transport is a response to the sinking of the oil tanker erika on 12 december 1999. despite the adoption of a large number of amendments by the european parliament, such as the exclusion of classification societies having any commercial, personal or family links with the owner or manager of the ship, the improvement of transparency by requiring classification societies to make all relevant information available to all interested parties on an internet site, and finally the control of classification societies whose classified ships have had too many accidents, parliament and the council have still not reached agreement on two crucial points and that is why, in the event of adoption of these recommendations, a conciliation procedure is required. first, the european parliament proposed to set limits on the financial liability of classification societies in the event of accidents due to negligence, inconsistency or omission in their duty of control. the council is in favour of legislation which allows member states to set the ceilings to be paid, although the amounts set by parliament in this respect are minimum amounts and not ceilings. secondly, the council did not accept the idea of regular consultations with accredited bodies to ensure the equal value of their technical standards in the light of the provisions of imo resolution a.837 (29), the idea of regular reporting on the essential progress of these standards to the commission, or the idea of collaboration with port state control authorities. since my group is convinced that a common position is possible on these two outstanding issues, we believe that the conciliation procedure is important.
in writing. - the report which originated this proposal states that 'a number of transport companies in the european union are using all sorts of ploys to employ cheap equipment and staff from third countries where the costs of equipment and staff are well below those in the european union'. this means that many land transport employers employ drivers who are underpaid and work in precarious conditions for journeys outside their home countries. but what worries the author of the report is not the situation of drivers, their too low wages or their unacceptable working conditions, but the resulting "distortions of the conditions of competition". the solution envisaged is to 'introduce a uniform driving licence', which would be compulsory in all the countries of the european union. it would have been better to have made it compulsory for road haulage companies to pay the same wages, whether the driver is from the union or not. the introduction of a minimum wage, aligned with that of the country where it is highest, would have been the best way of combating 'social dumping'. but the european authorities prefer to impose a single administrative form throughout the european union rather than imposing on road haulage companies salaries and working conditions that are appropriate for all their drivers, whatever their origin. the proposed reform does not therefore concern workers and we therefore abstained.
in writing. - the van dam report, which aims to introduce a uniform certificate for drivers of goods transport operating in europe, is a positive point. but we do not take the rapporteur's position on the question of 'fair competition' in this sector. the single market has liberalised road freight transport. the airlines then used and abused all the ploys to employ cheap equipment and staff from third countries in particular. a system of complacency has developed in this field, similar to that which exists in maritime transport. the pursuit of profit at any cost by transport managers leads to over-exploitation of the workforce, which considerably aggravates the risk factor of this mode. we insist on the need to harmonize the labour law of road drivers operating in europe on the basis of the most favourable acquis for employees, starting with their training, working time and conditions, remuneration and pensions. in addition, it is imperative that member states hire sufficient number of inspectors and controllers to enforce existing legislation. for these reasons, and mainly for these reasons, we are voting in favour of this report.
in writing. - as we have no particular preferences for the duration of the sessions, we abstained on the proposal for a calendar. we believe, however, that whatever the majority of members votes, the employees of the european parliament, both statutory and non-statutory, must not suffer in any way from this decision, particularly by a reduction in their salaries. there is no reason to punish staff for a choice which only affects the way members work or even their personal conveniences.
in writing. - it is our responsibility as responsible politicians to take care of the health of europeans, especially the youngest. the increase in the use of alcohol by children and adolescents calls for our utmost vigilance. that is why i voted in favour of this recommendation from the european parliament which calls on the member states to take measures to protect young people. it is therefore desirable that awareness-raising measures be carried out in the countries of the european community to make children, adolescents and parents more aware of the dangers of excessive alcohol consumption. children and adolescents are particularly receptive to messages, and appropriate instruction can lead to tangible results. remember, youths are the prime victims of these fatal accidents that result from the abuse of alcohol. so spreading relevant messages, educating them from an early age about the dangers of excessive drinking, could help to avoid some of the tragedies we have experienced. but we have to differentiate between alcohols. for example, we know that moderate consumption of wine can have health benefits. that is why we do not want to condemn the producers in any way. our goal is to curb the excessive consumption of alcohol among young people. however, producers have a role to play. so parents should not make teenagers the primary target of their commercial and advertising campaigns. we know the impact these can have on young people, and temptation must be regulated in favour of prevention. finally, a reflection on the warnings to be affixed to products, such as the one existing in france in the field of advertising, should be carried out to judge its possible effectiveness.
in writing. - the use of alcohol by adolescents, and increasingly by children, is a real concern and we must do everything we can as responsible adults to protect young europeans from abuse or, as the rapporteur says, from harmful use of alcohol. that is why we shall vote in favour of mrs stihler's report and most of its amendments. i would add, however, that the protection of children and young people against a number of perversions must be absolute. yes, we must protect europe's young people from alcoholism. but it also needs to be protected from drugs, including what some would call "soft" drugs. it must also be protected from the actions of perverts, from the sexual practices that some leftists advocated in the 1970s to "awaken the middle class" and justify their shameful pedophilia. that is why i am surprised that a report like mrs stihler's can coexist in this house with the speeches of activists for the decriminalisation of cannabis use or against the death penalty. there can be no double standards when it comes to the health, the balance and the future of our children.
in writing. - the european institutions have long been pushing, with subsidies, for intensive agriculture and livestock farming that correspond to the interests of the agro-food industries. intensive livestock farming and the massive use of animal meal have led to bovine spongiform encephalopathy. even though the responsibility of animal meal for the spread of this disease was clearly established, the european institutions helped to conceal the disease and to distribute subsidies to encourage production and marketing. in view of the scale of the disaster, the european authorities changed their attitude, much too late. under the guise of financing the reparation of the errors of the previous period, they have rushed into a policy of 'purchasing for destruction', which the european budget has difficulty following. now, after having pushed for intensive farming, efforts are being made to "promote" extensive livestock farming and "organic agriculture". we abstained on this report which in fact calls for an end to a chaotic 'agricultural policy' in which the only constant factor is the payment of large sums in the form of subsidies which only partly benefit small farmers and to a much greater extent the cattle sector and the capitalist enterprises which thrive in the sector of feeding, processing and marketing of meat.
in writing. - the european commission is chasing bse. failing to treat the disease at its root in 1990, which jacques delors and his men refused to do in order not to hinder the glorious march towards the single market first, and the euro second, we have since then been constantly multiplying financial and technical palliatives to deal with the endless effects of the health, commercial and financial catastrophe in particular. this is the case with the new measure for beef cmo, which has been very well reported on by mr sturdy. to save the market which it has led to its ruin, the commission is returning to its ideological malthusianism. the special premium for male bovine animals and suckler cows would be capped again at 90 head or 1.8 gbu/ha. this would limit the supply of meat to meet the declining demand. each state will set the individual ceiling for each of its producers. our colleague mr sturdy proposes a series of amendments to maintain the income of farmers, especially when they are farmers. for example, the premium for bulls is proposed to be increased. the commission is also proposing to increase the current budget of eur 10 million, which is insufficient, to promote beef. the summit is reached with a special purchase regime of cattle over 30 months old to store and unload them at an unknown date, like a patient is cryogenically frozen in the hope of resuscitation when medicine has evolved. when we know that public stocks are increasing by 50 000 tonnes a month, that in april 2001 the commission had already bought back 175 000 tonnes and that the cattle sector in 2001 spent 7 billion euros in credit, we can see the extent of the financial disaster that the jacques delors team has planned by knowingly turning a blind eye to the beginnings of the esb case. the new measures proposed by brussels, which are ineffective, are intended to increase the slate by 1 billion and that is not the end of it.

in writing. - we are not against the decision to 'grant unlimited access to the european community market for all products originating in the ldcs, with the exception of arms and ammunition' because there is no reason to impose customs duties on products from the poorest countries at the borders of the european union. but it is clear that this measure, which is presented as being in favour of the poorest countries, will mainly favour the multinational companies established in these countries, which are generally the only ones producing and selling on the international market. it is a sign of hypocrisy and false appearance in this area that the only three products for which the application of this decision is delayed are bananas, sugar and rice, that is to say three products whose production and marketing are in the hands of powerful trusts, competing with each other for control of the international market. the commission has also proposed that the community should be able to provide aid to the poorest countries in the developing countries, in order to help them to develop their technological capacity and to export finished products. that's why we abstained. the report rightly concludes that the gap between the 48 poorest countries and the rest of the world has "grown wider again". the development of these countries, where a large part of humanity lives in conditions beyond description, would require an international sharing of wealth that is absolutely incompatible with a world economic order based on inequality, exploitation and plunder of poor countries for the benefit of the capitalist class in rich countries.

the council. - the council has not discussed the specific matter raised in the question. contrary to what the question implies, there is no community legislation on arms exports. the question cannot therefore arise as to whether a particular transaction is illegal or not in relation to community law. the code of conduct to which the honourable member refers was adopted on 8 june 1998 and is based on common criteria for transfers of conventional arms. according to the implementing provisions of the code of conduct, each member state will 'examine on a case-by-case basis the applications for export licences for military equipment submitted to it, in the light of the provisions of the code of conduct'. the decision whether to grant export licences is thus taken by each member state and it is not for the council to assess such individual transactions. the code requires member states to exchange information on their arms exports annually in the council, which allows for a common assessment of the functioning of the code. the annual assessment of the functioning of the code is reflected in an annual report in accordance with implementing regulation 8. the council's general policy on the conflict in western sahara is to give full support to the efforts of the united nations and the personal envoy of the un secretary-general, mr james baker, to find a solution to the conflict. the council is convinced that the un process provides the best framework for a rapid, lasting and agreed solution which would also enhance stability in the whole region. it is clear that any solution must be acceptable to all parties and must be based on full respect for fundamental democratic principles and human rights. in line with these political objectives, the council is willing to contribute to the process and to help create a climate of trust and confidence between the parties concerned. in line with this, the union proposed a number of humanitarian and confidence-building measures to the parties concerned at the end of last year. the union is in close contact with mr james baker and is examining how best to support the un's efforts. i would also like to stress that the european union is the largest donor of humanitarian aid to the sahrawi refugees, with 20 million euros in aid over the last three years.

same strategic principles when it comes to the future orientation of the slovak republic. however, as the president of a young democratic country, i cannot fall victim to the feeling of self-satisfaction with this rare political consensus. ever since i assumed my presidential office i have been trying to impress not only on the political leaders, but also on all those who are not indifferent to the future of slovakia, that the direction of the country must not depend on a momentary euphoria or on the fleeting political preferences of those in power. this is the reason why i and a group of experts are drafting a medium-term and a long-term vision, which should be adopted as a constitutional statute by the national council of the slovak republic with the support of the broadest possible political spectrum. this document – may i call it a state doctrine – should define in very clear terms and at the highest legislative level the future orientation of slovakia to the european and transatlantic structures. it would convincingly dispel the doubts with which i am often confronted during by trips abroad in my discussions with the friends and observers of slovakia who ask: "what changes can be again expected in the foreign policy orientation of slovakia after the next elections?" as i have said, we are pleased with the public support for the integration ambitions of slovakia. however, we cannot ignore the worries or mistrust among citizens of the eu member states who fear that the enlargement of the union could have undesirable consequences. i can understand their concerns – they are natural and human. at the same time i have the impression that these worries are often conjured up artificially. it is not our wish to disturb what has been achieved in the integration process in past decades. we have to jointly focus on two areas. we – in the applicant countries – must thoroughly prepare for membership and, together with the eu members, we should alleviate the doubts concerning enlargement. and we must work together to strengthen european solidarity and the feeling of togetherness. europe is not only a map. i am convinced that the basis for its permanent revival is an ongoing honest dialogue with the citizens of the unifying europe. the entry of each new country will enrich the common house by its spiritual, cultural and historical heritage. we want to contribute to the enlargement of the common market but at the same time we want to be a contribution to the economy and thus contribute to greater stability and security for all of europe. you are familiar with the fact that the slovak republic was not invited to open accession negotiations in 1997 in luxembourg because of its failure to fulfil the copenhagen political criteria. this was not a good situation for slovakia. the european parliament was the first to respond to the new situation in the slovak republic through its resolution of october 1998, which acknowledged the changes in the style of government of the country and its new orientation after the elections. i would like to take this opportunity to state how highly i regard the relations between the european parliament and the slovak republic which, especially during the last two years, have gained a new momentum. the relations between the european parliament and the national council of the slovak republic have also intensified thanks to the activities of the joint parliamentary committee which i personally highly appreciate. parliamentary democracy is also greatly strengthened by the joint meetings between the president of the european parliament and the presidents of the parliaments of applicant countries. the next such meeting is to be held in a few days in bratislava. slovakia was invited to open negotiations on accession to the european union in 1999 in helsinki. today – after 17 months of negotiations – we note great progress. i am convinced that by the end of the swedish presidency we will provisionally close negotiations on more than half the chapters. at this rate our country has a chance to catch up with the countries that had started negotiations earlier, and to complete accession negotiations by the end of 2002. we make no secret of our hope that the citizens of the slovak republic will also cast their votes in the 2004 elections to the european parliament. the path of integration is interspersed with exceptionally lively political discussions and, sometimes, disputes. we are happy that we have got rid of the one-sided monologue of political elites we knew in the past. this path is not a smooth one, but the prospect of future membership of the european union multiplies the sorely needed pro-reform energy. i want to assure you that we have no shortage of this energy. the year 2000 was the year of the "economy". we continued implementing the reforms launched by the slovak government after its coming to power in 1998 with a view to restoring stability at the macro-economic level. structural adjustment brought improvements in the effectiveness of the corporate sector. however, if i want to take a realistic view of the economy of my country, i must consider it from the point of view of the everyday life of people, their economic possibilities. and here i realise – as confirmed in my direct contacts with the citizens of my country – that economic reforms can have painful consequences for the socially weakest groups of the population. i am convinced that the current – and the most difficult – phase of the reform will soon bring its positive effects. in this respect, i feel that the slovak government may have lost some time when, during its first year in power, it was too absorbed with pointing to the mistakes of the previous government and pronouncements of the need to eliminate their consequences, rather than immediately and constructively tackling all the problems, especially in the economic field. it is too late to say now that if the style of government had been more flexible right from the start, today the citizens could enjoy the fruit of all those sound economic steps. this too is the reason why in every political or professional discussion on the subject of economic and legal reforms i stand up as an advocate of the reforms, even though i always view them in terms of their benefits for the majority of our citizens. this year, 2001, is the year of "legislation". in february the slovak parliament passed the long awaited amendment to the constitution, compatible with the constitutions of eu member states. the amendment has put in place the legal prerequisites for the integration of slovakia. the amended text explicitly provides that the slovak republic may delegate the exercise of some of its powers to the european union through or on the basis of an international treaty. the amendment also lays down the precedence of legally binding acts of the european union over the laws of the slovak republic. moreover, it sets out the procedure for the transposition of legally binding acts into the national legislation in the form of laws and government ordinances. other necessary steps include the taking of measures for implementing public administration reform, completing structural reform, strengthening the banking sector and building a modern state administration. the national legal system of the slovak republic is based on the principles of democracy and the rule of law. through its constitution and the ratified international instruments on human rights, the state guarantees the enjoyment of rights and freedoms to all citizens without any distinction. however, unemployment and the adverse economic situation in some regions of slovakia have created serious problems for dealing with the issue of the roma national minority. in my opinion, finding effective solutions in this area is one of the most important tasks of society as a whole. the serious attention given to this problem by the government is expressed through the government's strategy for addressing roma national minority issues and the set of measures for its implementation. i take the view that this is not a problem of slovakia alone, but a broader european problem whose solution is very complex and requires a partner-like approach. the visit to roma settlements in slovakia by commissioner günther verheugen exemplifies the commitment to a common approach to dealing with the roma issue, which is one of the key areas that will require our attention in the future. during my years as the mayor of the city of kosice, situated in the region with higher concentrations of the roma population, i learned the basic precept – effective assistance requires active involvement of the roma themselves in the solution of their problems, otherwise the efforts will be wasted. the project on eliminating the disproportions of the roma national minority, launched on my initiative, envisages the participation of the representatives of individual roma groups in its implementation. the first experience gained indicates that the level of legal awareness and democratic thinking – even among educated roma – has been marked by decades of a paternalistic approach by the state to the roma community whose members find it difficult to exercise their powers. this is why i believe that this issue will still have to be addressed by the generations that come after us. i have also brought my initiative to the attention of the presidents of other visegrad group countries; we agreed to adopt a common procedure with the president of the czech republic. i fully agree with the individual approach and the assessment of the countries on their merits. this is the reason why we internally are striving to make the slovak republic take its place among the first countries to enter the european union. we make no secret of our ambition to do it together with our neighbours – the czech republic, hungary and poland, our partners in the visegrad cooperation process. this cooperation, which strengthens our good neighbourly relations, is being positively received both at home and abroad. not only does it enhance the atmosphere of regional european allegiance, but is also an important element of integration. in this connection, on my initiative and in cooperation with the president of the republic of poland, several cross-border cooperation projects were launched under the patronage of the chancellery of the president. because of their positive results i plan to extend similar projects also to other border regions – those with hungary and the czech republic. i attach great historic significance to the creation and functioning of the visegrad grouping whose aim is to encourage close cohesion of an mutually beneficial cooperation within the central european region as the basis for its future integration into economic, political and security structures. these common objectives of the v-4 countries contribute to the development of europe as a whole and to expanding the zone of stability to the entire continent. the idea of the accession of visegrad countries to the european union as one group has logical implications for the definition of the schengen-type border whose length will depend on the map of the enlarged european union. when speaking about the future of the european union, the discussion on which was launched in the wake of the nice summit, i would personally prefer to speak about the near future and the distant future. it would not be easy to mix everything together and to try to resolve all the issues facing the european union by 2004. i support the opinion that the candidate countries should be given a chance to effectively contribute to the exchange of views in the preparation for the 2004 intergovernmental conference. it is personally hardly conceivable for me to see the prospective members of a family left standing at a closed door during the discussions on important matters that concern everybody, older members, newer members and prospective newcomers, especially if the latter are expected to enter the family within the time horizon in question. we all, both members and candidates for membership, want a stronger europe. we may agree with many, although not all the opinions. thus, it would not be appropriate to delay the process of enlargement on the ground of what i consider to be unjustified worries about the enlargement bringing the threat of "dilution" of the european union, or endangering the possibility of the continued political integration. i am convinced that the slovak republic and other candidate countries are no less prepared for further integration than some current members. our objective must be to further build the european union as a political community. i agree with the words of the president of the european parliament madame nicole fontaine according to whom we cannot continue building the european union in "closed circles". at a certain stage of development, several issues may emerge and require solution, while it is not always possible to resolve all of them. but the process must continue and the system must remain open. an important part of the entire european integration process is the building of the european identity. national identity plays an important role in the life of individuals, because it is the means for their self-identification and affiliation with a certain group. as the president and a citizen of the slovak republic, i have no worries about the loss of sovereignty after our accession to the european union, because in an integrating europe, a sovereign country is one that takes part in the decisions that concern the development and direction of the european union. the entry of the slovak republic to the european union will be the real completion of sovereignty of our country. (applause) the future of slovakia lies with the european union which will become the area of freedom, security and justice. i am speaking to you as a european to europeans, facing a unique challenge and immense responsibility. let us turn the ideal of common spiritual values and historic experience into the reality of a unified and prosperous europe, attractive to all citizens of its countries and serving as an example for other regions and continents. the slovak republic declares its willingness to share in this common responsibility. thank you for this opportunity of addressing you (loud and sustained applause)

- the next item is the report (a5-0167/2001) by mrs schleicher, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the proposal for a council regulation on the statute and funding of european political parties (com (2000) 898 - c5-0081/2001 - 2001/0011 (cns)).
- madam president, i just wanted to go back for a few seconds to what happened this morning. my group is a little concerned that procedural battles could overturn this text, which is important to us. we hope that the fact that there has been some sort of passage this morning will not put the future of this text in jeopardy because, for us, it is imperative that there be transparent funding of these european political parties. we know very well what those who refuse this financing mechanism expect. they still prefer a system where the suitcases pass in the shadows with tickets in them. let us be clear: the copy that has come out of the committee on constitutional affairs is not yet good. it doesn't really provide transparency. the democratic threshold for access to this funding is far too high. as for the nature of the funding, we are terribly concerned that private companies can finance political parties as they stand. we know very well what this also means: when a company funds a political party, it expects benefits in return. it's called organized corruption. so we hope, because there are now very good compromise amendments on the table, that transparency will be increased, that the democratic threshold, as my friend andrew duff said, will actually be lowered, five at once, and a quarter of the member states after nice, and above all, that private funding will be totally banned, because we, the greens/efa group, are not called upon to organise corruption, even in transparency. i am here to announce that our group will not vote on this report in the end, if private companies can buy political parties at european level with their money.
- madam president, the proposal for a regulation on the statute and funding of european political parties is not only inappropriate for all the reasons i will explain in my explanation of vote, but also lacks any legal basis. it is based on article 308 of the treaty establishing the community, but this can only be used where there is community competence for which there is no provision for action. the court of justice made this clear in its opinion of 28 march 1996 on the possible accession of the community to the european convention on human rights on the basis of article 308. it stated that the use of article 308 in such a case was impossible because there was no prior general competence of the community to define and amend fundamental rights. the court therefore concludes, in paragraph 30 of its judgment - which i shall quote in full - that 'as an integral part of an institutional order based on the principle of conferral of powers, this provision (article 308) cannot constitute a basis for extending the field of community competence beyond the general framework resulting from all the provisions of the treaty and in particular those which define the tasks and actions of the community. in any event, it cannot serve as a basis for the adoption of provisions which would, in substance and in their consequences, lead to an amendment of the treaty outside the procedure provided for in the treaty to that end. " today we find ourselves in exactly this situation with the european political parties. article 191 of the treaty mentions them, but it has only a declaratory value, since it does not confer any task on the community in relation to them. this article cannot therefore in any case be used as a starting point for the use of article 308. there is no community competence, so there is no article 308, that is clear. finally, i would add, in conclusion, that the reform proposed by the treaty of nice, which seeks to create the missing legal basis, has not yet been ratified, and i hope it will never be ratified, because it is contrary to the french constitution and to the general principles of a free society, according to which political parties must be free.
- madam president, we are therefore faced with one of the innovations of this parliament which is certainly not lacking in imagination or brutality when it comes to strengthening, securing and protecting the closed-loop system which it calls 'democracy'. madam rapporteur, for the good authors, your text is called teratogenesis, that is to say the creation of monsters, a discipline in which the good dr frankenstein illustrates himself before you. it is therefore proposed that we create european political parties ex nihilo, an exceptional phrase since it is not a party - they will not participate in the expression of universal suffrage whose framework remains national - since it is not a political one either, since the sole purpose of this text is to allow the large groups in parliament to escape a decision of the european court of auditors, and all this is european only because it is neither african nor asian. in reality, madam rapporteur, behind the pompous name of a european political party there is a scheme as old as the world, the great raffle for the benefit of the raffle organizers or, if you prefer, a comfortable pension awarded to the parliamentary groups that are most docile towards the institutions that this parliament is nevertheless responsible either for monitoring - such as the commission - or with which it intends to share the decision - that is, the council - a pension granted by these institutions themselves. in plain english, it would be called a concussion.
the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. we are firmly convinced that article 191 of the treaty sets out an important principle. i quote: 'political parties at european level are important as a factor of integration in the union. they help to build european awareness and to express the political will of the citizens of the union. if this is the case, then if the european parties are to play their assigned role, they must be placed on a solid and legitimate basis in an open and transparent manner and must be given the necessary resources for their work. in summary, this is the rationale behind the proposal for a regulation on the financing of european political parties which we are debating today. first of all, i would like to thank mrs schleicher for her excellent work. i would also like to thank the other committees on behalf of the commission for their amendments, in particular mr marinho of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market and mr costa neves of the committee on budgets. i would like to return briefly to the question of the legal basis for the proposal and, in the light of yesterday's debate, to stress once again that the commission, as the guardian of the treaties, has of course examined very carefully what the legal basis is and can be. article 191 is merely declaratory in the wording of the maastricht treaty and contains no specific provision which would enable the necessary rule to be adopted. we understood the urgent appeal that was made to us last year after the court of auditors' report criticizing the practices of the past, namely to find ways and means of establishing a solid legal basis. as you know, we have decided to take a two-pronged approach. the first step which has now been taken in nice was to include a specific provision in article 191 so that in future it will be possible to adopt a legal act on the financing of european political parties by qualified majority voting and by co-decision. at the same time we have proposed a transitional arrangement on the basis of article 308. that is a sound legal basis for this proposal. we have been strengthened in this respect by the political signal given at the highest political level in nice. we are pleased that the legal affairs committee of this parliament also supports the concept of the transitional arrangements based on article 308. the commission has tried to follow two principles in its proposal. firstly, we wanted to leave room for manoeuvre and development in the definition of european parties. the commission has also been asked to present a report on the implementation of the european year of the environment, which will be presented to the european parliament in the autumn. as regards the definition of european parties, let me say quite clearly that european parties do not have to follow a specific european political course, but they must respect the values of democracy, the rule of law and respect for fundamental rights. as the amendments originally submitted to the committee on constitutional affairs showed, there can be a wide range of views on how exactly the principles of funding should be implemented. the commission has tried to find a consensus and a middle ground. i would like to deal with the main amendments before the house. we share the view that there should be a reference to the charter of fundamental rights. we also share the view that european political parties should have legal personality. we also welcome greater or high levels of transparency in private donations to political parties, i.e. the disclosure of these donations. we also consider the amendments which would allow the provision of parliament's services to political parties against payment to be open to discussion. however, it is guaranteed that this will not lead to hidden party financing. the right arrangements must be found. the commission's proposal is based on the principle of subsidiarity, which is the principle that the member states must be represented in the european parliament. let me note that after a long discussion the commission has explicitly chosen an absolute number and not a relative number, i.e. not a third or a quarter, because that would naturally raise the question, particularly in view of the enlargement process, of what happens if you have different numbers in the enlargement process during one legislative period. would it require an adjustment? what does a quarter mean in relation to the number of member states, 21 or 23? so, we have to find extra arrangements all the time. for this reason we therefore explicitly suggest the number 5. we felt that the most appropriate procedure was to settle disputes about the fulfilment of the condition of article 1, that is to say, the fulfilment of the criteria for european parties, independently of parliament. but this is a matter of political judgment, in which we take parliament's position, and therefore could accept amendment no 13. we cannot accept amendment no 22 on the duration of the regulation. we have special legal and constitutional difficulties with two amendments. firstly, amendment no 16, which would prohibit subsidies to publicly owned undertakings. apart from the difficulties of delimitation, we consider it difficult, in the light of article 295, to give a legal basis for such a ban at european level. secondly, the commission has considerable difficulties with amendment no 21 on sanctions. we can accept the second sentence: 'unjustly received aid must be repaid'. i would point out, however, that this is simply a repetition of normal budgetary rules. the principles mentioned in the first sentence are of course not to be objected to, but the procedure is inappropriate. grants are awarded by the commission in accordance with the usual rules. article 274 does not give the council or parliament the right to intervene in the implementation of the budget. the term 'appropriate sanction' used in the amendment is too vague and would raise legal problems. as regards the amendments adopted in committee, the commission can accept the following amendments: 1, 2, 3, amendment no 5 (first sentence), 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 17 (in part), 18, 19, 20 and 21 (in part). as regards the amendments tabled directly in the plenary, the commission could also accept amendments nos 23, 31, 32, 34, 37, 56, 58, 62. the same is true of motions for resolutions 33, 46 and 57, which are open to discussion. however, i would like to point out again the risks involved. i would like to make a brief comment on the duration of the programme. the commission has proposed that the scheme should expire after the second financial year of validity. why this temporary? i would like to point out once again that the experience gained in the last two years must also be incorporated into the next regulation. the issue of party financing is a politically sensitive area. it is therefore important that this matter be discussed and regulated in a transparent and open manner. the commission hopes that we will have such a transparent system very soon. it's in the democratic interest. this is in the democratic, common democratic interest. - the next item is the report (a5-0153/2001) by mrs gebhardt, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the initiative of the portuguese republic, the french republic, the kingdom of sweden and the kingdom of belgium with a view to adopting a council decision establishing eurojust to strengthen the fight against serious forms of organised crime [10357/2000 - c5-0396/2000 - 2000/0817 (cns)).
- madam president, ladies and gentlemen, in the face of the growing increase in organised crime, the european union has multiplied initiatives to strengthen the fight against criminal organisations and to improve cooperation between the investigating and prosecuting authorities. the tampere summit has given new prospects to this police and judicial cooperation, long considered the poor relation of european unification. eurojust, composed of prosecutors, magistrates and liaison police, has been the focus of all attention. but how can we envisage the proper functioning of a unit which is to be the future european public prosecutor's office in the absence of prior harmonisation of the laws of the member states and a minimum approximation of their procedures? is it not the aim for the member states to achieve the highest possible standard which ensures both sufficient procedural guarantees and effective justice for all citizens, while respecting human rights, including the right of defence? it is clear that we are dealing with a body which is not subject to any control by the european parliament. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. another point to keep in mind is the processing of data that the unit is responsible for. eurojust will also be responsible for collecting information on criminal records, police reports and registers in the member states as part of a network. questions are being asked. what protection will be given to the processing of this data? who will have access to them, who will use them? what right of reply and defence, or even of correction of incorrect or outdated data? the spirit of my amendments will be the condition for our support for this report. yes, the european union needs a supranational judicial structure to coordinate and strengthen public action throughout the eu. the stakes are of the utmost importance. it presupposes the will to implement a common criminal policy which will go hand in hand with a minimum of surrender of national sovereignty, whether the states want it or not. with eurojust, the aim is to give europol a genuine judicial partner. the full effectiveness of eurojust will depend on the complementarity and added value that the unit will be able to bring to other actors in the judicial and police worlds. i am not saying that we should be in favour of a european union. why do we have to have complex coordination between different countries to centralize an investigation if the magistrate in charge of the case has no means to carry out his investigation or to ensure the conviction of the persons charged? in conclusion, rather than endlessly speculating about the possible powers of a genuine european party, would it not be better to decide on a structure that would really stand out for its speed, its efficiency, its availability to the citizens of europe by giving them all the guarantees?

in writing. - i would remind you that the european commission's proposal, which is the subject of the report we have discussed today, aims to establish a community action programme 2001-2005 to support and encourage cooperation in the fight against social exclusion. the aim of this programme is to encourage member states to combine their efforts in the fight against poverty and social exclusion in europe through an open method of coordination. to be effective, this coordination must be based on national action plans to combat exclusion with guidelines drawn up at european level. the method has been found to work well in employment matters. the european parliament considered this text at first reading in november last year under the french presidency, which had supported many initiatives in the social field and was keen to make the fight against poverty a priority on the european social agenda. in the common position, the council adopted, in whole or in part, 25 of the 47 amendments adopted by parliament at its meeting on 16 november 2000, whereas the commission had tabled 31 amendments. i am very sorry to say that the council has rejected some very important amendments. it refused to refer to the revised social charter of the council of europe (1996, to which the charter of fundamental rights of the european union must now be added). it did not want to withhold funding of up to 90% of the activities carried out by ngos under the programme to combat poverty and social exclusion, the same rate of funding having already been accepted for the programme to combat discrimination. the funding of the programme is also a stumbling block. the european parliament, believing that it is necessary to have the means to achieve its ambitions, wanted to increase the budget from eur 70 million to eur 100 million, but in vain! the refusal to include explicitly the involvement of the european parliament in the monitoring of the programme is equally questionable. i have of course voted in favour of the amendments to reinstate the provisions which have not been approved by the council and/or the commission. i think that this programme must be as voluntary as possible. it must be an instrument for promoting equal opportunities for all citizens and a strong political signal from the european union. the overall positive statistics on growth and employment should not make us forget that too many people remain on the margins of our society.

in writing. - the commission's proposal to create a statute and funding for european political parties, like the schleicher report which supports it, has no legal basis, as i explained in the main debate. the persistence of the main federalist groups in pursuing the adoption process gives the true measure of the respect for the law in the europe they are building. the same could be said of the french government, which in its note of 9 may sees no objection to the use of article 308 in such a case. in substance, the proposed text reverses the logical course of a free society. at the national level, political parties are created by citizens, irrigated by their participation, and only in a second stage can the law eventually grant them public funding. the new text would do the opposite at european level: public funding from the community budget would be used to 'bring to life' european political parties which today are non-existent or have no real consistency. but the perversion does not stop there. tomorrow these artificial creatures will be invoked to justify the existence of a so-called 'european political scene', which itself will be produced as proof of the proper functioning of a 'european democracy'. and this largely invented 'european democracy' will in turn serve to justify the subtraction of powers from the national democracies, the only truly real ones. this anti-democratic machine of plundering the people is running at full speed, activated in this case by the lure of profit, since the ectoplasms that today call themselves "european political parties", supported by their friends in the european parliament, are eagerly awaiting the moment when they will be able to feed themselves on public funds. in addition to these fundamental reasons for our opposition, there are many other reasons for the irregularity of the text presented, because it gives a 'status' to political parties which should remain free, because it has been biased in favour of supporters of supranationality, because it establishes genuine political justice, because it introduces indefensible discrimination to the detriment of national parties acting directly at european level. it is from such texts that we can see how much there is a lack of constitutional review of secondary community legislation in france.
in writing. - the debate on the schleicher report during this part-session reveals particularly worrying undemocratic tendencies within the community institutions and particularly within this parliament. democracy is first and foremost respect for the law. but everyone knows perfectly well, even those who claim otherwise, that this project to finance european political parties has no legal in writing. - the eurojust judicial coordination unit, as it is now presented following an initiative by several member states, aims to ensure a good liaison between national prosecuting authorities in crossborder crime cases. this coordination excludes any act of authority towards the member states and any desire to integrate national judicial systems. it aims to improve the cooperation between the different judicial actors and is part of a clearly intergovernmental framework. we welcome this approach because it is the most realistic: it does not dream of a general merger of national legal systems - an impossible dream, which only delays concrete solutions - but it seeks, on the contrary, to work on the basis of existing judicial networks, removing the technical obstacles which might impede the smooth running of their relations. for once, the parliament's report seems to be in agreement with this realism: it does not reject this initiative a priori, as it has tended to do in recent times, on the pretext that it would come from the states, and not from the commission; it shall not make its usual calls for the establishment of a supranational european public prosecutor, a unified body of law or federal criminal courts; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. however, this apparent moderation is fraught with several pitfalls. firstly, the amendments proposed by the european parliament seek to strengthen the centralisation around the eurojust unit, in particular by requiring the removal of national correspondents, thus surreptitiously renouncing the idea of a 'network' on which the system should be based. above all, these amendments completely overturn the intergovernmental spirit by transforming requests for investigations or prosecutions expressed by eurojust into decisions binding on the member states, and by removing any room for manoeuvre for the member states in the application of judicial acts carried out on their territories. we find this surreptitious alteration of the original text completely unacceptable.
in writing. - of course, we must adopt a policy of strengthening the fight against all forms of corruption, both at national and european level. we have said this time and again, especially since the schengen agreements have abolished checks at the borders of the member states. all these serious questions, which concern the very exercise of justice, public freedoms and public order, can only fall within the competence of the states. it must be remembered that justice is a royal right, that is to say, a right organized by the national public power. however, in the face of the rise of all forms of organised and crossborder crime, and in the face of growing insecurity and violence, interstate cooperation between the police and judicial services of the member states is desirable. but now, under the guise of this cooperation, europe is trying to impose on us a communitization of our judicial system and our internal public order, in particular by creating a european public prosecutor's office. the nice council of december 2000 rightly rejected the creation of this supranational prosecutor, considering that the latter measure was dangerous for the respect of human rights and democracy. the european parliament is once again ignoring the deep feelings of the member states. following an old habit of going in through the window in disguise after going out the door, he tried, with the help of mrs guigou, then french minister of justice, to make eurojust an embryo of a european public prosecutor's office. thus, a single prosecutor's office, independent of the member states, could, at its discretion, decide to arrest, prosecute or extradite persons, without any possibility of appeal to the judicial authorities of the states concerned. any progress on the common security ? no, it's more like a new step towards confusing the skills.
