- the following reports are requested for joint debate: - report (a5-0206/2001) by mrs karamanou, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, on the proposal for a council framework decision on combating the sexual exploitation of children and child pornography (com (2000) 854 - c5-0043/2001 - 2001/0025 (cns)) - report (a5-0183/2001) by mrs klamt, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, on the proposal for a framework decision on combating trafficking in human beings (com (2000) 854 - c5-0042/2001 - 2001/0024 (cns)).
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to return to the signing by the european union of the additional protocol of palermo, which was entitled 'protocol against trafficking in human beings, in particular women and children'. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i do not think that it is enough to talk about human trafficking. it was in palermo that the specification "women and children" was proposed. the amendment calls for the purposes of sexual exploitation to be formulated before those of labour exploitation, and i think that is very right, because we know very well - let us not be hypocrites - that trafficking concerns first and foremost women and children. we know that by putting the exploitation of labour before the exploitation of sex we are betraying reality. that is why amendment no 1 is important to me and i hope the commission will be sensitive to it. it is also important to me that trafficking should be considered a crime and not a crime. all sexual exploitation is a crime, not just a misdemeanor; we must know this, we must emphasize it, we must be aware of it and we must not play with these inaccuracies. i thank our various committees and rapporteurs for insisting on this. i would add that in all the amendments there are some very important additions to the status of victims. they deal with at least three points. firstly, there is the fact that we can speak of incitement, which may be one of the punishable causes. incitement, not just fraud. the distinction between these two concepts is obviously a thin one. then there is the vulnerability of the victims, beyond the pressures we could easily identify; i think the vulnerability of the victims is important, too. finally, it was the council of europe, in its recommendation of may 2000, which insisted on the point of 'the non-applicability of the argument of consent'. that's another important thing. the victim's consent or non-consent is not always relevant; it's not even relevant. i think we must be vigilant in this respect and recognize that consent is not an argument to exonerate those who are involved in trafficking. that is why these reports are important to me. i thank both rapporteurs. i would like to say, unlike others, that i would obviously like to see more cooperation between the member states. how can we combat trafficking if there is no cooperation between member states? does this proposal provide for sufficient cooperation? it's not safe, and i personally wish for more. and this is so that we can identify all the victims, both men and women, because, of course, men can be victims of trafficking and sexual exploitation, too. men and women, but especially women and children. i would remind you that one of the amendments proposes that we recognize that adulthood begins at 18 and that persons under 18 are to be considered children.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this report raises the question of a phenomenon which, according to what is said, exists, at least as far as public opinion is concerned, at the highest levels of some of the member states. there are reasons for the explosion of child pornography, and those reasons are the first to be addressed. i'd see two. the first is the explosion of pornography itself and the second is the progression, alas, of the disregard of children and childhood. the explosion of pornography itself is due to the disappearance of moral standards, to the domination of this spirit of pleasure, the bitter fruits of which are seen. we are now seeing the results of the slogan 'play without restraint' which was used by some of the members of this parliament in the 1960s. it inevitably leads to the search for extreme sensations, to the search for violence, sadism, and it is the fruit of a trivialization that spreads in newspapers, in the cinema and on television. that's the first factor. the second is the contempt of childhood. it must be said that it begins very early, since we are proud, at the same time as we are discussing the ill-treatment of certain children, to present as a right, as a progress of civilization, the fact of organizing the elimination of unborn children in our public hospitals. it should not be surprising that our civilization is headlong in this regard. the 'right to the child' outside the family bond, outside normal sexual relations, the 'right to adoption' by homosexuals, for example, are also claims that are making their way, including in the conservative press, and all this cannot be without impact. the report is not intended to be a criticism of the excellent provisions of the report. the council's legal instruments, however, are a little different: why a framework decision rather than a directive when it is a question of amending several very important provisions of the criminal code in each of the member states? i should also like to say a word about the methodology used in the report. the commission's draft was drafted in terms which were sufficiently general to encompass all kinds of incriminations. we wanted to complete them. has not the editorial staff been considerably increased in certain areas? on the other hand, we support the definition of aggravating circumstances as the employment of children under 16 or of children with physical or mental disabilities. a particular point is raised by amendment no 26, which amends article 8 (3) of the draft. this amendment is intended to cover the case where a state, we are told, applies the principle of 'double criminalization' to its own nationals who are guilty of child pornography. in such a case, however, he must take action. what exactly is meant by the term 'principle of double incrimination'? is this the principle which jurists know by its latin expression, non bis in idem? it would then be a question of the principle of non-double incrimination, that is to say, the refusal of an indictment against a national as soon as he is prosecuted in another member state. i think we need to revise the editorial on this point. the definition of pornography is more comprehensive in the report than in the original draft, such as that of material which can be used for child pornography or the responsibility of those who have custody of children. i would like to warn you, however, about the internet. it's hard to ask for the impossible. the internet itself is no more responsible than the post office is for criminal acts that can be prepared by mail. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the postal services are not subject to any form of control. with these reservations, we are in favour of the main points of this report and also of the inclusion of interpol alongside europol. we hope that this report will help to eradicate this abhorrent phenomenon.
- mr president, we must congratulate the authors of these two important reports which honour the work of our parliament. the proposed measures, which we will support, are aimed at preserving the integrity of those who need us most, namely children. they are the future of the world, they are also the most vulnerable and have already, unfortunately, in their pre-natal uterine life, to suffer from the selfishness of adults, without moving anyone, since they are deprived of a voice and a real face. we shall support both reports by voting for the amendments which go further than the council's proposal. in particular, we would like to say that these are criminal acts which should not be tolerated, and that these measures should be applied when the children concerned are under 16 years old, as we voted in committee. in parallel with these measures, the real and root causes of these evils should be tackled, namely, inter alia, the lax attitude towards pornography in which most european nations are indulging. under the pretext of freedom of the press or individual freedom, a minority of individuals are allowed to disseminate through film, books, magazines, minitel, and now increasingly through the internet, all pornographic literature that violates the dignity of the human being and stimulates the sexual instinct in an anarchic way without restraint, without shame and without respect. the first step in preventing such criminal acts is to adopt a family policy which promotes the child's proper integration into society. we all know from experience that a child who is properly integrated into a family is better protected against the evils of our time, whether it be drugs, human trafficking or pornography. he is also more able to resist these evils if he is confronted with them.
- mr president, the proposal to set up a european food authority is a direct result of the very serious shortcomings which have emerged in the commission's handling of the mad cow case. it was the white paper on food safety which proposed the creation of the body we are discussing today. the whitehead report has the merit of pointing out a number of ambiguities in the draft regulation, but without always proposing the means of removing them. the rapporteur rightly stresses the need to draw very precise boundaries between the advisory and advisory role of the european authority and the risk management role of the member states and the commission. the early warning system should therefore not be placed under the control of the authority. and why have we substituted the word 'agency' for 'authority', which creates confusion and seems to imply that this body is an executive, which it should not be? the report also rightly emphasises the need for networking between the european authority and the agencies of the member states, but it is silent on the modalities for implementing this close cooperation. how will the consultative forum, which should in principle be the instrument, function? no particular elaboration has been made on this important point. we have, at national level, a remarkable scientific expertise in food safety, whether we refer to the british fsa or the french fsa. it is essential to avoid creating a european structure which is competitive or redundant in relation to these national bodies, which must continue to provide the elements of assessment which enable the european agency to play its coordinating role, since the latter is not in any way vested with superior authority over the national agencies. finally, on the need to work actively to achieve consistency between high european standards, as proposed, and existing international standards, a problem which is furtively addressed in the report, i also regret that parliament has not really dealt with this essential point so that our initiatives do not penalise european producers.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the whitehead report on the establishment of a european food safety authority seems to us to be moving in the right direction, both in its analysis of the situation which led to the proposal for the creation of this authority, in the tasks which it will be entrusted with and in the method proposed to enable it to function optimally. it should be remembered that this initiative is unfortunately the result of a series of repeated scandals, linked to agricultural productivism on the one hand and the monopoly of large-scale distribution on the other, which have led to a hygienic industrial agriculture, but have not prevented the development of scandalous by-products, such as dioxin chicken, trafficking in veterinary products of all kinds, and above all the underlying bse crisis. addressing all of this is one of the agency's main objectives to ensure the health and safety of consumers from the "fork to the fork". it must have a dual role: to ensure safety throughout the food chain and to guarantee the quality of any product for the consumer. to this end, it will work upstream of the institutions, because every citizen must have the right to healthy and safe food. but like the professional, he must be aware of the rules involved and the cost involved. in order to apply the principles of transparency and independent monitoring, the food authority must, as from the beginning of next year, propose principles which this document develops properly. it must be able to provide analytical data on any product, including genetically modified organisms, vaccines and pesticides, which may at some point enter the food chain. the failure of hygiene as the only benchmark has been proved with the animal meal scandal. such an agency must be able to give a list of good practices, of labels to products with local specificities, farming qualities, rather than just industrial standards that do not prevent salmonella or dramatic epidemics. its main task is to coordinate the national agencies so that they all recognise the same references and that their scientific assessment and risk prevention role is sufficiently publicised. it is clear that it must require the same controls and traceability rules for all the countries of the union, whether for their exports, imports or consumption. as for the place, it is of little importance as long as transparency and traceability are respected by all.
- mr president, commissioner, bovine spongiform encephalopathy, dioxin and foot-and-mouth disease are the plagues that have struck europe, and they have been spreading in a chain of events that has caused panic among consumers in the member states. the neglect of certain governments has contributed to, if not exacerbated, the impact of these calamities. how can we oppose the creation of a european food agency in the face of growing consumer concern, which is exacerbated by a media coverage that is almost sensational? however, this agency project already mentions the food authority and that is where my fears begin. will it be an additional european technocratic level, one more? will this authority prevail over the national food safety agencies, with the tentacular drifts that often follow? or will the authority simply act at the level of coordination, as i would like, leaving the member states to manage food security themselves? in this respect, it is too easy to disregard the irish vote, because it is a significant part of the aspirations of the peoples of europe and europe, let us not forget, if it is to survive, can only be built with the consent of the peoples.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to thank and congratulate our rapporteur on the importance and quality of the work he has done. i hope that this regulation establishing the european food authority will help to restore confidence to european consumers. it is therefore of the utmost importance that this authority, which is to be the backbone of the union's food safety strategy, should be operational as soon as possible, and in any case by the beginning of next year. the rapporteur is quite right to stress the need to distinguish clearly between the tasks and responsibilities of the future authority and those of the commission. it should be clear that while the authority is responsible for the day-to-day operation of the early warning system, which is a key tool for risk assessment, the commission, as the policy-maker, must retain responsibility for risk management, which is the control of the action to be taken. in the same vein, it must be stated that, although the authority is to be distinguished by the competence and scientific independence of its experts, it has no political legitimacy of its own. in this respect, it is regrettable that the name 'agency' has been abandoned, since it is more appropriate to describe this structure whose powers must remain technical or scientific and must in no way become regulatory or executive. that is why it seems to me appropriate, as the commission proposes, to place this authority under the triple umbrella of the commission, the council and the european parliament. finally, i would like to stress, as other members have done before me, that without a reorientation of our choices and our common agricultural policies, no authority, however efficient, will ever be able to put a stop to the deep crises such as those we have recently experienced.
in writing. - the commission proposal on the european food authority is officially aimed at improving the prevention of crises such as mad cow disease. but in reality, we see a perfectly designed system being put in place, designed to hinder member states who would like to make use of their national safeguarding powers in the event of a public health crisis (as france did by maintaining, at the end of 1999, to the commission's great dismay, a unilateral embargo on british beef) and thus to preserve as much as possible the sacrosanct freedom of movement of products. although the new european body's sole purpose is to provide scientific advice to the community institutions and the member states, it is clearly intended to circumvent or neutralise the advice of national food safety agencies, such as afssa in france, to prevent governments from having any legitimacy to rely on them. the new body is headed by a board of 16 members, of whom 4 are appointed by the european parliament, 4 by the council, 4 by the commission, the last 4 being representatives of consumers and industry appointed by the commission (article 24). half of the members are therefore appointed by the commission, and all by european institutions. none are designated by national food safety agencies, which would have been necessary to make the whole work as a network. but that is clearly not the point. to make matters even more complicated, the executive director is appointed by the administrative board on a proposal from the commission (article 25), and the members of the scientific panels are appointed by the same board on a proposal from the executive director (article 27). who could believe that such a montage would not support the commission's positions? article 22 states that the new system will provide 'the best possible scientific advice', so as to be sure to devalue all others. the central body is called the 'european food authority' (abbreviated 'the authority', with a capital 'a'). the name should have been 'agency', since this body only gives opinions in theory, but the commission is absolutely attached to 'authority', you can guess why. it is also a 'food authority', not a 'food safety authority', in order to extend its scope of action to the broad areas listed in article 21. among these, genetically modified organisms are found, modestly placed at the bottom of the list. who can doubt that one of the first "advice" of the "authority" will be to advise the resumption of the authorization of gmos? we are dismayed, once again, to see that national states are allowing themselves to be trapped in such crude traps, which will lead them tomorrow to no longer protect their citizens. but after all, maybe that's what they want.
in writing. - i voted for this report. i am not in favour of the creation of an agency. in recent times we have seen a proliferation of these new entities: maritime safety agency, european aviation safety agency, etc. a new community bureaucracy is emerging. i'm sorry to hear that. however, there are circumstances which may make it necessary to consider the possibility of setting up a special authority. that's the case here. the existence of this report is the result of a sad fact: the european commission has not been able to respond effectively to the various food crises. the commission has also been asked to provide a report on the implementation of the directive on the protection of consumers and consumers' interests. the action of the food authority must be guided by two main principles: it must be given a clear mission and a separation must be established between what is the responsibility of the scientific authorities on the one hand and what is the responsibility of the political authorities on the other. the authority should focus on identifying and assessing risks, coordinating its activities with those of national agencies and providing all necessary information. in no case shall the food authority be responsible for the management of the early warning system. the consumer is the instrument and the decision on the measures to be taken must be entirely and exclusively a matter for the political sector. finally, as regards the location of the authority, i voted in favour of amendment no 188 in its entirety. france is a great country and a founding member of the union. it must show its partners its commitment to europe by implementing european directives as soon as possible. and yet, so far, my country remains among the worst students. i simply want to send a strong signal to the french politicians with this vote that this situation should be reversed. france will thus enhance its prestige and gain a greater say in future negotiations.
in writing. - our abstention on this text does not mean that we are disinterested or neutral in the problem of paedophilia, which we strongly condemn. it merely means that the text is inadequate on some points and ambiguous on others.
in writing. - we support the approach of affirming the need for a framework decision which defends the need for strong and concerted action to combat the sexual exploitation of children and child pornography, the latter experiencing a particular development with the internet and new technologies. this fight must be waged in all directions, because the consequences for children are disastrous and, from this point of view, we support the fact that the possession of child pornography is also a crime. the main problem is to prevent this necessary fight against the sexual exploitation of children and child pornography from being used by the supporters of a backward morality and leading to excesses that kill liberty, especially in relation to certain sexual information materials or certain fictions. thus, it cannot be said that any depiction of children engaging in "sexual behavior" is wrong. this is the ambiguity of a number of amendments which deal with virtual productions. there may be a legitimate concern, but the risk of slipping is real. we are therefore in favour of a firm fight against the sexual exploitation of children and child pornography. but there is a real risk that this just struggle will be used for reactionary purposes in a number of amendments. that's why we abstain.
in writing. - the commission is today proposing regulations against human trafficking and sexual exploitation which we can only approve, but which conceal a less commendable approach to illegal immigration. the commission, which is frequently accused of using its new powers of initiative under the amsterdam treaty in an overly favourable way towards immigration (proposals on family reunification and on temporary protection in particular), is seeking to clear its way by including trafficking in human beings for the purpose of exploiting their work. it claims to be contributing to the fight against illegal immigration. but in reality, it is an alibi. a closer look at the text reveals that the approach chosen tends rather to defuse repressive measures. the offence of 'trafficking in human beings for the purpose of exploiting their labour', as described in article 1, does not require the illegal crossing of a border, which is the first criterion of illegal immigration. as a result, the definition of this offence is vague and covers a wide range of cases, not just illegal immigration. in the context of this broad definition, the person who is the object of trafficking is presented in the commission's explanatory memorandum as a 'victim'. for a crime to be committed, the victim must have been forced to do so, which is not the case for illegal immigrants, who usually come voluntarily. in these circumstances, these so-called measures against illegal immigration, which are drowned in the fight against all kinds of exploitation, including child pornography, cannot be effective. they only serve to provide a false counterpart to other immigration texts which are lax. fortunately, the member states, and in particular france, have used the right of initiative which they still have until 1 may 2004 to make other proposals, more precise, more appropriate and therefore more effective: a draft framework decision aimed at strengthening the criminal framework for the repression of aid for illegal entry and residence; the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the eu's external assistance programmes, in particular the implementation of the european union's external assistance programmes. the commission has also adopted a proposal for a directive on the liability of carriers of illegal immigrants. if the member states had not taken these rebalancing initiatives, the commission's current texts would have little meaning, at least as regards illegal immigration.
in writing. - human trafficking and migration, which are purportedly voluntary but are in reality forced by poverty, have this in common: they both grow in the soil of poverty of most of the world. without a profound social change that puts an end to a system which, in order to accumulate wealth in the hands of the privileged class in rich countries, impoverishes the working classes of the planet, neither voluntary emigration nor human trafficking will be put to an end. we voted for the text to express our condemnation of those who profit from this kind of trafficking or sex trade. it must be noted, however, that this deliberate resolution does not even go as far as it is supposed to go, if only by granting the victims of trafficking not a temporary residence permit but the full right to remain in the countries of the european union if they so wish.
in writing. - the recitals in the draft which affirm the need to take firm measures to oppose trafficking in human beings and the references to un texts seem to us to be generally correct. of course, the notion of exploitation at work could be extended (references are to the charter of fundamental rights which is too restrictive). the main danger is that human trafficking and immigration are being equated or confused. that is why we supported the amendments which recall that the fight against human trafficking must not be used to repress the undocumented, or which concern the right of residence for all victims. we also voted for the amendments which seek to make what was originally called an offence a criminal offence, given what human trafficking means in terms of exploitation, humiliation, physical and psychological violence. finally, we want to make it clear that our positive vote on this proposal for a framework decision does not in any way mean for us any acceptance or legitimization of the various european systems of police and judicial cooperation in place.
in writing. - we can only vote against this collection of nonsense which, in its first recital, says that the poor countries have 'the possibility of improving their economic situation, reducing poverty ...' if they know how to use this 'revolution of information and communication technologies'. in many poor countries, the majority of the population not only do not have electricity but do not even have adequate food. it is easier to draw up and vote resolutions of this kind, or even to give a few subsidies to computer manufacturers to get rid of unsellable stocks, than to feed the people of these countries, or, better, to give them the opportunity to feed themselves instead of plundering them and forcing them to abandon even food crops in order to produce for western markets. it takes a great deal of ignorance or a high degree of cynicism to claim that 'information and communication technologies make a significant contribution to direct democracy'. the people of a number of poor countries, particularly in africa, would be satisfied, in terms of the "contribution" to democracy by the great powers of europe, to see them stop supporting, financing and arming their dictators. but it would be too much to ask european governments to abandon indigenous dictatorships that protect the interests of their trusts. the people demand democracy ? let them settle for the internet!
in writing. - we voted against this report to denounce the hypocrisy of a text which claims to oppose the increase in the theft of art objects in the european union and their illicit trade. the author of this article neglects to mention that not only national museums in european countries but also private collections are filled with art objects looted over the centuries from countries in the mediterranean, the middle east, asia, latin america, and africa. while the british museum, the louvre, and the pergamon museum in berlin are filled with wonders of ancient art, in greece, little remains except stucco copies. in museums, these artworks are at least on public display. the same cannot be said for private collections. and since the text purports to prevent illicit trade, it should first define as illicit all purchases which allow very rich individuals to appropriate and preserve for their private use cultural property which should be the heritage of all humanity and accessible to all.
mr president, since this morning we have been talking specifically about ozone and its serious effects on human health, but also on ecosystems and the environment as a whole. i myself, in my department in france, chair a network of air quality monitoring and whenever it is very nice, it is full sun, and there is no wind, i fear the consequences of car traffic. i know that at that point there will inevitably be a breach of the limit values, what is commonly known as an ozone peak. what can we do in these conditions ? what can we do to meet the kyoto protocol and address the problem of climate change? we know that it is human activity, industry, motor traffic, which are causing the exceeding of the limit levels of ozone in our urban environments, but this ozone then, with the winds, and depending on the terrain, spreads to areas which should be preserved. it is therefore essential to set clear objectives and to have real, valid air quality monitoring networks. early warning systems in the event of ozone levels exceeding the limit values which may be harmful to the health of vulnerable persons such as children, the elderly, and persons with cardiac or respiratory problems must be effective. the european territory must be meshed in such a way that everyone is duly informed. but we must be aware that it is difficult to reduce overruns in spain, greece and italy, and that in the southern countries of europe it is much more difficult than in the northern countries. local authorities must take the right measures in terms of urban planning, in the context of sustainable development, without, however, undermining the competitiveness of our enterprises. it will be necessary first of all to raise awareness among those who can change their behaviour, but above all, to succeed, to make all the states feel responsible and to make our decisions not only european but also international. president bush has arrived in europe; we must not forget that the united states is also responsible for this.

substitution and not of complementarity, would like to see develop in parallel, in a closed way. on the contrary, efficiency and subsidiarity require that we go beyond the association programme and the council. the union's action plan on drugs for 2000-04 was drawn up on the basis of the debates at the second interinstitutional conference on drugs policy in europe held in brussels in february 2000 and the eu strategy on drugs endorsed by the european council in helsinki in december 1999. this action plan was endorsed by the european council at its meeting in feira, portugal, in june 2000. the action plan, which is now being implemented, calls on the commission, in cooperation with the member states, to establish a procedure for the voluntary monitoring of so-called non-scheduled chemical precursors of synthetic drugs in cooperation with the chemical industry. the commission is also invited to report regularly to the council on the control of the diversion of illicit chemical precursors, on measures taken in the previous year and on measures proposed for the coming year. on the basis of a proposal from the commission, the council recently adopted, on 5 june 2001, a regulation amending an earlier regulation on measures to make it more difficult to divert certain substances for the illicit manufacture of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, in order to extend the definition of scheduled substances to natural products containing such substances, to extend cooperation between the authorities of the member states and the chemical industry to non-scheduled substances and to give the commission responsibility for drawing up guidelines to assist the chemical industry in achieving the objective of the abovementioned cooperation. in particular, these guidelines shall provide a regularly updated list of non-scheduled substances commonly used in the illicit manufacture of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, in order to enable the industry to monitor trade in such substances on a voluntary basis. the european union is developing its activities in cooperation with, in particular, the key countries of origin and transit in order to combat the illicit trade in drugs. as regards latin america and the caribbean, the third high-level meeting of the so-called cooperation and coordination mechanism has just started in the city of cochabamba, bolivia. an eu/central asia action plan will be adopted in the coming weeks. the fight against drugs is an important part of cooperation with the united states in the framework of the transatlantic dialogue and with russia in the framework of the partnership and cooperation agreement. in preparation for the accession of the candidate countries, the drugs component of the phare programme is an important element in the fight against drug trafficking. europol has also opened negotiations with 23 countries on cooperation agreements. in most cooperation systems, measures to combat illicit trafficking are concentrated on drug trafficking by sea, control of synthetic drugs and increased police and customs cooperation.

- doc. a5-0149/2001 by mrs torres marques, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 77/388/eec with a view to simplifying, modernising and harmonising the conditions for invoicing in the field of value added tax (com (2000) 650 - c5-0008/2001 - 2000/0289 (cns))
commission. – madam president, it gives me great pleasure to discuss the commission's proposal on invoicing with parliament today. this proposal stems from the slim exercise, during which traders themselves identified the current divergent rules on invoicing in europe as a major obstacle to the smooth running of the internal market and the development of electronic commerce. it is an important element of the new vat strategy adopted by the commission last june focussing, in the short term, on simplifying and modernising the present vat system. two problems have been pinpointed. firstly, there are the 15 different sets of rules on vat invoicing that place an enormous administrative burden on business. various speakers have already drawn attention to that tonight. the compulsory set of requirements is indeed different in each member state. this means that when a trader makes taxable supplies to several member states, he has to respect different obligations when drawing up invoices in each of those countries. the second problem is that the current legal framework for electronic invoicing also differs across europe. in most cases it is very restrictive. electronic invoicing is sometimes not possible at all. when it is allowed, it is subject to diverse technical requirements or to prior authorisation from the tax administrations. it is therefore extremely difficult to use it in cross-border trade. hence the need to set up a common legal framework, for both paper and electronic invoicing. that is why the objectives of the present proposal are the following: firstly, to create a common set of 12 obligatory vat requirements on invoices across the european union; secondly, to set up a common legal framework for electronic transmission and storage of invoices. by creating a single set of rules, such a new framework will enable businesses to save on administrative costs. moreover, i should like to stress that this proposal will also enable tax administrations to carry out tax audits more efficiently. i am pleased to say that this opinion is shared by the european parliament – as evidenced by the report drawn up by the rapporteur, for which i thank her very much indeed, on of the commission's behalf. the commission would like, in particular, to welcome the positive contribution of the rapporteur for the committee on economic and monetary affairs, mrs torres marques, as well as the helpful ideas put forward by mrs plooij-van gorsel, in her opinion on behalf of the committee on industry, external trade, research and energy. given that the council is currently considering this proposal, and in view of the commission's strong desire to address this issue in a timely manner, i believe that the most appropriate course of action at this stage would be for the commission not to accept formally the amendments put forward by parliament, but to endeavour to take them on board as much as possible during the negotiations with the council. however, it will not be possible, i am afraid, to take into account some amendments, in particular those relating to the advanced electronic signature, which the rapporteur proposes to make optional rather than mandatory. i should like to stress that the commission's proposal is already a compromise between the most flexible and most restrictive legislation. but i should also like to stress that the electronic signature is an important tool in securing the authenticity and integrity of what is, after all, a valuable commercial document granting the right to vat deductions. i share the argument that there is a need to postpone the date of entry into force, to enable businesses to adapt to the new rules. but such a date could only be decided once the council has reached agreement on the content of the proposal. i personally am confident that such an agreement will be reached rapidly. the council has already started to discuss the proposal in detail and it will do its best to come to an agreement before the end of this year, as requested by the stockholm summit. i should now like to make two remarks to mr garcía-margallo y marfil and mrs kauppi. mr garcía-margallo y marfil has reproached the commission for not supporting the strategy which would lead to a single vat system. the commission's ambition remains that of a single point-of-origin vat system. but the complaints and reproaches which mr garcía-margallo y marfil directs at the commission should be addressed to the member states, since it is with them that the problem lies. mrs kauppi made a remark about the costs of electronic signatures, in particular for small and medium-sized enterprises. i remind her that the costs cannot be a real obstacle, since these signatures are inexpensive. one can buy the cheapest ones for eur 20 or eur 30. the savings in administrative costs more than outweigh initial outlay. in conclusion, parliament's support for this proposal is important in order to achieve a good result. i thank parliament and the rapporteur very much indeed.
- thank you, chief. contrary to custom, i'm going to give the floor to a speaker who was scheduled but who got a little confused about the times. i therefore give the floor to mrs arlette laguiller.
- madam president, i apologize for intervening after the commissioner, but i am a bit of a computer victim, since i had the timetable on the screen and i thought i would be speaking at about a quarter to ten. thank you for letting me speak. the present situation in the 15 countries of the union, where there are 15 regulations and 25 different types of mandatory vat invoicing, is indeed an aberrant situation, but what is unfair is the very existence of vat, not the way it is invoiced. and if we intend to vote against this report, it is not to oppose harmonization, but to express our opposition to the very existence of value added tax, and more generally to any indirect tax on consumption. it is a particularly unfair tax because it is imposed on everyone, including those on modest wages and even those on unemployment benefits. by the mere purchase of a consumer item, even a piece of bread, the consumer becomes a taxpayer. what is worse is that this tax, vat, is not proportional to the income of the taxpayer. the billionaire will pay his taxes at exactly the same rate as the lowest paid employee. in a country like france, vat accounts for almost three quarters of government revenue, twice as much as income tax. this means that it is the working majority of the low and middle income population that bears the bulk of the tax burden. it's not fair in itself; this is all the more so since, on the other hand, the trend in public expenditure is towards increased spending in favour of employers and the propertied class, to the detriment of the public service. taxation should be used to reduce the gap between the richest and the poorest, but it widenes it. we are in favour of abolishing all indirect taxes throughout europe and replacing them with a substantial increase in taxes on corporate profits and a very progressive income tax, particularly on high capital incomes. in addition, this would have the advantage of solving the problem of the harmonization of invoicing which is of concern to the council.
- this debate is over. the vote will take place tomorrow at noon.

two-thirds of those requirements from within the commission. in addition to measures which enabled redeployed staff to perform other higher priority activities, we also proposed that explicit termination of service arrangements should be made available so that over a two-year period the commission could offer reasonable severance conditions to 600 officials whose skills are not easily adaptable to the changed and changing needs and tasks of the institution. the purpose of the proposed regulation being considered by the house is, therefore, to authorise such a termination of service scheme for 300 commission officials in the course of this year, and another 300 in the course of next year. the proposal is based on the same mechanism that has been used in previous termination of service regulations related, for instance, to successive enlargements of the union or to renewal of responsibilities in the on research directorate-general. application for inclusion in the scheme is therefore voluntary, but the new scheme differs from previous ones, particularly on the following major points. first of all, candidates for early retirement will be selected solely according to the interests of the services. secondly, financial conditions are set at a lower level – 65% of final salary instead of 70% – than has been customary in all previous termination of service arrangements. thirdly, this early retirement proposal has a neutral budgetary impact. the difference between the cost of the total remuneration of 600 officials before termination of service and the cost of the allowance they will receive afterwards will finance the recruitment of 258 new officials. the 342 remaining posts will be given back to the budgetary authority. these elements of the new scheme will help to ensure the achievement of the overall objective of gaining a better match between commission tasks and resources. it will also ensure that the ceiling of heading 5 of the financial perspective is fully respected. in response to the amendments proposed by mr miller, the commission cannot accept amendment no 9, which asks for the expenditure for the early retirement scheme to remain non-compulsory. we cannot accept that amendment simply because of the statutory reality that allowances for officials who have left the service are legally defined as compulsory expenditure. having made this point, i turn to the more positive and more complex position of the commission on the other proposed amendments tabled by mr miller in the report. i will come to the amendments by mr ferber later on. the commission can accept amendments 8, 10, 11, 17, 18 and 19 and which are aimed at ensuring that the arrangements of the scheme are properly implemented, that the measures under consideration do not preclude the adoption of a new permanent early retirement scheme for all of the institutions. as miller said in his speech, these arrangements should be drawn up and adopted at the earliest possible opportunity. the amendments that i have just listed are also aimed at ensuring that further single measures of this kind should in future be unnecessary and, therefore, precluded. all of the amendments tabled by the rapporteur are in line with the commission's intentions as regards the implementation of the scheme and introduce improvements and refinements to the proposal that we originally submitted. we therefore welcome them very warmly. since the commission will soon be proposing the introduction of a permanent, flexible retirement scheme into the staff regulations, further single measures of this kind are highly unlikely to be necessary in the future. the house will know that the most important political points in the discussions on this early retirement scheme that have so far taken place in the council and in parliament relate to the fact that the proposed scheme only concerns the commission, which is committed to implementing the scheme in a budgetary neutral way. in this context, i refer to amendments nos 1- 6, 12, 13 and 16, all of which seek to extend the field of application of the proposed regulation and require the participation of all european institutions and of parliament's temporary staff in the early retirement scheme. i understand the interest of parliament and council as employing institutions in this matter and, as members of this house will know, i am not unsympathetic to their objectives. however, i wish to say most emphatically that, if progress is to be made to everyone's liking, budgetary neutrality must be observed in all of the institutions that implement a scheme of this kind. there are three reasons for that. the first, very obviously, is the clear need for public understanding and acceptance. that in itself requires that any developments in this area should be budgetary neutral. secondly, if the commission alone guaranteed budgetary neutrality, the adoption of the scheme by the council would be very unlikely indeed. thirdly, heading 5 of the financial perspective provides budgetary means for all institutions. the margins for the years to come, which the commission has promised to respect, would be further reduced if budgetary neutrality were not common to all institutions. taking these realities into account, it is clear that the success and the acceptance of the whole early retirement scheme may well depend on all institutions' accepting budgetary neutrality. in adopting mr miller's report, therefore, this house would need to confirm that its participation in an early retirement scheme will be subject to the same conditions as those applied by the council and by the commission. i am sure that that requirement is well understood and supported across this house. finally, before responding to the two amendments tabled by mr ferber, i must say that i heard mr miller's comments on mr ferber's amendments and think that, whatever glorious future offers itself to my good friend mr miller, i can safely predict that he will not be made head of the diplomatic service. in response to mr ferber's amendments, the commission feels that amendment no 21 would significantly reduce the effective scope of the measure by restricting the number of eligible candidates for early retirement. indeed the restriction would be so significant as to actually have an impact on the geographical balance of the scheme. that would clearly be unacceptable to the commission and to the great majority of this house. amendment no 22 by mr ferber would introduce new conditions, notably a 50% tax so negative and complex as to significantly reduce the effectiveness of the commission's proposals. we cannot, therefore, accept that amendment either, and i hope that, on reflection, the honourable member, mr ferber, whom i know very well and have every reason to respect, will understand and accept the commission's view. i am extremely grateful for the constructive approach taken in this report and, indeed, the improvements made on the original proposal, because it has received close and enthusiastic attention from members of this house. i am sure that that constructive attitude will continue to characterise our discussions on reform, since as honourable members know, i regard the understanding and support of this house for all our reform proposals to be absolutely critical.
- thank you, chief. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at noon.
- the next item is the report (a5-0202/2001) by mr harbour, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on universal service and users' rights relating to electronic communications networks and services (com (2000) 392 - c5-0429/2000 - 2000/0183 (cod)).
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by praising the quality, the richness and the importance of the european commission's draft directive. i must, however, regret that this text, which is an integral part of the telecommunications package, has been taken out of the industrial committee's competence in substance and given to the legal committee, which seems to me to be becoming a very bad habit. i believe that, even though they are contained in the same directive, universal service and consumer protection are two areas which are related and important, but different. the protection of consumers requires guarantees, clarity, simplicity and, above all, transparency. the amendments voted in committee are in that direction. others could have gone further if a majority of the committee had wanted to. universal service is a much broader concept and its objectives are more varied, if not more complex. universal service requires a definition at a given moment, but also the modalities and mechanisms ensuring its evolution over time. it presupposes, of course, that there is a financial provision for it. finally, i would remind you that it is independent of the legal nature of the undertaking which issues it. i welcomed the text of the european commission, but i remain convinced of the need for a framework directive for all european universal services. i would like to conclude, on a personal note, by reaffirming that universal service cannot and should not be what might be called a leftover, a sore-skin, of liberalisation. for me and my friends, this is a value and an objective in itself, which is one of the conditions for the social cohesion that has founded our europe. it must therefore be willed, defined, affirmed and decided as such.

- the next item is the report (a5-0186/2001) by mrs fourtou, on behalf of the committee on petitions, on petitions declared admissible concerning silicone implants (petitions 0470/1998 and 0771/1998).
the rapporteur. - madam president, as you said, in 1998 the committee on petitions received two very important petitions. one was submitted by a belgian woman on behalf of the self-help group for women who have been victimized by silicone, accompanied by about a thousand signatures; the other, by a british citizen, called for a ban on silicone breast implants. at the beginning of 1999, after studying the petitions, the executive committee issued a response which can be summed up as follows: the results of the scientific studies currently available do not appear to justify a ban on silicone implants. the position of third countries and the member states of the union on the subject was set out in the annex. in march 2000, the european parliament's directorate-general for research sent the committee on petitions a working document on silicone breast implants. this research status report, together with international references from medical institutes, scientific associations, universities, the medical press, etc., leads to a conclusion which can be summarised as follows: at present, there is no definitive answer to the question whether silicones cause inflammatory reactions that indirectly stimulate autoimmune responses. that is, there is currently no scientific evidence that women who have had breast implants are more prone than others to serious diseases, connective tissue diseases, and that they have a special lymphocyte response. in view of the complexity of the problem and not resigned to closing the examination of such painful petitions, parliament requested an independent scientific study from the stoa and, in may 2000, dr moreno presented his conclusions in the form of three options. option one: status quo, not a ban. option two: a complete ban on silicone breast implants. third option: not a total ban, but the adoption and implementation of specific measures essential to improve the situation with regard to patient information, follow-up and surveillance, quality control and assurance and basic research. the european commission, the committee on the environment and the committee on women's rights, which were asked for their opinions, opted for this third approach. commissioner liikanen confirmed in march 2001 that the commission was preparing a communication on silicone implants, aimed in particular at strengthening european standards, surveillance, introducing a system of patient consent, and continuing research and development. finally, on 29 may 2001, the committee on petitions, after taking account of the complaints of the petitioners and the opinions of the committees consulted, which i thank for their thorough work and for their help, unanimously adopted a resolution on the basis of option 3 of the stoa, which will be voted on tomorrow in plenary. its main recommendations are: free access and information for all patients, a health warning for all advertising of breast implants, very strict supervision of the surgical procedure, the establishment of an implant database, continued research and development, and a ban on implants for cosmetic purposes in patients under the age of 18. this is the first time, madam president, that the committee on petitions has tabled a resolution in plenary which is the direct result of the demands of citizens of the union. the committee on petitions is pleased that it has thus been able to play its full role as an active listener to citizens.
commission. – madam president, first of all i should like to congratulate the european parliament on the way it has followed up the question on silicone breast implants, which was put to the committee on petitions, and in particular the rapporteur mrs fourtou. i would say that i was privileged to take part in this procedure and i highly appreciate the respectful and professional way the committee dealt with the issue. it gave a chance to the citizens to come with their serious problems and concerns. the committee wanted to hear the scientific opinion on the issue, the experts, and then draw its conclusions. this is a new departure for our institutions and i hope it will pave the way towards closing the gap between the citizens and the european institutions, a problem which faces all of us. the draft resolution has a strong independent scientific basis in the report drawn up by professor moreno at the request of parliament. the draft rightly distinguishes between measures to be taken at community level and those that should be taken mainly at national level as part of health and consumer policy. the draft resolution reflects the consensus between our institutions and member states, with whom we have been discussing the subject over the last few months and who share our concern to improve the situation that was highlighted in such an impressive way by the petitioners. the commission will adopt a communication on breast implants within the coming weeks, before the end of july. it is now subject to internal commission consultation procedures. our communication intends to reinforce the implementation of the medical device directive on issues such as conformity assessment, standardisation, monitoring, clinical data etc. it also addresses recommendations to member states that fall under the chapter of health policy, in particular on the highly important issue of informed patient consent. women have a right to the fullest possible information regarding the risks and benefits of breast implants before surgery so that they can take a well-informed, deliberate decision. the commission services had a meeting with the representatives of the petitioners, in particular concerning informed patient consent and we received a number of useful suggestions. the commission's communication will be sent to parliament as soon as it is adopted.

- madam president, madam president-in-office of the council, mr president of the commission, it is too early to produce an exhaustive analysis of the irish 'no' to the treaty of nice. but we can already make some observations about it without much risk of error. the first concerns the official reactions to the eruption, which caught all european officials off guard. the ministers spent a half-hour in luxembourg on monday on what one of them described as a "historic incident". that is what i would call practicing the politics of the ostrich. does he not see in this rejection a new and serious symptom of the crisis which is shaking the european construction to its core? almost three quarters of the irish people said 'yes' to the community when their country joined in 1972, and the same proportion of irish people today refuse to say 'yes' to the union treaty, and national and european leaders saw nothing coming! we are facing a problem that goes far beyond nice and ireland. the irish 'no' vote is, in my view - and this is my second observation - after other warnings elsewhere, the first of which is the growing abstentionism in the european elections almost everywhere, above all the ransom of a europe that is being built without the citizens and far from them. where have we had great public and pluralist debates, with cards on the table, on the issues to be mastered, the difficulties to be overcome, the values to be defended and finally the political choices to be made in full transparency, democratically? an example which relates directly to the irish case: in the midst of hell, the states concocted, at the summit, a europe of defence with vague missions and independence improbable in the eyes of the entire public. they often glorified this new achievement with accents perceived as militaristic, particularly, but not exclusively, in neutral countries. who's surprised by a comeback? this is true in other areas, notably economic and social. and what of those leaders of the richest countries who are recklessly cultivating the net contributor syndrome and are raising the spectre of renationalizing agricultural aid and the structural funds, thereby feeding the pernicious 'every man for himself' tendency. the federalist overreach of the current institutional debate may have caused some dizziness in countries anxious to preserve their place, role and identity in a future larger whole of which they perceive neither the nature nor the contours. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the process of european integration, and it has been a very active participant in the process of european integration. so my third and final observation on the question that everyone is asking is: what do we do now? firstly, i think we must respect the rules of the democratic game. the treaty is not ratified unanimously; whether we like it or not, it must be put back on the table. secondly, we will gain by going to the heart of the debate with the citizens of all our countries on the direction of europe and the political, institutional and financial implications of our choices. finally, we must not allow opponents who are ashamed of enlargement to use the pretext of this crisis to get the sine die postponement of this potentially great and beautiful, but obviously complex and costly pan-european project. here too, a responsible debate is needed to assess, in the open, the conditions for success for all, since it is true that there is no ambition without effort, and no european project without solidarity.
- mr president, the foreign ministers of the union countries, who on monday chose to continue ratifying the treaty of nice, as if the irish had not said no in a referendum, have chosen the worst possible solution. it may well confirm to many that the european institutions under construction are deaf to the demands of the citizens and that, once the ideological disguises have been stripped off, they are ultimately nothing but an attempt to confiscate the powers of the people. the 'no' vote in the irish referendum, following the 'no' vote in the danish referendum last september, is a warning. the people are turning away from a europe in which they do not recognize themselves. to hasten federalism in these conditions would be to rush to ruin. the gothenburg council may still have a chance to set the record straight. what should he decide? first, to suspend ratification of nice by annulling the conclusions of the general affairs council on monday. secondly, to send a strong signal to the applicant countries, inviting them to join the union immediately, without an additional treaty by accession to the intergovernmental part of the existing treaties. then announce that the additional provisions on enlargement will be included in the accession treaties. finally, to reopen another intergovernmental conference, this time aimed at establishing a europe which respects its nations. the igc should be based primarily on national parliaments and not on the new confiscation structure which is being invented. that is what we propose, mr president, in our counter-report on the treaty of nice.

president of the commission. mr president, a brief reply to some of the points that have emerged from the debate. first of all, i am very pleased to see that this parliament has taken very seriously the will expressed by the irish people, not only because it represents - although the vote was not very large - a whole people but also because it represents a whole country. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. it is a lesson, and i am glad that there is a common will - and i thank the swedish presidency again - the great step forward in the unblocking of the social directives. they've been standing still for a long time. he's now taken another step forward. i would also like to thank mrs diamantopoulou for her work in this respect. finally, reference was made to the speech i made a few days ago on the need for a european tax. i would like to reiterate this concept, to clear up any misunderstanding and to begin with you, the house, a reflection on this very sensitive subject. the commission is working, is carrying out technical work on the feasibility and possibilities of this tax, which is to replace existing taxes, which will in no way constitute a new burden for european citizens. we have been clear about this since the first time we spoke about it and we must be clear about this now. we must also make it clear that this attitude is in response to an explicit request from the council and parliament. we must reflect on these issues because the institutions must live in a democratic context also from the fiscal point of view and, therefore, the objective of this hypothetical and eventual tax is to replace the current system - which is complicated, opaque, not transparent - of national contributions and to strengthen the perception of a democratic way of accumulating resources and a transparent way of spending the resources accumulated. this is absolutely our duty, and we must also reject as far as possible the attitude which is often common in our member states, which is summed up in the expression 'i want my money back', that is to say, a kind of confidential accounting which is the accounting of the national states, of which the european institutions are a passive object. i think that this must be changed and i repeat that this is a necessary step for all democratic institutions: the commission's proposal is to have clear resources - which can of course be transfers of national taxes to european taxes but which must be clear, specifically dedicated to the european institutions - and to respond with equal clarity to european citizens. i think these are the methods we should always use. if we use these methods, the attitude of the people of europe will be a much more positive attitude, a much more understanding one, because they will understand what we are doing with their trust and their money. finally, let us also remember this lesson from the irish referendum and the reflections that followed. the people of europe must and want to give their opinion on a strong and bold project. they want to have a say in a comprehensible project, they want to know what part of their destiny they want to share with the other european countries. they have no preconceived hostility, no new closure; they only have the right to understand, the right to know every step that is in front of them, every step that will guide their lives. we are the arbiters - and we will be in the near future - of decisions which are important for all european citizens, and we must take this path, we must go in this direction. and the convention - as it will be made - is the first delicate step in this new phase of the european institutions. in writing. - in the aftermath of the referendum in which ireland said 'no' to the treaty of nice, we have heard almost all the biased interpretations which show the undemocratic drift of the federalists. to continue the ratification process as if nothing had happened, some questioned the "relevance of the referendum", on the grounds that the turnout was low. perhaps they think that decisions taken by the eurocrats alone would be more democratic? in any case, the low irish participation is mainly due to the demobilization of the 'yes' supporters, and this is also due, of course, to the treaty of nice. the second interpretation is flawed: the 'no' vote is attributable to specifically irish causes, the concern to preserve neutrality in defence matters, the desire not to become a financially contributing country, the desire to preserve restrictive legislation on abortion... but these one-off explanations are not enough. there is only one great reason for the 'no', explicit or underlying: the desire of the irish people to retain their freedom of decision in the face of an invading europe, as the treaty of nice would further strengthen it. third interpretation: we are told that by rejecting nice, the irish would have rejected the intergovernmental method of treaty negotiation, because it was too obscure. this may be true, but it should not be taken to mean that in the future governments should be replaced by more supranational preparation or review mechanisms. on the contrary, we must strengthen the power of each people. finally, perhaps the worst are those who, seeing in the irish vote a reaction against a europe indifferent to its citizens, explain that the only remedy would be to put in place, as soon as possible, a european constitution. of course, this remedy would only aggravate the problem by reinforcing supranationality. let us read the results of this referendum with common sense and simplicity: it is a rejection of federal europe.
in writing. - we voted against this proposal because the europe it mentions in some respects is not ours, it is not the europe of the working world. it is the europe of merchants, bankers and large industrial groups, a coalition of their respective states. the european community is a europe which has been painstakingly built up for half a century by the bourgeoisies of european countries, condemned to agree with one another in order not to disappear from the world economic scene, and yet which are rivals to one another. the difficulties it faces in expanding to eastern european countries merely reflect its fundamental nature. the future is certainly the unification of europe, of all europe, on the basis of complete equality of its peoples, and the abolition of frontiers. but it cannot be the result of an agreement between capitalist groups which are exclusively concerned with their own profits and not with the interests of the people. the emergence of a truly unified europe under the democratic control of its people is linked to profound social transformations, ending the domination of private financial groups over the economy and society.
in writing. - at the next european summit in gothenburg, it is very likely that the fifteen will once again demonstrate their inability to build a democratic and social europe. europe, mired in its inability to support a just and lasting peace in the middle east, will continue to watch israeli aggression against the palestinian people without being able to enforce un resolutions 242 and 338 or to demand the dismantling of settlements. with the euro only a few months away, europe will also be unable to intervene against the dictatorship of the market, leaving transnational trusts like marks & spencer and danone to lay off thousands of employees, while their profits amount to several million euros. a european law is needed to prohibit stock market layoffs, as is a tax on capital movements and the abolition of tax havens. but, more than that, the fifteen, after the failure of the treaty of nice, will continue to promote a europe entirely devoted to liberalism by continuing the privatization of public services and the questioning of social protection systems. the recent rejection of this treaty by ireland demonstrates once again that europe cannot be built without the consent of the peoples. referendums on the future of europe must be held and the charter of fundamental rights must be revised and amended. the democratic deficit between citizens and their representatives must be reduced as a matter of urgency. in gothenburg, the future of europe will not be played out in palaces turned into bunkers but in the streets, with the progressive forces.
