in writing. - the european parliament's report on the ecb's 2000 financial year and the ecb's report on the same subject seek to eliminate differences in assessment and present a unified front on the eve of the physical exchange of coins and banknotes. however, as soon as we scratch the surface, contradictions emerge, and they are very serious, because they point to defects in the construction of the single currency that are very difficult to correct. let us take institutional issues as an example. first, on the powers of the council of ministers: the european parliament's report calls for greater economic coordination and stability programmes (paragraph 5 of the resolution), which implies a strengthening of the eurogroup and its means of action. on the contrary, the ecb report points out that 'the first two years of the euro's existence have highlighted the satisfactory nature of the economic policy framework at the european level' (page 3). it thus appears that the bank is fiercely defending its independence, well aware that the rise of policy in the management of the single currency, within a non-optimal monetary area, risks leading to difficult conflicts. but is technocratic management preferable? in fact, neither of these two ways is feasible. second disagreement: transparency: the european parliament report again calls (paragraph 4) for the minutes of the meetings of the governing council to be published, indicating the positions taken (for or against). this proposal is repugnant to the ecb, for a good reason which the european parliament insists on not seeing: in the specific case of the euro zone, made up of separate nations, conflicts between governors would easily be assimilated to conflicts between nations, which would damage the credibility of the euro, which is already too weak. we are reminded once again of the suboptimal nature of the monetary area of the twelve. third, on voting in the governing council: the ecb report defends the principle of 'one member, one vote', because the governors of the national central banks deliberate 'in complete personal independence', and not as representatives of their countries (page 181). the european parliament's report also takes note of the reform of article 10 of the statute of the ecb introduced by the treaty of nice, which could make it possible in the future to weight votes according to the size of countries (paragraph 17 of the resolution). such a reform would be in line with the wishes of the large countries, especially germany, which complains of the ecb's "immobility", implicitly attributed to the disproportionate weight of the small countries in the governing council. however, the operation is far from being carried out, as it seems to be contrary to the spirit of maastricht, the ecb's position and the interests of the smaller countries, which will have their say. once again, the single currency of several nations is struggling with its contradictions.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to say - and my colleague mr wuori has nothing to do with this - that it is a little surreal to have mixed human rights and fundamental rights in the same joint discussion. the european union is not a party to the treaty of rome, but it is a party to the treaty of rome, and it is not a party to the treaty of rome. there may be an intermediate zone, namely the candidate countries, where human rights and fundamental rights are mixed together because of the forthcoming accession of these countries to the union. i would like to explain the reason for the new title of the report and the validation by the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs of the method chosen for this year's report. our report is now called the report on fundamental rights and no longer the report on human rights. we did want to adopt a broader and more neutral concept. the new method is based on the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which serves as a reading grid insofar as it is a new, innovative element of political life and it is up to parliament to make this charter come to life. it was therefore quite natural that its committee responsible should take the charter, which we adopted in plenary, as the framework for this report. we have come to the conclusion that since there is an annual report, it should be an annual report. let me explain. a report is based on fact. the report was therefore to be an annual report because it is interesting to carry over the facts from one year to the next and to check the year after what has happened to the resolutions of our parliament. so why did you choose the bill of rights? i think it was necessary. it is indeed a highly european text, since it is the product of the convention, that is to say, of the combination of the three elements of legitimacy which made up the convention. the convention is also cited as a model for the development of other european texts. the charter is a complete text because, for the first time, it incorporates both civil and political rights as well as economic and social rights and, therefore, it allows a broad sweep of fundamental rights. i mean, it's a reference text. beyond the debate on whether or not to incorporate it into the treaties, it is already a reference text, since the european court of justice uses it and the commission itself has undertaken to ensure that its services are guided by the charter. finally, it is also a reference text - as i mentioned earlier - for the applicant countries, because we cannot accept a country into the union if it does not respect the values defended by the european charter of human rights for its inhabitants. i would also like to say, and i agree with mr wuori, that we must have credibility: in order to be able to pass a critical judgment on others, we must also have the political courage to pass one on ourselves. we have here, with the report, the instrument for doing so. what was the working method ? i would remind you that the charter of fundamental rights sets out a minimum number of rights to which every citizen of the union is entitled. so we took the 50 articles of the charter and checked whether they were applied in the 15 countries and at the level of the union. the report's outline follows the charter's outline, which is found both in the resolution, since the chapters of the charter have been taken up, and in the explanatory statement. the sources are many and varied: the council of europe, of course, with the work of its committees, national parliaments, ngos, civil society, the vienna observatory, a network of lawyers. in fact, we have used all the sources, we have not felt that we should deprive ourselves of any of the important and verifiable sources at our disposal. i would like to stress here the lack of resources of the committee on civil liberties to do this work. the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy has nine people, an administrative unit to do it. the committee on civil liberties is not, and you will find in the resolution a request for resources to enable us to do this work properly. we also call for - and i take this opportunity to thank those who helped me to draft this report - a network of lawyers. it seems important to be able to rely on a network of national lawyers who would feed the team of rapporteurs and help to collect information. finally, we ask for cooperation with the other committees of parliament because, since the charter deals in particular with environmental rights and economic and social rights, the committees responsible for these matters must naturally have a say in the application of the charter in the european union. the philosophy of this report is not to stigmatise any particular state, to highlight any particular nonsense. quite the opposite. in any case, the rapporteur believes that 'zero defect' is a utopia in human rights, but that human rights and fundamental rights in europe mean that when a mistake is found, one can lodge a complaint, see the offender convicted, that there is an administrative inquiry and that there are regulatory or legislative decisions which prevent the reproduction of the said mistake: this is the respect for human rights that we are entitled to claim. finally, this report has two parts. it's the rules. there is the resolution, which emerges amended from discussions in the committee on civil liberties or in the plenary assembly, and the explanatory statement. i simply want to say that no country has been spared and that those who will take the trouble to read this report will find in it, both in the explanatory statement and in the resolution, proposals for solutions in the spirit of what i was saying earlier. in fact, this first report is intended as a draft, the framework for a new method. if the plenary follows the rapporteur's proposals and the report voted in committee, we will therefore have a much more collegial work, based on collaboration inside and outside parliament, on dialogue with ngos, on dialogue with our natural partners, the national parliaments; we will have a report which will be detailed, verified by a whole committee and which i believe will be awaited, perhaps feared, by public opinion. that's my wish. - ladies and gentlemen, although the adoption of the charter of fundamental rights last year in nice represents a step forward for human rights in the european union, it is only a minimum standard of protection to which every citizen is entitled. unfortunately, this is still not enough to cope with the plight of thousands of people, whether refugees, immigrants or undocumented people, especially women and children. at no time are states, european or not, called to account or condemned for the violations committed. the reports before us today are proof of this: however good they may be, and we can thank our rapporteurs for this, they merely list the many cases where fundamental rights are a cause for concern. human rights and fundamental freedoms are universal and indivisible. they must know no borders, no nationality, no gender. we must reaffirm this forcefully and vigorously. these rights will only be realised if all citizens are aware of their existence and have confidence in those who ensure that they are applied and respected. it is therefore essential to promote them and to make them visible and accessible to all. in order to be constructive, it is necessary to establish a dialogue with all those concerned with the recognition, promotion and defence of fundamental rights, in particular those who are closest to the most disadvantaged citizens who are victims of discrimination. another key factor is the ratification of international instruments and their application in everyday life: the right to move freely, to live with one's family, to be a citizen. any society can only flourish in peace, and there can be no peace without justice. beyond the generous speeches in favour of human rights, nothing will be achieved without the political will to achieve real equality of rights for all those men and women who contribute to the wealth and construction of europe and to european citizenship. rather than speculating about the structures that the european parliament might have in the future, we must give ourselves the means to ensure respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, including social and political rights, without which the principles of the rule of law and democracy would no longer make sense.
- the european parliament is a key player in the design and implementation of the union's human rights policy. its influence on the amendment of treaties in this direction is becoming increasingly evident. we must therefore focus in depth on the human rights situation in the member states, when the shortcomings of our systems are becoming apparent. in my own city of lyon, i am confronted every day, in a very real way, with the problem of the suffering of refugees and human trafficking, especially trafficking in women. we must therefore harmonise our laws and adopt a legally binding instrument to ensure that victims of trafficking in human beings are genuinely protected. we should be able to extradite human traffickers without any problems and confiscate the proceeds of their criminal activities to feed a european compensation fund for victims. we should be able to grant humanitarian residence permits to victims of human trafficking and domestic slavery, and we should be able to guarantee that those arrested and detained in police stations have access to legal and medical assistance at the first opportunity and, where appropriate, to an interpreter. we should be able to move quickly to better protect unaccompanied minors, in particular by providing them with the assistance of a guardian or legal counsel as soon as possible. on the other hand, i would call for a certain degree of consistency in our parliament. if the community's immigration policy, which is the subject of a report currently being examined by the committee on external economic relations, were to be based solely on our selfish economic interests as european countries, it would not really guarantee all the fundamental rights that we are defending today.
- mr president, the author of the cornillet report has identified the many areas where, even within the european union, human rights are totally or partially violated. we shall be voting on a number of proposals which could represent progress. but even in these cases we would like to express our reservations, since these are recommendations which the states concerned will either respect or not. the legislator is known to be much more restrictive in commercial law. in its explanatory statement, the report refers to the charter of fundamental rights proclaimed in nice, touting a text that combines both civil and political rights and economic and social rights as a coherent whole. but what good are labour law proclamations as long as the bosses of companies have the royal right to hire or fire? what does the right to housing mean when, as the text itself admits, 11.8% of the population of the european union lives below the poverty line and therefore cannot afford to buy adequate housing? we shall abstain on the whole of this report because declarations of good intentions are not enough to constitute a policy in favour of the poorest and most oppressed sections of the population.
- mr president, the annual report on human rights in the world is a good summary of the current issues. but the european union must make its position on three points clearer. firstly, history shows how difficult it is to enforce human rights in countries where economic development is lacking or very low. this is a fact which needs to be emphasized more. this implies that we should set up a methodology for global development which would group together convergent criteria around a principle which i shall call the 'principle of evolution'. the report also points to a number of countries which do not respect human rights. in order to avoid falling into the trap of 'double standards' and to give europe credibility in its approach, we must insist more on the indivisibility of human rights within and beyond the borders of a state. finally, we must be aware of the particular responsibility of those countries which have achieved a high level of democracy and development and which, instead of being an example, continue cynically to flout human rights. developed countries must become an example for developing countries, not the other way around. our action is based on duration. we must say loud and clear that human rights are a universal value and not a circumstantial value. on this basis, it is imperative that europe should consider the creation of a human rights engineering which takes account of our political will. the credibility of europe is at that price.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the increasingly unstable situation in which the remaining part of the republic of yugoslavia finds itself, as indeed the whole of the balkans, obliges us to extend this year, and probably for a long time to come, the aid we are giving to the countries of the region. it also forces us, and above all it should force us, to face the reality of our failure, face it head on, and ask ourselves what caused it. the reason is simple. the european union has only pretended to follow a logic of peace. in reality, it has only covered up a real war logic with humanitarian rhetoric, a war which served the interests of several powers and which aimed to destroy yugoslavia, which was done in a few years. but that is something that only geopolitical reasoning can explain. but although it is the only way of grasping the reality of the balance of power between nations, that is to say, of diplomatic life itself, we persist in refusing geopolitical analysis. but it would show the obvious truth, that three powers pursuing convergent interests in the balkans. firstly, germany, which was never unaware that, after the first and second world wars, the yugoslav system was created partly against its interests, at least against its european expansionism; the european union is a country which, as soon as it was reunified in 1990, played a major role in breaking the serbian barrier, its old enemy, and in finding its allies, the slovenes and the croats, two precious mediterranean neighbours, by the way. similarly, turkey has easily found its way back to the albanian collusion and its armed wing, the kla. in a way, under the pressure of the entire muslim world, turkey has regained very old, very old positions in the balkans, and it has done so, of course, against the interests of europe, but in the interests of the united states, which, like any empire, knows very well that it must divide in order to reign and which found, which finds its own today by stirring up very old conflicts, by reawakening very old quarrels in what should be called a great turkey that is settling in the balkans, to the great disadvantage, we can understand, of greece. in short, europe has worked against itself and this is another sign of its inability, in my view, to conduct rational diplomacy.
the rapporteur. mr president, this is indeed a rather technical title, namely the creation of executive agencies with certain tasks of managing community programmes, a rather important reform and an element that is not peripheral to the administrative reform under way in the commission. i will say at once that the committee on budgetary control and this parliament can only look with great sympathy and a positive a priori at the principle of the agency proposed to us, since, through the creation of this agency, the commission is responding to a fundamental concern of parliament as it was expressed in the context of the 2000 budgetary procedure. the aim was to dismantle the technical assistance offices, which were poorly controlled and outside the commission's authority, and replace them with establishments which would have both the security attached to the public nature of the institutions and the flexibility of management and operation necessary for the accomplishment of a number of tasks, particularly the execution of certain programmes. in short, we said: let us abolish the bat, but not replace them with the central services of the commission, let us invent something new. these agencies are something new. the commission's proposal is part of a wider package, a policy of outsourcing which has three components: the privatization of certain specific and specific tasks, which we want provided that the private persons who will be responsible for these tasks are not entrusted with integrated administrative tasks; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the proposal for a regulation before you deals only with the statute for agencies. so, commissioner, you have the support of the rapporteur and the support of the committee on budgetary control. i don't mean to doubt you, but you know me, we agree on everything. we have a number of points of agreement and a number of points of disagreement. as regards the first, as i said, we agree on the principle of agency. we also agree with the management arrangements for this agency, which will include staff seconded by the commission, since we want the agency to be clearly subordinated politically and administratively to the commission, and staff who are more flexible, recruited on the basis of temporary contracts adapted to the flexibility of managing programmes of limited duration. we also believe - and i think we agree - that these new bodies should be subject to the same controls and the same reporting, audit and competence obligations of olaf as the central services of the commission. i think we share the same view on this. however, there are still a number of points on which we have some doubts. the first of these is the definition of tasks which may be outsourced and entrusted to executive agencies. let us say that on this old question - the committee on budgets and the committee on budgetary control are in agreement on this point even if some of us do not quite agree - we want these outsourced tasks to be really outsourced because they are temporary and because they require the use of temporary or specialised staff, but not to be systematically outsourced simply because they would cost less because of the use of lower paid and less qualified staff. that is not our objective. secondly, we believe that the commission's legal responsibility must be full and direct. there is a point of law that can separate us, but i do not think that, on the substance of things, we are really opposed to each other. we also want to see these bodies given discharge at the same time as the commission - and this is a very important technical point to which mrs theato, chairman of the committee on budgetary control, is particularly attached. we don't want to separate them; we don't want to have to deal with countless separate dumps; we want to vote unanimously on discharge, both for operational appropriations and for operating appropriations. i am now coming to my conclusion: there are still two points which separate us and which are a problem within the committee. firstly, the rapporteur wanted - and the committee on budgetary control has not yet followed this - that 25% of the staff of the agency should actually come from the commission. the committee on budgetary control has not granted this request. we have tabled an amendment on behalf of our group to reinstate this requirement, but with an amendment and after negotiation with the commission services, specifying that this 25% should be reached only after a certain period of time, in this case 18 months, which would allow the agency to reach its cruise speed. i would like to convince my colleagues in the socialist group to support this proposal. i don't despair of succeeding, but i haven't succeeded yet. finally - and this is the last and most important point - there is the nature of the staff regulations and contracts. we are opposed to this, and i am concerned because i have seen, after the cocobu vote, proposals for regulations which have worried me. we are concerned that staff will be subject to non-renewable statutes. if this is the case, we will have lower quality staff, lower loyalty and will not be able to ensure continuity of service at all times, thus causing disruptions detrimental to the interests of service recipients and programme recipients. i would ask you, commissioner, to make a firm commitment to this. we want continuity of service and that the staff employed by these agencies can be renewed as needed and not be hit by a blind, automatic guillotine in the middle of the programme. that, madam commissioner, is the view of our committee. i'm going to stop here. i come to the conclusion that we support the principle of your proposal, but we are waiting for clarification on the points i have raised. i thank you, mr president, for your patience and i thank my colleagues for their warm support.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the european parliament has played an important role in the whole debate on the commission's administrative reform. the committee on budgets and the committee on budgetary control have also played a central role in the question of outsourcing. the rapporteur, mr bourlanges, in particular, has given the needs to focus more on its core tasks overall. this is the whole context in which the issue of externalisation is discussed, namely under the question 'what tasks can be done in a different form than within the commission's administrative structures now?' the concept of outsourcing provides for three methods and procedures, namely outsourcing in the form of delegation of tasks to executive agencies, then in the form of delegation of tasks to national agencies, i.e. decentralisation, and in the form of contracting out to third parties. the framework regulation on executive agencies defines a new form of community body, which is to serve the commission and is to be responsible for supervising and implementing community programmes on its own behalf, including the related implementation of budgetary resources. the regulation therefore provides the framework for the creation of executive agencies, which the commission will set up as and when necessary. i would like to emphasize the following points: an executive agency is an instrument in the hands and under the control of the commission. this also makes it clear that it is wrong to equate the issue of outsourcing with privatisation, which is often said in the discussion, especially with the civil servants. mr bourlanges, you have made it very clear that this is not the case. it means that the commission's responsibility for the implementation of the budget, as laid down in article 274 of the ec treaty, remains unlimited. that is a point which has just been made by the committee on budgetary control and by you, mrs theato. an executive agency shall be set up by the commission. the management bodies of the agency shall be appointed by the commission. the commission shall exercise control through its departments. the operational appropriations managed by the agency shall remain in the general budget of the european union and shall be managed by the agency in its capacity as authorising officer by delegation of the commission. the prerogatives of the budgetary authority are preserved. the budgetary authority shall authorise the grant to the agency's administrative resources. the establishment plan of the agency shall be submitted to the budgetary authority in the framework of the budgetary procedure. we cannot accept the proposal that a fixed percentage of the staff of the agency should be commission officials. but i would also point out, with regard to the duration of contracts, that the creation of executive agencies only makes sense for tasks which are now not one-year tasks but rather longer-term tasks. this means that the contracts for the contract staff are correspondingly longer. i would also like to mention that the european parliament grants discharge for the implementation of the administrative and operational resources of the executive agency. to sum up: the commission can accept the following amendments: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12 in part, amendment no 16, paragraphs 1 and 2, in part, and 17 and 21 in part. i would like to thank the committee on budgets and the committee on budgetary control for the critical examination of our proposal. their contributions will make our proposal more balanced and bring us one step closer to the desired increase in administrative efficiency.

commission. – i would like to make two brief responses to this debate. two points which should be obvious to all of us, as democrats concerned about issues such as global social equity, but nevertheless important to make. first of all, most speakers in this short but interesting debate, with one unfortunate exception, have drawn a clear distinction between violence and open discussion of the serious issues which will be on the agenda at genoa. there is a real danger in occasionally implying that there is a moral equivalence between people who go to these conferences with a balaclava helmet in their back pocket, prepared for violence against police officers and against property they do not like, and the democratically elected leaders of the governments who are meeting in the city where the demonstrations are taking place. once you blur that distinction, it seems to me that you are on a very slippery slope indeed. at göteborg, i do not believe that a government could have made a greater effort to involve civil society in the discussion of what was happening. we still saw those scenes of violence on the streets of that otherwise peaceful city, however. so i think it is very important that the message from a democratically elected assembly like this is very clear: that there is no moral equivalence between violent demonstrators and those who are elected. secondly, i will not trouble the chamber with a detailed exposé of my views on globalisation, but i want to make one obvious point. while it is true that most people have done better out of globalisation this time round, with the combination of opening markets and technology. it is also the case that too many poor people in rich countries have been left behind and too many poor countries have been left behind. too many poor people face not the opportunities of globalisation but the challenges of globalisation; the dark side of globalisation. the transmittable diseases; the drug trafficking; the illegal trafficking in human beings; the transnational crime; the environmental degradation; and the sheer grinding poverty. the only way you can address issues, such as the decline in aid flows during the 1990s, is through multilateral efforts. now how you make multilateral efforts without world leaders coming together as they will in genoa later this month beats me! you need the democratic leaders of the world to get together to focus on these problems and then to try to give some impetus to solving them. the problem is not that we have these summits, though i wish the media would focus rather more on what is actually discussed at them rather than what happens on the fringes. the problem is not the holding of these summits, the problem is ensuring that the institutions which then try to follow up the summits have the maximum legitimacy and credibility with the world's citizens. they will only achieve that if we are more successful in making multilateral solutions stick. therefore, when we talk about the kyoto protocol at genoa, it is very important that we are able to do so in a way which leads to action on climate change and not the collapse of what has been an extremely important effort by the international community to address a major change. i do not understand those who say that we should not have g8 meetings. i would have responded as well to what mr bertonotti had to say about the role of the churches. as a member of the church he referred to, i have some views about the way it could contribute rather more to the debate about universal human rights as well to the debate about social equity, but since mr bertonotti was unfortunately not able to stay until the end of this debate, i will sit down.

in writing. - by multiplying free trade areas, by abandoning customs duties, by a system of unilateral generalised preferences, by giving customs duties as gifts to the 49 least developed countries, under the pretext of receiving everything but arms, and above all by submitting to the demands of the masters of the empire, from gatt to the wto, the european commission has cut the financial branch on which the european budget was based, that is, customs duties, which represented more than 55% of community resources in the 1960s, to only about 14% today. in addition, with the abandonment of the community agricultural preference, the common agricultural levy on imports of agricultural products from the commonwealth, central america or elsewhere, which protected it, is disappearing. it now produces only about 2% of community resources. so much so that the european budget now receives only 17% of its resources from customs duties and this agricultural levy. however, since these first two historical resources are the only ones specifically belonging to the community and making it financially autonomous from the member states, their decline makes the community budget dependent on payments from the national states. this is illustrated by the importance of the gnp levy, the fourth historical resource of the european budget, which dates back only to 1988. this tax, which is constantly increasing and already provides more than 45% of community resources, is in fact a conventional contribution by states to the financing of an international organization. we have now reached the surprising situation in which the european commission, the heart of federal integration, has pursued a global customs policy which has reduced the union to financing itself like any intergovernmental organisation governed by the most intergovernmental international law. in writing. - the social fabric of many coastal areas has been altered in recent years by the restructuring of the fisheries sector and traditional agriculture. although some regions have experienced an exodus of their native population, most coastal areas are experiencing an increase in overall population pressure, as well as significant seasonal variations in occupancy, mainly related to tourism. large-scale urbanisation and development work can threaten the coastal environment if carried out without sufficient knowledge of coastal dynamics, accelerating coastal erosion. in addition, pollution from land and sea is increasingly contaminating soil and drinking water resources. the coastal territories are the focus of recurrent antagonisms and conflicts. the lack of integrated management of marine and terrestrial resources causes serious tensions between the different sectors of activity, such as fisheries, agriculture and services, which has the effect of undermining the sustainable development of coastal areas. the strategy proposed by the commission is an interesting approach to solving the fundamental problems facing the coast, namely the lack of information, the insufficient participation of the population in projects, the lack of coordination between the various spatial planning authorities and the absence of a genuine partnership involving the economic sectors concerned, regional and local authorities and interregional organisations in decision-making. however, the strategy for coastal areas must be one of the first examples of the implementation of the guidelines developed in the 'community development plan', since the principles laid down therein are obviously valid for the coastal areas of the union. it could even be an excellent opportunity to give new impetus to a particularly inert csdp, whose real impact is still very limited. finally, i would like to join those who regret that the commission proposal does not take account of climate change, which seems to be having an impact on sea level rise and the frequency of storms, contributing significantly to the risk of flooding, coastal erosion and shoreline compression. even if we are only beginning to realise the new challenges that coastal regions will face in the coming decades, the integrated coastal zone management strategy cannot afford to ignore them.

in writing. - it is never too late to say that the european union must actively promote human rights and democracy in all its activities around the world. respect for human rights must be a priority in all eu activities, including its efforts to prevent conflicts. it is important that it 'exports', as it is often said, common values such as the principles of freedom, democracy, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms and the rule of law, which are its founding principles. i would stress, however, that it must respect national sovereignty and not fall into the trap of interference. the european institutions must work together to devise more effective ways of doing this. the rapporteur proposes that the council and the commission should develop more targeted joint strategies in the field of human rights. the eu presidency is invited to ensure that its work programmes automatically include sections on well-defined policies and actions to promote human rights and democracy. specific annual priorities should be set, together with detailed rules for their implementation. these strategies should be reviewed annually and ensure consistency between the various community policies concerned. as far as the european parliament is concerned, i think it is important to improve its own structures dealing with human rights issues. i welcome the suggestion that a special 'representative' be appointed, who could be a vice-chairman of the committee on foreign affairs: he would look at all the problems of human rights and also follow up individual cases of violation of human rights. in writing. - the european union is ill-placed to give lessons in human rights. it invokes, among other things, the 1948 universal declaration and the covenant on economic, social and cultural rights... but does not respect them. what has it done to put an end to the scandalous hemorrhage which debt repayment is for the countries of the south? the member states do not pay the who the sums needed to combat aids or tuberculosis because public deficits must be reduced: the maastricht criteria require it. to prevent conflicts, "a more consistent policy of crisis prevention" would involve putting oil multinationals, such as total fina elf, whose role as a warmonger in southern sudan or the congo is increasingly evident, out of harm's way. the report also calls for the eu to respect the right to asylum and the 1951 convention by abolishing 'waiting areas' and 'detention centres' rather than 'tightening visa requirements' as the report advocates. and it is not enough to "regret" that roma are victims of severe discrimination. they must be granted asylum and the mass expulsions, as belgium in particular has done, must be condemned. only freedom of movement and a policy of legalising all undocumented persons will make it possible to respect the right to asylum and to combat human trafficking effectively. as regards freedom of the press and the fight against 'excessive concentration of media', a populist predator, led by italy, offers an instructive picture of the double language of liberal europe.
in writing. - since we are talking about human rights, i will speak again about the violations of the rights of intellectuals of all specialties who dare to express independent opinions in history, which leads them, for example, to reexamine certain aspects of the second world war and the concentration camp drama. unfortunately, today, tragedy is exploited in a daily and shocking way for political or financial interests that have little to do with the memory of the victims. indeed, at the present time in europe there are thousands of historians, sociologists, researchers, academics or simply citizens who are persecuted for the sole crime of wanting to practice a free examination of the dogmas, which are changing, which the official authors claim to impose. as in 1999, i will mention only one example, taken from the rhône-alpes region, from which our rapporteur, mr cornillet, comes. a young historian, mr. plantin, who was destitute and whom i did not know, was convicted of the sole crime of having mentioned in a bibliography in a scholarly journal that he edited works that corrected historical errors that no serious historian now adheres to. he was arrested. his personal computer was confiscated. each of the usual grant-making associations that sued him won large sums of money at their own expense and at the expense of their rural artisan printer. the judges of the court of appeal of lyon, dominique fournier, jean-luc gouverneur, marie-odile théolleyre, also banned its publication in a judgment worthy of the stalinist courts. the counsel for the court of cassation, bruno cotte, christine chanet and guy joly, failed to do their duty by failing to censure in this case the manifestly abusive use of a law on publications for young people. moreover, under pressure and in all illegality, professors régis ladous and claude prudhomme have taken the ridiculous and odious step of cancelling mr plantin's thesis eleven years later, which they had, in full knowledge of the facts, given the mark "very well". and all this in the 21st century, in france, as in other european countries! of course, such persecution only reinforces the doubts about official dogmas. she is unworthy and intolerable. it has to stop as soon as possible.
in writing. - certain recommendations in the cornillet report are undoubtedly positive. the extension of the right to vote to non-eu citizens, the abolition of the aznar protocol, the complete denial of the right to asylum, the unrestricted recognition of refugee status, for example for all persecuted algerians, measures against discrimination against the roma and the recognition of the rights of homosexuals are measures which we support. but sometimes good intentions are thwarted halfway through: detention centres and waiting areas are effectively nameless prisons where conditions are inhuman. 'limitation' or 'placing a cap on the length of detention' are insufficient recommendations that maintain the criminalisation of asylum seekers and undocumented persons. minors must not be subjected to the degrading detention that article 32 seeks to "humanize" for them. in order to enable victims of human trafficking and domestic slavery to free themselves from their persecutors, a general regulation must be enacted in europe. a permanent residence permit would be much more effective against operators than a 'temporary permit ... for the duration of the investigation and the legal proceedings'. if the recitals and amendments concerning the right to vote or the rights of homosexuals are retained, we shall vote in favour of this report. otherwise, we will abstain.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to welcome the initiators of the first world congress against the death penalty, which i believe was the culmination of the work of abolitionists all over the world. during these three days, a very important work was done and i would also like to commend here the personal commitment of our president who, together with her counterpart from the council of europe, launched an appeal to the states for a global moratorium on executions, a moratorium which has been signed by 40 countries present here in this house. to fight for the abolition of the death penalty - as has been said here - is to fight for the strengthening of human dignity and the extension of human rights. i believe that the european union is doing this and must continue to do so, but i also believe that sometimes it is important, in an assembly such as the united nations, to sweep in front of its door. i am referring to the fact that countries such as turkey, russia and armenia, which are members of the council of europe and are seeking to join the european union, must abolish the death penalty from their respective penal codes. i believe that this is a sine qua non condition for their membership or non-membership and a guarantee that this fundamental principle of human rights will be respected in the european union area. secondly, as robert badinter has pointed out, i think the debate has made a tremendous progress: 100 countries have already abolished the death penalty. and even in the united states, five or six years ago, almost 80 percent of the population was in favor of the death penalty. today, it is only 66 percent. it means the fight is moving forward, and that's good. however, there is another case which is very symbolic of the fight against the death penalty: it is the case of moumia abu jamal. of the 3,700 people who are still on death row in the united states today, moumia abu jamal is a symbol of the fact that he is in prison and on death row because he is black, and in that sense, he reminds me a little bit of the struggle of nelson mandela. he's in prison because he was an intellectual writer, and in that he reminds me a little of solzhenitsyn, and because he dared to write at a time when we didn't write against the excesses of the philadelphia police. and finally, he was an activist, an activist as we say in english. for these three reasons he is now on death row and i think it would be a great sign if a country like the united states, which claims to be the world's largest democracy, abolished the death penalty and decided to release mumia abu jamal. imagine the weight that this would have on countries like china and other countries that, of course, continue to practice this barbaric practice! i am counting heavily on the belgian presidency to take this idea forward, which we fully support here.

- mr president, commissioner, like it or not, we are indirectly responsible for the fate of 250 million children between the ages of 5 and 14, according to the international labour office. they make carpets in nepal or luxury shoes in thailand; they work in coffee and cocoa plantations in africa: and all this for export, for our goods. in europe, this takes more subtle forms: apprenticeships give rise to abuses of schedules; children are used as models; we're all obsessed with young athletes, who make us happy in front of our tvs. then there are the things that we all hate: the sexual abuse that destroys whole lives, the pornography and the prostitution. i think that our position must therefore be one of unrelenting firmness. forced child labour is a hindrance to their intellectual, physical and psychological development, and i think that, therefore, we cannot continue to have countries signing conventions, releasing themselves from labels, knowing that they are doing this as if they were going to buy a pair of shoes. the minimum that can be demanded at the september conference is the right to education, the right of every child to leisure, the right of every child to be informed of his rights. we must at least get that. if we do not get it, it will mean that children's rights are like socks: when they are dirty and have holes in them, they end up in the garbage.

commission. – i would just like to say that it is a pleasure to listen to the debate and to take part in it, not least since it was so ably moved by my friend mr maccormick. it is an important debate as part of the preparatory process for the un special session on children. the commission, in coordination with member states, firmly supports a rights-based approach founded on the convention of the rights of the child. since 1992, for almost one decade now, all cooperation agreements between the european union and third countries have incorporated a clause defining human rights as an essential element of the agreement. this includes the rights of the child and respect for the core labour standards as set out in the eight ilo fundamental conventions. the commission strongly supports efforts by the international community to eliminate child labour across the world. in this regard, the commission particularly supports the work of the ilo which adopted a convention in 1999 banning the worst forms of child labour, some of which were referred to during the debate. on 15 september 2000, the commission underlined its support for the ilo's efforts against child labour by adopting a recommendation to the member states to ratify this new convention. while there is no specific community competence in children's matters, the european commission recognises children as a particularly vulnerable group within the overarching policy focus on poverty and vulnerability, and the concerns about children as well as about human rights and gender issues are an integral part of our development policy objective of poverty eradication, especially in social sectors such as education and health. whereas there is no explicit focus on children in development cooperation, echo has made children a priority for our humanitarian assistance this year. promotion of the rights of the child is also a high priority for funding under the european initiative for democracy and human rights where the promotion of the rights of the child was chosen as a priority theme for funding under the budget this year. as a complement to the european union's intervention in international fora such as the un, the commission offers substantial support to projects designed to address the plight of children affected by conflict, and there were several references to that problem. since the beginning of 2000, more than eur 40 million have been spent on projects providing assistance and protection to children affected by armed conflict. the commission is therefore active in supporting children's rights both at the political level and through practical initiatives. i am grateful for your indulgence, president, but this seemed to me to be a sufficiently important subject on which to make those remarks. commission. – firstly, on vietnam, may i say that i share the concerns of honourable members about the human rights situation and, in particular, about recent developments in that country. these appear to suggest that the progress which has been achieved by the vietnamese government, both politically and economically, since the 1992 constitution was adopted may be slowing down or even going into reverse, particularly where political freedoms are concerned. the european union's policy toward vietnam, as it is towards all countries, is to encourage and support continued progress on human rights and democratisation and to raise concerns both publicly and in private where abuses or a deterioration in the situation is observed. in vietnam, permitting freedom of opinion and freedom of religion are of paramount importance to the european union. the constitution of vietnam guarantees freedom of belief and religion, and in recent years the state has developed more cooperative arrangements with the catholic church. however, the constitution also specifies that it is forbidden to violate freedom of belief or religion or to take advantage of it to act against the laws or the policies of the state. this provision obviously reflects the desire of the vietnamese authorities to try to control the pace of change and to maintain their grip on society during the transition process. it is also plainly a restriction on freedom of opinion, and the press law is similarly restricted. the cases mentioned in today's debate seem to me to be more concerned with freedom of opinion than with freedom of religion, a freedom which of course the european union holds to be equally important. father ly has called publicly for the united states not to ratify its bilateral trade agreement with vietnam, linking this action to human rights issues. similar calls have reportedly been made by members of the unified buddhist church of vietnam. these calls are clearly contrary to the government's policy and difficult for them to tolerate in a society unaccustomed to public dissent. what is needed in vietnam is continued progress in the country's reform programme so that the administration learns to deal with a wider range of views and to appreciate the value of accommodating dissent in the system of government. we will continue to support progress and to take every opportunity to draw attention to the fundamental importance of freedom of opinion. the first article of the ec-vietnam cooperation agreement which we signed with the government of vietnam in 1995 states that respect for human rights and democratic principles is the basis for our cooperation. we will shortly be holding in hanoi a meeting of the ec-vietnam joint commission at which all aspects of our relations will be reviewed including our shared commitment to respect for human rights. in the meantime, the commission delegation participates with the member states represented in hanoi in all eu démarches to the government of vietnam on human rights issues, as well as in the regular discussions on human rights which the eu missions pursue with the vietnamese authorities. i can assure parliament that in this process, we will continue to raise particular issues of concern and individual cases, and will continue to encourage action to address human rights abuses in vietnam. i will make those points when i am in vietnam myself later this month. i would have referred specifically to a point raised by mr dupuis, but since he is not here, i will pass on. the second subject that i would like to deal with is south africa. the commission shares the european parliament's view that south africa/eu cooperation should seek to redress the existing inequalities inherited from the apartheid era and to work to improve the living conditions of the population with programmes targeting employment, health, education and housing. that is what our european programme for reconstruction and development is about. we strongly share the european parliament's concern that there is an urgent need to combat the hiv/aids problem in south africa and i am sure – as i said this morning during the debate on the forthcoming g8 summit – that will be one of the subjects which is discussed then in genoa. the commission also agrees that there is a need for a climate of greater security in south africa as a prerequisite for a peaceful society and for economic development. we fear that the crime situation is not only a threat to the inhabitants of the country and to its social fabric, but also threatens south africa's reputation abroad, discourages foreign investment and has a detrimental effect on the economy as a whole. as the house knows, the priority areas under our current multiannual indicative programme for the years 2000-2002 are poverty alleviation through the provision of basic social services, private sector support and the consolidation of the rule of law and promotion of human rights. the commission has funded two programmes to support the south african police force. the most recent one is currently being implemented. while it is true that last year saw no new projects or programmes in the health sector, the public health sector support programme 2000, which was agreed in 1999, became operational during the course of the last year. programmes under consideration for funding in 2001 include a major health programme on primary health care, and that will also cover hiv/aids in selected provinces. preparations for the programming of the next multiannual indicative programme are about to start and they will take place in the course of the next year. in this programming phase the commission will give very proper consideration to the concerns and interests expressed by the european parliament. i now turn to belarus. i want to say how important it is for parliament to discuss this subject and i very much take the point raised by a number of honourable members about the importance of raising our concerns on belarus with the russian federation. that is something we have done, are doing and will continue to do. i welcome this timely debate. i congratulate honourable members on highlighting the extremely worrying situation in belarus. the commission shares the deep concerns contained in the resolutions that are before us today. i join parliament in calling on president lukashenka to reverse the present alarming trend towards increased authoritarianism by decisive action to improve human rights, press freedom and democracy. in the short term this means, in particular, ensuring free and fair elections and addressing the situation of missing opposition figures and political prisoners. improved cooperation with the osce will be a vital ingredient in this. the presidential elections on 9 september will be the next test of the democratic credentials of the country and we are in close touch with the osce-odihr discussions over the desirability of an international election monitoring mission. there are some – i emphasise ‘some’ – encouraging signs of greater unity among opposition parties. however, all the indications are that the authorities will again fail the democratic test, just as the parliamentary elections last october fell disappointingly short of the conditions established by the osce. the european union has a clear position: as long as the present intolerable situation remains we cannot consider closer economic or political relations with belarus. unless and until there are significant improvements, our financial assistance will remain limited to direct help to those involved in promoting civil society and democracy, and humanitarian assistance where it is needed. the european union has condemned the recent government decree on external funding for non-governmental organisations, and we are urgently seeking clarification on how it might affect our own assistance programmes. speaking personally, i would prefer to see our present limited assistance suspended, rather than have it subject to prior approval by the authorities. our restrictive policy on political dialogue has not prevented the european union from repeatedly airing our deep concerns about prominent public figures who mysteriously disappear or who are imprisoned for political reasons. recently the european union has raised the cases of the former interior minister yury zakharenko, the former head of the election committee, viktor gonchav, the businessman anatoly krasovsky and the photographer who was referred to in the debate, dmitry zavadsky. it is disturbing that despite this pressure there has been no progress in these cases. the debate today has highlighted a further case: the imprisonment of professor bandashevsky, following his work on the alarming social and environmental consequences of the chernobyl disaster. european union heads of mission in belarus have recently undertaken a study into the impact of chernobyl on public health. the commission is keen to discuss with member states how the european union should respond to these disturbing findings and on how we should react to professor bandashevsky's imprisonment, taking account of the strong views that are felt by honourable members. i have no hesitation at all in defending a fair, but tough, line on belarus, but it is a pity that it is necessary. belarus is a country at the heart of europe that has the potential to become an important political and economic partner for the union, particularly following enlargement. this is the positive message that we must continue to send to the people of belarus. in this way we can lend our support to those forces in society that are pressing for the reforms that are so necessary, the reforms that will one day assuredly arrive. finally, i refer to the important speech made by mr khanbhai, who raised a number of very important issues, triggered by the position of burundian refugees in tanzania. the commission is concerned about the lack of progress towards peace in burundi. how could we not be? we are concerned about the continuation of violence against the civil population resulting from persistent clashes between the burundian army and the rebels. in the current circumstances a voluntary return of burundian refugees in tanzanian camps is not, frankly, likely and a forced repatriation is hardly advisable. the continued and growing presence of a huge burundian refugee population in tanzania is causing tension between the two governments. by the end of may there were approximately 523 000 refugees in camps in western tanzania, of whom over 383 000 were burundians. in particular, the tanzanian government is accused of not preventing burundian rebels from using refugee camps as bases for their attacks. in reaction to recent allegations by the burundi government to this effect, tanzania's president mkapa suggested an immediate forced repatriation of all refugees, without taking into account the prevailing security situation in burundi. the government of tanzania has since reassured the unhcr that its policy towards the burundian refugees is not in question, and it undertook to respect its earlier commitment to facilitate a gradual voluntary repatriation once the security conditions in burundi permit. for our part, the european commission will contribute eur 25 million towards the implementation of the unhcr plan for voluntary repatriation of burundian refugees to be launched once the situation is favourable. for now, the commission is taking the necessary measures to assist the government of tanzania to cope with the refugee population. through the humanitarian aid office, echo, the commission is funding more than a third of the total humanitarian aid available to refugees in tanzania. last year echo's budget for aid to tanzanian refugees was nearly eur 27 million. this was increased to over eur 32 million this year. mr khanbhai also raised a number of important issues about the management of our assistance and development programmes and about our representation in africa and in other parts of the world. i look forward to future opportunities to discuss those matters with him and the whole house, not least in the context of the communication which we have just produced on our external commission. – the commission is well aware of the information referred to in the proposals for a resolution submitted to parliament and in the press concerning illegal exploitation of natural resources in the democratic republic of congo. this information has been broadly confirmed by the commission's interlocutors on the spot, including non-governmental organisations and in an interim report by the united nations, to which a number of honourable members referred. the honourable member referred to that report during a speech which made a powerful case for an international criminal court able to extend its remit around the world, not unlike the tribunal at the hague focused on the balkans. that report covers the illegal exploitation of the drcs natural resources and other wealth. it was presented to the security council by the secretary-general, kofi annan, on 14 april 2001 and it was the subject of a heated debate. the secretary-general decided to extend the mandate of the experts who compiled the report by three months, so that they could add to the research and the information already provided. the report will be an important point of departure for the international community, which will have to take a position on it. the profits to be made from coltan mining and other mining by the warring parties in congo are bound to have an impact on the devastation in kivu. the region's decline began under president mobutu and has a number of causes, one of the most significant being ethnic tensions. the situation became much worse following the genocide in rwanda and rwanda's intervention in both the country's wars which were originally fought to secure external borders. the international community is aware of the link between economic interests and the continuation of the war in kivu. the only lasting solution is nonetheless to advance the peace process and to build legitimate institutions able to regulate the exploitation of resources. this is the objective supported by the commission through its activity in the democratic republic of the congo. that is the context in which we envisaged the gradual resumption of aid in tandem with the implementation of the lusaka agreement and the progress of the congolese dialogue. honourable members, and particularly mr van den berg, focused their arguments on the relationship between the illicit trade in some commodities and the conflict. we know the problems that have been caused with diamonds elsewhere and the arms trade. it is extremely important, where we can, to take initiatives and pursue them on both. that is why we have been so active in working at the united nations on small arms and we must make use of the community's competences, when we can, and with the member states deal effectively with the illicit diamond and with other illicit trades which have caused so much suffering and impoverishment in africa in particular, but in other countries as well.

- b5-0493/2001 by mrs salafranca sánchez-neyra, on behalf of the ppe-de group, on the earthquake in peru, chile and bolivia on 23 june 2001; - b5-0503/2001 by mr medina ortega and mr linkhor, on behalf of the pse group, on the earthquake in peru on 23 june 2001; - b5-0518/2001 by mr puerta and others, on behalf of the gue/ngl group, on the earthquake in peru; - b5-0519/2001 by mrs muscardini, on behalf of the uen group, on the earthquake in peru;
commission. – as the house knows, a strong earthquake struck southern peru on 23 june 2001. up-dated figures from the un office for the coordination of humanitarian affairs indicate that almost 190 000 people were affected and some 35 000 homes damaged or destroyed. through its humanitarian aid office echo, the commission reacted, and i am grateful for the generous remarks made by the honourable member, mr medina. the commission reacted very promptly. a decision to allocate humanitarian aid amounting to eur 1.15m was taken two days after the earthquake to help meet the first urgent needs of the victims. this is the first time, in fact, that the commission has made use of its new system for responding immediately to the sudden onset of humanitarian crises which came into operation less than two weeks ago. furthermore, five emergency humanitarian operations are already under way. the spanish red cross is distributing food aid and emergency relief items for 1 000 families to the tune of eur 250 000. oxfam is spending eur 200 000 on emergency water storage and distribution facilities and sanitation. save the children fund – eur 300 000 on blankets and tents. medicos del mundo – eur 100 000 on blankets, medicines, water tanks and plastic sheets for shelter. the international federation of the red cross – eur 300 000 on shelter, food and support to the rescue efforts for health, water, sanitation and other relief supplies. that is how our emergency relief is being spent and i think it is being spent in sensible ways. according to information received from the field, the international response has been generous and the immediate needs seem to be covered. nevertheless, the commission services continue to monitor the situation in case additional aid is required. a debate on a resolution on the peruvian earthquake is not perhaps the most appropriate framework to discuss the political situation in peru, but i would nevertheless like to stress that we are extremely satisfied with the capacity shown by peru and its transitional government to carry out transparent and clean elections after the political disasters described very effectively by the honourable member in his maiden speech. we shall look forward to hearing from him many times in the future. it was a pretty vigorous maiden as maidens go! the european union observation mission for the elections was extremely positive. like honourable members, i discussed the catastrophe and the european response on tuesday with president toledo during his visit to parliament. we want to congratulate the interim government and the people of peru for the maturity shown in this situation and for the support and cooperation provided to our team in the field. i was able to say to president toledo when he was here with us that the approximately eur 60m in programmes for the alleviation of poverty blocked by the conduct of the elections in 2000 will now be released. we want to proceed with those projects as rapidly as possible. i follow very much the point raised by mr medina, you want to get on with those projects as soon as possible and i know that poverty alleviation is one of the new president's priorities. we also want to sit down with the new government to discuss programming our future assistance. the president himself underlined his commitment to reforming the judiciary and making sure that there is in place a rule of law in the institutions to make that rule of law effective. i feel that that is a very important way in which we can see the encouragement of more private investment in peru and more confidence on the part of the international community. we all express our condolences to those who have been affected by this terrible earthquake but at least it has given us the opportunity of expressing in this house once again our solidarity with democracy in peru and our encouragement of the new peruvian government.

mr president, commissioner, i am speaking on behalf of my colleague, dominique souchet, and i am presenting the position he has taken in the committee on fisheries, which is also my own. this annual report - whatever the merits and efforts of the rapporteur - always seems repetitive, agreed and rather vain. the vacuity of this exercise highlights, if need be, that of a process: the pop process, i.e. the multiannual guidance plans, which has the main effect of generating fraudulent behaviour, benefiting some fleets at the expense of others. the purchase of near-wrecks from outside, in order to break them up and thus have unnecessary reserves of kilowatts, has distorted the mechanism from the outset. in some states, this perversion has even become a national sport. it is therefore not very sensible to complain indefinitely about the poor quality of the statistical data on pops. it would be dangerous to adopt the logic of punishing and sanctioning the member states, as proposed by the commission, which would in fact affect the professionals. what is needed is simply to acknowledge the failure of the pops instead of trying to artificially prolong the life of this inefficient and counterproductive system. despite their high cost, these pops have not achieved their objective. the tacs, which are added to the total allowable catches, were poorly designed from the outset and have caused the second-hand market to explode, to the detriment of young artisanal fishermen who are entering the profession. everyone admits to this failure in private. it would be healthy to have the courage to publicly admit it and face the consequences. the main one should be to provide in the new common fisheries policy, alongside the abolition of pops, for the refocusing of sustainable resource management on a renewed, better-adapted, multiannual, improved tac and quota system, based on refined resource assessments through a substantial increase in scientific research and close involvement of professionals in the process. by wanting to prolong the policy on pops, the commission risks taking the wrong path, and we warn it against this. it is not by doing so that it will reconcile fishermen with the common fisheries policy.
in writing. - we shall vote in favour of the resolution on the european union strategy for the bonn conference on climate change. it is responding to an emergency by affirming its willingness to move forward in the face of president bush's unilateral denunciation of the kyoto protocol. it also includes positive articles, such as reaffirming the need to promote "clean development" by promoting technologies that exclude nuclear energy, the large-scale use of fossil fuels and the use of carbon sinks. or as one that favours domestic policies and measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, rather than the use of 'flexible mechanisms' (whose resolution calls for a 50% cap). or one which demands, beyond the prudence of the formulas, that the wto submit to environmental priorities decided outside it by an international conference, by acting to prevent countries which would not respect the kyoto protocol from obtaining competitive advantages. this resolution shows how bad the situation has become today. the union is reduced to defending the kyoto protocol, which was far from good. the kyoto protocol is too much about the mechanisms of an unequal market. the protocol sanctions the successive setbacks in environmental policy since the rio conference, under pressure from established interests and supporters of economic liberalism. we cannot be satisfied with the way things are.
in writing. - no one has been able to prove that the climate change we are concerned about is not the result of a natural climate cycle that has been evolving since the origin of our planet. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be consulted on the future of the european union's environment policy. in this sense, i support the idea of assisting developing countries to ensure that they respect the environment. i do not share the idea of setting up a 'censor' which would sanction states according to criteria which i cannot accept and which would exclude nuclear energy amongst others. on the other hand, if we are consistent, we should develop without delay, through tax incentives, clean energy sources such as biofuels. in conclusion, let us be firm in the objectives to be achieved, but flexible in the means to achieve them.
in writing. - the two recent mining accidents mentioned in the explanatory memorandum were ecological disasters whose impact extended far beyond the regions where the accidents occurred. in the case of baia mare, after the disaster, the main shareholder, an australian, withdrew his capital and washed his hands of the destruction of the fauna and flora of the tisza and a large part of the danube. if we want to prevent this kind of disaster from happening again, the minimum would be to impose binding legislation, making not only the mining companies concerned but also all their owners and shareholders responsible for the damage caused, or else all their assets and capital, including those invested in other sectors, would be seized. it is useless to make mere wishes or even recommendations if the sacred right of property is not called into question when its exercise has disastrous consequences for the whole population, and not just for the present. we voted on some of the proposals in this text, but we abstained on the whole, because of its arbitrary nature.
in writing. - the report by jonas sjöstedt follows on from a commission communication and deals with a very important issue, too often neglected: the impact of mining activities on the environment. it draws lessons from two recent major accidents: the donana mine in spain, in a metal concentrate mine, and the "maia mare" gold mine in romania. in view of the flagrant inadequacy of the current rules and standards of monitoring, it is essential to revise the community's environmental policy so as to include mining activities (and in particular the management of their waste) systematically. the aim is to define clearly the responsibility of mining companies which today abuse the laxity of regulations. we shall vote in favour of the report by mr jonas sjöstedt.
