- the report (a5-0243/2001) by mr hans-peter mayer, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the draft council regulation on the statute for a european company (se) (14886/2000 - c5-0092/2001 - 1989/0218 (cns)) and - the report (a5-0231/2001) by mr menrad, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the draft council directive supplementing the statute for a european company with regard to the involvement of workers (14732/2000 - c5-0093/2001 - 1989/0219 (cns)).
mr president, the proposal for a directive on the involvement of employees in european society gives us the opportunity, and this is the first time, to establish at community level a precise definition of what is meant by the right of employees to information, consultation and participation in all undertakings. it makes the inclusion in the commercial regime of a company which would choose this new status conditional on the conclusion of a negotiated agreement on the involvement of employees. the green group is not making light of the fact that the proposals for the rapid adoption and effective implementation of this directive are being put forward, says mr menrad's report. we will of course do so in the conviction that this necessary condition is far from sufficient to consider that european legislation really meets the needs that are being felt at the moment. we must, as soon as the vote has been taken, go on and get the job done. as you know, this directive will apply tomorrow only to employees of companies who choose this new status, a small minority. this is why we must of course guard against any triumphalism and advertising. we shall only have made progress if we simultaneously adopt this directive, revise the directive on european works councils which we shall be discussing shortly, and approve the directive on information and consultation of employees under conditions somewhat different from the position adopted by the council. this legislative work, to be carried out in conditions which guarantee a real social and citizens' debate, requires the use of the codecision procedure. i would like to stress in this connection that the green group refuses pressure which in fact limits its right to legislate under the guise of efficiency and speed, especially as the matter is old, as everyone knows.
- mr president, first of all i should like to congratulate and thank our rapporteur for the tenacity and efficiency he has shown in this matter of worker participation, which for several years has been the stumbling block in the negotiations on the status of the european company. the first proposal for a regulation dates back to 1970, but it was not until the nice european council that agreement was finally reached on a draft directive on the involvement of workers, supplementing the draft regulation on the statute of the european company. it is therefore a fragile balance, which was achieved at the council meeting on 20 december. it is important to maintain this balance. that is why amendment no 4, which requires member states to take appropriate measures to ensure that negotiations are provided for in the event of restructuring, seems difficult to accept. it is tantamount to calling into question the agreement that was so difficult to reach. the same applies to amendment no 7, which seeks to remove the limiting list of rights of the body representing workers in matters of participation, which in practice leads to the establishment of a system of participation which does not take account of national specificities and calls into question the mechanism for safeguarding the rights of participation provided for in the annex to the directive. the status of the european company has been awaited for more than 30 years by economic and social actors. let us therefore, ladies and gentlemen, take care to respond to the need for simplicity and flexibility expressed by the companies and not, therefore, to complicate this status by adding new constraints which would discourage the companies concerned, and in particular small and mediumsized enterprises, from using this new tool to their advantage.
as rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, i should like to begin by thanking mr menrad for having taken account of the main points of the proposals put forward by our committee, particularly - and i will not go into detail - the definition of information, consultation, strengthening of the procedure, strengthening of the role of trade unions, lowering of the thresholds for the establishment of these committees and reducing the time limits for the establishment of european works councils. i would like to stress three points which i think are important. the first was mentioned in paragraph 12: this is the reference to the 1998 directive on redundancies which provides for the possibility for workers' representatives to refer to a competent authority on the basis of information provided by the company's management, when they believe that alternative solutions have not been explored to avoid redundancies, site closures or that the legality of the procedure is in question. i believe that, in the face of the problems that arise in european-sized companies today, including sometimes mergers and acquisitions authorised by the commission and its competition authority, the question that is being asked - and which was raised after the marks & spencer case by your colleague, mrs diamantopoulou, the commissioner for social affairs - is whether employees, their representatives and works councils can bring an action against the european commission arguing that social law is sometimes disregarded because it is purely financial and purely stock market transactions. i therefore support amendment no 5 by mrs ainardi and mrs figueiredo, which i shall be voting for. the second point, which is linked to this amendment, is that of sanctions. i think we must not only provide for significant and dissuasive sanctions but also say - and this is implied in one of mr menrad's paragraphs, but i would have liked it to be more specific so that workers and citizens would know - that when there is non-compliance with the information and consultation procedures, decisions to cut jobs or close sites can be annulled. i shall conclude, as mr menrad did, by asking the commission to understand the urgency of this request from parliament, not to wait until 2002 and to make a proposal which reflects the wish of the vast majority of our groups to see the rights of workers in european-sized enterprises strengthened.
mr president, the interest which workers and citizens are showing in european social policy is being eroded by the many examples of restructuring and redundancies. it is clear in this context that the revision of the directive on works councils is an essential means of restoring this credibility. what do the employees who are victims of these restructurings say about the possibility of using this directive? in a few examples, they say that the current legislation on the right to information and consultation, in the absence of a precise definition, is regularly flouted by companies; they do not have the administrative and judicial remedies necessary to verify compliance with this directive; that the law is applied only too 'sparse' or not at all in many transnational enterprises below the current threshold; whereas it is unthinkable that mergers should be authorised on the basis of criteria relating to competition law alone and that the social, territorial or environmental impact of mergers should not be taken into account; that they are deprived during the merger periods, during which the old concertation structures are no longer operational, while the new structures are not yet established; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the report by mr menrad, which is the result of open and cooperative work with the social partners concerned, the members of the commission, who held a wide public hearing on the subject, calls, in my view, for the remediation of these shortcomings by the precise definition of information and consultation, the proposed lowering of the thresholds for employees required to set up a works council, the request for the maintenance of specific places for consultation during merger periods, the request for the annulment of decisions taken without respecting the procedures and the imposition of sanctions, including financial ones, for companies which are in breach of the rules and, finally, by taking into account the opinion of employees and the provision of evidence of compliance with the procedures of the directive, prior to the authorization of mergers. in this context, these proposals are supported by our group. it is obvious that the revision of the directive must be started effectively and rapidly - and this requires a collective effort.
mr president, at a time when thousands of european employees are facing a wave of restructuring, redundancies and social plans, the menrad report on european works councils must, if not change the situation, at least provide new support for employees to cope with very difficult situations and influence decisions in progress. at a time when growth is showing worrying signs, it would be useful to reflect on the content of this growth and on the need to change it by promoting employment stability and skills. there is an urgent need for genuine consultation of employees, an urgent need to put an end to the attitude of treating men and women as goods which have become useless because the financial return is considered insufficient by the shareholders, even beyond the real economic situation. the menrad report is the fruit of very important work by our colleague, whom i also want to congratulate. it is also the result of the desire of the committee on employment and social affairs to hear the representatives of the employees of the major european groups. it is on the basis of these hearings that the menrad report makes a serious assessment of the situation, showing the need for major changes to the content of the directive. i agree with many of the proposals made in this report. i would like to mention a few of them which i believe represent important advances for employees. the requirement, for example, in paragraph 2, that regular information and consultation be given prior to the decision of an undertaking or group in order to enable workers to exercise a real influence on the management decision-making process, information which may even go, in particularly serious cases, as far as the possibility given to employee representatives to obtain time for negotiation prior to the application of the decision, as indicated in point 14. i would also mention point 2, with the development of a clause according to which management decisions will only have legitimacy if the information and consultation process, as defined in the directive, has been properly carried out beforehand, or point 13, which proposes to introduce sanctions in case of non-compliance. finally, there is the demand by the companies for reimbursement of the funds and aid provided and their exclusion from public procurement for those who do not comply with the law in this area. these proposals are in the right direction, but i think that for the effectiveness of action for employment, for the improvement of economic performance in europe, we could have gone further in the right of employees to participate in the future of companies. that is the meaning of the amendment tabled by my group, which calls for the possibility of employee representatives having a suspensive veto. the aim is to give the employees' representatives the assurance that their alternative proposals will at least be studied and taken into account. many of the disastrous decisions for companies, for jobs, could have been avoided if the employees had been able to influence those decisions. this right, which is an expression of social justice and democracy in business, is also a guarantee of economic and social efficiency. once again, the menrad report is an important step forward. that is why he has the support of my group.

mr president, i will not vote against this report for the sole reason that a number of trade unions want it to be adopted, whatever i may think of their policy. but i won't give my approval for it. in return for a limited extension of the prerogatives of the european works councils, the report calls for the approval of the requirements of competition and confidentiality of information. he also stressed that the role of committees was to reduce the risk of conflict, which he said was a success factor for companies, in other words for their bosses. in france, it is clear that in all decisions which are essential for the lives of workers, the final decision belongs to the employers. the works councils are rendered powerless, as in the case of the unacceptable dismissals at moulinex, aventis, danone and many others, or they are so involved that they endorse the decisions of the employers or even appoint the victims of the dismissals, as at aom-air liberté. the only right that would be a right for workers would then be the right to employment, i.e. the prohibition of dismissals, at least in the beneficiary companies.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in april 2000 the european commission presented a report on the state of application of the 1994 directive on the establishment of a european works council for - mr president, 1075 formal complaints, 470 reasoned opinions, 178 referrals to the court of justice, twice as many as in 1998. this 1999 review of the application of community law reflects a deep malaise. we must face the facts: europe is over- and under-legislating. it may even legislate in areas where it has no competence. it did so in 1979 for the birds directive and more recently, without any legal basis, on the status and funding of european political parties. the member states are slow to transpose community law into national law, and the number of disputes is increasing because european regulations are often restrictive, cumbersome, unsuited to local realities and far from the concerns of our fellow citizens, when they are not directly opposed to their will and the republican principle. last year, for example, the french government declared its disagreement with the genome directive. mrs guigou, minister for justice, considered this directive, and i quote, "incompatible with french bioethical laws, with the industrial property code and the civil code which prohibit the marketing of the human body". can we, in the name of europe and its qualified majority, impose legislation on a people who refuse it? it's a matter of substance. should we standardize everything and sacrifice our differences, the true wealth of europe? that's not our opinion. moreover, in a democracy, it is not the court of justice that makes the law through case law, but the elected representatives. the european parliament, the only body elected by universal suffrage, does not have a genuine right of legislative initiative, a monopoly jealously guarded by the commission. europe will not solve its problems by insisting on the application of bad legislation through fines and penalties, as article 15 would like. there are limits to obstinacy, and when a text is wrong, we must have the lucidity and courage to amend it, as we propose in article 12. it is therefore necessary to legislate less in order to legislate better, to respect national wishes and democracy by applying the principle of subsidiarity as much as possible. for example, a regulation on the transport of hydrocarbons is urgently needed, but it has just been referred back to the greek islands for commercial reasons. contrary to recital m, we do not consider that the strict application of community law contributes to the emergence of a european nationality which we do not want. we are too concerned with respect for identities, democracy and the right to be different.
- mr president, community law is giving rise to increasing difficulties in its application, since according to the commission's own report, it opened 2270 cases in this respect in 1999, compared with only 124 in 1978. this increase is due, on the one hand, to the constant proliferation of community law and, on the other, to the increased severity of the commission, which has had effective instruments of repression at its disposal since maastricht, in particular articles 226 and 228 of the ec treaty. the report under discussion today in the european parliament is a further step in the direction of repression, since it calls on the commission to make greater use of these articles, to threaten member states with fines or penalties more often, and even to propose a new system of automatic sanctions for those who do not transpose community directives quickly enough or well enough. but why do member states, which are supposed to have accepted the directives in the council, then delay in implementing them? it's the big question that everybody's avoiding. i shall give three additional replies. firstly, it is a perverse effect of the extension of qualified majority voting which keeps the institutions in what i would call a kind of normative illusion. we believe that because we have voted by a majority at the council table, everything is settled. but in reality, if the minorities had good reasons and if the application does not follow on the ground, nothing is settled. and to set the record straight, europe is being thrown into a spiral of repression that a better consensus would have avoided in the first place. second reason for non-application: the inadequacy of certain parts of community law, such as the 1979 directive on the hunting of wild birds, which was later tightened up by the court of justice behind the very backs of the council. in a case like this, which is a directive, note that, adopted unanimously, what we lack is the possibility of automatic revision after ten years, at the request of a single member state. finally, the third reason for non-application: certain directives remain untransposed or poorly transposed because government representatives in the council wanted to buy good european behaviour by turning a blind eye to future difficulties which they knew were inevitable. this is what happened in france, for example, with directive 98/44 on the patentability of living things, which is now found to be unenforceable because it is contrary to several essential parts of our law. unfortunately, this is a customary behaviour of french leaders, right up to the highest level of the state. today we agree to sign this or that european text because we do not dare to raise objections, and tomorrow we will be able to implement it. that is what they have just done again with the treaty of nice, and france will pay dearly for it.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, in the wake of what malcolm harbour has just said, i shall move very quickly to the technical problems which concern the legal affairs committee. i would like to say, however, commissioner, that i welcome the progress made in the area of consultation since our last plenary session. i thought, as did several members, that it commission. – madam president, the minister has set out with great clarity and comprehensiveness the situation in the middle east at the moment and, as the minister has said and everyone in parliament knows, the situation in the region has gone from bad to worse and threatens to become worse still. in considering what i should say this morning i was struck once again, by the difference between the strength of the adjectives and the nouns that we use to describe the situation and the strength of the verbs we use in trying to resolve it. it really is an intensely difficult problem. the continuing violence – according to the news this morning there has been another suicide bombing in jerusalem – and the endless recriminations and refusal of the parties to rise above their grievances and choose the path of peace is not only profoundly regrettable but also frustrating for everyone in the international community who is trying to find a way out of the current impasse. both parties, as the minister said earlier, have failed to seize the opportunity offered by the recommendations of the mitchell report, offered again in the tenet plan. but again we come back to the point that there is no better basis for an end to the violence, for laying the foundations for a peaceful and prosperous future, than mitchell. what is the alternative? the alternative is more bloodshed, with an international dispute turned into a bitter feud and continuing collateral damage internationally, as we are seeing this week at the conference in durban. so what can the european union do in these circumstances? the minister has explained, very clearly the extremely important role the presidency has been playing, trying to mobilise international opinion around proposals which offer a way forward. the minister has also noted the efforts made by all the european union foreign ministers and, of course, javier solana, who has been attempting to bring israelis and palestinians together and to get them to return to the negotiating table. we obviously have to continue to urge all concerned to implement all and not just some of the recommendations of the mitchell report immediately. we will go on doing that and delivering that message. we must also urge the parties to reduce the level of distrust which has been built up in recent months. they must reaffirm their commitment to the fundamental long-term goals of the middle east peace process, secure borders for israel through the negotiated establishment of a viable palestinian state on the basis of the relevant un resolutions. palestinian leaders must make clear day-by-day their unequivocal condemnation of and opposition to attacks on the innocent and violence in all its forms. it is sometimes suggested by critics that we in the european union have not been sufficiently strong in our condemnation of terrorism. that is a grossly unfair criticism. for example, in its statement after the attack in jerusalem on 9 august the presidency unreservedly condemned the bombing of a jerusalem shopping centre and it abhorred that cowardly attack, which mainly claimed the lives of innocent civilians. after the attack in haifa on 12 august, the presidency once again put out a statement condemning recent suicide bomb attacks in the strongest terms and pointing out that these attacks targeted at israeli citizens are hateful and repugnant in the extreme. so we have made clear our opposition to terrorism in all its manifestations, but if we are to stand a better chance of ending the cycle of violence and weakening the position of radical forces. palestinians need to be able to see a real prospect of an improvement in their daily lives. this should include the implementation of existing agreements between israel and the palestinians. for a start, the lifting of the closures, the transfer of tax revenues, safe passage between gaza and the west bank, reopening of the airport and creating export facilities that will allow palestinians to benefit from their agreements with the european union and with other partners. (applause)i cannot, for the life of me, understand why anybody should suppose that further impoverishment of the palestinian territories and increased employment among young palestinians can have anything to do with the restoration of security. i am sure that we all took away rewarding reading matter during our summer break. i spent a good deal of my summer reading about the 1930s and about the relationship between economic impoverishment, economic hardship and political extremism in country after country. we must go on reiterating the point that trying to do so much damage, putting such a tough squeeze on the palestinian territories, is not to restore security or the way to lay the foundations for a future in which both parties can live happily and amicably together. (applause)third-party monitoring of the proper implementation of those agreements and a functioning dispute settlement mechanism would obviously help to address palestinian frustration with the current non-implementation of existing agreements. all this would help to bring about a revival of the palestinian economy, give palestinians a stake in their own futures and improve the prospects for a better future to be achieved by political negotiations. these efforts need to be supported by a range of confidence-building measures to overcome the current deep distrust, not only between the leading politicians, but also between the two peoples. this is an area in which parliament has quite rightly taken a particularly strong interest. i want to remind parliament that in the past two years alone the commission has allocated about eur 50 million to peace-building programmes fostering israeli-arab and israeli-palestinian cooperation in particular. these programmes promote peace through joint projects and awareness campaigns for tolerance and peace. we have an important role to play in supporting the voices of moderation wherever they exist. the sad fact is that the longer this dreadful situation continues the fewer moderates there are going to be, but they show considerable courage in their own communities and they deserve our continuing support. the commission stands ready to use all the instruments available to it to help alleviate the very severe financial difficulties facing the palestinians. our package of support for the palestinian authority is a successful example of how the european union can deliver assistance in a sensible, fast and effective manner and i am extremely grateful to parliament for its support in our work. european support for the palestinian authority budget is secured until november and the arab states are currently considering extending their budgetary support until the end of the year. it is still too early for any concrete announcement regarding further commission intervention. we have just reached mid-term in our current support operation and we are awaiting palestinian compliance with a number of conditions to be followed by an evaluation and assessment of the pretty grim macroeconomic and fiscal outlook. palestinian needs in 2002, and the contributions of other donors will have to be looked at in the context of an assessment of the economic situation in the palestinian territories currently being carried out by the world bank. it is expected that this exercise will be concluded by the end of september. once these data are available, the commission will consider how best we can contribute further to international efforts. of course, we will keep in the closest touch with parliament about our assessment of the financial requirements of the palestinian authority and about our continuing determination to ensure that even in the present appalling circumstances our financial assistance depends, as far as the palestinian side is concerned, on transparency, proper budgetary prudence and a commitment on the palestinian side to fight corruption. those are all points that have all been made to us by members of this house and they underlie our determination to secure a proper agreement between ourselves and the palestinians before we started releasing money in budgetary support. in the meantime, i can only repeat what the minister said so ably a few moments ago. what is required is a recommitment to mitchell as rapidly as possible. unless we see that, the situation will get even worse, with considerable damage right across the region. the council. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the last fifty years have undoubtedly seen great progress in the construction of europe. the european project has a strong appeal and has contributed to peace, stability, democracy and prosperity. the attraction is so great that the european union is preparing to double its membership today. the enlargement process is not in itself a new experience for the union, but the current enlargement process is unprecedented in its scale, the diversity of the candidate countries and its political and historical dimension. in the debate today i would like to discuss with you three questions: 1 why the enlargement, although i think it is obvious in this hemisphere, 2 and that will probably interest you more: what is the state of the negotiations and how should we prepare for the future? why the expansion? you, madam president, and the honourable members know this, but perhaps some of what i am about to say will seep through the walls of this hemisphere and reach the public opinion, which still asks itself this question regularly and which, of course, has every right to do so. the future of europe and the enlargement of the union are now inextricably linked. enlargement is the future of europe. in accordance with the objectives set out in helsinki, the nice european council enabled the union to take in the new member states. we could easily have rejected the compromise reached in nice, but we chose not to do so in order not to send the wrong message, namely that of a europe without a decision and without a heart, and at the wrong time, namely on the eve of european reunification. the enlargement gives concrete form to the generous and open vision of the original european project. the decision to do so, which was rightly declared irreversible at the gothenburg european council, reflects the importance which the founding fathers of europe attached to international solidarity then and which the member states still attach to it today. enlargement of the union is a historic duty. the peoples who have been separated by history for far too long must be given the chance to unite. in addition to the real historical challenge, enlargement is also a political project. this project requires a great sense of responsibility on the part of us, the european leaders and elected representatives. we must now do everything we can to ensure that our fellow citizens in an enlarged europe have a stable, secure and prosperous future. enlargement was and is a matter of urgency in order to prevent any destabilisation in the countries which are now candidates for membership and the manifestations of such destabilisation. i am thinking here of the growing influx of refugees, the increase in crime, and so on. the unfortunate events of the last ten years in the balkans have shown that a region cannot be stabilized without initiating and strengthening the enlargement process or the association process. in some countries of the former yugoslavia, this destabilisation has led to the deterioration of the rule of law and the emergence of new hotbeds of international crime. the union will have to make a full effort to combat transnational criminal networks. it is in the context of a desire for stabilization that the process of association and stability has been launched since the zagreb conference, which naturally leads to a european perspective. the positive effects of future enlargement are already being felt. in central and eastern europe, stable regimes have been established which have adopted common values or values which they share with us, such as democracy, the rule of law, respect for human rights and the protection of minorities. the remarkable improvement in security in europe and new prospects for economic development are the direct result. the enlargement, although it has yet to be translated into action, is already making europe more prosperous and increasing its influence. we also see, to be purely materialist, that the number of foreign direct investments, and i mean european foreign investment, in the applicant countries is increasing. the union has today become the main trading partner of the 13 candidate countries. so there are a lot of benefits for the member states . the enlarged europe will have 500 million citizens, and in economic terms we will call them 500 million consumers. this is sufficient to enable the union to assert and defend its specific character, also in the economic field, in a world which is becoming more and more 'a village', to speak to a canadian sociologist.
- madam president-in-office of the council, i thank you for a very comprehensive speech and i now give the floor to commissioner verheugen, reminding him that our distinguished guests have a limited speaking time in principle, with all the necessary flexibility, of course.
in writing. - i express the greatest reservations about the new draft statute of the european company because it seems to me complicated, useless and likely to lead us, little by little, to results that we do not want. the demand for a unified legal framework for public limited companies at european level, over and above the diversity of national laws, is an old federalist demand, almost as old as the community, since the first discussions were launched in 1959 and the first formal proposal of the commission dates from 1970. but this idea clashes with national rights which are deeply rooted in the mentality of each people, for example social law - concerning the participation of employees, in particular - or tax law. for 30 years this issue has been discussed without any progress being made, and everyone had finally resigned themselves to its immobility, which may mean, by the way, that a solution is not so urgent and that we could live without it. suddenly, at the nice council last december, the french presidency, no doubt anxious to show results at any cost, managed to get an agreement approved. but in reality the status thus obtained consists of a juxtaposition of national social rights, from which the partners may choose, but without any tax provision. the new proposal therefore seems both complex and insufficient. in fact, no one has ever been able to properly evaluate it. the committee on employment and social affairs in our assembly states that 'according to certain organisations (which ones?), a european company statute would save european industry €30 billion a year (according to what calculations?) '. but it is precisely the european industrialists who wrote to meps on 24 august 2001: 'we would like to reiterate our position: a european company status will not offer any significant economic benefits unless it is accompanied by an agreement on an appropriate tax regime'. but that agreement does not exist today. the states still want to retain their fiscal powers. in these circumstances, the european company status, which is of little immediate interest, seems to be pursued mainly because of the mechanism it could set up to destabilize national rights by means of a supranational status, which the committee on employment and social affairs even dreams of making applicable to small enterprises. if this project were to be pursued, it would lead to confusion and the dispossession of the states, without any real benefit for europe. it is true that in its present state it is likely to remain unused. it's the best thing that could happen. but the ideologues of unification will not give up so easily.
in writing. - the european council directive is intended to grant additional rights to workers in european companies. these alleged rights are limited to the participation of 'workers' representatives in the administrative or supervisory organ of the european company'. even taking parliament's amendments into account, these minority representatives will not be able to influence any decision. the legislator also wants to restrict their right to speak to their colleagues by imposing confidentiality. as a result, these representatives are invited only to endorse the policy of their bosses or to remain silent. we refuse to endorse this charade. that is why we abstained on this text.
in writing. - it seems to me important to mention the context in which this proposal for a directive is situated, the purpose of which is to supplement the regulation on the european company with regard to the involvement of workers. the first proposal for a european commission regulation dates from 1970. it was presented to the european parliament in the late 1980s. the main points of this directive include the compulsory participation of workers' representatives, the obligation to inform and consult the administrative or supervisory bodies and the obligation to obtain their agreement before implementing decisions such as the cessation or relocation of activities, the reduction or expansion of activities, the modification of activities, the creation of subsidiaries or holding companies, the election procedure and the modus operandi of workers' representation in accordance with the practices in force in the member states. these proposals failed on the question of participation. it took many more negotiations before an agreement was reached at the nice european council on 20 december 2000. as regards the proposal for a directive on the organization of information and consultation of workers, it is provided that the level of participation is freely negotiated between the participating undertakings and the workers, represented by a special negotiating group. if the result of the negotiations should lead to a reduction in participation rights, the majority required to decide to adopt such an agreement shall be the votes of two thirds of the members of the special negotiating body representing at least two thirds of the employees. if negotiations fail, an alternative regulation guaranteeing the right to participate is provided for. the amendments tabled by our european parliament aim to establish minimum requirements for information, participation and consultation of employees; to approximate the detailed rules of application adopted by the member states in so far as this does not affect acquired rights; ensure that even in the case of a significant restructuring occurring after the creation of an se, negotiations on subsequent worker participation are provided for; provide clear provisions governing the disclosure obligation of the management body, in particular as regards the content of the information; ensure that the election or appointment of employees' representatives to the administrative or supervisory organ of the se is carried out in accordance with the provisions of the laws in force in the member states. i should like to say in conclusion that i voted in favour of the amendment to amend the legal basis of this proposal. it seems to me that the european parliament must co-decide on legislation which will affect 75% of european workers!
in writing. - thirty years of hard negotiations, derogations and exceptions, a legal basis which serves only to give illegitimate powers to the brussels commission, an attempt to turn a directive into a regulation by imposing an implementation group... the european community is a gas factory. and it is not, to say the least, a subject that is very much in demand among economic and political actors. it must be said that the only interest of european society is to be imposed as a pure element of supranational law. it is like the single currency: an ideological construct designed to replace national structures by force and to impose an uncontrollable level of community decision-making. some claim to be concerned about workers' rights. but the directive clearly places these rights above the absolute right of the boards of directors to set up a european company. it even allows a regression of their right to participation. we are simply facing another step in the process of globalisation, which begins with the standardization of the european system. it is certain that in this context it would be advantageous for all ultra-liberals to have a globalised wage-earner himself, with the lowest possible rights. a kind of perverse version of the unification of workers worldwide that the so-called "anti-globalization" left-wing extremists are calling for with great force of slogans today. for the greatest perversion certainly lies in this objective alliance between capitalist internationalism and subversive or marxist internationalism, to impose levels of decision-making that go beyond the nations, their democratically appointed governments, their democratically elected parliaments. and yet it is the nation that is the only level where the social and political rights of workers, the freedoms and prosperity of all exist and can be best defended.
in writing. - we did not want to prevent the report from being adopted by voting against it, in order to take account of the wishes of a number of trade unions. but our abstention means that we reject proposals which, under the pretext of extending workers' rights, clearly take the view of employers' interests. we are told that there are 'competition imperatives', but we are not told that there is an imperative to ensure the right of workers to live and to receive a wage. the author of the report said that helping the bosses was an imperative. on the other hand, as regards the rights of workers, it is limited from the outset to the right to be informed of the dismissals which will be imposed on them and there is no question of preventing them. the simple right of veto is denied to works councils, even though, in the face of the proliferation of collective redundancies, including in large companies which have been making huge profits for years, only the prohibition of redundancies could protect workers. so what is this 'employer-worker partnership' that the report is advocating, where one partner has the right to make decisions that ruin the lives of many workers, or even of an entire region, while the other has no right, not even to save his job?
in writing. - first of all, i would like to point out that the main objective of directive 94/45/ec is to remove the obstacles to information, consultation and communication with the staff of community-scale undertakings. it is true that this directive was transposed within the deadline. it is also true that its application has resulted in the creation of many european works councils. for example, some 650 works councils have been set up in companies employing at least 1000 people, and at least 150 in two member states. however, there are still 1 800 enterprises in the eu which meet the conditions, including thresholds, for the establishment of a european works council under the directive. in addition, the recent restructuring and collective redundancies that have highlighted the shortcomings of european legislation are still on everyone's mind. it is unacceptable that employees should be informed by the press of decisions affecting their company. we have to answer to the european citizens who are increasingly doubting the existence of a european social model. this period of industrial change should give us the opportunity to reflect on how to improve existing arrangements. this is what the report of the parliamentary committee on employment and social affairs does, since, in its implementation report, it sets out guidelines for the european commission to follow when preparing a proposal to amend the european works council directive (planned for 2002). the following improvements are to be made: a precise definition of the notions of information and consultation of workers; a general obligation to convene extraordinary meetings of the european works council as soon as possible and at the appropriate time; the introduction of a strengthened consultation procedure on specific issues of particular interest to workers; the reduction of the number of employees in the undertakings covered by the directive from 1000 to 500 for the whole undertaking and from 150 to 100 per establishment in at least two member states; the commission has also proposed that the directive be amended to include the introduction of sanctions, at national and european level, for non-compliance with the directive. i therefore also ask the european commission to incorporate these suggestions into its proposal to amend the european works council directive.
in writing. - less than 5% of the companies covered by the 1994 works council directive meet the staff representatives more than twice a year; 60% have not even set up ecs and in the few cases where they have been set up, this has been at the expense of the representation of workers in national enterprises, particularly in terms of hours of delegation and training. this is a clear example of the refusal of employers to inform and consult workers' representatives, their willingness to decide alone the fate of millions of employees. the latest social plans drawn up by the management of aom, marks & spencer, lu-danone and moulinex have again demonstrated that the interests of employers and stockholders are opposed to those of employees and the needs of the population. today, what is important for employees in terms of social welfare is to be able to prohibit dismissals, and not just to be informed about them before and differently. the proposals in the resolution concerning redundancies are symbolic and have no effect on the thousands of employees whose jobs have already been lost. we support all measures which provide better information and more rights for employee representatives and all measures which give more means to mobilize the necessary forces to defeat the employers' plans.
in writing. - it is a sign of the impotence of the european authorities that after eight years of negotiations they are not even able to obtain reliable information on the production of waste, especially industrial waste, and on its treatment. it is a way of confessing their inability to pursue a policy in this area that would limit the damage and prevent ecological disasters now or in the future. the explanatory statement makes plain the "lack of unanimity" among the member states, the "vigorous opposition of the council" and the refusal of "the professional circles". the treatment of certain wastes, such as those from the nuclear, chemical or oil industries, would require international cooperation. but the impotence of the european authorities reflects the impotence, if necessary, of the national states. neither of them intends to run afoul of the private interests of the large industrial groups, nor to impose on them, in order to safeguard the environmental interests of society, draconian measures which could reduce their profits. we abstained because of the deliberate nature of the proposals in this report.
in writing. - we voted resolutely against the koukiadis report because, with a frighteningly good conscience, it proposes to increase repression to better apply community law, without first examining whether the multiplication of cases of misapplication would not translate into a widening of the gap between europe and its peoples. at no point does the report ask whether the failures to apply the law that have been found are not the result of a kind of defensive reaction of nations or individuals against a right that they feel is outside their own, too tacit, or adopted according to anti-democratic procedures. the solutions proposed here and there in the reports of the european parliament or the commission are to increase the dose of supranationality, to strengthen the sanctions and to promote a faster and more direct application of community law by bypassing the national parliaments more. in the commission's recent white paper on european governance, we even find the puzzling thesis that european law is too detailed because the council and parliament would add to the detail, lacking sufficient confidence in the commission. the commission should therefore be given a freer hand to improve the quality of community law! in particular, there is a movement underway to speed up the transposition of directives into national law by means of expeditious methods such as the ordinance method recently used by the french government. these methods, which remove the fundamental role of national parliaments, will only increase the disconnect between community law and the reality of the member states. the only solution is to restore the role of the nations and national parliaments in european decision-making.
- like all the rapporteurs who have already spoken, i am pleased to see that the negotiations are moving forward and are moving well for all the candidate countries. despite the difficulties, the work is considerable. let us say that on the technical side we can only congratulate the negotiators on the efforts they are making, commissioner, we congratulate you. however, i would like to stress two points which have not been forgotten but on which we believe more should be done. i am thinking first of all of the social consequences of enlargement. it seems that the commission, the council and all of us should do more to deal with the disorganization of society which will inevitably result and already results from the economic reforms being forced on the applicant countries. the restructuring of companies, privatization and modernisation of working methods, which we consider necessary, create unemployment, disrupt social protection systems and have a negative effect on families and individuals. let us try, let us try to do more to limit these social disturbances which could, if not dealt with, turn into serious political disturbances. the second point i would like to make is that of contact with public opinion, both in the candidate countries and in the member states. negotiations are the work of specialists. i commend them again for their seriousness. but the accession of a country to the union affects its entire population. the polls show it. as the deadline draws near, the number of opposers increases, as do anxieties and worries. we should inform and explain more, and de-dramatize as much as possible. this is a huge public relations task which the commission - and we too, of course - should be doing more of.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, following today's debate on enlargement, we are going to have to take a decision on a comprehensive draft resolution drawn up by our colleague mr brok. the text does not treat lightly the decision of the irish people to reject the treaty of nice and does not conceal, i quote, 'the uncertainty which this decision creates over the future of the enlargement process'. we are therefore pleased to see mr brok repeating in paragraph 2 of his motion for a resolution the recommendation we made the day after the irish vote to provide for alternatives in the accession treaties. on the other hand, it is absolutely unacceptable to take the result of the irish referendum as a hostage to justify abandoning the intergovernmental process. if the current practice of igcs is often opaque and unintelligible, this is not due to the method itself which associates governments democratically elected by their peoples. it is quite possible to make the intergovernmental process more transparent and understandable. this is what must be done in a pragmatic way, avoiding the ideological drift which, when a decision is unpleasant, leads to the conclusion that, in order for it not to happen again, it is necessary to destroy by majority vote the legal framework within which it was taken. we are in the order of magical thinking, or, as our colleague georges berthu said last night, of the normative illusion. the lesson to be drawn from the irish referendum is certainly not to make the process of european integration even more undemocratic.
- the next item is the commission communication on the white paper on the reform of european governance. i now give the floor to the president of the commission, mr romano prodi.
president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, 18 months ago, speaking to this house, i announced that one of the strategic priorities of the new commission was to reflect on the state of the union's institutions and to promote new forms of governance. on that occasion, i promised that the commission would publish a white paper before the summer break in 2001. we have done our duty and i am particularly pleased to be making the first presentation of the white paper to the european parliament. this is not just for protocol reasons: the central theme of the white paper - bringing europe closer to its citizens - is one of the main concerns that parliament and the commission share. as representatives of the citizens of europe, you are by definition the legitimate link between the union and its peoples. the specific proposals which will be made by this house in response to and in completion of the white paper will therefore be of great help in charting the course to be followed in the coming years. i shall be glad to open a thorough debate on your proposals at the next partsession of parliament, which will be held in brussels in 15 days' time. since the beginning of my presidency, i have expressed the firm conviction that we must rethink the way we build europe, to set an example of innovation in the relationship between citizens and political institutions in a historical period when transparency and accountability are becoming the new rules of governance. the nice summit, however, changed the political environment in which this project is to be developed. after the adoption of the nice declaration on the future of europe by the intergovernmental conference, a new debate on the future of the european union and its ultimate aims has been launched. political leaders and citizens have made their voices heard. europeans expect a lot from europe, and they expect their citizenship of the union to be loaded with symbolic and practical meanings, as the debate on the charter of fundamental rights has clearly shown. i therefore hope once again that this charter will be fully incorporated into the treaties. europe has finally begun the great debate on a more complete democracy. disillusionment, absenteeism from elections and a decline in confidence in political parties as the vehicle of popular consensus are worrying and widespread phenomena. they concern not only the european institutional level but all relations between citizens and their representatives, whatever the level of representation. the citizens of europe are anxious because they sense the force of the epochal changes that our democracies are experiencing. the impact of globalisation and changes in society have been rapid and brutal and have profoundly affected the daily lives of all of us. the european union project has been a hope for many years and is today the only example of a concrete, operational and democratic response to the challenges of globalisation. in the face of accelerating globalisation, the european model of democracy, competitiveness and social solidarity is the only one capable of providing the prospect of stability that our citizens seek. they realise that each member state, on its own, would not be able to withstand external pressures to dismantle our societies. many events have called into question our ability to accomplish this great task. the commission has not yet taken any action to combat the problem. for this reason, it is an urgent and exemplary duty to question our governance rules in the face of all, in order to prepare new ones. in fact, to talk about governance is to talk about democracy: european democracy, its functioning, its problems, but also its prospects. the commission has therefore devised a three-stage process: in this first phase, the white paper addresses the issues of european governance 'in the same treaties'. we are convinced that much can be done by changing the way our institutions and the member states operate, by applying the rules in force in a better and more consistent way. the commission will then make its position on the laeken process known. finally, in a third and subsequent phase, the commission will indicate its priorities with regard to substantial amendments to the treaties. in preparing its proposals, the commission will take utmost account of the views expressed during the debate on this white paper, and in particular of the criticisms and suggestions which you, the parliament, will make. in drawing up the white paper, the commission wanted to maintain a concrete and operational approach. we have therefore focused on european governance in two ways: first, relations between citizens, organised bodies of civil society, central and local government and the european institutions; secondly, the functioning of the european institutions and the relations between them. nor could we convey to our fellow citizens the message that the only instrument capable of solving the still open problems of governance at european level is the amendment of the founding treaties. i personally do not trust such a simplistic solution. so we felt it necessary to fix our house first; then, we'll discuss how to rebuild the city. that is why the commission has chosen to focus its white paper on ways of improving the current system, making better use of the options we already have under the current treaties. many problems can be solved by courageously applying the rules already agreed and abandoning the practices that have diverted the european project from its original objectives. let us see how we have actually proceeded in this first phase. openness, participation, accountability, effectiveness and consistency: the five pillars which form the basis of the analyses and proposals contained in the white paper complement and reinforce the two fundamental principles already enshrined in our treaties: subsidiarity and proportionality. the white paper's proposals are designed to improve the functioning of the community method by acting on three lines: first, the definition of the union's political initiatives through greater involvement of citizens; second, the effective implementation of these policies; thirdly, the distinction between the roles and responsibilities of the european institutions and the need to focus on their core functions. let me now briefly explain all this in detail. first, citizens must be more involved in the formulation of union policies. it is not a question of upsetting the institutional balance or of offering improper representative roles to actors who are not democratically entitled to them. you know my thoughts: parliament, this parliament, is the seat of the democratic representation of the peoples of the union. but it is a new challenge: the commission's proposal is based on the principle of subsidiarity, which is the principle that the community should be able to take action in the field of justice and home affairs. our task should not be to counter this expression of democratic wealth but rather to channel the complexities of societies and find the right methods to dialogue - albeit with different methods - with local authorities and civil society. at the root of all this is a communication deficit: if we want to bring the european union closer to its citizens - that is, to make brussels less remote - we must explain the union's policies in clear and simple terms and make them open to public debate. in this context, the creation of a european network, in which all levels of government participate in the definition, implementation and monitoring of policies, should be encouraged. the white paper proposes a systematic approach to the creation of this network, which will require the best possible contacts with national, regional and local organisations and bodies, in order to build and implement the decisions of the union, in the strictest respect of the constitutional organisation of each member state. the commission should also be able to provide information on the implementation of the union's macro-financial assistance. i do not, of course, consider that structures such as non-governmental organisations can represent public opinion in the same way as the european parliament or the employers' associations and trade unions represent their members. we must also ensure that the internal organisation of ngos is based on democratic principles. the european commission, however, wants to make use of their energy and commitment, and the white paper analyses the modalities of such cooperation. we therefore propose in the white paper minimum standards for consultation with a twofold objective: make it as clear as possible who we have consulted, who has given us advice and whether we intend to follow that advice and how we intend to do so. this will allow parliament to assess the quality and impartiality of the consultation process in taking its decisions during legislative procedures. let us now turn to the second question, namely what can we do to make the european union's action more effective? community law is often criticised as being too intrusive; the european union is a global player in the field of education and training. both of these criticisms contain some truth, and we must take that into account; the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, and we can take account of this, since the existing treaties offer us a range of instruments which enable us to take action in line with the needs. moreover, now that the internal market is in many ways complete, there is much less of a need for new legislation in this area. the union must therefore focus on the correct and effective implementation of the rules in force, in order to make the internal market work better and to minimise distortions of competition. what can the commission do to ensure that european law is of the highest quality? i would like to mention briefly five lines of action outlined in our white paper: firstly, we intend to take steps to ensure that the public can trust our scientific advice and, more generally, our way of consulting experts. secondly, legislative activity must be set up by better assessing the type of measures to be taken; thirdly, the circumstances in which community legislation must be supplemented by other forms of action, such as self-regulation or the open method of coordination, must be defined more clearly. fourthly, the commission intends to concentrate its efforts on those areas which really require it to assume political responsibility. other activities should be entrusted to union agencies, the role and tasks of which will be discussed further in depth; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's legal framework is properly applied. this is a matter of serious concern, since the quality of implementation of community law is disappointing. the direct responsibility for the ineffectiveness and unpopularity of european legislation falls, in no small part, on the member states. to remedy this situation, the white paper recommends the use of regulations instead of directives in many cases where this instrument is more appropriate. it is clear, however, that the clarity of our primary law depends to a large extent on the work of the council and, in the case of codecision, of this house. on the eve of enlargement, we must therefore ensure that european law is of the highest quality and that it is applied correctly and effectively. the commission has clearly set out in its white paper the steps we are going to take to put our house in order. we hope that this will encourage the other institutions and the member states to do the same quickly. the third and final type of change aims to make the distinction between the roles and responsibilities of the institutions more understandable by focusing on the essential political tasks. the treaty has been weighed down by institutional practices which have confused and altered the project of the founding fathers. the current treaty, when properly applied, clearly distinguishes the roles of the parliament, the council, the commission, the court of justice and the other institutions. in practice, however, citizens are confronted with actions that confuse this clear distinction of roles. they no longer understand who proposes, who decides, who controls. and they understand even less which institution is responsible for each act, that is, whether the responsibility lies with the european institutions or with the member states. we must act urgently and decisively to remedy this situation, and we do not need to amend the treaty immediately to do so. the need to focus on the essential tasks, as recommended in our white paper, entails a new formulation of the policies of the european union and therefore a reorganisation of the way in which the three institutions - council, parliament and commission - operate and cooperate with each other. the committee system is the prime example of the distortion of the system: the council, the legislator, becomes the executor, while the parliament, the legislator, is excluded from this stage. the commission, which represents the executive, must mediate with the legislator on the details, but without the council having to assume the political responsibilities that follow, since it is in fact the national administrations - that is, the member states themselves - that participate in the meetings of the experts. the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council and the european parliament on the basis of a proposal from the commission. the union's major political priorities should be expressed and discussed at regular and solemn political events, such as european council meetings, the annual state of the union address by the president of the commission to the european parliament, and other solemn and political events. this brings me to the question of how we can improve the way in which the commission, the council and parliament work together. the main obstacle to clear policy formulation is the impenetrability of the council of ministers' working methods and the increasing difficulty, especially in the general affairs council, of finding a synthesis of sectoral interests before the european council. much can and must be done to improve european governance in this respect, and without the need to amend the treaties. that is what our proposals are aimed at, but it is a profound change. i believe that this house too must concentrate on its fundamental tasks: the commission's proposal for a regulation on the common organization of the market in bananas is based on the principle of the free movement of goods, and the commission's proposal for a regulation on the common organization of the market in bananas is based on the principle of the free movement of goods. the white paper suggests, with great respect but with equal firmness, that the european parliament should 'abandon the current role of accountant on matters of detail in favour of control more based on political objectives'. as guardian of the treaty, it is my duty to point that direction. however, it is not for me, but for you to decide what organizational changes are necessary. finally, changes should be made to the way in which the three institutions work together. the return to its basic tasks must be - mr president of the commission, the introduction of your white paper on european governance does raise the problem of a declining confidence of the citizens, illustrated by the 'no' vote in the irish referendum. but the remedies are extremely weak. the best governance would be better transparency, better consultation, better communication, better participation, a more open method of coordination, etc. in short, mr president, these are changes in behaviour which are certainly desirable on the part of the european institutions, but which will remain marginal if they are not part of a profound change in the balance of power within the institutional balance. the citizens think, and we think, that certain problems can be better solved by better european cooperation, but at the same time they are massively and consistently attaching the main legitimacy to the national framework. in these circumstances, the conclusion is very simple: to strengthen the legitimacy of european cooperation, to restore contact with the citizens, it is necessary to give a paramount weight, a much more visible place, to the nations in the european decision-making process. this is the fundamental condition for genuine democracy, a word which is hardly found in this white paper. everything else is just gossip. for example, why is it that in your white paper you find developments on the involvement of the regional and local levels in european policy, on decentralised management, on co-regulation with various organisations, which are not identified, and why is it that you find nothing on the essential role of national parliaments in the european decision-making process? i understand, mr president, that in your position you could not solve this problem, but at least the white paper could have raised it. the best communication you wish for is of no use if european policies are not articulated around the central place of national democracies.
president of the commission. - madam president, i should like to begin by thanking all the speakers who have spoken, because they have made a very useful contribution to this debate, which is the basis for a more in-depth analysis. i would therefore like to touch on some basic points, some starting points of this document so that together we can then work to improve and complete it. we have described a path in this document, but this is the first proposal: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. i therefore took note of the criticisms made and i take note of them with pleasure, because this is a first proposal which needs everyone's input to be final. second point: language, name, all that stuff. you are right, yes, but in all honesty, i have read a lot of national laws, i have tried to make a lot of them. name one that is understandable as common citizen language! they all have a special language. we have done our best to make it appropriate, but there are concepts which, in their technical nature, end up being a problem for the average citizen. our role is precisely to explain, to act as a bridge, but we cannot give up the precision of the proposals. this includes the discussion of the term 'governance'. i understand perfectly well what mr dell'alba is saying, except that the problem is that we do not use just one language here, but fortunately and proudly 11 languages, which will become 20. we must try to adapt. the title we came up with is not a title i like, precisely because working with dictionaries is not like finding a unique word. it is part of our duty to understand each other as well as possible, even if we sometimes fail to do so with the precision we would like. finally, relations with parliament. i did not make a speech today to please parliament. the same words i have said today about the role of parliament and its relations with ngos, civil society, the different functions they have, are words that are familiar to me, that i have already said a thousand times and that i have tried to put into practice in all honesty in these eighteen months in my relations with you. if our relations are certainly more effective, more operative, smoother and more open than they were before, it is precisely because i believe that the new europe must be based on a fundamental role for parliament. finally, i am reproached for many shortcomings: the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, for example on the question of clarifying the role of local authorities. i remember we set a limit in this white paper: the treaty of rome was not changed. so when i am asked about a change of powers, that is not the subject of the white paper. we must make this enormous effort to adapt our approach to the tasks we have, but with the treaties unchanged. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. so in the third phase we will be making an active contribution, and we will have to work together on institutional reforms. in the face of the decisions of nice, we had to take this into account and have a methodology which respects the necessary changes. but look, democracy is made of rules, but it's also made of practices. i think, as we have seen in my speech and in your debates, there is room for improvement in the way we work on unchanged legislation. so i think we have to work together in this direction. there are some particular points which have emerged from the debate, points which seem to me to be of particular importance. there was a speech on the question of the delegation of powers to the commission. the commission, in line with what i have said on unchanged legislation, does not require more powers but wants to organise its work in a more transparent and efficient way, returning to the way the treaties establishing the union were set up, where, in the institutional organisation envisaged, the council and parliament decide, the commission implements, not in technical detail, and parliament controls. in the end, the commission will probably do less than it does today, but it will avoid the confusing part of the comitology practice, which drags out the processes and makes it absolutely unclear what our role is and what your role is. in this case there is an identical interest of parliament and the commission, because we are both plagued by this practice of comitology and we are both dissatisfied. so what we say to each other in our individual speeches about the inadequacy of this process, well, we say to ourselves here in the chamber because that is how we remedy it. an objection was also made to the direct responsibilities of local authorities in the decision-making process. let us remember that this cannot happen, even if it is based on the discourse of decentralization, of subsidiarity. the aim is to take account, in a transparent and organised way, of the views of those who are the final users and implementers of the common policies, and this in compliance with the institutional structures of each member state. we cannot enter the sacred organization of the member states. they provide for the role of meetings, they provide for their institutional structure, and if we go in there, we are violating and, above all, we are going against the principle of subsidiarity to which we are absolutely and profoundly committed. i should like to comment very briefly on some of mr swoboda's objections, because he has touched on points which need to be addressed. one of them is a point that may seem trivial: the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the programme. i do not think that these are enormous resources, but it is clear that parliament will have to tell us in the debate that it must agree and that it must give us the resources we need. i think that, although we have not made any calculations at this stage, this is a modest speech, but it is one of the subjects we must discuss together, because parliament is the budgetary authority. another point: delegation of powers and agencies. these are delegations on practical and technical activities, not political delegations, because delegations on these matters are not allowed, they are matters which must be dealt with by the institutional authorities. finally, another very important question from mr swoboda: the commission's basic tasks, the political priorities. i repeat that the commission has undertaken - and i have not mentioned it by chance in the annual commitments - to explain to parliament each year what its political priorities are. this is the practice we have envisaged, proposed and which i believe we will have to follow rigorously because every year, as happens in the most democratic and transparent government structures, political priorities are presented to parliament and discussed in front of parliament. that is why this white paper, on the one hand, is in my view a new and strong attempt to advance democracy and transparency; on the other hand, it is a new and strong attempt to improve the quality of the information society. on the other hand, it still has some vague aspects, but because it is a proposal, we could not present it completed today: it must be refined and developed with our cooperation. it's a framework, a blueprint, and i thank you for the objections i received today because i believe they will help us profoundly in our future work. finally, in thanking you, i would just like to say that we must see all this in the three steps of the great european reform that we have envisaged and which will be implemented in these three years: first, the reorganization of our internal working methods; secondly, to help us together to plan how we shall organise the great process of reform of the institutions, hence laeken; thirdly, how to carry out the process of institutional reform. i present this white paper definitively and it becomes our instrument of self-regulation. perhaps mr dell'alba can call it this: the commission's proposal is to be seen as a step in the right direction, and it is to be seen as a step in the right direction.
