commission. – mr president, i should like to congratulate mr coelho, the chairman, and the honourable members of this parliament who participated in the work of the temporary committee on echelon, especially the rapporteur, mr schmid, for the comprehensive and well-written report on the echelon interception system. i should also like to thank parliament as a whole for this very important debate. the commission has been following the parliamentary work over the past year with great interest. the issue touches on complex technological and political considerations. the report presents a large number of references to the existence of a global interception system. these build up a body of evidence. the commission stated on 30 march last year: “it is the very nature of intelligence activities that those that are not involved in those activities are not able to confirm nor deny their existence”. even though the commission is not involved in intelligence gathering activities, we do not question the findings of the european parliament. the report by the echelon temporary committee is based on careful and thorough work. the european union is founded on respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, based on article 6 of the treaty and the eu charter of fundamental rights. as the guardian of the treaty, the commission attaches the utmost importance to the observance of those principles. the abuse of large-scale communications intelligence is something that can make an individual living in a democratic society feel very uneasy. privacy is a fundamental right. any derogation from this right has to be specifically provided for by law, necessary for the achievement of objectives, in the public interest, proportionate and subject to adequate checks and guarantees against any form of abuse. the commission is determined to look at the practical implications of the eu charter of fundamental rights where, in particular, the protection of communications and personal data will be further enhanced. the commission has already stated that it considers it would be preferable for the charter to be integrated into the treaties for the sake of visibility and legal certainty. at the same time, the community has to act within the scope of the powers conferred upon it by the treaty. the findings of the committee concerning the compatibility of a system of the echelon type with eu law distinguish between two scenarios. first, the use of such a system purely for intelligence purposes and second, abuse of the system for the purpose of gathering competitive intelligence. the commission shares the opinion that the operations envisaged in the first scenario in the interest of state security fall within the scope of title v of the treaty on european union, which sets out the framework for the establishment of a common foreign security policy. this lays down no provisions on intelligence activities. member states remain responsible for the conduct and supervision of intelligence operations, unless the council decides otherwise. the eu treaty does not empower the commission to exercise its prerogatives as guardian of the treaty in this field. maintaining an interception system for the purpose of gathering intelligence, even in the context of a member state’s defence or national security, is outside the scope of the directives in force on data protection. as to the second scenario, the gathering of competitive intelligence does not come within the scope of a common foreign and security policy. it is not an activity that would be allowed in pursuit of a common foreign and security policy. as far as community law is concerned, such activity could fall within the scope of data protection directives. this is the case if data gathered by echelon-type systems is collected or subsequently passed on to commercial undertakings for purposes unrelated to the prevention of criminal offences or state security matters. we are all aware that electronic communications play an increasingly important role in everyday life. properly functioning electronic communications infrastructures are crucial for our economies. as was stated in lisbon, europe wants to become the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world. a precondition for this is the need to build trust in electronic communications. this concerns both our citizens and our businesses. the development in technologies can bring protection against surveillance. it is reassuring that the use of fibre-optic cables instead of satellites for transcontinental communications has decreased the possibilities for large-scale routine interception. the argument that the rise of the commercial internet has significantly diminished the possibilities for interception is convincing. today the majority of internet communications by cable no longer leave the european continent. the commission has taken important steps over the past years to develop a policy to improve the security of electronic communications. encryption has been mentioned here often. the availability and free circulation of encryption products and technologies in the european union has now been ensured with the dual-use regulation in place since september 2000. the support, through the community’s research framework programme, in particular with the information side of technologies programme, has improved the conditions to develop top-of-the-range european encryption products in order to enable eu citizens, companies and governments to protect their communications. i would ask for your support in this context in our discussions on the next framework programme. however, it is not sufficient to guarantee a widespread use of encryption. citizens and small businesses are not always aware of the potential effects. we need to inform them about the possibilities of encryption. we need to empower them. in june this year the commission adopted a communication on network and information security. the purpose is to tackle this awareness problem and to further develop a european approach on security-related issues. i am pleased to note that the conclusions of the report under discussion are very much in line with the approach adopted by the commission. the honourable members are aware that there is already a legal framework in place at eu level addressing data protection and obligations for operators. there is also an emerging policy on cybercrime, which will be discussed later today. network information security is now coming as a third element to complete the picture. however, communication is not meant to contain a fully fledged action plan. we have already initiated some broad action lines where progress needs to be made. i will highlight some of them. to raise awareness, public information and education campaigns should be launched and best practice should be promoted. a european warning and information system is needed to strengthen the activities of computer emergency response teams – crts – or similar entities and improve the coordination amongst them. i have noted parliament’s support for this idea. then we need to examine how best to organise at european level proactive and coordinated measures to develop forward-looking responses to existing and emerging security threats like the european information security observatory. finally concerning the legal framework, we will set up an inventory of national measures which have to be taken in accordance with the relevant community law. here i reply to mrs plooij-van gorsel’s question. i would also like to mention that further action is needed to support the development of technology, to streamline standardisation and certification work, and for the introduction of security in government use and better international cooperation. as a next step, it is our intention to develop a road map before the end of this year containing concrete actions with firm deadlines in order to start putting a european information security policy in place. finally, the commission is constantly improving the production of its own information systems in terms of availability, integrity and confidentiality, especially in view of the changing nature of the various existing and potential threats. the entry point to the commission networks is constantly monitored and actively tested. similar efforts are conducted through projects for secure video conferencing, secure telephone systems and encryption of databases. furthermore, security audits of commission information systems are conducted on a regular basis. a new information system security policy has been drafted and is currently being prepared for discussion within the commission services. in addition, the commission is reviewing its overall security policy as a result of internal reorganisation activities and policy developments. the new internal commission security provisions will follow the model of the council security regulation adopted earlier this year and will be based on the following principles: proportionality of security measures in relation to existing risks; shared responsibility and accountability of staff, management and security experts; the creation of all elements into a coherent security strategy, such as personal information and physical security; and finally, close cooperation between european and national security organisations. the commission intends to allocate additional resources to the security domain. however, scarce technical and human resources, especially in the field of information security specialists, hamper the full deployment of security policies. this concern is common to most public administrations including the european institutions. i welcome the support in the report to allocate more resources for the task to be undertaken and i sincerely hope that parliament as a budgetary authority will follow the position of the committee. the trust of european citizens and businesses in electronic communications and the well-functioning of information infrastructures has become crucial for economies. let me reiterate once more that the commission attaches the utmost importance to respect for human rights and respect of rule of law.

in writing. - we are opposed to terrorism because of the means used but also because its perpetrators generally aim to impose an oppressive regime on their own people. we are, however, disgusted by the hypocrisy of the report, which, while attacking terrorist groups, excludes state terrorism when it is, or has been, the work of states which call themselves democratic and which are now members of the european union. to take the case of france as an example: when generals claim torture and murder during the war against the algerian people to prevent them from liberating themselves from colonial oppression, is this not legitimizing terrorism? or should we simply be silent and excuse this kind of ignominy, on the pretext that these acts of terrorism were committed knowingly, or even on the recommendation of the highest state authorities? and how many acts of terrorism by the uk in india or kenya were committed before decolonisation? how many are the uk committing in sierra leone today? the report does not mention state terrorism, which is no better than small group terrorism. but on the other hand, it has the cynicism to list among the aspects to be combated "extremist ideological conceptions" or "intellectual support", which obviously opens the door to all the attacks on the simple freedom of opinion. we therefore voted against this report.
in writing. - i would like to express my support for this own-initiative report calling on the member states of the european union to improve coordination in the fight against terrorist acts. in recent years, the european union has seen a resurgence of terrorist activities on its soil, which have not spared any state. the traditional means of judicial and police cooperation are often insufficient to combat this new form of terrorism, which is the result of the activity of internationally organised networks established in several countries, exploiting the legal loopholes of the territoriality of prosecutions and sometimes benefiting from powerful logistical and financial support. we must of course condemn these acts which traumatize entire families and create a climate of terror in the regions most affected. but above all we must make concrete proposals to put an end to these heinous acts. that is the subject of this report. among the interesting proposals are: :- the creation of a 'european search and seizure mandate' for the purpose of combating terrorism, in the context of action against organised and non-organised crime, trafficking in human beings and crimes against children, illicit drug and arms trafficking, corruption and fraud,- the introduction of minimum rules at european level on the definition of criminal offences and sanctions applicable in the field of terrorism,- the abolition of formal extradition procedures and the adoption of the principle of mutual recognition of criminal decisions in respect of terrorist offences,- the adoption of relevant legal instruments to approximate national legislation on the compensation of victims of terrorist offences. like the rapporteur, i also believe that it is essential to work on the prevention in writing. - in its explanatory statement, the report calls on the commission and the member states to make a greater commitment to culture. this is indeed a good reason, since he also states that in the year 2000 only 0.1% of the community budget was allocated to culture, and that this was followed by the audiovisual sector! but what does the report mean by the term 'european culture' which is constantly mentioned by the authors? apart from the ambiguity of this expression, how does it differ from the universal culture, rich in the contributions of all the continents? in one of its recitals, the report sets out in the cultural context such areas as copyright, the right of succession, the liberalisation of the telecommunications market, international competition law (financing of cinematographic works, single book price, theatrical subsidisation, media concentration, etc.). we pretend to talk about culture when in reality it is about markets, if not business! the report does not, however, address some very basic questions. is simple access to culture ensured for all those living within the union? are they all even literate? have they all been able to attend school to the best of their ability? these questions are not of interest to the european authorities, who are too concerned with regulating competition in the cultural business. we have therefore voted against this report.
in writing. - i welcome the fact that the european parliament, the representative body of the aspirations of european citizens, has used its right of initiative to urge the european commission to propose concrete measures in the field of culture. since 1974, it has stressed the importance of developing a cultural policy at community level. and for good reason: culture is a fundamental element of the identity of the european union, it is the basis on which people come together, recognise each other and feel a sense of belonging to the same space. the aim is not, of course, to promote a european cultural policy aiming at uniformity. it is, on the contrary, a matter of highlighting cultural and linguistic diversity and the sharing of a common heritage. at a time when our fellow citizens are doubting the european project, we must work to strengthen the feeling of european citizenship. this is a necessary prerequisite for the elaboration of a european constitution. this is the view taken in mr ruffolo's report. he's throwing up a lot of leads. the commission is therefore asked to submit to the european parliament and the council a proposal for a recommendation in which it will undertake to submit to these two institutions an annual report on the cultural policies of the european union and the member states and invite the member states to contribute actively to the elaboration and implementation of a three-year plan for cultural cooperation; - to establish a european cooperation observatory; - to convene, with a view to the evaluation and revision of the framework programme 'culture 2000', a second forum on culture which, on the basis of this resolution, will redefine the values, objectives and forms of european cultural cooperation; - to carry out a study on the possibility of approximating, at community level, the principles governing the tax treatment of works of art and artistic work; - to reaffirm, in the run-up to the next wto summit, the position of the european union. i would like to end by recalling that i, as rapporteur for the sixth framework programme for research and development (fp6), proposed amendments to strengthen research in the cultural field.
in writing. - the question of the harmonization and homogenization of safety rules in air transport is now a pressing one. the air traffic has grown considerably, and safety issues must be dealt with with particular attention. we do not dispute this necessity. however, we are not in favour of the creation of the european aviation safety agency (easa) on the basis proposed. the challenges are clearly linked to the deepening of the international market. easa is supporting the liberalisation of airspace and is a tool in the standards war with the united states. in fact, it is a matter of making things consistent, rather than competitive. easa becomes a mandatory part of the deregulation announced for air transport; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not disrupted. these staff are currently informed or consulted, but have never been recognised as experts. this is worrying at a time of massive restructuring and layoffs at aom, sabena and swissair, among others. this agency must concentrate on one mission: safety, by integrating employees into its work and by harmonizing the achievements of each european state from the top.
in writing. - the debate which has just taken place in this house on the forthcoming enlargement of the european union has given us a triple satisfaction. first, it appears that as of 2004, 10 out of 12 candidate countries (probably with the exception of romania and bulgaria) could become members at the same time. mpf members think this is great news, which will make up for a long wait. secondly, we have seen a change in tone towards the candidate countries, which are now treated as states worthy of respect. the resolution also stresses that 'the european union must ensure that the dignity of the peoples of the applicant countries is never undermined by making unnecessary demands'. we had often denounced the arrogant, even contemptuous attitude of the federalists, who demanded that the countries of the east abandon their sovereignty. hopefully this new development will go beyond a change in vocabulary. finally, as a third reason for satisfaction, paragraph 10 of the resolution seems to mean acceptance of a more flexible europe, made up of differentiated circles. we believe that this is a more realistic position, provided that the circles in which france will be represented are not dominated by ultra-federalism: this would be to accept flexibility for the whole in return for increased rigidity for a sub-set, which would be illogical. the resolution adopted still contains, however, unsatisfactory and even unacceptable passages: for example, it is contradictory to call for both better control of the external borders of the candidate countries and a relaxation of their asylum policy; it is hardly responsible to call for the application of structural policy to 'the whole of the union' after enlargement, when it should rather be concentrated, for a limited period, on the new member states; it is unacceptable to say that the lesson to be drawn from the irish referendum is the need to find a method of treaty revision which can circumvent such opposition (recital e). the change of tone does not yet seem to be in keeping with national democracies when they say no!
in writing. - despite an optimistic presentation, the reports give a bleak picture of the eastern european countries, which make up the vast majority of the applicant countries. "alarming levels of corruption", "overcrowded prisons", "enormous trafficking of women and children for prostitution and sexual exploitation", "high unemployment", "poverty", "severe environmental degradation", "unpromising economic prospects", "accelerating hiv spread", oppression of minorities, discrimination against roma - these are some of the terms used to describe one eastern country or another, or, in some cases, all of them. despite all this, the report welcomes the fact that privatisation is proceeding - including in the health sector, which is excluding a large part of the population from care - and that foreign investment, as well as exports, are increasing in many of these countries. the return of these countries to savage capitalism and the growing domination of western big business are already resulting in a considerable increase in social inequality. yet, apart from some moralising admonitions, what the reports ask of the governments of these countries is first of all to remove the last obstacles to the penetration of foreign capital and to increase "the flexibility and mobility of labour", that is to impose on their working classes even greater exploitation. we are in favour of a europe that is totally united from one end of the continent to the other, so we did not vote against enlargement. our abstention expresses our opposition to the domination that the european union is seeking to impose on these countries with the collaboration of the privileged sections of the latter, as well as to the anti-worker policy imposed under the pretext of enlargement.
in writing. - in this enlargement process, the council puts the 12 candidates on the same level without taking into account the specificities of the eastern european candidates, while imposing on them an overall change of system which makes this enlargement a qualitatively different issue from any previous enlargement. the european union is asking each candidate to prove his ability to cope with competition by destroying his environment, his social protection system and the means of a genuine policy of modernization and full employment, thus expanding poverty and unemployment. instead of continuing to give satisfaction to those who have privatized the most and reduced their budgetary expenditure, we need an audit of the real socioeconomic effects, a moratorium on privatization, public development aid, the redefinition of a european project for society for the european union, open to the east and the south, protecting employment, the environment, health and living standards. instead, the eu is preparing to welcome these new countries as second-tier members, tasked with applying the acquis communautaire and excluded from the benefits of the cap or the structural funds. the people must be consulted beforehand, in particular by means of a referendum, and europe must commit itself to respecting their response, whatever it may be. that is why we did not vote for the continuation of the enlargement process in these circumstances.
in writing. - it's probably a very big adventure that the enlargement. but it has been reduced to a commercial takeover or a merger of companies, instead of being the major historical event of the reunion of christian peoples who are coming together, at a time when the age-old enemy is threatening the south again. in this battle between the camp of freedom and enlightenment and the camp of fundamentalist darkness, ukraine and russia, the advanced sentinels of the west, would have had their place. the term 'acquis communautaire' sums up this ridiculous technical deadlock of a political issue at the top. in some thirty chapters, from agriculture to taxation, the environment, smes, education and transport, the legislation of the candidate countries, their administrations, their sociologies and even their morals have been scrutinized by a police eye which must remind these former countries of the proletarian morality of the heavy practices not yet forgotten. the member states are thus criticised for their criminal law which prohibits such sexual practices. many are being scolded for their fraud and corruption, as if the european vat had not been a factor in massive tax evasion since 1993. and malta has even been criticized for attracting too many offshore companies through a preferential tax regime. as if ireland had not done so and as if the united states had not practiced this system on a huge scale with the fsc; the european union has been condemned by the wto but tolerated by europe, which is descending all the "ladders" of its submission to the empire. at no time is enlargement an opportunity for a dialogue of experiences and an exchange of successes. poland rightly points out that its agricultural achievements are worth the achievements of a europe with 8 million animals slaughtered for foot-and-mouth disease or bse and 136,000 people who are incubating the deadly atypical creutzfeld-jakob disease. instead of enriching and preserving the heritage of plant and animal biodiversity of these eastern countries, not to mention their heritage of social ties not yet broken by ultra-capitalist savagery, the european commission is degrading this historic event to unconditional annexation. an anschluss in short. this explains why the case was handed over to a german commissioner and the european parliament's report to a member of parliament who happened to be german. it is true that things are clearer this way. there is enlargement, but as in 1990, it is still german. the parenthesis of 1945 is closing. the empire is rebuilding. mitteleuropa is here. eternal in its geography and history.
in writing. - at a time when the member states of the european union are finally drawing up, following the erika disaster, a more binding system for maritime safety - an area where the common interest is obvious - it is regrettable that the place reserved for this essential subject in the various resolutions concerning the candidate countries directly concerned is so discreet. everyone remembers the images of the wreck of the erika and the mention of its home port: valletta. it is well known that the merchant fleets of six applicant countries are on the 'black list' of the paris memorandum. apart from turkey, these are malta, cyprus, latvia, romania and bulgaria. the adoption by these countries of the erika i and erika ii packages and their commitment to tackling the issue of accommodating flags of convenience must be a priority in the accession negotiations. the security of our coastal regions depends on it.

in writing. - this report 'exhorts' poland to speed up the effective and genuine implementation of the acquis communautaire so that it can meet the commitments it has made and benefit fully from the benefits that future membership of the european union will bring. but what is the actual content of the acquis communautaire that the population and in particular polish farmers can expect? we certainly support the demand of all the applicant countries, and poland in particular, that they should not be treated as second-tier members. but reforms of the cap and the structural funds require much more than narrow budgetary calculations. agriculture is a major issue for the satisfaction of needs and fundamental rights, from the right to food sovereignty to health and environmental issues, to regional balances and jobs. the candidate countries like poland should be fully involved in the redefinition of another european agricultural policy. the polish industrial apparatus is suffering the full effects of this race for europe, which has taken this country from being a favourite for membership to being an outsider. the revenue used has left entire regions in disaster with an official unemployment rate of 16%. the socioeconomic failure of poland will be that of the so-called 'liberal' recipes imposed by accession. that is why we did not vote for this report.

in writing. - cyprus is now the most advanced candidate country in its negotiations with the european union (23 out of 29 chapters provisionally closed), and therefore, on paper, accession can be envisaged as early as 2004. but in practice this will pose serious problems because of the illegal occupation of the northern part of the island (37% of the total territory) by turkey since 1974. the european union considers that the cypriot government in the southern part represents the whole of the island, in accordance with international law, and that it is therefore negotiating for the accession of all the inhabitants. it is right, because to do otherwise would be to recognize a change of border imposed by force. but the result could be the inclusion in the union of a closed zone (since communications are cut off, except with turkey), where human rights are not respected (the european court again condemned turkey on 10 may for its behaviour in cyprus), and where the economic situation is beyond all standards. how do you deal with such contradictions ? the poos report which our assembly has just adopted rightly states that if turkey decides to annex the north of the island, 'it will be the end of its own candidacy for membership of the european union'. but if it does not, and if it refuses to resume negotiations, that is to say, if the present situation persists, what then? at the very least, turkey's attitude is not what one would expect of a country that wants to be a candidate for membership of the union.
in writing. - we approved several points in this report which could improve the protection of air passengers, but we did not vote on the whole because: - it seeks to exonerate airlines from a whole series of malfunctions by blaming them on airports and air traffic control, whereas it is the very operation of air transport as a whole according to the rules of profit which causes damage to passengers; - the deregulation and liberalisation of the air transport sector, falsely praised in the report, has accelerated the race for profit and therefore the resulting damage to passengers and air transport workers alike. it is a mockery of the world to pretend to believe, as the report says, that passenger safety could be improved without affecting competition and by relying on the voluntary commitment of airlines.
in writing. - we voted against this report not only to denounce its complacency with regard to the eschelon system, without the ridiculous hope that the european parliament could influence the decision of those who set it up, but above all to denounce the whole system of relations between states, as well as between financial and industrial groups whose universal espionage is only one of the many consequences. political and military espionage is used as a tool in the rivalry between great powers in their competing efforts to control the world. the industrial and commercial secrecy advocated by all the defenders of the capitalist order in order to conceal from their own populations the many ways of appropriating and squandering social wealth is inevitably complemented by industrial espionage. all these practices, which are shared by all the states that can afford them, are an attack on democratic freedoms and human rights. the report is concerned only with protecting european manufacturers against the handicap of their little secrets being discovered by their american competitors through the eschelon system. even the amendments made by some of the amendments we voted for do not change our opposition to the whole report, nor our disagreement with all the minority positions, the most innocent of which differ from the majority text only in the absurd desire to improve, control or moralize a system which is neither controllable nor moralizable. and we are certainly not advocating the "free market logic" which is just the law of the jungle.
in writing. - i was one of the people who signed up for a commission of inquiry. for efficiency, i joined the temporary committee. today i do not regret it! our committee (of which i was a member) did a good job and mr g. schmid, its rapporteur, was particularly competent. a few months ago, most political leaders simply denied the existence of echelon. at the beginning of september 2001, everyone (or almost) recognizes that this illegal american spy network covers a good part of the world and "watches" corporate markets and the private life of citizens! the system is less efficient than we feared, but it exists and it is intolerable! the rapporteur proposes measures. several groups consider them insufficient. i can understand some of them being real democrats. but i do not accept lessons from those, especially on the far right, who care about individual freedoms "as their first shirt". the important thing, the fundamental thing, for me is that the file is on the public square. in the wto negotiations, in the development of new technologies and in research (see my amendments on the sixth rdp), nothing will be quite as it was before! no one can say he didn't know! with the excellent schmid report, which i am voting for, our fight in this area is only just beginning.
in writing. - the main consequence of mr schmid's voluminous report is that we almost forget the question we asked in the beginning. neither the rapporteur's talent nor the courtesy of the chairman of this committee can make us forget that the strategy followed throughout this work was to drown the substance of the case in a general debate in which, from moral judgments on the activity of the secret services to uncertain considerations on technological complexes, we tried to talk about everything, about everyone except echelon and those who help to make it work. these fundamental questions - at a time when the european construction is so short of breath - should have been better treated than this regrettable silence. so we have to ask them again. firstly, since the participation of european union member states is proven in echelon, is there, yes or no, a clear violation of the eu treaty in this case? and if so, what sanctions are envisaged? in your report you answered the first question in the affirmative. but what did you learn from it? none, because you have not even raised, not even to explain your refusal to use it, the painful but logical problem of sanctions. we are therefore breathing a sigh of relief in london and berlin, since a breach of the principles of the treaties does not even attract a remonstrance from this parliament, which is so quick to be moved by the slightest attack on the rule of law in every corner of the planet! secondly, since our work has shown that the european union cannot undertake any major operation in the field of defence and security without the technical and logistical support of nato, is it really serious to lay the foundations for a european equivalent to echelon without first making a political clarification of the relations between echelon's european member states and the union, and above all between the union and nato? the reason for your embarrassment is that as long as its technical and financial links with nato are so obvious, so-called european solidarity will give way to atlantic solidarity, a legacy of the cold war, which is contrary to the existence of an independent common european defence and security policy. in short, the majority of this parliament - the same majority that adopted preventive measures of 'apartheid' against the new democratically elected austrian government, or that seriously considered putting under surveillance the government of silvio berlusconi - is exempt from taking measures against member states which are now found to be aiding and abetting an activity which contravenes the provisions of the treaty, seriously harms european businesses, and constantly threatens individual freedoms. the least that can be said is that there are undoubtedly two scales, two measures, and that simple fairness allows us to call this a real scandal. but for once, we could have avoided the real problems raised by echelon and had a real debate on the foundations and objectives of european construction: we could have understood the european nations as they are, with their own history and loyalties. we could have asked ourselves what kind of europe we wanted to build. the default response thus provided - that of a europe of the fog and the unspoken, cowardly consenting to submit to the law of the strongest - is in many ways quite appalling.
in writing. - my opposition to the motion for a resolution drawn up on the basis of the report of the temporary committee of this parliament on the echelon communications interception system is motivated by two main reasons. on the one hand, the proposed agreement between the european union and the united states does not seem relevant because, beyond good intentions, it is likely to remain without practical effect. on the other hand, if echelon is likely to constitute, as its promoters claim, an effective multilateral instrument in the fight against organized crime, terrorism, drug and arms trafficking and money laundering, then it is not a mutual goodwill agreement that should be signed with the united states. what needs to be negotiated is the possibility for any state wishing to become involved in active international cooperation in these essential areas to join the eschelon system, which would then become an open system. on the other hand, the draft resolution is used as a pretext to deal with a multitude of subjects which are completely outside the scope of the temporary committee. in the middle of this heterogeneous patchwork has slipped, in paragraph 5, the federalist obsession to see the next igc give the charter of fundamental rights a binding character and make it a legal basis for appeals, as if the current protections provided by both national constitutions and the universal and european declarations of human rights were null and void. this is a serious misrepresentation of the debate on eschelon which cannot be accepted.

- mr president, like the members before me, i support the principle of the reform of competition policy proposed by the commission. i say yes to decentralization. the present centralised method, the overloading of files, is not without some arbitrariness. they don't provide legal certainty. but i think that the reform will inevitably raise a very interesting issue, namely the clarification and development of the rules. and that's where i have a few differences. article 3 is obviously essential. it establishes the primacy of community law over national law where practices are liable to affect trade between member states. but this is not acceptable without clarification. for example, when it comes to services of general interest or other tasks which are essential for the states and regions, i am convinced that there is a need for exceptional regulations. at the very least, the commission will have to - as the economic and social committee proposes - present an interpretative communication on this subject. article 10 is another important article. it provides that the commission may make observations to the states on grounds of community public interest. here again, clarifications are necessary. jonathan evans points to the case of heavy investment. the services of general interest should also be mentioned here. two final points. the rapporteur is right to point out that it is contradictory to end prior notification and to establish a register. i think we should delete the registry. he is right to want convergence of national laws. that's the whole problem. this requires respect for the cultures of others and a balance between competition and social and environmental standards, including the service of general interest. so, go to the langen report and other reports.
mr president, we have been waiting for a long time for a directive on the quality of blood, which is essential to ensure the safety of donors and recipients at european level. from this point of view, my colleague mr nisticò's report, supplemented by the many amendments voted almost unanimously in committee, is in favour of greater protection of human health, in particular by requiring increased medical control of donors and by strengthening the responsibility of doctors and blood establishments at all stages, from collection to storage and at the time of processing blood derivatives. there is still, as we have just seen, a question which is not the subject of a consensus between us: free or paid donations. we are very attached to the principle of free blood donation, which has been acquired in many european countries without any shortage, and we cannot accept that it should be called into question for two essential reasons. first, from an ethical standpoint, we cannot advocate the selling of blood or any body component. the human body is not a commodity. in fact, we find it extremely shocking that companies can profit from the free blood donation. secondly, the remuneration of the donation may be counterproductive in terms of quality. financial-lure donors may be led to deny that they have any health problems, which can have dramatic consequences for their own health and that of the recipients. the recent news of the hundreds of thousands of chinese who are now suffering from aids because they have sold their plasma is a tragic illustration of this and we do not want the same thing to happen in europe tomorrow.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to say a few words on the proposed amendment to article 3 of the ombudsman's statute, and i refer to mrs garrett's report. giving access to all classified documents emanating from a member state without the consent of that state, even when it is a question of documents which may relate to diplomatic or defence matters, seems to us to be a very dangerous precedent, especially if this review is somehow imposed on the member states. the perverse result of this measure, if it were adopted, would obviously be that member states would be encouraged to retain classified documents rather than to disclose them to any community body, and that is why my group cannot support this proposal. as regards the bösch report, we do not entirely share mr bösch's optimism in his analysis of the european ombudsman's activities. the work of mr söderman's services certainly seems quite remarkable, given their modest means. but the fact that just over 1 700 complaints were received in 2000, of which only 297 were declared admissible, does not prove that the institutions of europe are administering things properly. it shows above all the lack of information on the part of citizens about their means of defence against certain aspects of the eurocracy in brussels. as for the content of the complaints, mainly against the commission, they seem to us to be symptomatic: refusal of information, lack of transparency, delay in payment, abuse of power, injustice and even discrimination are the main complaints. it is in the light of these grievances that i think we should continue our reflection.

- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as regards the fruit juice directive, i should like to express our agreement with the council's proposal, which seems to us to be moving in the right direction, namely that of effective consumer protection, which must be provided with clear, easily understandable and objective information enabling consumers to make informed choices in terms of both quality and food safety. the higher production costs linked to the effort and quality guarantee must also be clearly recognised on the labelling. there are currently two main categories of fruit juices, depending on whether they are concentrated or not, each corresponding to a specific product type and a specific production process. however, current labelling practice does not allow consumers to distinguish clearly between these two categories. in order to eliminate this source of confusion in the minds of consumers about the real nature of the product they are buying, the finnish presidency has proposed the introduction of two simple, clear and objective definitions. the term 'fruit juice' would be reserved for unconcentrated juices, while juices based on concentrated fruit juice would be given a sales denomination which corresponds to their characteristics. thus, the consumer seeking a more authentic and natural product will be able to easily find it on the shelf under the clear name 'fruit juice' knowing that he is prepared to pay the price corresponding to the specific qualities associated with this product, while the consumer wishing for a more standardised and more economical product will be able to turn in full knowledge of the facts to a juice based on concentrate without ambiguity about its nature and its specific characteristics. the definition of these two categories of juice, corresponding to two different names, seems to us, mr president, to be a real step forward in consumer information, and that is why we will support it.
in writing. - we voted on this text as it stands after the amendments proposed by the committee on the environment and public health of the european parliament. and we voted against all amendments that would jeopardize or restrict blood donation based on voluntary, voluntary and non-profit. we only regret that the report does not provide for a formal obligation for companies to allow their employees the time they need to donate blood and to remove the cumbersome authorization procedures which discourage goodwill. we are opposed to the whole economic system that is driven by the pursuit of profit. the profits made directly or indirectly from the trade in human organs, cells and tissues are one of the most abject manifestations of this system, an expression of the fact that society has not emerged from barbarism.
in writing. - the european directive on quality and safety standards for the collection, testing, processing, storage and distribution of blood had to be amended to increase the protection of donors and recipients. the safety of recipients deserves to be further guaranteed both by the traceability of the entire blood supply chain and by the guarantee of highly qualified staff in all blood transfusion facilities in europe. greater security increases confidence in the supply system and, in turn, encourages donors to donate their blood. but this directive must also be based on principles. blood is not a commodity. the charter of fundamental rights of the european union states that the human body is not to be used for commercial gain. we must therefore clearly affirm the principle of gratuitousness. by donating, the citizen performs an act of solidarity. this implies, as the european socialists have argued, that blood and blood components should be collected only from voluntary donors.
in writing. - i have, like many colleagues, been approached by blood donor organisations concerned about possible changes to existing legislation in this area. everyone agrees that the shortage of blood and plasma in the european union is a matter of regret, and rightly so, but we must not under any circumstances let up our vigilance as regards the quality of these products, especially since half of the european union's needs are met by imports! this directive, as amended by parliament, amends, integrates and complements the legislation currently governing the quality and safety standards for the collection, testing, processing, storage and distribution of human blood and blood components in europe. the aim is to adopt stricter requirements for donor eligibility and screening and to establish a community-wide quality system in blood establishments. this would be complemented by an equivalent system of control and approval in the member states. finally, common standards would be defined for the training of staff and for the traceability of blood from donor to patient. of course, these measures will not prevent member states from maintaining or introducing more stringent protective measures. it is also desirable to reduce the european union's dependence on imports of blood or blood components from third countries. this requires information campaigns to be carried out with potential donors. but in no case should we imagine a system of remuneration for these products. the european parliament's report rightly emphasizes the importance of the voluntary nature of blood donation, while acknowledging that the social contribution of donors and the meritorious nature of their donations should be emphasized. as a blood donor myself and an advocate of the cause of blood donation, i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. - i voted for this report. the initiatives advocated in this report will, i believe and hope, help to avoid the disasters we have seen, particularly in france with the case of contaminated blood. we cannot ignore the tragic outcome of this event, which has left such a deep impression on our minds. it is therefore our responsibility at european level to set high standards for the quality of blood and the safety of blood collection, to be demanding about storage conditions and traceability and to impose strict control rules. blood is not a commodity like any other. it is not a commercial good and nothing should make us deviate from that idea. i remain firmly opposed to any commercial use of human blood and i am in favour of the principle of voluntary and unpaid donation. firstly, for ethical reasons: our parliament, and in particular its committee on genetics, has made many references to ethics. but does ethics require us to introduce a fee for blood donation? should the relationship between the doctor and the donor be based on trust or on a single financial relationship? as far as ethics is concerned, we have voted a charter of fundamental rights which clearly states that it is forbidden to make the human body a source of profit. coherence must be part of our political commitment. the second reason is scientific: studies have shown that the safety of the blood supply seems to be better guaranteed by the practice of voluntary donation, that the blood thus collected is less likely to transmit infectious diseases. in a directive on the quality and safety of blood, this scientific finding cannot be ignored. for cultural reasons, finally: in france - and the support of the various associations that have contacted me shows this to me - we cannot accept the idea of payment for blood donation, particularly for the reasons i have mentioned earlier.
in writing. - in recent years, food scandals have been highlighted in the news and consumers are rightly demanding to be very informed about the products they buy. information to the consumer must be as clear and legible as possible, while avoiding the multiplication of categories. therefore, the sales denomination of fruit juices should not be confusing. it is therefore imperative to inform the consumer of the difference between fresh fruit juice and fruit juice obtained from concentrate. these two distinct names will enable the buyer to make an informed choice. similarly, some fruit juices are produced by mixing fresh fruit juice with juice obtained from concentrate. the mere mention of 'fresh fruit juice' would be misleading to the consumer. it is important that the labelling in this case includes an additional statement that the final product also consists of concentrate. the name 'concentrated' or 'partially concentrated' must then appear directly under the name, the size of the characters being sufficient to ensure that the consumer is informed. this provision also applies to nectars obtained from concentrate. these decisions are intended to provide the consumer with the clearest possible information, but also to avoid penalising producers. the manufacturing processes of these two categories of products differ in technical, economic and organoleptic aspects. the production of fresh fruit juices requires a high quality of product processing, particularly during the pressing and pasteurization phases, whereas the production of fruit juices obtained from concentrate does not entail the same requirements.
in writing. - i abstained on the joint resolution on the bonn conference on climate change. it is a far too enthusiastic assessment of the negotiated agreement. it is hard to believe that the kyoto protocol "gives new impetus" to kyoto, is a "key instrument" in a "global strategy against global warming" and represents "an extremely positive message for all citizens concerned about globalisation". the alarm should be sounded: nine years after rio, no effective measures have been taken and the ambitions of the states have been particularly diluted. the bonn agreement includes positive points, such as the refusal to present nuclear energy as a 'clean' energy. but it marks a further setback for the "market-for-all" proponents, which can only worry and not reassure "citizens concerned about globalisation". the joint resolution remains very ambiguous on this essential question. paragraph 9 'regrets' the place given in bonn to 'carbon sinks' and 'flexible systems'. but paragraph 6 proposes that the 2003 climate conference focus on these "systems" (the international emissions trading scheme) rather than the essential public policies required to combat climate chaos. the mere fact that an agreement was reached in bonn with japan, australia, canada and russia should not hide the fact that the content of this agreement is far from responding to the urgency of the issues at stake.
in writing. - although the text speaks of 'deepening democracy' and evokes 'a breath of transparency' and despite its very purpose of granting the ombudsman greater access to official documents, its whole spirit is marked by the concern to preserve the 'professional secrecy' of information to which the ombudsman might have access. instead of making institutions and their functioning more transparent, the function of the ombudsman only serves to conceal the fact that they are not so for the overwhelming majority of the population. we have therefore not voted for this report. and if we did not vote against it either, it is only because the french official authorities are against a little more flexible access - by the ombudsman alone! - to 'classified documents' on behalf of the europe of defence and are calling for the report to be rejected. we reaffirm our opposition to commercial and industrial secrecy and to so-called state secrets which are not so much intended to protect the state against a third state as to conceal the actions, even the most unworthy, of state institutions from the eyes of their own people.

mr president, after plundering zimbabwe for a century of colonial rule, after exploiting its working classes, after robbing its peasants of their land, the united kingdom has left a legacy of a situation where the best land still belongs to a few thousand rich white farmers. the great powers found nothing to complain about in the dictatorial and corrupt nature of the zimbabwean regime until its dictator, mugabe, had begun - to maintain his power - to make some demagogic gestures questioning the privileges of white farmers. france, which is less connected to this privileged class, continues to support the dictatorship without any scruples. the feigned indignation of all those here protesting against the violence of the mugabe regime seems, under these conditions, to be a hypocritical way of defending a privileged few against the right to life of millions of peasants in this country. even if some land occupations by groups of poor peasants occur in violence, this represents only a tiny fraction of the violence that has been imposed on them to plunder them. we, for our part, protest against the mugabe regime, both because of its dictatorial character and its corruption, but also because this dictatorship continues to protect outrageous social inequalities and the privileges of a small section of the population, including its clique and the rich white farmers. but we do not share this common resolution, whose letter and spirit we reject. it is up to the people of this country to settle accounts with mugabe and his dictatorship. it is not the complicit of the privileged minority and those who have led or supported colonial violence to give lessons of morality to this country. above all, we express our solidarity with the working people of zimbabwe and our support for their right to take possession of all their land without purchase or compensation.

government's only objective is to remain in power, even if it was forced to finish destroying a country which was considered, until recently, one of the strongest economies and democracies in africa. as many of you have mentioned - is the holding of presidential elections. the union's main objective is to hold presidential elections in 2002 under the best possible conditions to bring about change, already occurred and which should be manageable if we were only talking about the grain deficit and its consequences for the population. however, the serious instability in the country, the economic crisis and the social conflicts that are taking place there are an important factor in food insecurity, which we believe, in these conditions, is likely to worsen. so it is the interplay between the food situation, the agricultural deficit, in this case the cereals deficit, the economic and political context, that is carrying within it the seeds of a tragedy probably even more serious than the one we are experiencing now and which we must do everything to avoid.

- the next item is the joint debate on the following motions for resolutions: - (b5-0548/2001) by mr van dam, on behalf of the edd group, on foot-and-mouth disease; - (b5-0553/2001) by mr martinez and others, on behalf of the tdi group, on foot-and-mouth disease; - (b5-0555/2001) by mr mulder, on behalf of the eldr group, on foot-and-mouth disease; - (b5-0563/2001) by mr goepel, mr sturdy and mr maat, on behalf of the ppe-de group, on foot-and-mouth disease; - (b5-0573/2001) by mr lucas and others, on behalf of the green group, on foot-and-mouth disease; - (b5-0580/2001) by mr berlato and mr hyland, on behalf of the uen group, on foot-and-mouth disease; - b5-0584/2001 by mr jové peres and others, on behalf of the gue/ngl group, on foot-and-mouth disease;
- mr president, commissioner, in this outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease there are technical areas of uncertainty, political uncertainties and strategic questions. first of all, as far as the shadowy areas are concerned, how far from the known endemic outbreaks - turkey, asia, thrace for europe - how could foot-and-mouth disease, its virus, have possibly swam to britain, to an island? why this dogmatic refusal of a vaccine that is effective? france had, in the 1950s, before compulsory vaccination from 1961 to 1991, up to 300 000 annual outbreaks that disappeared with compulsory vaccination. how come we had the cow-pest virus and the cow-prion in the same country? these are questions that lead to political certainty, if not to lessons. in both cases, bse and foot-and-mouth disease, the british authorities reacted late and were overwhelmed, because the ultra-liberalism of the thatcher years left only 220 veterinarians compared to 8,000 in france. as with any developing country, australia, canada, and even the french army had to send veterinarians to britain. no vet, no surveillance network, which explains the spread. it is also the ultra-liberalism which has led to the closure of slaughterhouses and which has caused sheep to be taken from carlisle, from hadrian's wall, from northumberland, to the south and disseminated. the virus is spreading in britain and, after the removal of the borders, it is spreading in france as well. free movement means free contamination. a third certainty highlighted by a french parliamentary investigation report in june 2001 was that the spread of the virus was due to the illegal purchase of sheep at exorbitant prices - less than 90 euros a sheep for the muslim festival of eid el kebir. but alongside these certainties, there are questions for the commission. and it's good that mr. lamy, the strategist, is here. first, is the compensation system in britain becoming a contamination premium? it was suggested that the lucrative pay might be a benefit to having infected animals. the total slaughter of four million animals, most of them sheep, makes it possible to purge the surplus. and finally, does new zealand, the world's largest exporter, not have an interest in seeing its potential market share in europe increase as we cut? and, my god, if the treaty on echelon is an anglo-saxon agreement, we can exchange services. i, britain, the excess individual pay, you, new zealand, the opportunity to export more. cairn's group would be happy. doha would be a success. it would be good if mr lamy could shed some light on this.
commission. - to give a quick overview of the situation at union level, today there are no restrictions due to foot-and-mouth disease in the union, with the exception of great britain, and this has been the case since 25 june this year, 30 days after the last animal vaccinated in the netherlands was slaughtered and destroyed. in 14 of the 15 member states of the union, plus northern ireland, we have a rather favourable situation, which is the result of the implementation and effective application of measures to control foot-and-mouth disease at community level. i risk offending mrs lucas by referring to the international point of view, and from that point of view we strongly hope that the measures taken by france, ireland and the netherlands will enable them to obtain the necessary status from the international office for diseases of the animal health, which should enable third countries to lift the trade restrictions which are still in place. this - and i assure mrs lucas on this point - may not be the main point, but let us return to the case of the united kingdom, which is indeed a cause for concern since the 2000th outbreak appeared on 3 september. the situation in britain, although stable for almost three months, is of concern to us because of the persistence of outbreaks in or near areas that are subject to restrictions. many of you have mentioned the most recent cases in northumberland county, the area where the outbreak first began, which are of concern because they were reported three months after the disease was eradicated. radical measures were taken: slaughter of infected herds, neighbouring herds, contact herds and although the appearance of this limited but nevertheless worrying number of outbreaks was expected after a peak in disease in early april, the period during which a small number of outbreaks persisted is nevertheless excessive and the commission has required the uk authorities to step up their eradication measures. we are under time pressure, as things get more difficult in autumn and winter, both because of weather conditions and the animal migration patterns during this period. the current course of the disease is clearly at a critical stage. this is no time to loosen the controls. as has been said, and as many of you have pointed out, at this time of year we are beginning to see the herds moving and being subjected to various manipulations and therefore we believe that the movement of animals should be reduced to the strict minimum. the commission informed the parties concerned accordingly. in the case of the united kingdom again, the complex structures of bovine breeding, the absence of clinical signs in sheep and the slow spread within herds are all factors which complicate the problem and require us to use laboratory tests, the available capacity of which is now sufficient. so what is the commission's view? we will not say that the situation is satisfactory, it is not in this particular case, but the risk of spread to other member states is much lower today than it was in march and april last, at the peak, because all the restrictions imposed, particularly on the movement of untreated animals and products from great britain, are still in place. we are carrying out regular on-the-spot checks, the last of which was at the end of august, to ensure that the uk authorities are taking the appropriate action. other, sometimes important, areas of great britain have never been affected by the disease and there is a need for further reflection within the veterinary committee so that in these areas, and in due course, when the situation allows it, the resumption of trade can be considered under strict conditions. we shall be extremely cautious in this respect, because the northumberland experiment reminds us that the risk exists even in areas where the disease seemed to be under control. to return briefly to the third countries, if mrs lucas will permit me, a number of countries have maintained discriminatory measures against european products which go beyond the existing international standards and we are working on this with a number of our trading partners. many third countries have gradually lifted the rather extensive prohibitions with which they started; the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. and we will continue to work, our basis in this area being the wto sanitary and phytosanitary agreement. more generally, it should be noted that the crisis has already had a major impact on the community budget. we have decided to allocate eur 400 million to the four member states concerned this year, and the latest forecasts indicate a likely financial contribution from the union of something like just over eur 1.5 billion. we shall make the necessary arrangements for the budgetary procedure. this is undoubtedly an exceptional situation, we cannot foresee in the budget epidemics of such a magnitude and we will therefore have to make adjustments. that is one aspect of the question. the second aspect is, of course, the damage to the image of our livestock farming; it is now here, as a result of the slaughter of nearly 4 million animals. thirdly, the problem, as has been said, is also present outside the european union and we have some serious concerns following the recent outbreak in turkish thrace. finally, the commission hopes that in future it will be able to draw some lessons from the management of such crises in order to improve the current regulatory and legislative framework. for example, by introducing a number of additional requirements on intra-community trade in small ruminants, such as the restriction on the number of stopping points, which is probably a first step. secondly, we are working on a proposal on the identification and registration of sheep and goats, and another on the introduction of animal products by travellers. we are also working in the direction of adjusting our control procedures in the event of an outbreak of this type. i think we have enough experience now. let us not be fooled: the strengthening of legislation and the mechanisms, however necessary, will not be enough on its own to prevent the reappearance of such an epidemic. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the matter. i would like to conclude with a point that many of you have brought to our attention during the debate, and that is the question of vaccination. as regards the use of so-called 'ring' vaccination around outbreaks, i would remind those of you who are calling the commission into question in this respect, asking why the commission has not imposed emergency vaccination, that vaccination in our legal order today, marked by certain forms of subsidiarity, is the responsibility of the national authorities, whatever they may say. so there is a procedure which allows the member state concerned to use vaccination if it so wishes, and that is how it works. the system exists and is available to the member states, but it is not the responsibility of the commission. i think that is a clear answer to the questions put by mr van dam, mr martinez, mr mulder and mrs lucas.
- this debate is over. the vote will take place at 6.30 p.m.

- mr president, the dissolution in october 2001 of the main opposition party in mauritania, the union of new era democratic forces, and the arrest and subsequent sentence to five years' imprisonment, after a summary trial, of the leader of the popular front party, chbih melainine, call into question the fundamental principles of democracy, which are enshrined in the constitution of mauritania. but what is the value of this constitution? there is no freedom of association for political parties. the green party, which submitted its statutes several months ago, has still not been recognised and has not even received the receipt for its application. these anti-democratic maneuvers are taking place on the eve of the legislative and local elections scheduled for october. we have no guarantee for these elections, since there is no independent electoral commission. we consider the release of chbih melainine a precondition for holding elections in october, as well as the re-establishment of all opposition parties. it is to allow the participation of all these political actors that we ask that the elections be postponed. in order to restore democracy and ensure the holding of free and fair elections in mauritania, we call on the council and the commission to open consultations with the government in accordance with the procedure laid down in article 96 of the cotonou agreement.
mr president, two years ago, my first speech in this house was already about condemning the situation in togo. since then, although good people say that everything is getting better, togo is still in a political stalemate from which it is far from emerging. democracy remains a fleeting utopia. civil and human rights are constantly violated. and i believe that the passivity of the governments of the countries of the union does nothing to promote change. the usual condemnations by parliament remain rhetorical and without effect. the amount recently paid by the commission for the organization of the new elections - cfaf 4 000 million - was considered insufficient by the government, which took the opportunity to postpone the long-awaited parliamentary elections once again. in complete violation of his previous commitments, president eyadema and his government are even considering amending the constitution to allow him to run for re-election. finally, one of the opposition figures, mr yawovi agboyibo, was arrested and sentenced a month ago on false charges. the fact is that he had denounced the terrorism in areas where the opposition was dominant, terrorism expressed in rape and extortion, even the murder of opponents. mr eyadema seems less than ever ready to fulfil his obligations to his people and his commitments to the international community. again, parliament must strongly condemn these abuses, demand free elections on the scheduled dates and ask the council and the commission to open consultations in accordance with article 96 of the cotonou agreement.
- mr president, the resolution calls for the release of yawovi agboyibo, who opposed the dictator yadema. we therefore support this resolution, but we say that those who approve of the policy of the great western powers are in no position to be indignant today, because this dictatorship which has oppressed the togolese people since 1967 has only been able to maintain itself with the support of the great powers, and more particularly that of france. so one can ask what the use of a resolution voted by parliament is if the dictator in power is then received with honors in government palaces and if he continues to receive subsidies that allow him to buy weapons to stay in power.
mr president, the attack on a train in angola on 10 august last, which killed 260 civilians and injured more than 150, is unacceptable and reprehensible, especially since several buses were also the target of deadly attacks in the weeks that followed. unita struck again, violating the 1994 lusaka peace agreement, which included the disarmament of the warring rebels. these acts of terrorism are unfortunately just another step in the civil war that has been ravaging the country for over 25 years, but above all, these acts of extreme violence against civilians further delay the prospect of holding elections scheduled by the government in 2002-2003. by announcing on august 23 that he would not run for the presidency, president dos santos is sending the ball back to the rebels. he said he was ready to hold free and democratic elections, provided the war stopped. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'common carrier' in the context of the directive. but mr savimbi, the leader of unita, says he wants to negotiate. in fact, we know that sitting on his diamonds, he wants only one thing: all the power. it is also our responsibility that is involved, because who supplies unita with weapons? who are the people who are helping to smuggle the diamonds? and the government is not transparent either. the lack of transparency in the management of oil revenues suggests that public funds have been used to strengthen the regime. the angolagate scandal has highlighted the role of europeans in this affair. the violence must stop, and dialogue must begin urgently. the angolans must vote and find peace. the european union has a role to play. we need to remind him, we need to pass this resolution and move forward.
