to participate in an election observation mission. if the united nations were to decide to coordinate this observation, we would have no objection. the conditions for the organisation and implementation of this observation mission have yet to be determined. of course, parliament's participation in this mission would be welcome if it were decided. as regards human rights in cambodia, the commission and the member states have been officially invited by cambodia to appoint and send observers to monitor the local elections. as such, we sent out an exploratory mission. the conclusions and recommendations of this mission will be examined by the council as from september, in order to decide whether or not we organise a community observation mission for the municipal elections. we are also prepared to support the smooth conduct of these elections through technical assistance projects. on the question of voter registration, mrs maes, the latest figures we have are of an overall voter registration rate of just over 80%, which is an improvement on the previous figures, although we are not quite at the total yet. as regards the past treatment which some of you have mentioned, i would remind you that we fully support the efforts of the united nations and the government of the kingdom of cambodia to reach an agreement on the tribunal to try the khmer rouge. as for the afghan refugees seeking asylum in australia, we are, like mrs kinnock, relieved that a solution has been found to provide the necessary assistance and protection to these men, women and children who were fleeing from one of the most intolerant regimes. your remarks, as i understand them, are not intended to put this or that third country on trial, but to look at what might, in the international governance system today, allow us to deal better with this type of situation. you are right: we cannot remain indifferent to this. we all know that other ships carrying other migrants from poverty, often in inhuman conditions, are appearing, including off the coast of europe. this is not a 'rest of the world' issue from which we can detach ourselves, nor can we consider it in the light of the problems it may pose elsewhere. there is clearly a growing unease in the international community about forced migration, whether for economic, political or criminal reasons, as this is how organized human trafficking networks should be called. mr medina ortega, we share the concern expressed by you and other colleagues that international instruments be adopted to prevent and deal with such cases and at least to update and adjust the 1951 convention to a situation that is not that of the 1950s. in this respect, we support the efforts initiated by the high commissioner for refugees and announced on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the convention. the high commissioner for refugees has played a significant role in the tampa crisis and i think we should all encourage him to put this kind of problem on the agenda for the consultations which, after the geneva conference next december, should allow us to update our rules, since they are indeed international rules. the importance of the protocols on human trafficking and smuggling, annexed to the united nations convention against transnational crime of december 2000, should also be noted. the community itself is a party to these protocols which, when they come into force - after a number of ratifications - will improve the common framework we have to fight this crime. as far as the union itself is concerned - and i repeat, this also concerns us - the treaty of amsterdam and the conclusions of the european council in tampere have laid the foundations for a common policy on asylum and immigration. i believe that the union, through these texts and various declarations, has reiterated its commitment and that of its member states to a humanitarian tradition, which should be reflected in the establishment of a common asylum system offering adequate protection to all those in need and guaranteeing the principle of non-refoulement. of course, this is not possible without preventive action in the countries and regions of origin. we started to move forward in this approach when the council adopted a number of action plans prepared by the immigration and asylum group. it just so happens that one of them is specifically about afghanistan and the surrounding regions. if this proves ineffective, we will have to go back to it and we are counting on parliament to take us in that direction. the channels of trafficking in human beings: we must strengthen the union's action, especially in cases where victims can benefit from international protection. here too, the commission considers that a more systematic and coherent approach is necessary. we shall be working towards this very shortly with a communication. all this is therefore becoming a timetable for action by the union. work has begun in the council. the pace of progress seems to us to be very slow, but this is not unexpected given the sensitivity of these matters for the member states. it is likely that a new impetus will be needed at the appropriate political level, probably at the european council in laeken. that is what the presidency seems to be thinking. we are convinced that parliament's support will certainly help us to move in the right direction. finally, on the attack on a train in angola, i have little to add. much of what has been said is consensual. the commission, like you, is very concerned about the continuation of this war, and deplores the fact that these clashes are intensifying and that several hundred civilians have again been killed in various parts of the country in recent weeks. we are fully committed to supporting the efforts undertaken in accordance with the union's common position to find a political solution to the conflict in angola. i have not heard from your speeches any serious criticism of this common position. we are therefore working towards its implementation by supporting any proposal to support initiatives emanating from the african union - there are some - or from african regional organisations, such as the southern african development community, with a view to developing the mechanisms put in place at the initiative of african countries to prevent and resolve conflicts. i would remind you that we are maintaining our humanitarian aid to angola, which is considerable, and that we are prepared to adapt the nature and the amount of this humanitarian aid accordingly.

- commissioner, without even waiting for 2002 and its international year of the mountains, we are all in agreement here, the 20 members who remain, to protect mountain agriculture, which accounts for, they say, 20% of our land. i come from a mountain area, from the sheep's transhumance. in fact, it is a dream farm, especially for the european commission. we are doing rural, forestry, biodiversity, the environment, we are fighting against soil erosion; we focus on quality, honey, meat, fruit, tourism, we focus on quality of life, and most importantly, we don't focus on productivity. we don't do it in the icu. we don't interfere with the united states in the world markets for wheat, oilseeds, animal protein. at its core, mountain farming is multi-functional without quantity. the 2006 cap reform aims to extend the austrian model to the whole of europe, including the plain. in the end, it is sissi the farmer who, accompanied by our commissioner, mr fischler, would be strolling among the haymills, the bells of the herds, the marmots, in the middle of the alpine pastures, caressing the rare breed cows, while mr bush's texans would have a monopoly on the meat market. so yes to mountain farming in the mountains, but no to an agricultural europe reduced to the wto negotiations, to nature parks with farmers who mike moore would have disguised as walt disney characters, and who would be responsible for entertaining anglo-saxon tourists by maintaining the landscapes.
in writing. - we agree with the author of the report in demanding that "free, compulsory and quality education should be provided to all children up to the age of 15". but even in european countries, where laws exist to this effect, the free provision is largely formal, as it does not include school supplies, which penalises children from the poorest sections of society, not to mention overcrowded classrooms and poorly equipped schools in working-class neighborhoods. these evils strike with far greater violence in underdeveloped countries, even where schooling is compulsory. the report claims that "solving the education crisis is one of the most effective strategies" to "break the cycle of poverty". it's turning reality on its head. without "breaking the cycle of poverty", that is, without stopping the plundering of poor countries and impoverishing their working people, even the best-intentioned speeches will remain speeches and even a minimum of education will continue to be denied to millions of children in poor countries. our vote in favour means that we agree with the intentions expressed under these conditions only.
- dear colleagues, it is with the emotion and sadness that inspires us all a horror whose scale seemed inconceivable that i open this extraordinary meeting. it is first of all to express our solidarity with the american people who have been struck by barbaric terrorism, our sympathy with the victims, whose number will undoubtedly be terrible, and our support for all those who are working hard to try to save a few more lives. i have already expressed my solidarity with president bush yesterday, on my own behalf and on behalf of the whole european parliament, and assured him that the europeans stand by the united states in the dramatic ordeal of its people. when terrorism strikes in a member state of the european union, it is each and every one of us who is affected. i feel the same sense of revolt and outrage at these monstrous attacks. today, the pain of the american people is our pain as well. it is this great democracy, which has done so much to help europe regain its freedom, that has just been struck. but it is also the sacred values of life and democracy that are being attacked. the date of september 11, 2001, will be indelibly etched in the memory of mankind. it calls for our calm but also for the closest cooperation of all countries which reject terrorism so that the perpetrators of these heinous crimes and those who have supported them are identified, hunted down, arrested and brought to justice and so that blind terrorism is finally eradicated from the face of the globe. it also requires the commitment of the international community to resolve peacefully the conflicts that fuel and sustain fanaticism. beyond declarations, beyond a common response to terrorism, which we are calling for, it is now up to all the actors on the international scene to assume their responsibilities. the time has come for decisive action, and i am convinced that urgent decisions are needed in the european union. i am glad that prime minister verhofstadt, minister michel and commission president romano prodi are here. the european union will only be credible if it has a common policy to combat terrorism. the european commission and the european parliament have made this clear, particularly at our last part-session. i would like the council to examine these proposals as soon as possible. since the tampere european council, the european area of freedom, security and justice has made some tentative progress, but it has fallen far short of what is required. it is urgent to go beyond this. even if the european union has also established its presence on the international scene, whether in the middle east, in durban or in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, yesterday's events demonstrate, if need be, the absolute necessity of establishing as quickly as possible a europe of defence and a genuine common foreign and security policy. an exceptional european council could give a boost to all these guidelines, because, as we know, history does not wait. i would ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to observe a minute's silence in memory of all the victims. - madam president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr president of the commission, we all lack the words to express the feelings aroused by the terrorist attack of unprecedented barbarity that has just struck the united states. the american people are going to have to overcome a deep trauma that is likely to worsen as the full extent of the disaster that they have just experienced becomes clear. in this unimaginable trial, he must be able to count on our unreserved solidarity. i would add that if these faceless monsters targeted the united states yesterday, they can, tomorrow, spread terror and death in any part of the world, including, of course, the european continent. my group therefore fully agrees with the statements and actions you have made on our behalf. these appalling attacks are a challenge to the entire human community, a challenge we must now learn to meet. i say 'learn' because, while we all agree that the perpetrators must be found and punished, we must also recognize that the questions raised by the tragedy of 11 september 2001 are more numerous than the certainties. i think that nothing would be more inappropriate, or even more dangerous, than to react to this radically new phenomenon with old conceptions which have just cruelly shown their limits. thus, the temptation may be great after such an outrage to call for a swift but incalculable retaliation. and yes, mr poettering, you are right, it would not be in the interests of peace to allow fanatical criminals to be mixed up with whole peoples, some of whose representatives have come precisely to express, sometimes with great dignity and a spirit of responsibility, a radical condemnation of the terrorists and their solidarity with the american people. finally, and more generally, no one should ever forget that we are all part of the same world. the most powerful nation in the world is not invulnerable. the entire international community is doomed to look together at the great problems facing the planet, the growing gaps, the broken dialogues, the oceans of frustration, and to cooperate as closely as possible to solve them in a lasting way. this is perhaps the most decisive contribution that europe can make to the world in order to meet together the challenge of civilization that we face. - madam president, mr prime minister, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the first thoughts we should express at this time are feelings of compassion for the victims and solidarity with the american people. the terrorist attack he was the victim of was not just aimed at the american people. he's aiming at the very heart of democracy itself. democracies are fragile and we know that they have a hard time dealing with this type of action. i am convinced, however, that the american people are capable of overcoming this ordeal, given their history and experience, and i believe it is important that this house should show solidarity with them at this time. i would therefore like to thank you, madam president, for organising this meeting. my group had applied for it, as had others. i'm glad it's going on. i hope that it will be followed later by a debate which will enable us to go deeper into the problems posed by international terrorism. as someone who has been responsible for leading counterterrorism action in my own country on two occasions, i would like to say that there is a first misconception that we must get rid of: there are no good terrorists and bad terrorists, there are terrorists. (applause from the left) and terrorism, in so far as it tries to impose its views on the majority by the force and the violent action of a minority, is never more than a manifestation of the totalitarianism and fascism that we have fought and must fight resolutely. but the fight against terrorism requires a permanent mobilization. and it is probably because we have lost sight of this notion and this obviousness that we are faced today with the tragic situation we are experiencing in the united states. i think the united states has made the mistake of probably thinking that it is out of the loop on this kind of action. unfortunately, we in europe have already experienced this: in germany, italy, france, spain and many other countries. and we know that terrorism is blind and can strike anywhere and at any time. we also know that to fight terrorism, we need political will. we must affirm this will. it also requires cooperation. if each state wants to keep for itself the information it has been able to obtain, if there is no real cooperation between the services concerned, then we will face further disasters. if, on the contrary, there is a consciousness at the level of the states and at the level of international cooperation, a willingness to put together all the information that can be obtained and also a decision to create, in one form or another, a permanent cooperation body that can analyse this information and propose the necessary measures, then we will have a chance of opposing, with some success, this type of operation. i would like to join in what has been said in this house, first by our excellent colleague mr poettering and others, mrs hautala, mr wurtz. there is nothing worse than that we should now be using inconsistent words to create solidarity between the terrorists and the muslim world. that would be the worst mistake, the worst stupidity. that is why, naturally, we cannot be satisfied with statements which do not represent much. but i think, personally, i would appreciate it, but i think our whole community would appreciate it if muslim religious leaders at the highest level would themselves condemn these attacks, to prove that there is no common ground, that there is no possible identification between terrorists who claim to have a deviant faith and the muslim religion, for which we must have the respect that it deserves. madam president, on this tragic day, we express our solidarity and friendship with the american people, victims of the most horrific terrorist crime. we also remembered that many europeans were working in the world trade center towers, and many likely died. we feel it only more deeply than beyond the united states, it is the whole west, of which we are an integral part, that was targeted. it is not just the united states, but the whole of western civilization that has just been the victim of an act of war, a new war, deadly but elusive, because it no longer meets the traditional criteria. some people believed that the world was becoming less dangerous after the collapse of the soviet union, and they found this an easy excuse for relaxing the security effort. it was a big mistake. we have actually entered a new era, where a major risk is that of rogue states run by people who are driven mad and blinded by hatred and ideology. worse still, more elusive than rogue states are the non-state terrorist organizations whose murderous madness no longer makes any sense. this new war will force us to revise all our strategic concepts. firstly, europe must understand that security must now be put before the abolition of checks at the frontiers or elsewhere. i'm not going to stress that point, which you know. secondly, we must strengthen our fight against terrorism and criminal organizations through european cooperation, global cooperation in the exchange of information and action, but also by putting our own countries in order first. it is hard to imagine what ideas may be implanted in other lands by the recent attacks on the world's first power. thirdly, we must resume the defence effort when it has become lax, as in my country in recent years. the threat is real and multifaceted. the rapid reaction force set up by the countries of europe is a good idea, provided that its democratic control, its variable geometry and the freedom of commitment of its members are better respected than today, as we have already had the opportunity to say. but, most of all, it is insufficient. while we are trying to eradicate terrorism, as you said, madam president, we must also make our territories more secure to protect our people. to make our territories more sacred, all appropriate measures must be taken. among them is the idea that president bush had some time ago put forward of a missile shield for the united states. europeans, on the other hand, had a rather negative view of the idea. today we must look at this question again. would it not be in europe's interest to start studies to have its own shield, either alone or in cooperation with the united states? well, we'll see about that. of course, it would not protect against the attacks of yesterday, but it would protect against other dangers that we have a duty to anticipate. of course, we also do not have the necessary technological means at the moment, but to acquire them would be a challenge worth taking up. it would be an unquestionable european project, madam president, which would undoubtedly demonstrate to the citizens the usefulness of cooperation which respects national sovereignty and is even intended to protect it. - ladies and gentlemen, i would like to draw your attention to a communication i wish to make to you on the security of our european parliament. as you know, the terrible terrorist attacks in the united states have given rise to quite legitimate concerns in our own european parliament. the sunday telegraph even reported very serious threats that had been made against us and that had been foiled. i would like to say that the european parliament has never been aware of these alleged threats. the day before yesterday, the prefect of lower rhine took the trouble to call me personally to tell me that he categorically denied the reality of these threats. moreover, as you know, this categorical denial by the french authorities was confirmed by an official communiqué. i would add that the british intelligence services also said they were not aware of this. i am thinking of writing a letter to the editor of the sunday telegraph to protest against the dissemination of such serious misinformation. - madam president, madam president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, my conviction and that of my group is that, since the day after the terrorist attacks in new york and washington, the need has never been more evident for the european union to show its identity and its usefulness in the conduct of world affairs. the next period, perhaps the very next few days, will no doubt provide an opportunity for him to demonstrate his willingness and ability to meet three challenges in particular that are thrown at him in these dramatic circumstances. the first of these challenges will be, in my view, to define ourselves as partners of the united states but not as obligated partners. wide consultation based on a working document presented in march 1999. the european parliament had the opportunity to express its views in june 2000 and the commission took full account of its recommendations made at that time. today's resolution, madam president, marks a turning point in the work on this subject. the belgian presidency, supported by the commission, intends to use the coming months to make decisive progress on asylum. this dossier, like that of immigration in general, should be one of the key elements of the mid-term review of the implementation of the tampere decisions and will therefore be drawn up by the european council at the end of this year. in this context, the council of ministers should hold a first policy debate on 27 and 28 september on the basis of questions whose answers will determine the level of ambition we all have in this area. because it must be remembered that the aim is actually to approximate national procedural provisions. i would add that this effort will extend to the other two proposals, the conditions for the reception of asylum seekers and the determination of the member state responsible for examining an asylum application. the three texts are linked. we must see them as a whole and i think that your parliament has always seen it that way. i would encourage the european parliament, if i may, to give its opinion on these two other initiatives as soon as possible. as regards procedures in particular, it is not to be hidden that there are very different positions on a number of important points. i think that this should not be surprising, because this initiative deals with many technically complex issues, which are still easy, but politically sensitive, which, in the present state of our policies, is a real problem. in addition, the first reading is not yet completed in the council's technical bodies. the delegations of the member states have therefore not yet had an opportunity to comment on some of the significant provisions. this is one of the reasons, madam president, why it is difficult to take a final decision on your amendments on appeal procedures now, because we still do not have the analysis and consideration by the council. finally, the discussions in the committee on civil liberties and the content of the excellent draft resolution tabled by mr watson confirm the feeling that there is at present, as you know and as we felt this morning, a clear divergence between the level of expectation of the european parliament and the ability of the council to reach an agreement which must be unanimous. the commission is a little bit between the two chairs, if you will. but it intends to take your opinion and any guidelines that may emerge from the ministerial discussion and then prepare an amended proposal, so as to facilitate a possible consensus. in this context, it seems essential to maintain the balance sought in the original proposal between, on the one hand, the concern to consolidate the rights of the asylum seeker, there is the necessary respect for international instruments, especially the geneva convention, and, on the other hand, the pursuit of an objective of efficiency and speed in the conduct of procedures and the achievement of a level of convergence that makes it possible to prevent the phenomenon of 'asylum shopping'. that is why the commission, and i repeat it and i would like to make it very clear to the rapporteur of parliament, has a lot of sympathy for the general approach which emerges from the draft resolution. but it will not be able to take up some of the suggestions which would tend to undermine the achievement of this dual purpose and which would, in the end, undermine the adoption of a text which we all want very much. for example, the distinction between the normal procedure and the accelerated procedure, which is in fact practised, at least virtually, in the member states, is a central point of this construction. acceptance of amendments to remove this would seriously jeopardise the chances of adoption of the proposal. on the other hand, the commission is certainly prepared to take into consideration the spirit or the letter, mr rapporteur, of certain amendments which could improve the protection of the applicant without calling into question the fundamental distinction i mentioned earlier. in the same vein, the commission shares the concerns expressed by various amendments aimed at further improving the quality of decisions, while strengthening the situation of applicants and aimed at increasing the efficiency of the national bodies dealing with procedures. however, the legislative approach is not necessarily the most appropriate to achieve such an objective, the achievement of which often depends on the improvement and convergence of administrative practices. these standards will more likely be met through the establishment of other cooperation instruments, notably the open method of cooperation, which the commission will propose to extend to the area of asylum in the coming weeks. in addition, certain amendments will find more room in your resolutions on the communitization of the dublin convention and the definition of the concept of refugee, to which i have just referred. other suggestions will have to be considered. the commission is therefore in favour of strengthening the link between this directive and international or european human rights instruments. in particular, compliance with the european charter of fundamental rights must be clearly affirmed and ensured. it is also useful to highlight the impact of the adoption of such a text in the context of enlargement and its relevance to an update of the international protection agenda. i am thinking in particular of the global consultation process initiated by the office of the high commissioner for refugees on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the geneva convention. finally, the commission can only agree with your concern to ensure a more systematic monitoring of the implementation of this directive. such a measure is also essential to accompany and accelerate the transition to the single procedure decided at tampere as the ultimate objective for the european union. madam president, in conclusion, the commission would like to confirm its full appreciation of the quality of the draft resolution submitted today. it shares the general spirit of the report. it must, however, clearly inform parliament of the difficulties which are being encountered. we will have to take these constraints into account in the preparation of our amended proposal and, beyond that, it is to be hoped that the european council in laeken will give the european union the necessary impetus to finally achieve the level of ambition set out in tampere in 1999.
- thank you, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place at 11 a.m. (the sitting was suspended at 10.55 a.m. pending the vote and resumed at 11 a.m.)
in writing. - we voted for both the oomen-ruijten report and the myller report because both propose to set emission ceilings for certain air pollutants. the projects, however limited, represent a small improvement on the present situation. however, it should be noted that, in order to respect capitalist interests and national selfishness, which is another way of expressing them, the proposed texts postpone application until 2010. when we try to protect private interests, even when we propose measures in the public interest, it is always the public who suffer.
in writing. - we voted in favour of the marinho report, which supports the initiative of france, sweden and belgium to have the council adopt a framework decision which would greatly facilitate judicial cooperation in europe: it would be to accept automatic mutual recognition of judicial decisions ordering the freezing of certain property or evidence in the context of investigations into specific offences. this method provides an interesting way of intensifying cooperation while respecting the criminal systems of the different member states. we would even be in favour of a little more clear-cut progress. the new mutual recognition procedure would apply to freezing decisions in the context of specific and narrowly defined offences: drug trafficking, fraud affecting the community's financial interests, laundering of the proceeds of crime, counterfeiting of the euro, corruption and trafficking in human beings. but other major offences are not on this list. but their suppression is urgent, as is the terrorism which we have just denounced once again in recent days. the amendment is aimed at introducing a more general definition of the offences covered: all those which can lead to a custodial sentence of a maximum of at least six months. if it were necessary to go beyond the freezing of property or evidence, further consideration should be given to a system of safeguarding rights which could be used effectively, but also quickly, by the member state to which the application was made.
in writing. - as was to be expected, the european parliament has just approved the commission's proposal for a directive on the granting of refugee status, which i denounced as lax in the previous debate. but parliament has also found a way to add amendments which further aggravate the shortcomings of this directive and strengthen our opposition. in particular, the original proposal provided that an appeal against a decision rejecting an asylum application would in principle have a suspensive effect (the applicant may remain in the country concerned pending the final decision), but that states could derogate from this in certain cases, in particular where the application is rejected as manifestly unfounded. the european parliament, however, has removed this possibility of derogation by means of an amendment no 85. it follows that even in the case of a manifestly unfounded application, the applicant may remain in our territory pending the final decision on his appeal. this intention was confirmed by the adoption of amendment no 5 which aims to create a 'right to remain in the territory of the country of asylum until a final decision is taken'. in addition, the adoption of amendment no 96 prevents member states from avoiding this disaster, since it prevents them from removing the possibility of appeal in the event that the asylum application has been rejected as manifestly unfounded. all these amendments are very serious, because they tend to keep asylum seekers who are notoriously abusive for months, waiting for a final answer which will necessarily be negative. but in the meantime, they'll obviously have gone underground. those who voted for these texts know perfectly well what they are doing. they want to encourage mass immigration, as is shown by the rejection of amendment no 126, which stated that an asylum application is manifestly unfounded if it is made only 'for economic reasons or for the sole purpose of escaping from a general situation of poverty or armed conflict'. the bad blow thus dealt to our countries can contribute to further destabilizing them.
in writing. - we voted in favour of all the amendments which seek to extend the protection and rights of refugees, and also for the report as amended. we are, however, against the passage which, by insisting on the 'prerogatives of control of immigration and entry into their territory' of the states, in fact restores to them the right to impose restrictive measures.
in writing. - after the attacks in new york and washington, all policies dealing with the movement of people can only be understood by giving the safety of citizens the highest priority. the implementation of asylum policy is not exempt from this imperative. in this respect, the recommendations of the watson report are now even more than in the past an example of what not to do, because they would seriously and dangerously weaken the level of security enjoyed by the citizens of our countries. the fact that we are constantly multiplying all kinds of guarantees, to the point of absurdity, as proposed in the watson report and in the amendments adopted by parliament, for the benefit of asylum seekers whose applications have been found to be manifestly unfounded, even though we know that three quarters of the applications are in this case, opens the way, under the guise of generosity, to the worst of errors. the 'benefit of the doubt' is a concept which is difficult to reconcile with the requirement of safety. at a time when the greatest rigour is at stake, our parliament is engaged in a lax attitude in favour of which illegal immigration can only be strengthened and the penetration of terrorist networks can only be expanded. why, moreover, do all the proposals in the watson report concern only asylum seekers and none the security of citizens of european countries? such a disparity, which is also reflected in the draft directive and the watson report, is unacceptable. it must be corrected urgently so that the legitimate right of genuine asylum seekers and the legitimate aspiration of the citizens of our countries to security and protection can be respected.
in writing. - we support the principles which guided the creation of the cohesion fund. like the rapporteur, we believe that the maastricht treaty 'has not provided for any support and cyclical adjustment mechanism in the context of economic and monetary union' and that the stability and growth pact has in practice led to a limitation of public investment'. we share the view that such funds are useful for planning the territory in an environmentally friendly way. but we also believe that the logic of these funds is contradictory to the neoliberal logic of european construction. it is very good to 'connect the island, landlocked and peripheral regions to the central regions', but it would be even better not to increase this spatial fragmentation by systematic privatisation of public services. from this point of view, the report does not go far enough in its criticism and postulates that the financial criteria of the euro and the stability pact can be made compatible with the requirements of genuine regional development. that's why we've been careful not to feed such a delusion.
in writing. - the report notes that the structural funds, which are intended in particular to promote regional development and gender equality, are still far from being fully implemented. its insistence on 'the implementation of a comprehensive policy for women' is commendable and points to a significant backlog. we also consider that 'there is a real risk that the programmes of economic and fiscal stability will tend to be achieved through a reduction in public investment, particularly in transport infrastructure and r & d in the least developed regions'. but the report does not go to the end of its analysis and does not stand out enough from the effects of such a trap. on employment, for example, it calls on states to 'subscribe to the employment policy process launched in amsterdam' and takes the 'national action plans for employment' as a reference. the latter, however, merely translate into operational terms the dogma of the necessary flexibility of labour markets and are in practice opposed to the fight against precariousness which the rapporteur is also calling for. we did not want to endorse such a position, so we abstained.
in writing. - we voted for this report without approving all the measures proposed. female genital mutilation is a barbaric practice which must be eradicated because of the violence it involves and its physical consequences, but also because of the motives behind it, which are designed to keep women in an inferior position. those who invoke traditions, customs, religion or any other nonsense in this connection are only covering up their resignation to barbarism with a veil of hypocrisy. those who dare to speak of the right to cultural difference only show their contempt for women in general and for the peoples whose women are victims of this barbarity.
in writing. - i thank our rapporteur, mrs elena valenciano martinez-orozco, and the whole committee for the quality of the work they have put before us and for the courageous social choices they are leading us to make today. it is precisely because female genital mutilation has dangerous health effects and leaves serious and irreversible consequences, causing serious complications in the event of sexual intercourse, pregnancy or childbirth which may lead to death, that i feel it is essential today to vote in favour of this report and, therefore, to condemn all forms of female genital mutilation, whatever their degree. the report deserves to be voted on all the more because it calls on the council, the commission and the member states to define all female genital mutilation as a crime and to punish any resident who has committed it, even if the crime was committed outside the eu's borders. this principle of the extraterritoriality of the offence must be firmly upheld. if there is any need to demonstrate the need to vote on such a report, i will give the following reason: the fact of being victims of such practices but also the fact of being born a woman in a place where there is a risk of genital mutilation must constitute a valid and necessary reason for granting the right of asylum or humanitarian protection: it is necessary that, within the framework of the asylum and immigration policy provided for in title iv of the treaty of amsterdam, the commission, the council and the member states take measures relating to the granting of a residence permit to victims of this practice and recognize the right of asylum to women, young girls and little girls who are at risk of being subjected to genital mutilation. it is in the name of equality, freedom and dignity to which every human being is entitled that it seems to me and that it must seem to us imperative to protect women and to vote without hesitation for this proposal. this is a matter of our political responsibility.
in writing. - the report puts on the same level what it calls "descending (from a superior to a subordinate) or ascending (from a subordinate to a superior) harassment, horizontal harassment between colleagues of the same level or mixed harassment". while denouncing harassment, the report therefore conceals that the reports at these different levels are not equivalent. the boss has a power over his employees that the employees don't have over their boss. those at the top of the hierarchy set up by the employer have the right to decide on the assignment, even the employment, of their subordinates. the new term "harassment at work" is based on the old exploitation reports. our abstention means that, while we agreed with the denunciation, even if it was extremely limited, we did not want to endorse his lies by omission.
in writing. - 8% of workers in the european union, or 12 million people, report having been victims of moral and sexual harassment at work. the effects are devastating to the physical and mental health of those who suffer it - mostly women. as the rapporteur points out, these practices are the result of the 'increase in fixed-term contracts and the worsening of employment insecurity'. the fight against harassment at work therefore requires that each worker be given back stable status, acceptable working conditions and a decent wage. but it is also necessary that each employee has more rights in the company: the right to organise, the right to defend oneself and the right to benefit from social services (occupational medicine for example). specific legislation on this issue also needs to be established in a uniform manner and applied in all eu member states. currently only france has legislated against harassment. it is also important to clarify the employer's responsibility in this area. this report is a step in the right direction and that is why we voted in favour of it.
in writing. - a few days after the terrible attacks in new york and washington, the president of eurojust, mrs michèle coninsx, who is also a belgian senior magistrate, has just made remarkable statements in a major paris daily newspaper dated 14 september. the question: 'is the islamist nebula strongly rooted in europe?' was answered by mrs coninsx: 'europe can provide a logistical retreat for these terrorists. the schengen area makes it relatively easy to cross borders". unfortunately, this is one of many recent findings in a variety of areas, such as drug trafficking, art theft, illegal immigration, organised crime, etc. we are all the more surprised to read the triumphant report on the schengen system which is being presented to us today. for example, the council's introduction states that 'thousands of travellers have crossed the open borders without hindrance, without any visible damage to security within the schengen area'. it is a question of whether the author of the council report is not suffering from hallucinations. the european parliament's report, on the other hand, not only repeats the same mistakes but also adds an injunction against the united kingdom and ireland, which are invited to participate fully in schengen, and thus to abolish their controls of persons at the borders. of course, this would be more practical for france, which would see the dramatic disappearance of the concentration of illegal immigrants waiting in the north of the country to be able to cross into britain. but that will not solve the fundamental question: how did these illegal immigrants get across europe to calais without being seen? is this not the overwhelming responsibility of the schengen system? in the wake of the terrorist attacks in the united states, we called for the european union to review all its policies to put the safety of its citizens first. we heard some fine speeches against terrorism yesterday in this house, but we can see that the usual drift is being repeated without any scruples.
in writing. - the schengen system, under the guise of the gradual abolition of internal border controls in the countries of the european union concerned, reinforces controls at the union's own borders and makes access more difficult. while it claims to facilitate the movement of people, schengen makes it more difficult for anyone not from the european union. our vote against this report expresses our opposition to the spirit and the letter of the schengen treaty. the enlargement of the european union by the integration of some eastern european countries makes the schengen treaty even more shocking, because the schengen borders will put additional barriers within the very national communities living in several countries at once. finally, even the slight advantages of the treaty, i.e. the end of internal border controls in the schengen area, are contingent, since they are at the discretion of the states which have the possibility of reintroducing such controls.
in writing. - the coelho report on the development of cooperation in the schengen area is not satisfactory for several reasons. today's proposal to strengthen the logic of schengen means to strengthen the exclusion of all those, asylum seekers and immigrants who for economic and/or political reasons aspire to live in the european union. this fortress europe is unjust and inhuman, as is daily shown by the treatment of immigrants in refugee centres, detention centres and other closed centres. the schengen europe is not democratic, as the rapporteur points out, emphasising 'the gaps that persist in terms of transparency and democratic control'. we need a different policy for the reception of migrants, in particular by regularizing all undocumented migrants and respecting fundamental rights. finally, what credibility can this area without frontiers still have, which allows the free movement of citizens, when the states arrogate to themselves the right to close their frontiers to peaceful demonstrators, as at the nice or genoa summits? the right to move freely in europe must be recognised as an inalienable right. for these reasons we cannot vote for this report.
in writing. - article 2 of the treaty on european union sets the objective of 'maintaining and developing the union as an area of freedom, security and justice, within which the free movement of persons is ensured'. in other words, the free movement of european citizens, to which the schengen agreements are often summed up a little too quickly, can only be understood, according to these same agreements, when freedom, security and justice are guaranteed to them. the current events, with the insane attacks that have just struck the united states, cruelly remind us of some realities: the theory of a western sanctuary, free from violence and in which it is no longer a question of granting rights without demanding duties and abstaining in principle from any coercive measures, has just been shattered. and while we do not believe that our obvious solidarity with the victims and the american people should necessarily lead us to participate blindly in any crusade decided on in washington, it is clear that the same type of threat is looming over our european capitals. i would just like to say, mr coelho, that in the light of the circumstances your report seems surreal to us, because from our point of view the reintroduction of border controls has never seemed more necessary than it is today. - the agenda calls for the commission's statement on the accident at the azf plant in toulouse and the review of the union's environmental protection policy. i shall now give the floor to the commissioner.
commission. – madam president, the accident in toulouse occurred shortly after 10 a.m. on 21 september at the establishment grande paroisse in toulouse. this fertiliser plant is owned by atofina the chemical branch of the total/fina/elf group. amongst other dangerous substances it held important quantities of liquefied ammonia and chlorine, combustibles, solid ammonium nitrate and fertilisers, as well as methanol. the effects of what seems to have been a mass explosion of ammonium nitrate were felt far outside the establishment's boundaries. according to the latest reports, 29 people were killed, 30 people are still in hospital in a serious condition and in total around 2400 people were injured. the accident also affected two other chemical plants in the vicinity. it rendered a large number of houses uninhabitable and affected the electricity distribution system. moreover, the psychological after-effects on the population that first believed it to be a terrorist attack are also important. this accident is perhaps the worst of its kind in europe since 1921, when an explosion at the basf company in germany claimed the lives of 561 citizens. last week a representative of the total/fina/elf group met with the responsible services of my directorate-general in order to provide detailed information on the accident. furthermore, the french ministry of the environment has provided information to the commission. however, the exact causes of the accident are still unknown and the three investigations under way by atofina, the ministry of the environment and the attorney-general might take a long time. azf was fully covered by the seveso ii directive, which aims at the prevention of major industrial accidents and the limitation of their consequences for man and the environment. its classical field of application are chemical plants and storage facilities. the directive obliges the operator of these facilities to put in place a major accident prevention policy, a safety management system and internal emergency plans. he/she has to prepare a safety report and send it to the public control authorities. these authorities have the task of inspecting the site at regular intervals and also of ensuring that its external emergency plans are put in place and tested periodically. furthermore, the public living in the vicinity of the plant must be informed of the risks arising from the facility and the behaviour in case of an accident. the directive came into force in 1999 and replaced the original seveso directive from 1982 that was adopted following major industrial accidents in the 1970s. this was the first piece of community legislation in the field of industrial risk management. it is no secret that member states were late with their transposition of the seveso ii directive into national law. no member state adopted transposition legislation in time or notified the commission hereof in time. therefore the commission started infringement proceedings against all 15 member states for non-communication or incomplete communication of transposition measures. in the meantime this resulted in the commission taking five member states to the european court of justice: belgium, austria, germany, ireland and portugal. for france, the commission decided on 18 july 2001 to apply to the court for incomplete transposition. however, i want to make it very clear today that the reasons for the court appeal being launched against france can in no way be related directly to the toulouse accident in terms of possible infringement of obligations under the seveso ii directive. at the moment, despite rumours in the press, the commission has no indication that there was either a deficiency on behalf of the operator managing the plant and complying with seveso ii or on behalf of the french control authorities responsible for inspecting the site. according to information received from the french minister for the environment, risk analysis, including possible accident scenarios, had been carried out by the site operator but these did not include a mass explosion of ammonia nitrate. the last updates were made in 2000 and 2001. a safety management system was in place and the site was inspected about twice a year. the last inspection took place in may 2001. internal and external emergency plans were in place. a land use planning policy established by the prefect imposed restrictions on all new construction activities in the vicinity of the plant. let me now come to the follow-up. just over a week after the accident it is still too early to draw any conclusions. the regulatory committee established under the seveso ii directive, chaired by the commission and composed of representatives of all member states is going to meet on 10-12 october to discuss, amongst other things, the accident and its follow-up. what is the repercussion of the toulouse accident on the foreseen amendment of the seveso ii directive? you might recall that after the baia mare accident, the cyanide spill in romania in january 2000, i created a task force that presented its final report in december last year. in parallel, after the disastrous fireworks explosion in may 2000 in enschede in the netherlands, my services organised two european expert seminars on pyrotechnic and explosive substances. the expertise and the resulting recommendations went into a draft proposal for an amendment to the seveso ii directive, aiming at broadening the scope and covering establishments that were previously not covered. the draft proposal has undergone a public consultation process involving all stakeholders and was foreseen for adoption by the commission in september. we should move forward with this amendment. this does not mean we should not take due account of the toulouse accident. there is indeed one very important aspect that made the consequences of the accidents in toulouse and enschede even worse, that is, the proximity of the establishments to inhabited areas. the new article 12 on land use planning in the seveso ii directive aims in the long term at the separation of hazardous industrial establishments and inhabited areas or other locations frequented by the public. although the inclusion of such a provision in community legislation for the very first time represents a major step forward, the commission and member states still have to gain experience with its implementation. moreover, this provision applies to the planning for new industrial sites, for new housing zones, and does not retroactively apply to existing situations, such as toulouse, where increasing density of population has led residential areas to continually spread closer to an industrial site that has existed since the 1920s. in order to assist member states with the implementation of this provision, a guidance document on land use planning was published in 1999 and plans for a european seminar on land use planning to be hosted by france were already under way before the accident in toulouse. in the near future my services will increase cooperation with the member states in order to develop an appropriate legislative and/or non-legislative follow-up to the accidents in the areas of land use planning, harmonisation of generic risk assessment methods and risk mapping.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0296/2001), on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a directive of the european parliament and of the council on the assessment and management of environmental noise (6660/1/2001 - c5-0245/2001 - 2000/0194 (cod)) (rapporteur: mr de roo).
- mr president, we all agree that noise pollution is disrupting the daily lives of our citizens. however, i am still a little surprised. we are simply asking europe to make up for the errors in the planning of the territory in each of our member states. why appeal to europe, when each member state can decide what to do in its own territory? we have already acted on the subject of tyres, aircraft engines; we can do that for pavement; our task is great. but why should we introduce standards which, in reality, are not only a matter for the member states but also have to take account of territorial disparities and, above all, encourage local authorities to adopt the necessary measures, in accordance with their local reality, rather than decide for them? that is the principle of subsidiarity, and i am particularly fond of it in this area. i believe that it is up to local elected representatives to decide what they should do in each commune, in each agglomeration, in each department, in each region. it's up to the local elected officials to decide. i'm one of them. i know very well what it is to establish a strategic noise map. we're hearing about airports. there are international airports, domestic airports; there are extreme disparities at airports. the impact of noise is therefore different. so why impose standards that won't apply to all of them? it should be borne in mind that airports are essential to the territories that have them. air transport infrastructure is a key factor for industries; the choice of location is often determined by the means of communication and the airports. is it worth pointing out that a derogation must absolutely be maintained for military airports? i agree with mr florenz on this point. the importance of this provision is well illustrated by current circumstances. i would like to end by recalling that the title of this directive is 'noise assessment and management'. management is therefore preceded by an evaluation. how can we claim to set limits in the absence of a precise, cross-sectional study based on commonly agreed evaluation criteria? this requires precise noise maps and requests for each member state to put in place effective action plans. i also believe that it is essential to involve our citizens in these initiatives, but this can only be done in agreement with each territory and with each local authority.

- mr president, the enshrinement of community competence in immigration and asylum matters by the treaty of amsterdam has raised many hopes, and one of those hopes was to see an immigration and asylum issues in all their complexity. thus, instead of zero immigration policies, which are inadequate and carry illegal immigration inherent in the system, they propose a flexible approach, flow management - the pirker report has the merit of being frank: it presents immigration as a simple commodity problem linked to the needs of the capitalist system. the report welcomes the fact that immigration is considered from an economic perspective, depending on the needs and possibilities of the member states. article 23 is very clear. each member state is free to define the skill profile and the number of workers required on the basis of the needs of its labour market. in other words, a quota policy is proposed as a community policy on immigration. with these positions, europe is far from recognizing the right to immigration. these are residence permits limited to the requirements of employers and the fantasies of demographers. even family reunification is subject to separate regulations for each group of immigrants, which are the antithesis of freedom of movement and of establishment and the right to live together as a family. immigrants are massively over-exploited and are victims of liberal deregulation. i conclude that only the general legalisation of undocumented migrants, together with the granting of citizenship rights, would be effective in combating the modern slavery which we are proposed to support.
mr president, the increase in the number of asylum seekers in recent years is causing serious problems for the member states, which are having serious difficulties in coping with the situation. as deputy mayor of the city of lyon, i see this problem on a daily basis. in my city, the number of conventional asylum seekers has doubled in just under a year. the two commission communications we are discussing today are certainly an important step forward. but we must go further and put an end to the present situation whereby some member states accept refugees from certain countries while others do not. we must ensure that the countries which are taking in refugees actually have the means to do so. however, these funds have recently been reduced. we can no longer give asylum seekers a decent welcome. in our cities, we have families who live under canvas. this is absolutely unacceptable: winter is coming and we are heading for disaster. but i would go further and call on the governments of the member states and the council to take the courageous decisions that are needed. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the process of european integration, and it is not only the european parliament that has been involved in the process of european integration, but also the european parliament itself.
in writing. - the two reports on the liquidation of the ecsc treaty deplore the fact that the council asks parliament to give it a discharge for activities which it has no means of controlling. parliament can vote as it wishes, but the council decides. it is certainly a way of recognising that parliament is only used to give a democratic guarantee to decisions which are not democratic. these two reports also point out that the so-called social aspect of the ecsc is being abandoned, precisely at the time when the accession of countries to which the european union intends to impose restructuring of their coal and steel sectors is being considered, in order to make it 'profitable', that is to say profitable for possible western investors. despite this 'social aspect' of the ecsc treaty, the restructuring of coal and steel in western europe has meant the dismissal of hundreds of thousands of workers, a tragedy for many. some regions, such as lorraine, have taken years to recover from closures and job losses. we can only imagine what it will be like for workers in poland, the czech republic and hungary, who will not even be offered benefits or early retirement. rather than turning the balance of the ecsc's liquidation into a research fund, which will benefit employers in one form or another, the sums thus freed up should be devoted entirely to the continued payment of wages to workers who are about to be thrown out on the streets as part of future restructuring. we therefore voted against both reports.
commission. – mr president, i wish to thank mr titley for another excellent and characteristically intelligent report, which we have read with very great interest. as his report and his speech have made clear, the issue of arms exports is tremendously complex and close collaboration is required by everyone in order to address its many different angles. there were a number of good speeches in the debate, some of which referred to the relevance of the appalling events of 11 september and their aftermath. i should like to respond to what mr paisley had to say. as he is not in his place, maybe my remarks will be borne to him on angels' wings. i agree with the definitional point he made. it is an enormously important point for us to make. some of us from spain or the united kingdom have personal experience of this; some of us have friends who have been murdered by terrorists. there is no such thing as a good terrorist. there is no distinction between good and bad terrorism. what is a terrorist? a terrorist is a man or woman or, alas, a deluded child who sets out in the morning to murder innocent men, women and children to make a political point – the propaganda of the deed. that is not justified. it is never justified. there are never extenuating circumstances, any more than there are ever extenuating circumstances from extrajudicial killings by a state. so i hope that when we start talking about definitions we will remember what terrorism really is. we will have views about the political roots of terrorism. we will have strong views about the importance of trying to find political solutions to some problems. however, i hope we will not be morally confused about what constitutes a terrorist act. during the debate on last year's report, i stated that the ultimate responsibility for arms exports belongs to national governments. however, it is also clear that some aspects of the arms trade lie within the remit of the common foreign and security policy, with which the commission is fully associated. the commission is making every effort to move forward with the implementation of those recommendations which lie within community competence and we stand ready to collaborate with member states where joint responsibilities are involved, for example when one is talking about dual-use goods. as parliament is already aware, the associated countries of central and eastern europe, cyprus, turkey, malta, and our eea/efta partners have issued declarations through which they align themselves with the criteria and the principles contained in the european union's code of conduct on arms exports. the union has continued to assist the candidates in their efforts to bring their legislation and administration fully into line with the provisions of the code. furthermore, the european union continues to urge the world's main arms exporters to subscribe to the principles and criteria developed in our code. we would react most favourably to the idea of drafting an international code of conduct on arms transactions, on the condition that it is based on the same principles as the european union code. the commission strongly supports the honourable member's call for the establishment of common rules for european union control of the legal trade in small arms and light weapons, as well as effective european union controls to combat and eradicate trafficking in these arms. in this respect we welcome the agreement reached at the july 2001 un conference on the illicit trade in small arms and light weapons. although the final text falls well short of the union's initial expectations, it marks an important step forward. it represents a delicate and hard-fought compromise, which would not have been achievable only a couple of years ago. if all parties involved were to adopt a more positive attitude, the agreement would become a more effective tool for addressing the concerns of all participants in the future. for the first time the international community has set out some principles for national and international measures which might curb the illegal trade in small arms. they aim to establish reliable controls on the production, export and transit of weapons; to apply reliable markings to them in order to trace their origin more successfully; to criminalise their unlicensed production and trade; to regulate the activities of brokers; and to destroy surplus stockpiles and all confiscated weapons. a new conference will be held no later than 2006 – i suspect that recent events may bring that date forward – and in the intervening period, biennial meetings will consider the progress made on turning the objectives of the conclusions into tangible reality. we will work hard with the member states to ensure an active and ambitious follow-up. the european union's commitment to concrete action in the field of small arms is illustrated by a number of projects currently under way or under consideration in different parts of the world. in cambodia the european union gives technical, administrative and financial support to the government and selected ngos for actions aimed at promoting the collection, control and destruction of weapons. we also support operation rachel, a joint south africa-mozambique project, to collect and destroy arms left over since the civil war. we provide equipment to the georgian and ossetian police forces as part of a programme which consists of the voluntary handover and subsequent destruction of small arms in the region. we also support the un regional centre for peace, disarmament and development in lima, which works to promote the control of small arms in latin america and the caribbean. we are also considering further projects in the balkans, africa and south pacific. during the past few months commission services have begun drafting ec legislation on a number of non-military items such as instruments of torture, to which the provisions of the code should, in our view, apply. work is now near completion, and the commission intends to submit a proposal to the council soon. this marks a first step in tackling the issue. compilation of a more extended list, which might include items that also have civilian uses – instruments of internal repression such as riot-control equipment, for example – would require the commitment of significant additional resources. if we are going to take on such a task – which involves establishing the eventual end use of the items and, perhaps, the identity of the end user – then we shall need more resources. however we will, of course, pay careful attention to what parliament has to say on that issue. progress in that field is conditional on the willingness of member states and parliament to make additional resources available for these purposes. so i repeat our gratitude to the honourable member, mr titley, for an important report. i hope that year by year we can continue to respond constructively to what he has to say. anybody who looks at the violence around the world, the violence often associated with the breakdown of states, from somalia to sudan, to sierra leone, to afghanistan; anybody who looks at the situation created by the breakdown of states knows how much the trade and small arms is responsible for continuing the violence and making the violence far more lethal. so this report is an important one, and i hope we can respond to it over the coming months and years with appropriately constructive behaviour.

commission. – madam president, the situation was already bad and now it is worse. i totally agree with what has been said this afternoon on the situation of the people in afghanistan. we put afghanistan on the list of so-called forgotten crises when we fixed echo's programme and priorities for 2001. we had a spending level of some eur 23 million, which would have covered the continuation until new year of the very last activity that we were funding there. in fact we had 29 european ngos delivering humanitarian aid inside afghanistan. they were all there on 11 september. on 11 september i was on my way to a mission to afghanistan and to pakistan. i was supposed to meet dr masood, the taliban leadership and to go around the whole country seeing the work of these ngos that we are funding. i had to cancel the trip. the morning after, we took the train back from london to brussels but our luggage was already in the aeroplane for islamabad. now, as i said, the situation is worse. winter is approaching. winter is such a dominating feature of reality there that even in normal years military fighting more or less stops simply because getting around is so difficult. so humanitarian aid now faces a really scary challenge. the international staff of the different aid agencies and ngos have all been withdrawn from the country. however, it is very encouraging to see that the local staff is continuing to distribute food – if the food has not been taken over by the taliban – and is still running health clinics and providing education where it is possible. obtaining real, true information is extremely difficult, but we can see that they are trying to keep these activities going even in this situation. of course the threat of an outside attack has resulted in large movements of population. this also has the effect that we cannot rely on people accessing the different storage centres for food as they used to, because they have fled into the countryside in their millions and lost the access to food they had in the cities. so the internal situation is extremely bad and the people who make it to the border look even weaker than they did before. some six million afghanis are considered to be totally dependent on food supplies from the outside. if no planting is possible before the winter sets in – and this is most probable – we are in for a very serious threat within less than half a year, even if things work out well in terms of stability. the very logistics of what is needed down the line, even on the basis of the best case scenario, pose a formidable challenge. we have supported the different un organisations very actively, and participated at the meeting of the afghan support group in berlin on 27 september. the un has launched a un-donor alert in support of emergency assistance. the alert calls for some usd 580 million from now until march next year to ensure that delivery of humanitarian assistance and the protection of what is estimated to be around 7.5 million afghans. usd 120 million is required immediately. funding of this appeal would, in fact, seem to be less of a problem than the overall question of accessibility to internally displaced people and refugees. there are conflicting views in the discussion as to whether emphasis should be placed on keeping the additional migratory flows within afghanistan or on encouraging pakistan and iran to open their borders, as the unhcr intends to do. my personal analysis of this is that we are only able to influence the choice of these people to a very small degree. things may happen and we will have to be very flexible in order to be able to do what we need to do as things develop. we have never had to draw up a contingency plan with so few given elements and so many unknowns. the need to keep food aid going was central to the discussion at this afghan group meeting. everybody agreed on the urgency, but concurred that the prospects for actually delivering such aid were quite poor. most participants argued that food-aid distribution without the presence of expatriates could expose afghan partners to undue risk. my earlier reference to afghan local staff continuing to do what they did before the expatriates had to leave relates to deliveries of existing food and other stocks. it is a far more difficult and demanding task to manage the convoys of new supplies coming in, given the internal situation that exists today. things are different in the north-eastern part controlled by the northern alliance and in the rest of the country. but from the humanitarian point of view it is quite evident that our activities must be targeted at the whole country. that is how it must be. we are using three financial tools to fund the aid to the afghan population. first – and this is to set the record straight – over the past ten years we have provided humanitarian aid of more than eur 400 million to internally displaced persons in afghanistan and refugees in neighbouring countries: echo funds, drought mitigation and response activities like food aid, agricultural rehabilitation, water and sanitation rehabilitation, assistance to internally displaced persons and to refugees in pakistan, as well as prevention of displacements and support for returnees. so this is more than just food aid. echo and the organisations working with our money have managed to build up a portfolio of meaningful activities that they have been able to continue. i add that one unfortunate international case is not representative of the situation of the 29 organisations that the commission is funding. it is a difficult situation but it is important to note that the organisations we are funding cannot be accused of the same kind of activity. they were able to work with expatriates until 11 september and to build up a portfolio of activity, which i was very much looking forward to coming to see. i pay tribute also to my predecessor in this job for laying the seeds of this kind of good cooperation with the european humanitarian ngos. we have, this year, committed eur 23 million to echo, channelled through ngos and different un agencies. as i said, this would have covered a continuation of this level of activity until the end of the year. then this terrible act of terrorism took place. we reacted immediately with an additional eur 4 million. this is committed for action through the world food programme, unhcr, and the international red cross. now our response has to go beyond this. we will approach the budgetary authority in order to get the green light for accessing and using funds from the emergency budget reserve, as in earlier years when echo's normal budget did not cover the needs that arose because of terrible events. we announced eur 25 million a week ago in the commission. it will form part of this operation and be directed at the immediate situation of the refugees. we will be asking for more money. but this is covered by the normal procedure for accessing additional money. the second line of support is ec aid to uprooted people. here we fund activities creating environments conducive to a sustainable resettlement of returnees and activities aimed at persuading people to remain in their villages. this budget line will commit funds from october for a budget of eur 19 million in afghanistan, eur 3 million in pakistan and eur 2 million in iran. funds are channelled through afghan ngos and un agencies. the third line is ec food aid and food security. since the beginning of this year this line has committed 30 000 tonnes of food aid to the world food programme and 7 000 tonnes to ngos. a further eur 7 million is now being requested by the commission for the wfp afghan programme. let me address some of the questions that have been asked. mrs nicholson mentioned that we should do more through unhcr and who to broaden the broad basis and improve the organisation of this assistance. in relation also to mr van den berg's remarks, from a commercial management point of view, if you will, the operation in afghanistan is a good case of cooperation between the un
