counsel. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to have the opportunity today to take stock of the results achieved at the third world conference against racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance, which was held in durban from 31 august to 8 september. the durban conference can be described as a success in several respects, despite the difficult political context in which the negotiations took place and despite the fact that the conference was announced in advance as a failure. firstly, in terms of concrete results: this is the first un conference devoted to the fight against racism, which culminates in the adoption, by consensus, of a political declaration and a programme of action. the durban conference was above all an opportunity to strengthen the essential fight against the racist tendencies, the tendencies towards discrimination and intolerance which are the daily realities of millions of human beings, who are too often the silent victims of violations of their dignity.
the commission. mr president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, the durban conference was a great step forward in the effort to achieve global consensus, global political agreement on issues of - mr president, madam commissioner, mr minister, many people have indeed asked themselves whether it is worthwhile convening the durban conference. but the international community must exist and must come together to discuss, even if sometimes conflicting interests may arise, and i do not think that leaving is necessarily a solution. the durban conference has at least had the merit of bringing the international community together on a subject which is undeniably a matter of common concern to all countries, since this scourge is global and no country is immune from any form of racism or discrimination. so it was an opportunity to take stock, to make a diagnosis, and what would that diagnosis be if there was no therapy? what could we expect from the durban conference? i do not yet know, mr michel, whether it will be a success in the long term. what we do know is that it has failed, that is to say, that there has been no final declaration, no confirmation of a world will to fight racism and no adequate instruments to do so. the aim of durban is to identify a whole series of global instruments, to draw up a road map, to develop new strategies to combat racism and action programmes - which you have listed, mr minister - from which the states can draw in order to be able, in accordance with the subsidiarity which is the key in this matter, to combat racism and discrimination. what lessons can we learn from this? i think we have avoided three pitfalls. the first, which you have already mentioned, is of course the middle east. any reasonable person knows that durban would not have solved the middle east problem. there have been attempts to make this the main topic. i think that this pitfall has been avoided, fortunately. the second pitfall is that of compensation. some would have liked compensation to be the main topic of debate. there was a real perversity, if not a perversion, because there was a risk that development aid would be reduced to a form of compensation. as mr michel has rightly pointed out, we are all aware of the historical weight of certain people in this area. we must work for solidarity between men and not for perpetual guilt which, in financial terms, would eventually cease, because all compensation paid in cash naturally ends up being paid out at some point. finally, the third pitfall is the list of victims. some of them wanted to make a list. this applies to us, to the roma and the sinti, and to the dalits. the risk of listing the victims is that, naturally, a hierarchy of victims is then established and some may be considered more victims than others, which would seem to me to be completely unproductive in terms of racism and discrimination. so, indeed, the declaration is acceptable and i would like here, quite officially, to thank mr michel for the essential role he has played as a mediator, intercessor, explainer - - doc. a5-0288/2001 by mrs langenhagen, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament on galileo (com (2000) 750 - c5-0110/2001 - 2001/2059 (cos)).
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, we are called upon to give our opinion on the implementation of the galileo programme, in the light of the decisions taken by the european council in stockholm on 23 march 2001. the council stressed the need to launch this satellite navigation programme without delay. our committee recognizes the value of such a programme, the essential feature of which is that it is european and of civilian origin, and therefore independent of the systems of military origin - the american gps and the russian glonass - and with a reliability and precision superior to the two existing systems. however, we propose the following to be implemented during the validation phases from 2001 to 2005, deployment from 2006 to 2007, and operational from 2008, essentially under the aegis of the european space agency and the commission. first, there is a need for precise monitoring of the financing, originally estimated at around eur 3 billion, in conjunction with the selection of partners, particularly industrial partners, and their participation, as well as a thorough analysis of the cost-benefit ratio and the economic and employment impact. we demand the utmost transparency and constant information from parliament on this matter. secondly, we insist that the use of the structures set up during the programme and its implementation must be limited to the civil sphere, and we recall that it is essential to develop, in this case, the use of space for purposes of general interest and public service. thirdly, the implementation of the galileo programme must not infringe the right to privacy or the protection of privacy. it must not, under any circumstances, be used for the purpose of surveillance of citizens. in particular, it must be developed with a view to protecting the environment and ensuring its safety, protecting the lives of citizens and natural resources, and detecting at an early stage, or even preventing, natural or man-made disasters. it must also contribute to the progress of european research in the definition of the sixth framework programme. finally, we propose - and this is an important point - the creation of an ethics committee with an advisory role, whose task is to ensure that the above requirements are met and which assists the commission and the european space agency in their decision-making tasks. i would stress - and i ask the commissioner to give us her view - that it is civil structures which will put the system in place. of course, we cannot say: "we will not vote for galileo if the military ever uses it", because when we set up transport, communications systems, etc., anyone can use them. what is important is that europe is independent and not dependent on the ussr or the usa. these various provisions seem to us to be realistic conditions which must accompany and justify the setting up of galileo, and we would also like to hear mrs de palacio's views on the creation of the ethics committee.

i know that we have it in this house by a majority, but also that some of the honourable members have shown considerable reticence, if not opposition. as the motion for a resolution clearly states, international cooperation is an essential element of the galileo programme. the aim is to ensure the interoperability of galileo with existing satellite navigation systems such as the us gps, or, in preparation, the russian glonass. in that sense - some of the honourable members have spoken about whether it is necessary or not - i would say that the idea is that they are compatible and mutually reinforcing. i would like to say, ladies and gentlemen, that, after what happened last month, the need for a second system to reinforce the existing system and to provide greater security and to be, at a given moment, not just a complement but an alternative to possible undesirable situations - when we are faced with an exponential increase in applications affecting all areas of our lives related to galileo - seems to me absolutely essential, not only for europe but for the whole world, including the users of the united states themselves. it is also important to have the support of third countries in order to have the necessary frequencies available, particularly in the context of the world radiocommunications conferences - the next one is in 2003. as you know, the allocation of frequencies is pending consolidation precisely in 2003. participation in the development of the galileo programme should be facilitated where appropriate. as far as the data transmitted by galileo is concerned, it is clear that the international and community instruments designed to protect it will apply. as mrs langenhagen's report emphasizes, we believe - and this is one of the particularities of the gps system - that galileo should provide a public signal, that is to say, a robust, precise signal which cannot be interrupted by military reasons, as in the other case, and sensitive applications, whether public - customs, judicial investigations or other - or private - banking transmissions. in closing, let me summarize the next stages of the program. at the end of the year, after receiving parliament's opinion, the council will have to adopt the statutes of the galileo joint undertaking and decide on the continuation of the programme to be developed by the joint undertaking in close cooperation with the european space agency. as some of the honourable members have said, the galileo project must be given the green light once and for all. the development phase, which is to run from 2002 to the end of 2005, should allow the first satellites to be launched to test the system in real life and the receiver sector to set up the receivers. as you can see, there's still a lot to do. your support is absolutely necessary and, in any case, we will keep this house fully informed of all the steps we are taking on this project.

amendment and that we can therefore, without having to go through a conciliation procedure, approve this report on the energy star programme today.

- the next item is the report (a5-0234/2001) by mr rübig, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament on innovation in the knowledgebased economy (com (2000) 567 - c5-0740/2000 - 2000/2336 (cos)).
commission. – i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr rübig, for an excellent report and the house for a debate displaying quality and commitment. it is widely recognised that policies that foster innovation are an underlying determinant of economic growth. i am particularly happy to present to you today the very latest findings of the eu’s innovation policy performance, namely the 2001 innovation scoreboard, which was compiled as a follow-up to the report last year. the 2001 european innovation scoreboard gives us a starting point for the union’s strategy to enhance its overall competitiveness, by providing a common measure of a country's performance using 17 indicators. i would also like to say that i share the rapporteur’s opinion in underlining the importance of education and training, something that has been noted by other speakers. one indicator called for in the report was added to the scoreboard to cover lifelong learning. eu performance in terms of growth and the standard of living relative to the us and japan highlights the key challenges that the eu faces in enhancing its competitiveness. in the past twenty-five years, and apart from temporary cyclical fluctuations, the eu has not kept pace with the us in improving its standard of living. the gap is now wider than it was a quarter of a century ago. at the aggregate level, the gap in living standards can be attributed to two factors: two-thirds to the employment rate, which is lower, and one-third to productivity. i will focus on the productivity gap. until the mid-1990s, the productivity gap between the eu and the us narrowed steadily. in the second half of the 1990s, however, the rapid acceleration of productivity growth in the us again began to widen the gap. until the early 1990s, capital-intensive industries spearheaded productivity growth. this changed in the mid-1990s, when research and innovation became the key determinants. the industries that achieved the greatest productivity gains during the late 1990s were predominantly research-intensive. the overall strategy for boosting competitiveness requires us to better combine union and member state efforts to develop more effective policies to foster and support innovation. national innovation policies should be reinforced, developed, and take a more consistent approach across the eu. this is why we need a regular benchmarking exercise to measure and compare the performance of eu countries, identify key areas of weakness and strength, and enable ourselves to design and fine-tune innovation policies accordingly. taking the eu as a whole, we still lag behind the us and japan on most indicators. we trail significantly in terms of private-sector investment in research and development. rapid increases in business research and development in japan and the us since 1994 have widened the gap with europe alarmingly. us expenditure in this area is now 74% higher than in europe. europe’s high-tech patenting activity is also too weak: us businesses apply for more high-technology patents in europe than do european businesses. japanese patenting in europe is almost as strong as us patenting. this patenting imbalance is an area that requires urgent attention. at individual member state level, the picture is different. i must say that, as regards many indicators, the best-performing eu countries are also world leaders, sometimes doing substantially better than the us and japan. i will give you some examples: the uk, ireland and france, for example, are world-leading suppliers of science and engineering graduates; the netherlands, sweden and denmark are ahead in home internet access; finland, the netherlands and sweden lead in public research and development; and sweden is well ahead in business research and development expenditure. however, differences in innovation performance between member states are still significant. countries such as denmark and finland, whose performance was already strong, continue to lead the field when measured by the innovation index, that is to say in terms of trends, not scoreboards alone. greece and spain are rapidly catching up with the eu average, while starting from a relatively low base. but change is important and positive. the four largest eu economies (france, germany, the uk and italy) are improving, but at rates below the eu average. a number of lessons can be drawn from these results. the union should: first, invest in education and training, as has been said here a few times; second, improve its performance in the high-tech sectors and promote entrepreneurship; third, help to step up business research and development by encouraging member states to introduce or increase the necessary incentives; and finally, promote the use of technologies in all sectors of the economy, including public administrations. i am pleased to see that several of these aspects are well covered by mr rübig’s report. i believe this report will help to generate a consensus on the way forward. this is necessary, as shown by the findings of the innovation scoreboard. the report expresses europe’s wish to reduce the union’s innovation deficit and achieve the goal set at lisbon and, hence, does a great deal to help improve the eu’s overall competitiveness. i hope that there will be an opportunity to come back to these issues in the commission’s 2001 competitiveness report, which will be presented in a few weeks' time.
- thank you, chief. the debate is closed. the vote will take place at 12 noon on wednesday.
- the next item is the report (a5-0311/2001) by mr mayer, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the problems of exhaustion of trademark rights (sec{1999) 2033 - c5-0354/2000 - 2000/2187{cos)).
- madam president, i would first of all like to pay tribute to the rapporteur who, in the face of extremely strong positions, was able to listen and propose an alternative acceptable to all in the form of a proposal for further reflection. this position is all the more important and necessary as this report addresses the crucial problems of globalisation and european integration. beyond the direct interests of consumers and producers, the economic role of the european union in world trade is at stake. some may be in favour of total trade liberalisation, others, myself included, believe that the community's exhaustion regime responds to the need to develop the integration of the single market, the preferred response to strengthen europe in the face of global competition. apart from this concept of integration, the challenge of this report is to support innovation, and god knows that in the previous report we talked about supporting innovation and creativity in the community. the trade mark is the first and most effective instrument for the protection of intellectual property. it is the guarantee of the authenticity and quality of a product for the consumer. it ensures the pre-sale, conditions the investments and, beyond that, the creation. a change of regime would lead to a decline in investment in research and development of european products, and the impact on jobs could be dramatic. the current system also provides better protection against counterfeiting, since the channels used by parallel importers are often those through which pirated products pass. in the light of the studies currently available, and i say 'currently', there is no relevant evidence to justify a change of regime which could be detrimental to innovation. i hope that the additional reflection proposed by our rapporteur will confirm this view.
commission. – madam president, this is an important subject and has been discussed at various places and at various times. it is important that the exhaustion regime for trade marks which the community applies provides for a proper balance between the interest of consumer prices and protection of trade mark rights. it has been stated by those who advocate a change to the community-wide exhaustion regime, that a unilateral change to international exhaustion of trade mark rights would have a significant impact on consumer prices. the commission is not convinced that this would be the case. according to the nera study carried out by a consultancy firm based in london which was submitted to the commission in february 1999, prices under international exhaustion would probably not be very different from those that are currently in force. mr berenguer fuster and the rapporteur have referred to alleged price increases in germany of films, perfume and cameras. as soon as this became known, the sectors concerned supplied statistics to the commission to show that prices have not increased as was claimed, but have remained the same or in some cases even decreased. the purported evidence concerning germany is not what it seems to be and, in fact, supports the case that the commission has put forward and not the case in favour of international exhaustion. there has also been a price study carried out by the swedish and the uk governments. it is very interesting to note, and significant for this debate, that of the items where comparisons between the european union and the united states were possible, the cheapest market was often within the european union. for some products, the united states was even the most expensive market. moreover, there were considerable price differences between member states. in general, prices in germany and france were lower than in the uk and in sweden. those differences exist within the european union where there is regional exhaustion for trade mark rights and not international exhaustion. in other words, for all member states of the european union the same exhaustion regime applies yet there is a 40% price difference in electronic goods between sweden and germany. this certainly goes to show that the internal market is not performing as it should be, but it also shows that the differences in prices have nothing to do with whether the exhaustion regime is regional or international. the price differences within the european union usually exceed the price differences between eu member states and the united states. in other words, the arguments in favour of the thesis that international exhaustion would lead to a decrease in prices is very tenuous. in fact the commission does not believe that evidence at all. furthermore, i should like to add that the price element is only one aspect of the exhaustion issue. it is also very important to consider the legitimate interest of trade mark holders in their home markets. for many companies the trade mark is their most valuable asset and that is not something we should take lightly. trade marks are also of value to consumers because they represent a sign of quality. the commission decided in may 2000 that there is no reason, at least for the time being, to propose any change to the current regime. the commission considers that there is now a proper balance between the interests at stake and that the current community-wide exhaustion regime is an appropriate way to protect the legitimate rights of trade mark holders. the commission has taken due note, obviously, of mr mayer's report and of the long and difficult discussions in the committee on legal affairs and the internal market. many arguments have been put forward for and against a change of regime. the commission recognised all those arguments from previous discussions in other fora. all the aspects mentioned have been thoroughly studied and analysed by the commission services and in my view no new elements have been put forward which would require further examination or which would give the commission reason to reconsider its decision. having said this, the commission intends to monitor the question of exhaustion closely and will certainly take any action necessary should new and important reasons emerge to consider abandoning the current exhaustion regime. in the meantime, the commission is, of course, willing to share with parliament our experiences concerning cases of possible abuse of trade mark rights but in order to make the report more useful and balanced the commission intends to take all relevant elements into consideration.
- thank you, chief. the debate is closed. the vote will take place at 12 noon on wednesday. (the sitting was closed at 11.20 p.m.) the next item is the report (doc.

in writing. - we know how much noise pollution can affect the daily life and health of our citizens. but europe must not be the fire extinguisher and compensate for the errors in land use planning. i do not question the overall objective, but to be effective we must act pragmatically, as has been done in the field of air quality. europe does not have to set up unilateral standards and impose them on everyone across the whole of the territory, without taking into account local specificities. europe is already doing something about tyres, aircraft engines, pavement... it is important that the provisions take account of these territorial disparities. the role of europe is to do more to empower the member states, to encourage local authorities to take the necessary measures in line with their local realities, rather than deciding for them. in this case, i am in favour of the principle of subsidiarity. the commission has already proposed a number of measures to reduce noise levels at airports. conditions vary greatly from one airport to another. each airport is unique (runway configuration, traffic distribution, etc.). the impact of aircraft noise differs from one airport to another and action to reduce noise pollution would be more relevant if undertaken at national, regional and local levels. moreover, it seems implausible that there is no distinction between international and regional airports! let us not forget that airports are also important for the territories. air transport infrastructure is a key factor for industries in their choice of geographical location and hence for employment. i would also remind you that the title of the directive is 'noise assessment and management'. but before management, there is evaluation. how can we claim to set limits without having carried out a precise, cross-cutting study beforehand, and yet agree on common evaluation criteria? the first step is therefore to set up a system which will make it possible to assess noise levels in the various member states and to have precise noise maps for each region. only once this information is known will it be necessary to encourage the member states to draw up an effective action plan, in consultation with all local authorities and elected officials.

in writing. - the geneva convention defines refugee status as any person who, "owing to a well-founded fear of persecution on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, is outside the country of which he is a national and who is unable or unwilling, because of that fear, to claim the protection of that country". (first article) it is time for the member states of the european union to implement the convention in full. france hypocritically refuses to grant algerian refugees this status. similarly, europe refused, in the midst of the kosovo war, to grant refugee status to serb deserters or to persecuted kosovars. how many bosniaks are still rotting in refugee camps in turkey because the union refused to take them in? how many afghan refugees are crammed into sangatte hoping to get to england because they know they have no chance in the schengen area? however, despite some reluctance, because the text proposes minimum standards for the reception of asylum seekers: a minimum level of assistance, such as the provision of full legal assistance to each applicant, at the expense of public money, or the justification by the authority or the court of the rejection of a refugee application, as well as specific assistance to vulnerable people, we will vote in favour.

in writing. - i am pleased to be able to speak on the galileo project at a time when the events of 11 september remind us of our capacity to manage crises. the galileo project aims to deploy a set of satellites in orbit, some 20,000 km above the earth. all these satellites would be linked to a network of ground control stations. this would provide worldwide coverage, allowing for significant improvements in air, sea and road traffic management and support for search and rescue operations. this technology is already available in the usa (gps system) and russia (glonass system). it is currently funded and controlled by the military authorities of both countries. the quality and continuity of its civilian use depend on the latter, which can stop or degrade the signal at any time. in europe, however, the galileo programme will be managed and controlled by civilians. its development is proposed in four stages: definition in 2000, development and validation until 2005, deployment until 2007 and operation beyond. the galileo system should therefore ideally be operational from 2008, thus responding to the wishes expressed at the stockholm european council and to the urgent needs of the european union in this field. this is what the report of the committee on transport shows. as far as the financing is concerned, i think it is important to clarify the terms of this before making a final decision. i also regret that some member states are reluctant to support this project. i therefore call on the commission to take the necessary steps to overcome these reservations. the commission will then be asked to draw up a general financing structure by 15 november 2001 if the 2008 deadline is to be reasonably met. the european parliament will have to be consulted on the draft prepared by the commission. once this project has been adopted, it should be able to encourage the participation of european industry in financing the subsequent stages in the medium and long term.

of the euro, due to its artificial currency character, stimulated our exports in a way that was unfair to our partners but, in any case, beneficial to our internal growth. i am not sure that this has not contributed, in some small way, to the american slowdown in recent months. finally, the third stimulus effect, which nobody is talking about but which is very real: the unwinding of private individuals in anticipation of the exchange of coins and notes on 1 january next. this is sterilized money that is being reinvested in the economy for about 50 billion francs this year in my country, which is far from negligible. in these conditions, we are already in full swing. further fiscal stimulus would only serve to raise new taxes which would make the future situation even more impossible. the real question we should be asking ourselves is: how is it that with the three combined stimulus factors i've mentioned, we're not in the middle of an economic boom? i see two reasons for this, apart from the accidental effect of the bombings, which has not yet materialized. the first is the overloading of our economies with taxes and various rigidities that the socialist period has just made worse in france with, in particular, the stupidity of the mandatory 35 hours. the second, as i have already said and will say again, is a perverse effect of the single currency. the euro may avoid some fluctuations in domestic exchange rates, as its defenders like to repeat. but in return it imposes a unified monetary policy on countries in different situations. this standard, as one economist put it, is not suitable for france and germany today, where it is having a recessionary effect. and it seems clear that the recessive effect of standardization now far outweighs the benefits of eliminating internal exchange. in this way, if we look at the situation as a whole, the euro is not acting as a shield but as an accelerator of the crisis. will we have to tolerate even larger budget deficits to compensate for this? that would be a paradox ! in any case, mr president, since europe is gone today, it will take a few more years of pain and tension before governments realise this first truth: everyone is much better off when everyone benefits from an economic policy adapted to their needs.
the commission is aware of the difficulties facing the community in the field of the internal market. i will begin by referring to our different economic situation from that of the united states. the starting point of the european union is totally different from that of the united states: our balances are not the same, what has happened in the united states has not happened in europe, nor is our institutional model similar. the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european union is able to take action in the field of human rights. for some of you, our concern is, it was said, to avoid intervention by the public sector. no, not at all. we have never raised this issue as a public/private sector debate. there can be more public investment, there can be more public action, but always within the rules laid down in the system we have agreed among ourselves so that the balance between monetary policy and fiscal policy can work more efficiently. a good example of the rapid reaction of a public decision is undoubtedly the ecofin decision on airlines and insurance coverage as a result of the political risks involved. from there, the great debate has been raised on the stability and growth pact. for some, the position of those who defend it is fundamentalist, for others dogmatic, some of you have even put forward the thesis of cancelling the pact. i would rather align myself with the presidency and those of you who have referred to something which i consider essential. the stability and growth pact is intended to be an instrument to facilitate countercyclical public finance. that was its aim and that remains its fundamental essence. so there is no dogmatism and no fundamentalism. we can discuss whether our past experience of applying the pact during periods of growth has led us to conclude that it only works in that direction. nor were we overly dogmatic in the growth period about exhausting the possibilities of the pact to reduce the public deficit in some of the member states, something which might even weigh on us at the moment. but let's go back to the logic of the covenant for a moment. the logic of the pact is to allow counter-cyclical actions. the flexibility of the pact is undoubtedly based on two fundamental elements: the first - exceptional circumstances - which it is not appropriate to analyse, since we are only talking about exceptional circumstances in the event of a deep recession or a fall in growth below certain levels, and the second, the normal application of the pact through the use of automatic stabilisers. in the specific case of automatic stabilisers, the element of flexibility is provided for in the pact itself and i can point out that we are not changing any position at all, but it is the very nature of the pact. the code of conduct adopted by ecofin last july already states that one of the fundamental elements of the stability and growth pact is the medium-term objective for the budgetary position, and it states very clearly that the assessment of the objectives of the countries must take account, explicitly, of the cyclical position and its effects on the budget. this means, as some of you have said, that the member states will certainly have to try to take this element into account when adjusting their stability programmes. the commission has insisted on several occasions that the cyclically adjusted deficit position should be included in the information on the stability programmes, and you are well aware that we have technical difficulties, not with regard to the concept, but with regard to the system for calculating this structurally adjusted position. this will of course not allow us to be more flexible, but to apply the pact to a different economic reality from that which existed when the various stability programmes were defined. and that means, therefore, that, in the commission's interpretation, the nominal targets, as i said in my first speech, should not be regarded as something absolutely unchangeable. the nominal targets are linked to certain growth assumptions. so, as i said, there are no problems, there is flexibility, there is no dogmatism, but rather we are in a different period from the previous one in terms of the implementation of the stability and growth pact. would a more expensive thesis solve the problems? i don't think he is. our position is that, in view of the european experience in recent years of rather procyclical behaviour in this type of decision-making, in view of the difficulty of restoring equilibrium, in view of the impact that some positions have had in recent months, it is not the right choice. that is why we continue to believe that the right choice, and i said that in my opening speech - some of you have also referred to this - is to go ahead with more europe. more europe means lisbon; more europe means, when we talk about lisbon, increasing our potential growth; more europe means more efficient systems; more europe also means taking more account of the impact of the crisis on international markets and also taking into account such important elements as international trade negotiations on development aid, all those linked elements which will undoubtedly allow us to improve the context. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is a matter of the european parliament's right to decide on the future of the community. a debate like today would have required a much longer answer, but i am afraid we do not have much longer. but i would like to comment on these ideas briefly so that the commission's position on this final point is clearly defined.

- mr president, in view of the millions of deaths in developing countries, the european commission's proposal for an action programme against communicable diseases in developing countries is a strong initiative which contributes to the affirmation of the right to health on the international scene. if the european union is to play a leading role in this fight and to make its action have a real impact, public health must become a priority of its cooperation in developing countries and thus be reflected in its budget. we shall therefore oppose the rapporteur's oral amendments on this point. that is a pity, because we worked very early on with mr khanbhai to strengthen his original resolution, and the votes in the committee on development produced a broad consensus. at the same time, the media coverage of the lawsuits brought by the pharmaceutical industry and the united states against south africa and brazil, which manufacture or import generic anti-aids medicines, has helped to lift the veil on the economic issues and pushed the european union to make a concrete commitment to the poor in terms of access to care. although it is consistent to tackle the fight against tuberculosis, malaria and aids in a single programme, it is nevertheless necessary to distinguish the specific problems posed by these three diseases. for tuberculosis, if there is a vaccine, its effectiveness is highly contested, and treatment is becoming increasingly resistant. there is no vaccine for malaria, and the drugs, while cheap, are becoming less effective because of the increase in resistance. there is no aids vaccine or treatment available to the people of the south because the patented pharmaceutical companies keep the prices high. we also regret that diseases such as filariasis, trypanosomiasis, sleeping sickness, ebola or the many forms of diarrhoea are not covered by the commission's communication, even though they cause an increasing number of deaths. efficient and coherent action against these diseases must therefore offer differentiated solutions for each case, but also combine measures at several levels simultaneously. first, prevention involves education and information campaigns, particularly for vulnerable groups (women, young people) carried out by influential local actors on the ground. so, in the prevention of aids, promoting condoms is a public health duty. the best prevention is to ensure that there are adequate housing, working conditions, nutrition and hygiene. it is therefore development policy as a whole, and all community policies, which must contribute to the key objective of improving public health. in the same vein, a more general reflection on the environment is needed. for example, the policy of dams, by increasing the surface of stagnant waters, has caused the number of parasitic diseases to explode. secondly, it is essential to strengthen or even create health structures and train the staff necessary for the detection, diagnosis, treatment and monitoring of these diseases. the european community's development aid, particularly under the edf, must concentrate on health services, which have been neglected for too long because of budgetary constraints imposed by structural adjustment. local health ngos must be able to receive funds to carry out their daily prevention and support activities. they should be involved in the development of programmes of assistance in this field and be integrated into public health action. third, everyone must have access to treatment. this means that medicines must be sold at cost to the people of developing countries. another solution would be for these countries to have licenses for the production of generic medicines. only the establishment of a regional or local pharmaceutical industry will eventually free the people of the south from the control of multinational firms over the price of medicines. trips agreements should be interpreted in this way and should reaffirm the right of developing countries to resort to compulsory licensing in the event of a public health emergency. we must make the pharmaceutical companies respect human rights. in fact, following the media pressure of the last few months, some of them have gotten involved and promised to lower their prices. but the measures are one-off, limited to a few products for a few countries, and over time. furthermore, they still reject the principle of compulsory licences. this refusal of compulsory licences forces us to question the duration of patent protection. it is also questionable whether the reduction in the duration of patents is not, after all, a great stimulus to research. fourthly, we must re-launch research, and this is a key point. new preventive and curative treatments must be found that are more effective and, above all, better adapted to local populations. to this end, an international centre for research on southern diseases, funded by public and private funds, would make it possible to completely detach research from the purely commercial interests of certain industrialists. and finally, and i think this is the most important point, we know that these people in the south who are dying of these diseases today are waiting for our help, and they've been waiting for a long time. i believe that we must develop these structures in a broad sense. all these concerns were largely incorporated in mr khanbhai's report. that is why we are calling for a vote for this one, and we hope that all these speeches, for once, will not be left unanswered, because the people of the south need us.
- the workers' movement will vote in favour of this report despite its shortcomings, because of the realistic assessment it makes of the catastrophic situation in the poor countries and because of the few measures, limited but positive, it proposes. it is shocking that three infectious diseases are killing five million people a year in poor countries and ten thousand a day in africa alone, and the number of victims is increasing. this is especially true because while there is no cure for aids, there is a cure for tuberculosis and malaria. nevertheless, malaria, which a few years ago seemed on the verge of being eradicated, is, as the report points out, once again the leading cause of death in sub-saharan africa, while tuberculosis, for which there are simple and effective treatments, remains the most common cause of death worldwide. the reason for this situation is simple. the manufacture of drugs is monopolized by large pharmaceutical trusts whose primary concern is not public health but profit. the recent and shameful lawsuit brought by a number of pharmaceutical trusts against south africa is a sign of an intolerable situation, even if the reactions of public opinion have to some extent pushed back these trusts. the report's proposal that the european union should have the right of developing countries to produce and market generic medicines within their own countries internationally recognised, without any cost due to intellectual property rights, is the least of these. nor would it be the least of things to impose on pharmaceutical trusts a bill of lading requiring them to manufacture drugs for diseases which the report says are neglected by the industry because they are not profitable enough. the report merely mentions a reduction in prices. for millions of people in poor countries, only free medicines, especially for malaria, could provide basic health care. the report claims to reconcile patent protection and access to health care in developing countries; in writing. - the bankruptcy of liberal dogma is becoming more and more obvious. the 'stability pact' and the undemocratic powers conferred on the european central bank are acting as real corsets, at a time when it is becoming particularly urgent to radically change the direction of european construction. the trade union and associative demonstrations triggered by the meeting of the ecofin council in liège and the debates of the european citizens' congress have underlined the urgency of the social and democratic demands made by the movements which oppose the prospect of a globalisation based on solidarity to the current capitalist globalisation. the ecofin council has nevertheless once again shown its autism. he has not made any proposals that are commensurate with the stakes. its debates continue to be characterized by a complete lack of transparency and accountability, as the fate of the tobin tax illustrates. the ministers reneged on their public commitments by referring the matter to the commission, whose hostility to such a decision, however elementary, is well known. similarly, the burning issue of tax havens is deliberately only addressed from the specific perspective of the fight against terrorism. the governments of the union are still not ready to change course. this is the essential question which is obscured by the joint resolutions put to the vote. and that is why we will vote against it.
in writing. - first of all, i would like to thank both our rapporteur in the committee on culture, youth, education, media and sport, mrs ruth hieronymi, and the whole of this committee for the quality of the work they have done and the interesting reaction they have had to the third report from the commission to the council, the ep and the esc on the application of directive 89/522/eec 'television without frontiers', the main purpose of which is to establish a legal framework to promote the free movement of audiovisual broadcasting services within the single market and to guarantee certain general interests such as the promotion of cultural diversity and the protection of consumers and minors. several reasons can be given for my vote in favour of this report; i shall confine myself to these. taking into account that 98% of households have a television, the report first of all aptly recalls that the social impact of television is becoming more and more marked, especially for children. the report also calls on the member states to strengthen their dialogue on the protection of minors and to define common solutions, without prejudice to their independence in the area of national restrictions on the protection of minors. what can be expressed in other words by saying that the audiovisual sector plays an essential role for democracy, for informing the populations and, through this, it is revealed to be a revealer of the level of freedom of expression and the plurality of ideas that can be expressed and heard. the report also highlights the importance of the audiovisual sector for the economy and jobs in the european union: in 1997, the audiovisual sector employed more than one million people in europe and its revenues were expected to increase by 70% by 2005. (intervention by the commission under article 137 of the regulation)
in writing. - the report makes the undeniable observation that 'economic europe is still incomplete'. the reasons for this incompleteness are not mysterious. each national state is primarily concerned with defending the interests of its own capitalist class and favours the national policy most suited to this objective. but there is no need for european institutions so that, beyond national rivalries, the possessing classes harmonize their policies by seeking to improve the profitability of their capital at the expense of the working classes. as regards wage freezes, the spread of precariousness, mass redundancies, savings on public services and attacks on social protection, capitalist europe does not need any institutional harmonization to be united. the berès report considers that 'sound public finances' are the first condition for 'strengthening the coordination of economic policies within the euro area'. however, it does not say how this financial balance is to be achieved. who 's paying ? capitalist enterprises or popular consumers through vat? who should benefit more from budgetary expenditure? the public services or the private employers ? without the tax gifts to capitalist enterprises, budgets could be spent more on public services without being in deficit. that is clearly not the direction of the report. it was not possible, under these circumstances, to endorse it by our vote.
in writing. - the berès report is interesting because it shows the failure of social liberalism, which thought it could combine acceptance of the amsterdam treaty with genuine social policies in europe. the report advocates the coordination of economic policies, but notes that the institutions that could do so do not exist. the ecb is monomaniacal, the parliament impotent, and the eurogroup semi-clandestine. the report merely begs the commission to keep parliament informed. the report contains much truth, however, because it is concerned about the institutional vacuum and the regressive policies that may be pursued under the influence of neoliberal dogma. but instead of saying out loud what is increasingly being discussed, that it would be reasonable not to apply the stability pact, the report merely advocates coordination of 'their respective stability programmes'. this rather pitiful desire to limit the damage cannot make us forget that this prison was set up with the active support of the social liberals, especially in italy and france. that is why we have not given our backing to waves of vague and informal injunctions which are intended primarily to make us forget that we have been gravely mistaken.
in writing. - the peijs report is a genuine neoliberal anthem which makes public finances and social protection the source of all evil. the report contrasts public investment, which is necessarily 'badly managed', with the private sector, which is by its nature efficient. its main function is to reaffirm the neoliberal dogma codified in the 'stability pact' signed in amsterdam in 1997 and to denounce the changes suggested at the gothenburg summit on automatic stabilisers. the report also calls for the introduction of a european social policy, which would be based on the principle of subsidiarity. it advocates the blind application of a policy which everyone will see to be in contradiction with the stated objectives of growth and employment. when the economy slows down, the stability pact contributes to the chaos by slowing down activity, because what is really at stake is to achieve a rate of unemployment that will again drive down wages and strengthen profits. it is absolutely essential to vote against this report, the implementation of which would represent a real danger for the workers of europe.
- mr president, would it be opportunism to dedicate a resolution of this house on extreme poverty to this day? i would like to recall that on 17 october 1987 father wrezinski, together with 100 000 people, witnessed the lives of the poorest families and people in our whole society and since that date the world day against poverty has reminded us every year that we have a duty to stand together to respect human rights when they are violated. if we vote today for this resolution, we pay tribute not only to the commitment of the families and individuals who themselves are facing extreme poverty, but also to the commitment of all the associations and all the citizens who are standing by them. on the other hand, throughout the european union, and especially since the lisbon summit, public authorities, both national and european, have been constantly stressing the need to combat exclusion, and in particular the need for a policy of integration. it is in this spirit that i am presenting today, on behalf of the group, this resolution which calls on the member states to develop genuine strategies for equal access for all to fundamental rights such as education, housing, health care, culture and sustainable employment. it is also in this spirit that we ask the european authorities and, for our part, our committee on employment and social affairs to be able, every 17 october, in liaison with the commission, to take stock of the policies pursued in this field and, thirdly, we ask, of course, for the future, that a plaque be placed on the courtyard of the european parliament in brussels in honour of the victims of poverty, like those placed on the courtyards of the trocadéro in paris, at the council of europe in strasbourg, in berlin, in rome and at the un. it is a simple but important tribute that we wanted to pay today by tabling this resolution.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, poverty in the world is a violation of human rights and an intolerable affront to human dignity. it affects hundreds of thousands of women, men, and children. the situation has worsened in the last six years. in the european union, 65 million people live on less than 60% of the national median income, not to mention the differences between the member states. it is thanks to social transfers and social assistance schemes that the poverty rate in the union has been maintained at 18%. but with the slowdown in economic growth, we risk a further worsening of exclusion and poverty. the analysis of the proposals of the associations and the work of the european fourth world committee intergroup clearly shows that the fight against poverty and exclusion must become a key element of sustainable development. the objectives set must be pursued and integrated into all policies, with more resources. i regret that the financial allocation for the programmes to combat poverty is still insufficient. the laeken european council will have to adopt policy measures on income, employment, housing, health, education, training and culture. our parliament should also have objectives guaranteeing the right to quality housing for all, fighting the steady decline in employment and services, reintroducing citizenship and equal rights. that is why, on the occasion of the world day for the abolition of poverty, which will be held on 17 october, the european parliament, in collaboration with the associations concerned, should also promote initiatives which raise awareness and mobilize people in favour of the eradication of poverty and misery. i hope that this day will be an opportunity to commit ourselves even more to the implementation of programmes to combat poverty, by developing economic and social policies that really tackle the root causes of poverty.

mr president, i would like to join the authors of the joint resolution in protesting against the lack of respect for human rights in vietnam. the european parliament has spoken out on this subject on several occasions, the last time being just three months ago, to denounce the violation of freedom of religious practice. the country, still ruled by the communist party, still represses on a daily basis any group or individual deemed a threat by the ruling power. my colleagues have said that freedom of the press, of opinion, of religion and association, of property and of voting rights are being violated. equally important, no international organization or independent observer is authorized to monitor the human rights situation in the country. we should remember that last april vietnam celebrated the 25th anniversary of its reunification. the vietnamese government, which has signed many international conventions on human rights, had a great opportunity to reaffirm its commitments in this respect. vietnam is claiming a place on the international stage and has the potential to become a prosperous country. unfortunately, the reality is very different. the population is poor, society is decadent, and the country remains underdeveloped. by signing a partnership and cooperation agreement with the european union in 1995, vietnam formally committed itself to respecting human rights and promoting democratization. the ec-vietnam joint committee meeting in hanoi in september reviewed all aspects of relations with the european union, including the mutually agreed commitment to democracy, good governance, human rights and the rule of law. i call on our parliament today to give the european commission its full support in implementing its partnership strategy in the region. we must give a massive boost to the reform process in vietnam. respect for fundamental freedoms of expression and conscience must be the basis for healthy and constructive cooperation with that country.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, when i was elected to the european parliament, i had a specific mandate: not only to represent réunion, the island from which i come, and even the outermost regions, but also to try to make the voice of the whole of french overseas countries heard. i am therefore pleased that our assembly has asked me to be its spokesman on the status of association between the overseas countries and territories, the octs, and the european union. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on the work he has done in this report. let me first of all venture a historical and political reflection on the relations of certain member states with their former colonies, relations which, in my view, are marked by the bond of exclusivity and by the guardianship, the pillars of the colonial pact. it is now time to break with this past and the guilt that accompanies it, in order to define a genuine responsible partnership on an equal footing between the overseas countries and territories, the acceding member states and the european union. we must move decisively in this direction, so that this new decision on association will be the real qualitative leap forward awaited by all the overseas countries and territories. this challenge is made more difficult by the lack of homogeneity in the oct and by the structural handicaps which mechanically impede their development: some 20 countries, all from four member states - the united kingdom, the netherlands, denmark and france - are small and island countries, most of them, with the notable exception of greenland, very far from the european continent, characterized by extreme economic and social diversity (the richest are in the community average, while the poorest are in a real situation of underdevelopment) and by a statutory diversity also in view of the links which the overseas countries and territories have established with their metropole throughout their history, relations characterized by a high degree of autonomy for some and by a strong state guardianship for others. it is clear that the commission's proposal, as presented, only partially responds to this challenge and to the legitimate aspirations of these territories scattered throughout the world. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. on the institutional level, i would first of all like to welcome the establishment of a forum to facilitate the partnership between the octs, the member states and the commission, although it is regrettable that decision-making is not also in the hands of the leaders of the overseas countries and territories. the commission has adopted a differentiated strategy in economic and financial terms, taking account of the extreme diversity of overseas countries and territories, but i regret that the amount of aid is essentially fixed on the basis of per capita gnp. i would have thought it more appropriate to supplement it with demographic and social criteria which more accurately reflect the vulnerability of these territories. i would like to take this opportunity to ask again for the creation of a specific development fund for the overseas countries and territories, separate from the european development fund, which i am sure would be more in keeping with the spirit and letter of the association. finally, on the commercial side, i should like to stress here that the share of the overseas countries and territories in trade with the community is very small, which makes the commission's defensive position incomprehensible. it is true that in certain areas, such as sugar, it is essential that the commission should exercise the greatest vigilance to prevent the rules of origin, which are also necessary for the development of all the overseas countries and territories, from being misused, with the effect of destabilising certain european markets, particularly in the outermost regions. however, not only for reasons of consistency, at a time when the union is fully opening up its markets to the least developed countries, but also in view of the common history of the octs and the european union, it is not clear why the union is refusing to grant the octs what it grants to the least developed countries. community solidarity cannot be a two-way street. it is therefore high time to demonstrate effectively that the overseas countries and territories are not the poor parents of our development policy. in other words, it is high time that we proved to these people in concrete terms that they are right to believe in the european union. i therefore wish to conclude by reiterating the wish that i have expressed many times in my report, namely that the tenth anniversary of the association status should be an opportunity to affirm a strong political will towards these territories which have been left to the whims of the winds on all the oceans of the world for too long, in order to commit ourselves definitively and resolutely to the path of partnership and responsibility, in other words to the path of development for all.
- commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by expressing my great satisfaction at being able to raise the question of the overseas countries and territories for the first time in this house. these twenty territories enjoy a special association regime with the european union, which, for the sake of simplicity, is less favourable than the status reserved for the outermost regions, which are integral parts of the union, but more favourable than the agreements concluded with third countries in the african, caribbean and pacific regions. my attention as a french elected representative from overseas is naturally drawn to the fate of the french territories and territorial collectivities concerned, namely, i quote them here with pleasure, new caledonia, french polynesia, the french southern and antarctic lands, wallis and futuna, mayotte and saint-pierre and miquelon. in his excellent report, mr fruteau welcomes the progress made in relations between the european union and the octs in institutional, economic and financial terms, although there are still many questions about the commission's proposals to meet the objectives set out in declaration no 36 on the octs annexed to the treaty of amsterdam. the report also calls for the establishment of a european union-wide network of national authorities responsible for the protection of the environment. in 1998, imports from the oct accounted for 0.21% of community imports and exports to the oct for 0.43% of community exports. liberalisation of trade with the octs can meet the objectives we have set ourselves. but particular care should be taken to ensure that this liberalization does not lead to a deviation from the objectives pursued. for several years now, imports from an oct (aruba, to say nothing of aruba) have been increasing, and they are a diversion from the spirit of the decision on association with the european union. these products exported to the union do not originate in that octs but are imported from acp countries for minor processing such as rice bleaching, rice screening, packaging or blending. these simple operations require very little investment and are therefore not a factor in development at all, as the luxembourg court of justice pointed out in its judgment in the emesa sugar case in 1998, their only interest is to provide easy added value for international operators. the increase in this type of dysfunction is all the more intolerable because it is contrary to the interests of the other octs, the outermost regions and the acp countries. in this context, without calling into question the objectives proposed by the rapporteur, which i wholeheartedly support, it is imperative to establish strict rules of origin to avoid these diversions which are detrimental to the economy of the whole of the overseas countries. in this respect, measures prohibiting the cumulation of origin for certain products, strengthening the list of insufficient operations or the systematic implementation of safeguard clauses do not in any way provide an adequate answer to the problem.
commission. – i wish to begin by saying that i totally support mrs sudre's remarks. the commission is always asked to ensure that there is coherence in what we do and we have a strong case of lack of coherence when we look at the trade practices that are at the heart of this debate. we have had good reason to do what we have done and i definitely hope that some constructive conclusion that ends this traffic will be part of the final solution for the whole matter. let me also congratulate the committee on development and cooperation and the rapporteur for a clear and generally balanced analysis of this whole matter, although i need to make some remarks. the commission proposal is based on the widest consultation of the parties concerned ever made in this field. thus, it is not surprising that some of the indications we have received as part of this wide consultation process point in different, even conflicting, directions. inevitably, some delicate compromises have had to be struck, for example in the trade sector. however, we have kept to the objective of giving an adequate and ambitious response to the expectations of the octs and to the challenges facing them. the motion before you today gives a positive assessment of several innovations we have proposed, such as the reinforced partnership procedure, the simplified financial regulations and the new role of civil society. in my view, other points also deserve to be mentioned, for example the extension of many budget lines, community programmes and provisions on trade in services to the octs. there is a tendency to neglect the importance, the scope and the opportunities for the octs to be able to access as users community programmes in general. this is new and should be highlighted. i have remarks to make concerning two chapters of the proposal – financial aid and trade. as to the european development fund, it is correct that, in respect of the past, financial aid will no longer be given to three octs – aruba, the cayman islands and the british virgin islands – because their gnp is now near or even higher than in the community. it is important that all members of parliament are made aware of this. we have to get out of the habit of having oct issues being discussed only in the few member states that have a direct part in the discussion. in the past, it has looked a little too much like a self-service shop. we are talking about community matters and they should be discussed at that level. for all the other octs, in the future funds will be granted following more objective, transparent and coherent criteria. income, gnp, has to be one of them, along with population, as we want to ensure that the taxpayers' money is spent where it is most needed, and this means in the fight against poverty. this is the cornerstone of the eu development policy, and i want to stick to this – also in respect of the clear support for this development policy in this house. transitional provisions have been proposed. substantial funds are reserved for social and environmental projects in medium income octs. secondly, money has to go where it is best used. this is why we have proposed to keep a reserve not only to cover emergency aid and the kinds of activities that cannot be programmed in advance, but also to grant additional transfers to those territories which use their initial amounts more efficiently. a real part of the story is that quite an impressive amount of money has not been well utilised. so this performance criterion is a necessary component and the reason we want to keep a reserve to solve this problem. the commission is looking into absorption problems but i have the impression that more efforts should be made by the octs themselves to use funds efficiently. i regret – but i have to tell you – that certain member states do not seem to share these priorities. again this is a matter for the community. we have to get out of the self-service syndrome. the reduction in regional funds is justified by the limited use made of them in the past. should this situation change, i would be very pleased to reconsider this point. the commission also wants to send a strong message to those octs defined as tax havens in the oecd analysis. unless and until they redress their practices, their allocations will and should be cut back. again let me remind parliament of the strong emphasis placed on the need for coherence. parliament's views on this matter have been made very clear to us. we happen to agree with them but we cannot say one thing in one document and then not apply it in an area like this. i share the view that different ways of financing oct aid than the edf could be considered. however, in practice this would only be possible when new budget guidelines are agreed in a few years' time. for the same reason, given the existing budgetary rules, the edf is currently the only real possibility for financing partnership meetings and evaluation studies. but let me repeat that opening access to active involvement in community programmes is an interesting additional way for the octs to benefit from our relationship. let me turn to trade. for too many years now this has been a bone of contention between some octs and the community. unfortunately, excessive expectations in this field have been generated despite our advice. when the community has been forced to take corrective measures those expectations have inevitably been disappointed. but part of the problem and the cases that have dominated this discussion were also the product of deliberate engineering of ways in which to use or misuse the existing system. we should not fool ourselves on this issue. so let me be very clear here. the commission has always supported a liberal trade attitude toward our preferential partners, in particular developing countries. the recent initiative on “everything but arms” is just one latest example. the octs will continue to enjoy the most favourable trade arrangement granted by the community. this is the current position and so it will remain. however, a line has to be drawn between supporting economic activities and tolerating purely speculative operations which have no development effects and, in addition, cost huge sums to the community, be it the community budget, consumers or productive sectors. in other cases, real abuses have been identified and stopped by our anti-fraud departments. it is only reasonable that when preparing new legislation we seek to eliminate the risk of this happening again. once more, such misuse has not served in any way the best interests of oct citizens and governments. let me stress that the oct association certainly includes the principle of preferential access to our market, but not an unconditional one. this is not only the view of the commission, as the council and the court of justice have consistently endorsed it. coherence with the other treaty policies and with the rule of the law must also be maintained. it is in the urgent interest of the octs that a favourable business climate is re-established as soon as possible. this has to be our main objective when formulating our proposals on trade. finally, let me express the hope that very soon we can reach the end of this long phase of transition and uncertainty concerning the future regime. the commission will, to this end, be available as a catalyst where needed to achieve a rapid conclusion in the council to end the long saga of this renewal of the oct regime. i definitely hope that parliament is giving a helping hand by this work of the rapporteur.

- madam president, commissioner, this is a very, very serious time. the worst-case scenario of terrorist air strikes on nuclear power stations, long denounced by the greens and anti-nuclear citizens, is becoming, by the force of events, an accepted hypothesis. proof that air strikes on nuclear power plants are plausible is that france has called on the military to try to defend its reactors. the french authorities, who have always dismissed the possibility of terrorist attacks, are now forced to recognize the fragility of their nuclear cathedrals. and will the surface-to-air missiles deployed around the hague reprocessing facility be credibly effective against a suicide attack ? the german authorities, like the vienna atomic energy agency, acknowledge that even the thickest of the reactors would not survive a crash. throughout europe and elsewhere in the world, the danger is very real, and multiplied by the impressive number of nuclear reactors. the security of citizens is not assured today. the citizens are worried and they have some reason to be. did the commission take these disaster scenarios seriously? how does it intend to ensure the safety of citizens today? and does the commission intend to launch, as in germany, this study on the safety of power stations? finally, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i regret that the other groups did not see fit to follow this debate with a resolution.

and installing video circuits to allow the pilot to visualise approaching people. secondly, the question of transponders. transponders transmit the aircraft's code and position to air traffic control. transponders must be secured and must not be able to be disconnected during flights, as was the case during the attacks in the united states. i would also like to draw parliament's attention to the question of aid to the european airline industry. i think it is very unfortunate that the commission has not taken the initiative in this area. with the economic shock affecting airlines, to say that - mr president, the promotion of transparency and public participation in the preparation of certain environmental plans and programmes is a laudable objective, which we fully support. the report does, however, raise a number of substantive problems, namely: first, the possible overlap of texts providing for public participation, in particular the directives on environmental impact studies, pollution prevention and reduction. secondly, the ratification of the aarhus convention. the latter was signed by the community and all the member states but ratified only by italy and denmark: it is therefore not in force! the report must not be used as an opportunity for the union to substitute itself, by means of a directive, for the will of the member states to be bound by an international convention. in addition, the addition of environmental policies to plans and programmes seems premature at this stage, pending the ratification of the aarhus convention. there is also the concept of the 'public concerned', which we support in order not to extend the scope of the text excessively. however, the two concepts of 'public' and 'relevant public' should be able to coexist, leaving it to the member states to decide on the most appropriate level of consultation. in the case of crossborder projects, for example, it would be advisable to extend the consultation to the general public. we shall support amendments nos 30, 31 and 32. finally, like the commission, we believe that the minimum conditions required to ensure effective public participation should be defined and that the member states should be left to decide the details of the practical arrangements, while respecting the principle of subsidiarity.
