in writing. - we will not discuss the medical arguments put forward in favour of limiting the consumption of antibiotics and other antimicrobial agents. the report does, however, mention the need to save on health care costs. although it may be justified in general, we reject any argument to that effect. we know all too well that when it comes to saving on medical expenses, it is always the consumption of the lower classes, and especially the poorest layers, that suffers. such "prudential recommendations", which are generally used by government authorities to take restrictive measures, result in the overconsumption of medical care by those who can afford it, while depriving those who cannot afford it of the necessary care. we therefore abstained on this report.
in writing. - according to the rapporteur, 24% of workers in the european union are exposed to mechanical vibration. these are mainly those who work in mining, construction, manufacturing, forestry and transport. vibrations transmitted to the hands cause serious and almost systematic disorders, such as the phenomenon of the "white hand" in loggers and foresters: narrowing of the carpal canal, poor circulation and nerve insensitivity. vibrations transmitted to the whole body cause low back pain, herniated discs and premature degeneration of the spine. however, despite the damage to workers' health that has been proven, a european directive has been under preparation for almost ten years! the reason why so much time has elapsed is that the bosses of these sectors and the equipment manufacturers are resistant, that they do not want binding standards, which would make the technological evolution have an immediate impact on the equipment used. in addition, companies do not always use certified equipment. and when they do, they may not review it regularly; so the vibrations are increasing. but above all, the working conditions imposed are considerably aggravating factors. the equipment concerned is often used by workers paid on the basis of output, under arduous conditions of intensive work. companies must be required to pay for regular breaks throughout the day. it is scandalous that workers continue to lose their health to earn a living.
in writing. - "public participation" in "environmental plans": we are of course in favour of this. but this report is, once again, a well-worn text where the good intentions displayed do not hide the ineffectiveness of the proposed measures. the news in france alone, with the reopening of the mont blanc tunnel against the wishes of the surrounding population, the failure to observe the protests of the inhabitants of the rhône valley against the noise of lorries on the motorway, or the route of the tgv line, shows how little the authorities take into account the public opinion when it is expressed. and, far beyond that, what control can the public exercise today to prevent a disaster like the erika from polluting hundreds of miles of coastline? what control can he even exercise to prevent a disaster, which unfortunately is not only ecological, such as the explosion at the azf factory in toulouse? in reality, as long as the public has neither the right nor the means to control the activity of companies like totalfinaelf, nor the possibility of forbidding them any savings policy to the detriment of society and their own workers, the expression "public participation" is an empty expression. we abstained.
in writing. - we voted against this report because it is a mere application of the schengen agreements, which we do not want to endorse either directly or indirectly. while the schengen agreements claim to organise the free movement of persons within the european union, they raise, on the contrary, obstacles to this freedom as far as, at any rate, those from outside the european union are concerned. we are in favour of the total freedom of movement of persons, whether they are from the union or not. the european treaties guarantee the free movement of capital without regard to its origin, to the point of allowing money from the arms trade, drug trafficking or even terrorism to be laundered on european territory so as not to touch the sacred banking or business secrets. our vote expresses our opposition to a europe for capital, not for men.
in writing. - the goebbels report on the means of avoiding international monetary crises is on the whole precise, serious and reasonable. it is all the more surprising that there is not a word about the euro in it, and that it does not recall the (so serious) argument that was once made that the euro, destined to become a major international currency, would discipline the dollar by forcing the us monetary authorities to abandon their "benign neglect". it is true that dissenting analysts thought that a bipolar international monetary system of dollar/euro (or tripolar, if the yen is included) would be more unstable than the old unipolar (or bipolar) system. in any case, it was an interesting debate, which should have been fully in line with the goebbels report, with the added benefit of experience, since the euro has been in force for almost three years, at least on international markets. the rapporteur is cautiously avoiding this question. why would you do that ? simply because the stabilising euro and the destabilising euro were based on the same basic assumption, namely that the euro would quickly become a second international currency, alongside - if not equal to - the dollar. which is far from the case. not only is the euro not a major currency, but it is depreciated, at the permanent limit of the crisis of confidence, and its international role is not developing. and, as a bonus, we are going to unsolvable problems between member countries! if the european union had not obeyed the dogmatists, if we had developed the ecu gradually while respecting the national currencies, the process would have been safer and simpler. finally, the experience of the last three years confirms what we have always thought: the false move towards european monetary unification will make life easier for the dollar. the fact that the president is in good health, despite the recent attacks, seems to be further evidence of this. the rapporteur is understandably reluctant to dwell on the subject.
in writing. - the goebbels report sets itself the ambitious goal of making the international monetary system work better. but for whose benefit? the question is rightly asked when the rapporteur says that 'the imf is the only institution concerned with the proper functioning of the world economy'. the victims of its structural adjustment plans will be delighted to hear this, and may not be convinced by the imf's request to take account of 'social aspects' from now on. in addition, the report made the significant choice of ignoring any tax on speculative movements (tobin tax) and the need to abolish tax havens. i have not voted against this report, however, in order to support two specific requests which we consider to be fundamental. we are in favour of cancelling the debt of the third world and therefore support the 'cancellation' of the debt of the poorest countries and the institution of a 'moratorium procedure' for the others. in our view, this should not lead to a rescheduling plan, but should allow the denunciation of an illegitimate debt. despite all these reservations, these proposals are rather in the right direction and i do not wish to stand in the way of that.

and paternity leave where children are adopted. the common position was hotly debated in the council on this issue and a delicate compromise was reached. it is unlikely therefore that any further - the next item is the report (a5-0335/2001) by mrs miguélez ramos, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on the establishment of a common classification of territorial units for statistics (nuts) (com (2001) 83 - c5-0065/2001 - 2001/0046 (cod)).
commission. - mr president, i would like to thank mrs miguélez and all those who have spoken in this debate. first of all, i would like to clarify two points which i consider essential. you can interpret whether a statistical classification can have a political impact or not; what i can assure you is that that is not the aim of this document, nor was it the intention of the commission. it is a document based on a proposal by eurostat which aims to seek the fairest possible treatment for all countries and regions of the european union. nor does this document prejudge regional policy in any way: who will be objective 1, who will be objective 2? will the present system of regional policy be the same in the future? we don't know that. we are talking here only about statistics; and we are talking about the system for making statistics as fair and as good as possible for all the countries of the union. what are we trying to do? we want to make a practice that we have been applying until now the norm. we want to do so because we think it is essential to give legal force to something which has so far been a matter of consensus between the member states and the commission. but we also think it is essential as a way of establishing the principles for enlargement and of continuing to apply the same criteria as have been applied so far. the nuts had no legal basis until now, and now they have one: that is the aim of this regulation. what criteria have we used to define nuts? there are three principles which are at the heart of our document. the first is that the nuts are normative regions; we therefore try to make their territorial definition correspond to existing legislative political definitions: a good definition, recognised by the member states, of units which, in many cases, already have government structures and comparable statistics, which therefore gives them sufficient reliability. as a second principle, we propose three nuts hierarchical levels. you, in your amendments, go further and ask for at least three levels. with the latitude we currently have in terms of producing statistics, it would be financially problematic for eurostat to work with more than three levels. that is one reason, but we also think that the three levels give us sufficient and valid information. the third principle is to try to make regional statistics comparable. the size of the nuts should therefore be as homogeneous as possible. but we are also aware that there are historical realities, legal situations in each of the countries, which make this principle impossible to apply automatically or mechanically and that specific assumptions have to be taken into account. there is a consensus among the member states that these principles, which have been the ones we have been using up to now, should also be the ideas of the new regulation. as i said before, not only to apply to our countries today, but also to the countries that are going to join us in the coming years. the regulation therefore meets a number of objectives, which you have been able to discuss in depth and to make some corrections to some of them. we are moving towards nuts broken down according to the existing regional systems, because we believe that it is the most efficient instrument we have at our disposal today for the collection, compilation and dissemination of regional statistics. in addition, we have set out criteria in the regulation for defining the regions so that the candidate countries have guidelines for creating a regional classification in their country. this objective is fundamental at the present time. another element i would like to stress is the need for statistics to be comparable and to be as unbiased as possible. they cannot be statistics produced and used for various political purposes. it would be very difficult to establish political interests which would undoubtedly lead to clear contradictions. the question is of course fundamental to the union's regional policy, but as i said earlier, let us not prejudge by a statistical classification what the future regional policy of the union will be. we want clear rules for future changes in the nuts breakdown because this will prevent future conflicts (some of which we have had in the past). modifications are inevitable. we cannot speak of absolutely permanent situations, but it is important that the nuts are not changed too often and that we have a system based on certain rules and pre-established principles. we therefore consider it appropriate that the amendments should not be made less frequently than every three years, otherwise monitoring difficulties would arise. the regulation, as it is designed, allows us to move forward and improve on what we have at present. you have made contributions with 11 amendments which, in our opinion, help to clarify and improve the regulation. the commission therefore considers that we can accept the 11 amendments tabled by the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism. finally, i would like to stress that the nuts regulation will be an important instrument for the achievement of comparable and impartial regional statistics in the european union, on which we can base the regional policy that we decide politically at the appropriate time. thank you very much.

- the agenda calls for the report of the european council and the commission statement on the meeting of 19 october 2001 in ghent.
- madam president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr president of the commission, between the extraordinary european council of 21 september and the summit in ghent on 19 october there were four weeks of events of strategic importance. what analysis did the fifteen make of it ? the targeted response they had supported in advance last month has now turned into a full-scale war, with its horde of destruction, civilian casualties, and helpless populations thrown onto the roads of exile. repeated mistakes in firing have destroyed a refugee center here, a hospital there, a residential area there, and even the northern alliance positions. every day that passes obscures a little more the ultimate goal assigned to these operations, which intensify, in a dizzying strategic blur. the protests are growing, the criticisms are increasing, the unease is spreading, including among the staunch supporters and the indispensable allies of a meaningful fight against terrorism. where are we going ? do we really think that this will lead to success in the necessary fight to neutralize these criminal networks and deprive them of the soil on which they thrive? what is the european council's assessment of this development, which is of the least concern, especially after the announcement of the imminent arrival of american troops on afghan soil, and moreover on the eve of ramadan and the approach of winter? the european council - i quote - 'confirms its strongest support for military operations and notes that these targeted actions are in line with the conclusions of the european council of 21 september last'. so there's not really anything to report... i am saddened and concerned by this attitude, because it puts europe practically out of the picture at a time when there are great expectations of europe, of a political europe, not a military europe, of a europe which is certainly in solidarity with the united states in tracking down terrorist networks, but which does not give unconditional support to washington's unilateral choices. in the period before the tragedy of 11 september, the european union had begun to exist on the international scene: in the middle east, in macedonia, at the durban conference against racism, it had made its mark on events. the same was true in the aftermath of the attacks, when europe supported the more realistic and responsible current of the bush administration, thereby contributing to the abandonment of the frightening notion of a crusade in favour of the constitution of a global coalition of unprecedented dimensions. unfortunately, since the start of the military operations, the european union seems to be in a state of tetanus. the new world situation makes its own intervention more timely than ever, on crucial issues which are at the heart of the serious crisis the world is going through, and first of all on the middle east issue. mr verhofstadt mentioned it briefly, mr prodi referred to it again, the european council communiqué rightly recalls the un resolutions, the respect for which is a condition for a lasting solution to this conflict; the american leaders themselves now seem to agree that mr the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the transition from the gatt to the wto has not only changed the size of the multilateral trading system, but also its nature. with the wto, trade rules are extended to a considerable number of new areas - services, intellectual property, investment, non-tariff barriers - often impacting areas other than trade. these rules have become disciplines with a dispute settlement mechanism that can lead to sanctions. finally, the enlargement to an ever-increasing number of countries, which began in the gatt framework, has led to a huge diversity of situations among the members with regard to international trade. the rules of the multilateral trading system no longer apply only to the countries that account for the largest share of world trade, or even just to one fifth of world production traded across borders. these rules apply to goods and services that will never enter international trade. all countries are affected and their internal rules are affected, regardless of their share of world trade. trade agreements have also had, in recent years, an increasing impact on other international rules in areas such as public health, the environment, social rights. for example, wto agreements or decisions have called into question the precautionary principle, environmental protection or access to medicines. this is partly due to the ambiguity of certain agreements, such as the one on intellectual property in the case of medicines; but we can also think about the scope of article 1 of the general agreement on services in relation to public services. the wto is an intergovernmental organisation whose democratic legitimacy is based on the principle that all members participate equally and have an equal say. in fact, many developing countries have been marginalized by the workings of the wto and have not been able to take part in the development of agreements and decisions. at least 24 developing countries among the members do not have a permanent representation in geneva and many others have delegations too small to follow their own work. many developing countries lack the skills. for developing countries, therefore, the formal issues here join the substantive ones, since rules and agreements more often reflect the interests of the trading powers who negotiated them among themselves - sometimes in "green rooms" or informal consultations, far too closed - than the interests of all members, and especially the poorest countries. for example, many developing countries have stated since the uruguay round that they did not, at the time they signed them, assess all the legal, administrative and financial implications of agreements such as the one on intellectual property, in the development of which they were not involved. in general, for the developing countries, six years after the creation of the wto, the situation is one of limited opening of the northern markets, great difficulties in the application of agreements and persistent marginalization in the functioning of the organization. this feeling is even stronger, of course, in the case of the least developed countries, which, 20 years ago, already accounted for only 0.6% of international trade and which now account for only 0.4%. the wto thus remains an organisation dominated by the trading powers, whose policies benefit the trading powers first. and two years after seattle, the multilateral trading system is still experiencing a triple crisis of democratic legitimacy, due to the unequal impact of world trade and the marginalisation of some of its members, due to the encroachment of certain wto rules on other essential principles, including at international level, and due to a lack of transparency and a weak integration of parliaments and society into the work of the world trade organisation. the wto has begun to recognize the need for reform. but this has not yet translated into the necessary changes. as you know, commissioner, our committee has therefore adopted by a large majority - 48 votes in favour, 5 against and 1 abstention - a report which is mainly characterized by a set of concrete proposals, grouped into four main chapters. first, the equal and effective participation of all members is crucial for a reorientation of the multilateral trading system. it implies a reinforcement of technical assistance. a number of actions have already been taken by the commission, and we encourage it to continue in this direction. but we propose to go further. for example, on the basis of a proportionate contribution from each of the wto member countries to world trade, to finance a fund or an increase in the budget of the organization, which would allow each member country to have a representation in geneva. we propose to support regional groupings - this has already been done, particularly for the acp countries, but we believe that more needs to be done; to establish genuine internal transparency; to enable non-resident countries to have rapid minutes of meetings, draft agreements, pending representation of all members; the commission has also proposed that the council should set up a committee of inquiry into the situation in the former yugoslavia, which would be responsible for examining the situation in the former yugoslavia and for examining the situation in the former yugoslavia. we also propose to reform the dispute settlement system, in respect of which there is still an inequality linked to the market weight of the various member states, so that for small countries, for countries which represent a small share of international trade, it is possible, in certain circumstances, to have recourse to financial compensation. secondly, openness to society and external transparency. from this point of view, we believe that much remains to be done to reach the level of other organizations, in which non-governmental organizations have been granted observer status. we believe that the dispute settlement procedure itself could, since it is a judicial procedure, be public, as are court hearings. thirdly, parliamentary control (this was discussed in the previous debate), both at national and european level, but also through a parliamentary consultative forum at the wto. as far as the european union is concerned, we propose a reform of article 133 and the opening of the 133 committee, as well as the assent of the european parliament on all trade agreements. fourthly, the balancing of international standards and the establishment of new relations between the wto and other international organizations. we propose that all other multilateral organizations - the international labour organization, the world health organization, etc. - should have observer status in the wto and that their views should be systematically sought by the dispute settlement body when there is a risk of conflict between trade and other rules. we believe that the european union should defend a true hierarchy of standards at international level, that is to say, recognize that business law, commercial law, cannot supplant the principles of environmental protection, public health and respect for the social rights of workers. it is indeed the ilo and it alone that should decide whether or not to take retaliatory measures and impose trade sanctions on a country, not the world trade organization. but i think that the world trade organisation must commit itself to respecting any decisions that may be taken by the ilo in this area. in conclusion, mr president, i would say that trade policy, which is one of the oldest policies of the union and the oldest of its common external policies, obviously involves economic interests, but that it also says a great deal - or at any rate that the european union says a great deal - through this trade policy, about its vision of the world of tomorrow and of relations between the north and the south, and about its conception of the division between what is the responsibility of the market and what societies must be able to continue to emphasize other principles, such as that of solidarity. this policy must therefore reflect the fundamental values and objectives of the european union. that is why we propose that the european union should place fair and equitable trade, a democratized multilateral system and a reformed wto at the centre of its objectives.

the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. on the one hand, we must welcome the real progress. the government had to act quickly in the face of the very serious financial crisis that turkey has been experiencing since the beginning of the year. a radical clean-up and rehabilitation programme was drawn up by mr dervis and signed by the three partners in the government coalition. it has been applied since spring under relatively satisfactory conditions, making it possible to initiate substantive reforms that have been delayed for too long and, more generally, to initiate the improvement of relations between the political and economic worlds. but in the short term, these unavoidable effects translate into a very sharp fall in national income, of the order of 8% this year, which is likely to have serious social consequences. and unfortunately, the deterioration of the world situation before and after 9/11 can only complicate the recovery effort. the year 2001 saw the real commitment to a process of turkey's approximation to european democratic standards. it is to be welcomed that in a particularly difficult economic context, a significant part of the turkish government and parliament's activity is devoted to substantive reforms linked to this european approach. in march, the government presented its national programme for the adoption of the acquis. it is a first catalogue of reforms. the timing and exact scope of the proposed measures remain unclear, but as early as september, the grand national assembly began considering several dozen constitutional amendments - some 34 - which were adopted in early october. the result is still far from today's democratic standards. the death penalty has not been completely abolished, non-turkish languages are no longer banned but not fully recognized, the national security council continues to exist, although the civilian population is more numerous. but above all, and most regrettably, the principle of the primacy of international law, and therefore, possibly, in the future, of european law, over national law, has been expressly set aside. nevertheless, there is undoubted progress, which has been welcomed by the european commission and the council of europe. furthermore, on 8 october, the government tabled a package of rights and freedoms legislation, including the criminal code and criminal procedure, the anti-terrorism act, the press act, the political parties act, the associations and demonstrations act. thirdly, outside parliament, this summer saw the beginning of a public debate on the taboo subject of the role of the military in turkish political life. finally, i would like to commend president sezer for his courage in denouncing corruption, a pervasive evil in turkish society, and for using his right of legislative veto against texts which marked a democratic setback. because there are delays, and the audiovisual sector from political power. the dissolution of the main opposition party fazilet has shown that the turkish political system is not stable and that legislative changes on the status of parties are urgently needed. in general, there is a persistent gap between good intentions and practice in the field of human rights, where progress is too slow. torture and degrading treatment of - mr president, i would like to join my colleagues in congratulating alain lamassoure on the quality of his report. i say "in the knowledge of the facts" because i know how passionate and exciting the debate on this subject has been for the last two years or more. i should like to elaborate on just two points in the report which have already been raised by mr brok and others. the first concerns turkey's geostrategic importance, which has been reinforced by recent events and by the european union's recognition of the need to join the coalition against fundamentalist islamist terrorism. i would like to say to our turkish colleagues in this chamber how vain it would be to fear that european defence will develop in competition with, in parallel with and in duplicate of what is being done within the alliance. european defence was built within the atlantic alliance and will continue to be developed there, simply because europe would not have the means to do otherwise. my second comment concerns cyprus. as has been said, the solution of the cyprus problem is one of the conditions - in my view a pre-condition - for any decision on turkey's eventual entry into europe. i do not believe that the turkish cypriot population is in real danger today and i think that a very important gesture on the part of turkey would be to agree, during the negotiations under way, to reduce, as a first step, the presence of its armed forces on the territory of cyprus or, preferably, to evacuate them.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, and a few of my colleagues who are still awake, european economic integration is an objective which most opponents of political integration accept without any stomach-ache. the promotion of short sea shipping is also widely welcomed, as it is essential to preserve the environment and to reduce significantly congestion on our roads. the commission's proposal for a common port form is a sensible, though not politically passionate, step towards simplifying port formalities. it should be noted that the forms currently in use vary widely between member states. the proposal for a directive would mean that the international maritime organisation's fal forms should always be accepted in our ports. for once we get a proposal from the commission that does not add any bureaucracy. this could happen more often. this is because member states are not obliged to require any forms; on the contrary, if a member state considers it necessary to have the information covered by the proposed directive, it must always accept fal forms. i support the commission's proposal and i think we should welcome it with open arms. i have made some technical amendments which are consistent with the initial position of the council of ministers. i believe that we can now, exceptionally, get through this in one hearing. i thank the members of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism for having succeeded in keeping the political animal lurking in all of us in check and not making their own amendments. we must not let our own brand on everything lead to the blurring of the objectives themselves and the delay in the timetable. this time, we avoided this cup with modesty. the joint introduction of imo fal documents contributes to the functioning of the common market and is a welcome improvement. i do not want to overestimate its importance, however, because it is only a very small part of a larger whole. we are not only going to bring dynamism to ports by unifying forms, but also by bringing more competition to ports. the significance of my report will depend to a large extent on whether we have the courage to accept the commission's proposal for the liberalization of port services without diluting it by excluding service groups. i hope that parliament will continue to build europe by breaking up monopolies. i am looking symbolically and appealingly at my esteemed colleague mr jarzembowski. finally, i would like to thank the commission and the council for their cooperation. europe needs constructive action and less politically motivated confrontation. i am confident that we can improve the position of maritime transport with the measures now proposed. you have the wheel, ladies and gentlemen. let us lead europe towards competitive ports!
- your holiness, it is with honour, with emotion and in a spirit of universal brotherhood that the european parliament welcomes you to this chamber of european democracy, and for the first time in a solemn session. despite the seriousness of the events in central asia which have led you to postpone your planned tour of europe, you have been determined to continue your visit to the european parliament. our assembly is particularly sensitive, your holiness, to this sign of interest. for the vast majority of the 380 million europeans in the union, of all nationalities, ethnic groups, religions and political persuasions, you are the embodiment of peace, tolerance between nations and religions, and the ideal of buddhist wisdom, of which you are the highest spiritual authority. 42 years ago, in 1959, faced with the invasion of tibet, you had to, as a young man, make the heartbreaking choice to flee lhasa, not to abandon your people, but because exile was the only way you had left to defend them anywhere in the world. inspired by a philosophical conviction which has never been contradicted, you also made the equally difficult choice not to respond to the invasion with violence and to reconcile, without relent or discouragement, the uncompromising denunciation of the injustice done to tibet and the call for sincere dialogue with the chinese authorities. the strength of your resistance comes from your spirituality, from a deep respect for human beings and life, and from your belief in the oneness of the world's human community. you have shown in a striking way, like mahatma gandhi, like nelson mandela, like andrei sakharov, that the peaceful expression of a noble cause makes it heard, respected and sometimes triumphant. in 1989, the nobel peace prize was dedicated to the recognition of the international community, the recognition that this community has for your person and for your tireless nonviolent action, thanks to you, and much more than yours, around the world, the cause of tibet has not been buried in indifference. it is seen as a just cause, and the younger generations are not lagging behind in this respect. (applause) i would like to thank on september 11th, the world was shocked to discover the new face of a monstrous terrorism. the european parliament has been a key player in the development of the european union, and it has been a key player in the development of the european union. i am convinced that this message will have a profound resonance throughout europe and beyond. therefore, your holiness, i invite you to speak. it is a great honour to speak and share some of my thoughts and feelings with you. as my prepared statement is in tibetan, i want to read in tibetan to show respect for my own unique, separate language. so i will speak tibetan. (loud applause) recently, in calcutta, at a function, at the beginning, as usual, i spoke in tibetan and then in my broken english. the next day a local newspaper reported very favourably on my remarks but said that the dalai lama spoke at the beginning in chinese. so i hope you will realise that this is not chinese, but the tibetan language. (laughter and applause)(the speaker continued in tibetan, what follows is a translation) madam president, ladies and gentlemen. it is a great honour for me to address the european parliament. i believe the european union is an inspiring example for a cooperative and peaceful co-existence among different nations and peoples and deeply inspiring for people like myself who strongly believe in the need for better understanding, closer cooperation, and greater respect among the various nations of the world. i thank you for this kind invitation. i consider it as an encouraging gesture of genuine sympathy and concern for the tragic fate of the tibetan people. i speak to you today as a simple buddhist monk, educated and trained in our ancient traditional way. i am not an expert in political science. however, my life-long study and practice of buddhism and my responsibility and involvement in the non-violent freedom struggle of the tibetan people have given me some experiences and thoughts that i would like to share with you. it is evident that the human community has reached a critical juncture in its history. today’s world requires us to accept the oneness of humanity. in the past, communities could afford to think of one another as fundamentally separate. but today, as we learn from the recent tragic events in the united states, whatever happens in one region eventually affects many other areas. the world is becoming increasingly interdependent. within the context of this new interdependence, self-interest clearly lies in considering the interest of others. without the cultivation and promotion of a sense of universal responsibility our very future is in danger. i strongly believe that we must consciously develop a greater sense of universal responsibility. we must learn to work not just for our own individual self, family or nation, but for the benefit of all mankind. universal responsibility is the best foundation both for our personal happiness and for world peace, the equitable use of our natural resources, and, through a concern for future generations, the proper care for the environment. many of the world´s problems and conflicts arise because we have lost sight of the basic humanity that binds us all together as a human family. we tend to forget that despite the diversity of race, religion, culture, language, ideology and so forth, people are equal in their basic desire for peace and happiness: we all want happiness and do not want suffering. we strive to fulfil these desires as best we can. however, as much as we praise diversity in theory, unfortunately often we fail to respect it in practice. in fact, our inability to embrace diversity becomes a major source of conflict among peoples. a particularly sad fact of human history is that conflicts have arisen in the name of religion. even today, individuals are killed, their communities destroyed and societies destabilised as a result of misuse of religion and encouragement of bigotry and hatred. according to my personal experience the best way to overcome obstructions to inter-religious harmony and to bring about understanding is through dialogue with members of other faith traditions. this i see occurring in a number of different ways. in my own case, for example, my meetings with the late thomas merton, a trappist monk, in the late 60s, were deeply inspiring. they helped me develop a profound admiration for the teachings of christianity. i also feel that meetings amongst different religious leaders and joining together to pray from a common platform are extremely powerful, as was the case in 1986 during the gathering at assisi in italy. the recent united nations millennium world peace summit of religious and spiritual leaders held last year was also a laudable step. however, there is a need for more of these initiatives on a regular basis. on my part, to show my respect for other religious traditions i went on pilgrimage to jerusalem – a site holy to three of the world’s great religions. i have paid visits to various hindu, islamic, christian, jain and sikh shrines both in india and abroad. during the past three decades i have met with many religious leaders of different traditions and have discussed harmony and inter-religious understanding. when exchanges like these occur, followers of one tradition will find that, just as in the case of their own, the teachings of other faiths are a source of both spiritual inspiration and as well as ethical guidance to their followers. it will also become clear that irrespective of doctrinal and other differences, all the major world religions help to transform individuals to become good human beings. all emphasise love, compassion, patience, tolerance, forgiveness, humility, self-discipline and so on. we must therefore embrace the concept of plurality in the field of religion, too. in the context of our newly emerging global community all forms of violence, including war, are totally inappropriate means of settling disputes. violence and war have always been part of human history, and in ancient times there were winners and losers. however, there would be no winners at all if another global conflict were to occur today. we must, therefore, have the courage and vision to call for a world without nuclear weapons and national armies in the long run. (loud applause) especially, in the light of the terrible attacks in the united states the international community must make a sincere attempt to use the horrible and shocking experience to develop a sense of global responsibility, where a culture of dialogue and non-violence is used in resolving differences. dialogue is the only sensible and intelligent way of resolving differences and clashes of interests, whether between individuals or nations. the promotion of a culture of dialogue and non-violence for the future of mankind is a compelling task of the international community. it is not enough for governments to endorse the principle of non-violence without any appropriate action to support and promote it. if non-violence is to prevail, non-violent movements must be made effective and successful. some consider the 20th century a century of war and bloodshed. i believe the challenge before us is to make the new century one of dialogue and non-violence. furthermore, in dealing with conflicts too often we lack proper judgment and courage. we fail to pay adequate attention to situations of potential conflict when they are at an early stage of development. once all the circumstances have progressed to a state where emotions of the people or communities involved in disputes have become fully charged, it is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to prevent a dangerous situation from exploding. we see this tragic situation repeated time and again. so we must learn to detect early signs of conflict and have the courage to address the problem before it reaches its boiling point. i remain convinced that most human conflicts can be solved through genuine dialogue conducted with a spirit of openness and reconciliation. i have therefore consistently sought a resolution of the issue of tibet through non-violence and dialogue. right from the beginning of the invasion of tibet, i tried to work with the chinese authorities to arrive at a mutually acceptable, peaceful co-existence. even when the so-called seventeen point agreement for the peaceful liberation of tibet was forced upon us i tried to work with the chinese authorities. after all, by that agreement the chinese government recognised the distinctiveness and the autonomy of tibet and pledged not to impose their system on tibet against our wishes. however, in breach of this agreement, the chinese authorities forced upon tibetans their rigid and alien ideology and showed scant respect for the unique culture, religion and way of life of the tibetan people. in desperation the tibetan people rose up against the chinese. in the end in 1959 i had to escape from tibet so that i could continue to serve the people of tibet. during the past more than four decades since my escape, tibet has been under the harsh control of the government of the people´s republic of china. the immense destruction and human suffering inflicted on the people of tibet are today well known and i do not wish to dwell on these sad and painful events. the late panchen lama’s 70,000-character petition to the chinese government serves as a telling historical document on china’s draconian policies and actions in tibet. tibet today continues to be an occupied country, oppressed by force and scarred by suffering. despite some development and economic progress, tibet continues to face fundamental problems of survival. serious violations of human rights are widespread throughout tibet and are often the result of policies of racial and cultural discrimination. yet they are only the symptoms and consequences of a deeper problem. the chinese authorities view tibet’s distinct culture and religion as the source of threat of separation. hence as a result of deliberate policies an entire people with its unique culture and identity are facing the threat of extinction. i have led the tibetan freedom struggle on a path of non-violence and have consistently sought a mutually agreeable solution of the tibetan issue through negotiations in a spirit of reconciliation and compromise with china. with this spirit in 1988 here in strasbourg at this parliament i presented a formal proposal for negotiations, which we hoped would serve as a basis for resolving the issue of tibet. i had chosen consciously the european parliament as a venue to present my thoughts for a framework for negotiations in order to underline the point that a genuine union can only come about voluntarily when there are satisfactory benefits to all the parties concerned. the european union is a clear and inspiring example of this. on the other hand, even one country or community can break into two or more entities when there is a lack of trust and benefit, and when force is used as the principal means of rule. my proposal which later became known as the ‘middle way approach’ or the ‘strasbourg proposal’ envisages that tibet enjoy genuine autonomy within the framework of the people’s republic of china. however, not the autonomy on paper imposed on us 50 years ago in the 17-point agreement, but a true self-governing, genuinely autonomous tibet, with tibetans fully responsible for their own domestic affairs, including the education of their children, religious matters, cultural affairs, the care of their delicate and precious environment, and the local economy. beijing would continue to be responsible for the conduct of foreign and defence affairs. this solution would greatly enhance the international image of china and contribute to her stability and unity –- the two topmost priorities of beijing –- while at the same time the tibetans would be ensured of the basic rights and freedoms to preserve their own civilisation and to protect the delicate environment of the tibetan plateau. since then our relation with the chinese government has taken many twists and turns. unfortunately, i must sadly inform you that a lack of political will on the part of the chinese leadership to address the issue of tibet in a serious manner has failed to produce any progress. my initiatives and overtures over the years to engage the chinese leadership in a dialogue remain unreciprocated. last september, i communicated through the chinese embassy in new delhi our wish to send a delegation to beijing to deliver a detailed memorandum outlining my thinking on the issue of tibet and to explain and discuss the points raised in the memorandum. i conveyed that through face-to-face meetings we would succeed in clarifying misunderstandings and overcoming distrust. i expressed the strong belief that once this is achieved then a mutually acceptable solution of the problem can be found without much difficulty. but the chinese government is refusing to accept my delegation till today. it is obvious that beijing’s attitude has hardened significantly compared to the eighties when six tibetan delegations from exile were accepted. whatever explanations beijing may give concerning communications between the chinese government and myself i must state here clearly that the chinese government is refusing to talk to the representatives i have designated for the task. the failure of the chinese leadership to respond positively to my middle way approach reaffirms the tibetan people’s suspicion that the chinese government has no interest whatsoever in any kind of peaceful co-existence. many tibetans believe that china is bent on complete forceful assimilation and absorption of tibet into china. they call for the independence of tibet and criticise my ‘middle way approach’. others are advocating a referendum in tibet. they argue if conditions inside tibet are as the chinese authorities portray it to be and if the tibetans are truly happy, then there should be no difficulty holding a plebiscite in tibet. i have also always maintained that ultimately the tibetan people must be able to decide about the future of tibet as pandit jawaharlal nehru, the first prime minister of india, stated in the indian parliament on december 7. 1950: “…the last voice in regard to tibet should be the voice of the people of tibet and nobody else.” while i firmly reject the use of violence as a means in our freedom struggle we certainly have the right to explore all other political options available to us. i am a staunch believer in freedom and democracy and have therefore been encouraging the tibetans in exile to follow the democratic process. today, the tibetan refugees may be among the few communities in exile that have established all the three pillars of democracy: legislature, judiciary and executive. this year we have taken another big stride in the process of democratisation by having the chairman of the tibetan cabinet elected by popular vote. the elected chairman of the cabinet and the elected parliament will shoulder the responsibility of running the tibetan affairs as the legitimate representatives of the people. however, i consider it my moral obligation to the six million tibetans to continue taking up the tibetan issue with the chinese leadership and to act as the free spokesman of the tibetan people until a solution is reached. in the absence of any positive response from the chinese government to my overtures over the years, i am left with no alternative but to appeal to the members of the international community. it is clear now that only increased, concerted and consistent international efforts will persuade beijing to change its policy on tibet. although the immediate reactions from the chinese side will be most probably negative, nevertheless, i strongly believe that expressions of international concern and support are essential for creating an environment conducive for the peaceful resolution of the tibetan problem. on my part, i remain committed to the process of dialogue. it is my firm belief that dialogue and a willingness to look with honesty and clarity at the reality of tibet can lead us to a mutually beneficial solution that will contribute to the stability and unity of the people’s republic of china and secure the right for the tibetan people to live in freedom, peace and dignity. brothers and sisters of the european parliament, i consider myself as the free spokesman for my captive countrymen and women. it is my duty to speak on their behalf. i speak not with a feeling of anger or hatred towards those who are responsible for the immense suffering of our people and the destruction of our land, homes, temples, monasteries and culture. they too are human beings who struggle to find happiness, and deserve our compassion. i speak to inform you of the sad situation in my country today and of the aspirations of my people, because in our struggle for freedom, truth is the only weapon we possess. today, our people, our distinct rich cultural heritage and our national identity are facing the threat of extinction. we need your support to survive as a people and as a culture. when one looks at the situation inside tibet it seems almost hopeless in the face of increasing repression, continuing environmental destruction, and the ongoing systematic undermining of the culture and identity of tibet. yet i believe that no matter how big and powerful china may be she is still part of the world. the global trend today is towards more openness, freedom, democracy and respect for human rights. sooner or later china will have to follow the world trend and in the long run there is no way that china can escape from truth, justice and freedom. the consistent and principled engagement of the european parliament with china will accelerate this process of change that is already taken place in china. since the tibetan issue is closely related with what is happening in china, i believe there is reason and ground for hope. i would like to thank the european parliament for the consistent display of concern and support for the non-violent tibetan freedom struggle. your sympathy and support have always been a deep source of inspiration and encouragement to the tibetan people both inside and outside tibet. the numerous resolutions of the european parliament on the issue of tibet helped greatly to highlight the plight of the tibetan people and raise the awareness of the public and governments in europe and around the world of the issue of tibet. i am especially encouraged by the european parliament’s resolution calling for the appointment of an eu special representative for tibet. i strongly believe that the implementation of this resolution will enable the european union not only to help promote a peaceful resolution of the tibetan issue through negotiations in a more consistent, effective and creative way but also provide support for other legitimate needs of the tibetan people, including ways and means to preserve our distinct identity. this initiative will also send a strong signal to beijing that the european union is serious in encouraging and promoting a solution of the tibetan problem. i have no doubt that your continued expressions of concern and support for tibet will in the long run impact positively and help create the conducive political environment for a constructive dialogue on the issue of tibet. i ask for your continued support in this critical time in our country’s history. i thank you for providing me the opportunity to share my thoughts with you.
