in writing. - as every year, the main subject of the second october part-session is the adoption of the community budget. this is the only area in which parliament can influence community policy, since it has the power of codecision with the council and, above all, the right of veto. in this europe of technocracy and democratic deficit, it is therefore one of the few powers exercised by representatives elected by universal suffrage. like last year's budget, the 2002 budget is a reflection of the construction of this liberal europe. this is a budget marked by austerity (0.3% of european gdp), with a general lack of resources, particularly for employment policy, enlargement, the treatment of food crises, afghanistan, palestine and the balkans. the rapporteur, mr costa neves, broadly supports these guidelines, proposing an increase in payment appropriations - which is rather positive - but also the setting aside of the structural funds and rather obscure transfers from the operational to the administrative plan - which is rather negative. for these reasons, we cannot support either the report or the draft budget for 2002.
in writing. -(de) budget debates are a highlight of parliament, as they provide an opportunity to review past and future policy. i'm afraid i can't do that for lack of time. let me therefore limit myself to one point, namely the situation of the regions of the member states which share a common border with the applicant countries. there is no doubt that the current border regions will benefit in the long term from the enlargement of the european union, as this enlargement offers new possibilities for organising regional economic, cultural, social and administrative collaboration. in the short term, however, there is a huge pressure to address the specific problems of the wide development gaps, particularly in the social sector. i would just like to remind you that the wage gap between east and west is about 60%. this raises questions that were not raised in previous enlargements and reaches a new dimension. without a strong response, it is impossible to deal with the problems expected in local labour and service markets. many commuters will hit the already tense labour market - in brandenburg and mecklenburg-western pomerania alone, unemployment rates above 20% are not uncommon. cheap services with wage costs some 60% lower than in the east pose a huge challenge to smes and the craft sector. according to local and regional governments and administrations, the commission's programme to support border regions is not up to the challenge. i am therefore pleased, on the one hand, that a line has been added specifically for border regions in the budget. secondly, i ask that the union should release additional funds as soon as possible, in order to convince the citizens concerned in the border regions that their fears and needs are not being ignored. we need a legal basis, which the commission must establish in the short term.
in writing. - we have of course voted against the ecsc budget, which continues, until the expiry of the ecsc treaty, to function as a pump for subsidies for the steel industry's shareholders. considerable sums have already been given to the employers in this sector, enabling them to reconvert into new 'juicy' sectors, while many workers whose jobs have been eliminated are still unemployed. this report proposes the integration of social aid into the budget of the european union; but the minimum guarantee required would be that all workers affected by future job cuts receive full pay until retirement age.
in writing. - the question of turkey is a direct reference to the question of the kind of europe we want. if it is put in terms of membership of a monolithic bloc, the turkish question will be extremely difficult to resolve. it is enough to think, for example, of the question of the common external border. so, in the event that the construction of europe moves resolutely towards a variable geometry, there is nothing to prevent turkey from participating in certain european policies in areas where there are real common interests. on the other hand, if we continue to have a rigid conception of the european union, there is no other way out in the long run than to reverse the helsinki decision and to resume an association process with turkey, of the same type as those we are developing with the other mediterranean states which geography and history have placed outside europe. i am also surprised to learn from the turkish ambassador that the rapporteur, mr lamassoure, is hostile to the amendments on the armenian genocide, when his own political family was actively involved in the recognition of this crime by the french national assembly. is there any double talk ?
in writing. - we voted against the lamassoure report on turkey's progress towards membership, because we cannot see how the rapporteur can reconcile his conception of a federal europe with strong supranational powers with the inclusion of turkey. the rule of law must correspond to the identity of a people, and the practice of democracy is part of this framework. we are already failing to find the european people. so what about the turkish-european people? the lamassoure report has, in fact, no other merit than to expose the contradictions of present-day europe. if it is necessary to establish strong cooperation with turkey, this cannot in any case be achieved through a supranational power which makes rules which apply uniformly to all, but must be the result of a dialogue between nations within the framework of a europe with variable geometry. the lamassoure report also omits the recognition of the armenian genocide of 1917, probably in an attempt to appease turkey. we think we should be more forthright and ask turkey to recognize this genocide. it is obviously difficult, but it would not be the first country to regret a dark episode in its history. the european union must then draw the consequences, in order to achieve genuine appeasement, by re-establishing diplomatic relations with armenia.
in writing. - there are pressing issues such as historical wounds that remain alive in the armenian community around the world. in its resolution of june 1987, the european parliament called on turkey to have the courage to open its eyes to its past so that it could look to the future. because historical truth is the guarantee of democracy. it is not negotiable, it cannot suffer from any financial or economic special interests. the question at stake today is not the recognition of the reality of the armenian genocide, since our assembly already had the opportunity to express its opinion in 1987. what i wanted to do, in asking for the lamassoure report to refer to the genocide, was not to rekindle ancestral hatreds or to fan the flames of intolerance, but to echo the legitimate concerns of the armenian communities. the children of armenia who were exiled at the beginning of the century to our lands are now waiting for justice. they want their ancestors to have a "moral burial". the duty of memory is all the more necessary at a time when the last witnesses to the exile, the last survivors of the massacres, are slowly dying out. i am convinced that joining the eu implies adherence to the founding principles which guided its creation: democracy, respect for human rights and minorities. this approach calls on each of the candidate countries to take responsibility for its past in order to make peace with its own history. i regret that our assembly did not follow my advice.
in writing. - i abstained on this motion for a resolution. i regret that the european parliament has failed to show consistency in rejecting the amendments calling on turkey to continue the dialogue on the recognition of the armenian genocide. last year parliament openly committed itself to urging the turkish government to publicly recognise this period in its history. today, under the guise of artifices, our european parliament has shown hypocrisy. as regards turkey's possible accession to the european union, i would remind you that the real question of europe's borders remains open. the people are not involved, and discussions are still going on about the country's possible membership of the union without raising the real question of europe's identity and outline. the commission and parliament would be better inspired to explore the paths of association rather than direct integration of turkey.
in writing. - this report on progress towards accession to the european union is presented in a very specific context. firstly, turkey is crumbling under the weight of its external debt (more than 120 billion) and must therefore devote almost 70% of its budget to paying it off. the debt spiral is being met by a programme of austerity and structural reforms leading to massive unemployment and sharp cuts in social budgets. the economic difficulties are compounded by a deteriorating political situation, particularly for prisoners of conscience, a persistent denial of the rights of the kurds and the non-recognition of the armenian genocide, and more generally a failure to respect the democratic rights of the turkish people. although the report takes into account the social impact of the prolonged economic and financial crisis and 'calls for the swift disbursement of union financial assistance to accompany reforms, including in the social field, and in particular with regard to the establishment of the rule of law and the promotion of civil society; considers that the volume of aid granted to turkey, despite its increase, is still not commensurate with the importance of turkey's trade relations with the eu, even though the report stresses 'the need to provide turkey with modern legislation on the right to strike and on collective bargaining', it is not for european governments, nor the turkish government, to set the conditions of accession. the decision is up to the people of turkey and they must be consulted by referendum. for these reasons we did not vote for this report.
in writing. - the european council in ghent has just taken note of a commission report on preparing for the changeover to the euro, which sets out 40 'best practices' suggested to banks, governments and retailers in the member states 'to make up for lost time'. this incidental remark by the commission should be of concern to us. why are we late when the date for the exchange of coins and notes has been set long ago and governments have had plenty of time to prepare for it? the most likely explanation is that the officials seem to have felt that the individuals, who were already caught in the trap, would be obliged to adapt. in these conditions, why bother? this attitude speaks volumes about the philosophy of an operation that has been falsely presented as being entirely focused on improving the comfort of citizens. moreover, when one looks through the list of the "40 best practices", one finds that these are small tricks of a minor level - from the early display of prices in euro to the extension of opening hours of bank counters - which can only have a marginal effect. but the main measures that could be envisaged to alleviate the citizens' difficulties, whether financial (compensating traders and micro-enterprises for their adaptation efforts) or technical (inscribing both euro and national currency values on banknotes and coins), have been resolutely rejected. it is true that the double inscription on banknotes and coins should have been thought of earlier and that it would have required a genuine concern to relieve the burden on individuals. but nothing is more foreign to the designers of the single currency. perhaps, after all, this is how citizens will come to realise, at the beginning of next year, that they did not really count for the creation of the single currency. and perhaps they will learn some general truths about the true nature of brussels.
in writing. - the informal summit in ghent, like the previous ones, showed the differences between the various heads of state, and they were widely commented on by the media. but beyond this apparent nonsense, a crucial issue was unanimously agreed: the eu is indeed at war, and it will strengthen its commitment to participate in the fighting. its repressive arsenal is making a leap forward: - the rapid intervention force will be established; - a european judicial area will make it possible to create a public prosecutor's office and harmonise sentences; - europol's prerogatives will be strengthened. the most immediate danger to the freedoms of citizens is probably the introduction of a european arrest warrant, which would allow for an increase in repression throughout the territory by creating a right of exception for all alleged terrorists. the definition of the term terrorist has been expanded to include all those who resist an unjust, intolerable order. of course, there was no room for a social europe at this summit, on the contrary: it called for wage moderation and a profound reform of the labour market. the social europe of ghent was in the streets: in the demonstrations organized by the youth and the working world. we shall therefore vote against this resolution on the outcome of the ghent summit, in accordance with these movements.
- we note that you want to send the council to retirement, which is quite normal given your political background.
in writing. - the poos report presents interesting technical reforms to enable the councils to work better 'with a constant legislative framework', without changing the treaties. but it is surprising that the most obvious reform to facilitate the work of the general affairs council (cag), whose overload is now the main problem, is not to be found in it: to split it into a general coordination council (general organization of work and institutional matters) and a foreign affairs council, which would obviously be purely intergovernmental. this simple and practical reform is not supported by the federalists, who fear that it will definitely attract the high representative for the cfsp to the new intergovernmental foreign affairs council, whereas they want to attract him to the community by placing him in the commission and at the same time giving it foreign policy powers. their proposal is not realistic. more generally, the poos report does not try to anticipate what the europe of tomorrow will be and to deduce from it how the council should evolve. it will be a europe with many and diverse member countries, and therefore necessarily a europe of variable geometry. for the same reason, it will be a europe in which the community method is often considered too rigid, and in which intergovernmental cooperation will have a large place, so a europe in which the distinction between the 'pillars' of the treaty will have a lasting existence. finally, it will be a europe where the current seizure of power by brussels will have ended - at least we hope so - and where national democracies will once again have a say. these broad lines lead us to draw up a pivotal position for the council in the future, which should give it a greater role as a driving force (the initiative for texts should be shared more widely) and a role of coordination between the pillars, between the different circles, between the national and european levels. this is the thinking that it would now be useful to open.
in writing. - our vote against the reform of the council does not imply any preference for its present functioning. it is not the constitutional form of the council that is important - although there is much to be said about its undemocratic character - but its content. the council's basic raison d'être is to manage the collective affairs of the possessing classes of the various countries of europe, provided that their respective interests are not contradictory and that a general consensus can be established. but the european council does not represent the interests of the majority of the union's population any more than individual governments represent the real interests of all their own people. the apparently democratic form of the appointment of national governments following elections does not prevent them from serving the big business in their countries. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. we do not endorse the present functioning or the reformed functioning of the european institutions.
in writing. - reform the council? the need for this, as well as the democratic deficit of european construction, is obvious to all european public opinion. strengthening democracy and transparency, and citizen participation and control, should be the sine qua non of this reform. and we should be careful not to explain, as the rapporteur does, that all the dysfunctions are due to non-compliance with the treaties or to the loss of power of the commission and the general affairs council. but beyond structural improvements, such as strengthening the role of parliament, putting the commission and the council under control, strengthening the power of citizens, directly or indirectly - through associations, trade unions, etc. - we should now discuss the meaning of this european construction which is dominated by liberalism, a construction at the opposite end of democracy and the satisfaction of social needs. new institutions for a different europe - that should be the subject of discussion and vote by the peoples of europe. that is why we did not vote for the poos report.
in writing. - we voted against the joint resolution by the pse and epp on the forthcoming wto ministerial conference in qatar in november, because it seems to us that it is once again setting us up in a trap by accepting the opening of new international trade negotiations without the rules of the game and objectives being sufficiently clarified. we conclude from commissioner lamy's speech yesterday that although he is trying to present a diverse range of objectives for future negotiations (liberalisation, regulation, integration of developing countries, taking sustainable development into account), liberalisation is still the number one objective. in addition, the wto's reference texts, which focus on a too strictly commercial view of trade, automatically encourage the adoption of this priority. it would be further aggravated if the inclusion of the issue of investment in the wto's competence were to be added to the negotiating mandate, which would risk reviving the multilateral agreement on investment (mai) of dismal memory. we are not suggesting that liberalisation is inherently bad, as some on the left think. but we feel that we should take a break now. we must take the time to draw up a clear balance sheet of the uruguay round. and on this basis, it will certainly be necessary to open negotiations, but with the following priority mandate: how to guarantee to each society, to each national democracy, the right to choose its model of life? liberalisation will only bring its full benefits if we have first given a concrete answer to this question.
in writing. - i regret that commissioner lamy was not more explicit yesterday on the differences between the council's negotiating mandate and the draft ministerial declaration of the doha conference. i thought i heard - but the commissioner was speaking in a low voice at the time - that they concerned, in particular, the further reduction in external protection and internal support for our agriculture which some states are calling for. i also regret that the joint resolution which this parliament has just voted is inconsistent in remaining silent on community preference, whereas it rightly stresses the right of wto members to apply agricultural policies adapted to their needs and conditions and in particular, for the countries of the european union, to defend a european agricultural model based on family farming, food safety and quality, environmental protection and territorial balance. food security has a strategic dimension which the tragic events of 11 september have brought to light in a new light. the european union cannot be dependent on imports for 75 per cent of its needs for a family of products as important, vital and strategic as oilseed protein crops. how can the european union condemn itself to zero growth in a crucial sector where world production is increasing by 5% a year? what would happen if there were a weather disaster in the americas? the fatal mistake of blair house, the absurd and severe self-limitation agreed in marrakesh, must therefore be corrected at the next round of negotiations. the complete elimination of animal meal makes it all the more necessary to be able to support the development of community production of vegetable protein: this objective must be a priority for the european negotiator. we will be extremely vigilant on this matter.
in writing. - we voted in favour of the report on 'opening up and democracy in international trade' to affirm our demand for reform of the world trade organisation in the sense of transparency and fairness (in particular for dispute settlement), as well as strengthening peoples' control. but there is a double ambiguity in this respect: at the european level and at the wto level. as far as the european union is concerned, successive reforms of the treaties have virtually eliminated the control and ratification of the common commercial policy by national parliaments. the treaty of nice, which is now being approved, virtually completes the work by eliminating them from the negotiations on services and intellectual property. the european parliament is not taking over, either in law or in fact. and anyway, even if it did get a real right of ratification the end result would still be an overall weakening of democratic control, due to the elimination of any direct power of the national democracies, the closest to the people. in this context, the european parliament's proposal to create a consultative parliamentary assembly within the wto is like the beginning of the establishment of a higher level of dispossession. the assembly would risk legitimizing the national democracies a little more than they do, and thus introducing "regulations" that would have the effect of imprisoning them even more. it should therefore be made very clear that the purpose of the consultative assembly is to improve information, but in no way to replace national parliaments in any way. for us, the first of the "regulations" to be taken into account is that each people, either directly or through its national parliament, has the right to choose its model of society and the laws that apply to it.
in writing. - the rapporteur of this text cannot be naive enough to think that the glaring inequalities in trade are due to the fact that the majority of the countries participating in the wto are 'marginalized because of non-inclusive working methods or the absence or weakness of their representation in geneva' or 'to habits inherited from gatt'. economic relations between countries, and trade relations in particular, are governed by the law of the strongest, and not by the 'democracy' which the rapporteur would like to introduce. the imperialist countries impose their law on the third world countries, and the united states imposes its law on the imperialist powers of the second zone. of course, it is not by giving the poorest countries a few extra posts of officials in the wto or any other international organization that the balance of power will be changed. in fact, the report's motives lie in the fact that this international trade, whose laws are based on the laws of the jungle, is the subject of protests and demonstrations. the european parliament, unable to change the substance of things, is called upon to give a democratic colour to relations which are the antithesis of relations on an equal footing and democracy. we have obviously not supported these sentiments and we voted against this report.
in writing. - tuesday, september 11, 2001: passenger planes carrying passengers crash into two symbols of american power, the twin towers and the pentagon. america is wounded in the flesh, but it is also a whole project of civilization that is struck. the lesson to be drawn from this horrible act affecting the united states, the main actor and beneficiary of an increasingly unequal globalisation, is that the industrialized countries can no longer afford to ignore the need to reflect on north-south relations. the floods in seattle, gothenburg and genoa were the first symptoms of this global split. it is now necessary to consider, in particular, the bodies regulating this globalisation. the report by our colleague, mr harlem désir, is very encouraging in this respect. in seattle, for example, the united states delegation had about 150 people, japan and the european union about 100, while most developing countries had only one representative. it is difficult in these conditions for the poorest people on the planet to make their voices heard. while the legitimacy of the wto cannot be questioned, its functioning and transparency and its effectiveness in terms of wealth distribution are more than questionable. the rapporteur's proposals to meet this triple challenge seem to me to be in the right direction, which is why i voted in favour of his report. but our action must not be limited to this: we must also act directly on the debt of the poor countries, show less arrogance and more respect towards our partners in the south, and stop trying to impose our way of civilization on them. the fourth wto ministerial conference to be held in doha, qatar, in november is an opportunity to seize so that words of goodwill can be transformed into concrete actions, as pillars of a more just and united world.
in writing. - one cannot help but be struck by the significant discrepancy between mr brok's report and the new course taken by international relations since 9/11. the rapporteur does indeed mention 11 september, but he does not draw any conclusions from it as regards the reorientation of the cfsp. on the contrary, it clings to the reassuring dogmas of the old way of thinking, organized around the 'community as a whole': the high representative for the cfsp must be made a community, decisions must be taken by a majority, and so on. the new international landscape which has emerged with the sustained fight against terrorism requires two levels of action: the national level, which has the decisive royal levers in this new form of war, and the global level, which is the only appropriate one for the broad cooperation needed. the european level is only an intermediate stage, often too narrow to comprehend the global circuits and networks of international terrorism. in times of tension, decisive cooperation tends to be organised directly between states. this was the case with the significant military contribution made by the united kingdom to the action of the united states, the tripartite summit in ghent and bilateral franco-german cooperation. the cfsp will have to adapt rapidly to the new diplomatic context. the necessary coordination between the various pillars, as well as between the intergovernmental and community aspects, will have to be organised around the council, which alone is in a position to play the pivotal role. the same need for efficiency should lead to the setting up of a specific foreign affairs council, separate from the general affairs council, as commissioner barnier also mentioned in his speech. without such developments, the cfsp risks being rapidly marginalized and confined to a purely declaratory role.
- doc. a5-0340/2001 by mr adam, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation on the common organisation of the market in sheepmeat and goatmeat (com (2001) 247 - c5-0214/2001 - 2001/0103 (cns)).
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to welcome the work of our rapporteur, mr gordon adam, and to congratulate him on his desire to give prospects to sheep and goat farmers, who are generally at the bottom of the income scale. the committee on agriculture has voted in favour of the principle of a flat-rate basic aid, a rural premium and a supplementary flexibility premium based on criteria of product quality, the environment or economic organization. the fact remains that the levels adopted by our committee will have to be better adjusted in plenary if parliament is to influence the council and thus be credible. the commission recommended a maximum of eur 28 per head. the committee on agriculture raised the amount to eur 44, which is far beyond the expectations of farmers and could also prove difficult to reconcile with the budgetary margins of manoeuvre. i therefore tabled again, on behalf of my group, two amendments by the rapporteur, aimed at restoring the basic premium to eur 25 per head and the premium for dairy herds - sheep or goats - to eur 20. in the meat sector, the maximum per capita support would be eur 39, which equates sheep producers and dairy cattle producers in terms of public premiums per hectare. this seems to me to be a perfectly logical reasoning, since these two types of livestock often coexist in the same regions and spaces, and sometimes on the same farms. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject. if the premium per hectare is at an equivalent level, this may result in a rebalancing of production, with the choice of the farmer being influenced by market prices. i am also in favour of maintaining a difference between the basic premium for the meat and milk sectors, because to do otherwise would mean that the sheep and goat milk economy is not profitable, which is something nobody can believe. that is why, ladies and gentlemen, i expect you to support these proposals, which i consider to be realistic and responsible.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the crisis affecting livestock farming in our european countries is of an unprecedented scale. if it is not stopped, its consequences will be dire for our economies, our societies and the life of our territories. in the beef sector, despite the soothing words of commissioner fischler - who would have us believe that the crisis is behind us - the bad sales are still going on. what i see in my country, for example, is that even with tragically low prices, which no longer cover production costs, farmers can no longer find buyers for their animals. desperation is winning. every day, farmers are forced to stop their work under dramatic conditions. to wait for the collapse of our farmers' numbers to happen would be a suicidal policy. in the sheep sector - i repeat - the european union is running a very large deficit and, when we look at the age pyramid of farmers, we can safely expect that this deficit will increase in the coming years. the income of sheep farmers is among the lowest in the agricultural world. the commission itself recognizes this. in the present situation, it is also evident in this sector that many farmers are in desperate situations and are forced to stop their activity because of insufficient income. in addition to the human and social tragedy it represents, it is also an ecological tragedy because sheep and goat farming is often the last line of defense against the barren land in areas where agriculture is difficult. that is why it has been essential for your committee on agriculture to substantially improve the proposal for a regulation presented by the commission in order to simplify, make it more predictable and increase aid to a sector which is suffering badly, which has such a significant economic, social and ecological impact and which offers cattle farmers, if it is sufficiently strengthened, the possibility of conversion. the very coherent proposals which have been put to you are designed to bring the system of aid to the sheep sector closer to the system for suckler cows, while respecting budgetary constraints because the com in the sheep sector is cheap in view of the number of customers of the farmers. these proposals also respect our international commitments, since the proposed reform is aimed at decoupling aid from an income insurance system, which can act as a safety net. the sheep sector today needs to be stabilised and strengthened, otherwise it will disappear in many regions. he expects a reform which is both generous and responsible: that is what your committee on agriculture is proposing. i hope that the house will follow us and that the council will listen to us.
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. first of all, mr adam, i should like to thank you very much for the report and the members of the committee on agriculture and rural development for their contributions to the committee and for the debate today. i am also very grateful for this, because it is important that we move this proposal forward quickly and vote on it soon so that it can hopefully be adopted by the council as soon as possible, so that this reformed sheepmeat and goatmeat market organization can enter into force on 1 january next year and thus the premiums under this new regime can be paid next year. the most important point of the reform proposal - and this has been emphasised by many - is the replacement of variable compensation payments by a flat-rate aid. this has a number of significant advantages. this new aid is stable. it's also predictable. this gives the farmer a corresponding degree of planning certainty. it is also much less bureaucratic, in particular because all the costly price reporting from which deficiency payments are currently derived and all the complex calculations in this connection will be eliminated. it is also much, much more understandable to sheep and goat farmers. it allows producers to respond appropriately to market requirements, since the support is not affected by price developments. the commission proposal also ensures budgetary stability and, overall, is more in line with the wto objectives. i think there is broad agreement on these principles - as the debate has shown. let me turn briefly to the main amendments. some of the requests concern amendments to the text, which are welcome. i can therefore accept motion no 11, for example, because a more precise definition of the terms 'producer' and 'production establishment' will contribute significantly to a better understanding of the regulation. i can also support motion no 16, which proposes that the premium be paid by 31 march rather than 30 june. this will enable the producer to receive the premium even sooner. i also welcome the proposal to change the definition of producer in less-favoured areas, but i think that this concept could be simplified even further. the wording of the amendment in this respect should therefore be adjusted even more precisely. i do not think it is necessary, however, to specify the additional premium for dikes or for salt marshes, as is proposed in amendment no 44. these should already be covered by the scheme for less-favoured areas. that is why i do not think this amendment is necessary. i also consider that motions for resolutions nos 1, 6, 9, 22, 36 and 37 are superfluous or are not useful in the context of the regulation. other requests concern the need for a certain degree of flexibility, which would allow member states to provide additional support to the sector or, above all, to manage the quotas allocated to individual member states better and more actively. the issues raised in this context in the discussions concern a whole range of aspects and possibilities, ranging from extensification and environmental concerns to the development of quality products, the improvement of marketing structures and the creation of producer groups. i would like to say that although i cannot accept the amendments tabled directly, i do understand the message they are trying to convey. i would therefore like to pursue the underlying concern further in order to find solutions which will better take account of the different needs of the sector in the various member states. but it's supposed to be simple solutions. i do not think we should introduce a new bureaucracy into the world. the same applies to motions 25 to 30 on the national financial framework, which should also be put in the context of the proposals for greater flexibility. it is necessary to ensure that these frameworks are also practical and can meet the objectives set out in the amendments concerned. amendments nos 12, 13 and 15 are the ones with the most direct effects. they therefore concern the issue under discussion here of raising the premium to eur 30 for all producers and raising the supplement for producers in the lessfavoured areas to eur 9. if these proposals were followed, the expenditure would rise to 2.7 billion euros. even the - as you have called it - more moderate amendments nos 45 and 46 would still lead to additional expenditure of eur 385 million. we have based our proposal on the financial framework agreed in berlin and i regret that i cannot take your views into account, especially since the heads of government stress the importance and immutability of this financial framework at virtually every summit. i must also reject the proposal to pay sheep and goat milk producers the same aid as farmers who are only involved in meat production. i am also interested in motions for resolutions nos 31 and 35, which propose additional premiums in the event of a significant fall in prices. the draft regulation already provides for a kind of safety net to be put in place in the event of price falls which disrupt the market. i therefore cannot support these motions. the proposal in motion 20 not to take the first 15 sheep units into account in the calculation of the stocking density under the beef and veal scheme raises a problem which is not really in the context of this regulation but in the context of the beef and veal market regulation and i must therefore reject this proposal in this context. i would like to assure you that we will come back to this point in the midterm review when we discuss the question of the beef regulation and its operation. the requests for annulment 5, 7 and 33 concern imports from third countries. these requests are unfortunately contrary to the international commitments we have made and cannot therefore be accepted. another important aspect is traceability. in motion no 8, it is proposed that this issue be included in the report on the environmental impact of sheep and goat farming due to be published on 31 december 2005. i understand that and i share your motives, but i think that this problem should be solved in the short term and that we cannot wait until 31 december 2005. the first step towards better tracing of origin requires the creation of a reliable labelling and registration system. since a proposal to that effect must be based on another legal basis, the proposed amendments simply do not fall within the context of this regulation, as this regulation would lack the appropriate legal basis. i think, however, that part of amendment no 42, which makes the granting of premiums conditional on compliance with the labelling and registration rules, seems to be a reasonable approach. i shall certainly put such a proposal to the council. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the possibility of adopting a new directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens. this question should be settled in the framework of the implementing rules. so there is no need for a council decision here, but this is the commission's competence. however, in order to avoid fraud, an efficient system of identification and registration should be operational for this reason too. in conclusion, i would like to thank you once again for the report and the amendments. there is a consensus on some points, and i will pass on your request to the council on some points, although i cannot formally accept the amendments in their present form, and unfortunately there are also some proposals which are beyond my financial capacity and which i cannot therefore accept.

mr president, commissioner, the gotthard disaster, with its many victims, completely contradicts the arguments which led mr gayssot to decide to reopen the mont blanc tunnel. we cannot simply mourn the victims. we must act now to put a stop to this tide of disasters once and for all. and we have good reason to demand that here. from an environmental point of view, the reopening of the mont blanc tunnel is contrary to the commitments of the european union and its member states to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. what good is it to vote for sustainable transport and the shift from road to rail if, at the first opportunity to show such determination to reverse the trend towards all-roads, this option is rejected? during the two years of work in the tunnel, rail freight transport did not increase; the commission has already taken the necessary steps to ensure that the transport of dangerous goods by rail is not affected by the increase in the volume of traffic, which is stagnating at 10.5 million tonnes per year, whereas rail capacity exists and the 13.5 million tonnes which pass through the mont blanc tunnel annually could have been absorbed by rail if the capacity for transit through the mont cenis, the southern axis of the river leman and the dijon-valorme axis had been doubled. it is incomprehensible that this railway solution, which represents a transit capacity of up to 20 million tonnes per year via the alpine routes, has been ignored. i would like the commissioner to listen to us on this, because i am making very specific proposals to him. but apparently he's not listening. i would therefore like to say to him that we do not agree with his analysis of the safety of the mont blanc tunnel. that is why we also refuse to reopen it. the €200 million of work carried out, without an impact study or public inquiry, does not meet the maximum safety requirements. the tunnel remains a narrow one-way tube (seven metres), covered with bitumen, which is flammable, without a central recovery hatch and without a parallel evacuation tunnel. the old ventilation shaft will be used for the evacuation. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission must therefore refuse to open the mont blanc tunnel and take up the proposals which the commissioner has not heard, but which are quite relevant alternative proposals to use railways for transit through the alps.
mr president, unfortunately the events of yesterday morning have brought us back to the mont blanc tunnel disaster, and this discussion we are having today is becoming even more topical. i fully agree with my colleague mr santini that the closure of a link like a tunnel under the alps creates real economic problems - which i understand very well - but i also believe that we cannot demand the reopening of a tunnel if all the safety guarantees are not respected. we do not know the real reasons for accidents under these tunnels, nor do we know what safeguards can be provided. what i regret is first of all that the council is not present to listen to this debate, whereas the commissioner has reminded us that this is a matter of the principle of subsidiarity. what i regret is that the council is not here to tell us what it wants to do in the context of a spatial planning policy. we never have answers to the questions we ask ourselves about the real transeuropean rail and motorway networks. so in this case, mr president, commissioner, i would like to see us together pressing the council to provide answers. we cannot go on indefinitely, when unfortunately catastrophic accidents occur, asking the same questions every time, still without answers two or three years later. i therefore believe that it is essential today that we consult the council and that we have a real spatial planning policy which takes account of the railways and which develops the transeuropean motorway networks so that such disasters cannot happen again.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, in 1999 the mont blanc tunnel disaster occurred. yesterday, another tragedy in the gotthard tunnel... this blacklist is not due to chance, but is the human price of a conception of the traffic of goods based on the "toll-truck", linked to the search for maximum profit, which generates terrible risks. since the mont blanc tunnel was closed, the asphyxiated maurienne valley has been able to withstand all traffic. the gotthard tragedy will generate another traffic transfer that we'll have to absorb. the number of crossing points is already too small in normal times. so there's a transitional situation to deal with. we must look at global solutions. in this context, the reopening of the mont blanc tunnel would require respect for vehicle spaces, regulation of road traffic, compliance with partial traffic bans, imposition and non-excess of maximum numbers of lorries, compliance with the limits set for the working time of road workers, and continuous monitoring of safety standards. finally, the commitment to develop the railway by using immediately the existing transversal lines, which are underused. the whole of europe's freight transport policy needs to be reconsidered urgently. the union's commitment in terms of financing investment must be adequate. i think that in these sensitive areas road freight traffic must be stopped, and that means that the means must be mobilised now for the rapid development of rail transport. the european union must now have the political courage to make new and bold choices. thank you.

- mr president, under the pretext of extending the mfa iv for one year to coincide with the expected reform of the cfp, the commission intended to tighten up this instrument, which has become as disastrous for our artisanal fisheries as it is ineffective for the regulation of fishing effort. thanks to the work of mrs attwooll and the committee on fisheries, i hope that the most unfair and dangerous aspects of this tightening up have been avoided, but more broadly, it is the very principle of the pdos that must be called into question. this bureaucratic and brutal system, totally foreign to the traditions and culture of the maritime world, has never been accepted by the professionals. experience has also shown that this instrument is crude, unfair, redundant and expensive. the perverse effects are terrible, coupled with a blockade of aid for new construction, it inflames the second-hand market and discourages young people from turning to fishing. that is why, in the context of the current discussions on the reform of the cfp, we must give priority to the tac and quota system. it is the instrument which must be used to bring the catch of fisheries into line with the resource. the new cfp must focus on the quota mechanism, which it will have to refine by making it multiannual, by improving transparency and scientific quality, by bringing it closer to fishing areas, by closely involving the professionals and by controlling it in an effective and fair way. mr president, commissioner, let us forget about the pops and refine the quotas, and we will do a good job.

in writing. - the adam report on the proposed reform of the sheep and goat production sector does not seem to us to take account of the fundamental problems facing small farmers, who have the lowest incomes in europe. we are happy to note the view of the confédération paysanne, which objects to the fact that the income of sheep farmers in france is 45% lower than the average agricultural income and considers that 'at european level, the com (common market organisation) in the sheep sector has not fulfilled its role of guaranteeing income to producers' and that the proposed reform 'shows no political ambition to revitalise the sheep sector'. the introduction of a flat-rate per head aid for sheep and goats instead of the current compensatory payment is detrimental to owners of smaller herds and does not improve their income. that is why we abstained on this report.

- mr president, the two government initiatives relating to europol which we are examining today, one on the definition of missions and the other on the rules for the transmission of data, provide the european parliament with an opportunity to raise a real question: the organization of democratic control over this office. this is a very important issue, since the police cooperation activities and, in particular, the management of the analysis files, which are held by europol, have a very direct link with civil liberties. today, europol is an intergovernmental body, and its control is carried out by national parliaments, firstly by governments meeting in the council of ministers for justice and home affairs or represented on the administrative council of the office, and finally by a supervisory authority with independent staff. the committee responsible in this house proposes to overturn this system, which has only been in operation since 1999, and would like to entrust the control of europol exclusively to community procedures, and therefore in particular to the european parliament. we do not think this is the right proposal. the european parliament is not, in our view, the appropriate body to ensure democratic monitoring of sovereign police activities, which are carried out by national services and have implications for the territory of the member states themselves. it would be better not to make any a priori judgments when europol is just beginning its activities and to give national parliaments time to organise and improve their controls. they are aware of this need. for example, last september the french parliament placed a reservation on the parliamentary examination of europol's draft agreements with eastern european countries, and then lifted the reservation when it obtained sufficient guarantees on the security of data transmission. we think this is a very positive step. it proves that effective control is being organized on the national side. to exercise this power even more closely, the french senate has just set up a specialised working group within its own body to monitor police cooperation issues. this is an example to be followed, mr president, and perhaps even developed by better coordinating the control activities of the national parliaments horizontally. why should they not set up an interparliamentary assembly among themselves to monitor europol and police cooperation? better still, why should the intergovernmental conference, which is due to meet in 2004 and which, precisely, is to deal with the role of national parliaments in the european architecture, not propose to develop such interparliamentary cooperation to the point of making it a new pillar of the union?

interest. and from this point of view, it is a question of which authority is responsible for services of general interest. in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, we advocate that all levels of the union, whether at european or local level, should be involved in both the definition of the scope of services of general interest and the way in which they are organised. we are concerned about the coherence between the overall approach to services of general interest and the sectoral approach. because there is no point in defining the framework if, behind it, sector after sector, we disorganize cohesion. our group will therefore oppose a number of paragraphs which fall within a sectoral approach which we will not support. i would like to emphasize the question of financing. the commission has just proposed a new text dealing with an exemption scheme for services of general interest. we will support such a proposal, but we believe that it must be complemented by an approach which allows for cross-financing, without which equalization is not possible and which in the long term threatens the operation of services of general interest.

proposals are based on the usual double language: on the one hand, reference is made to the interests of citizens, and therefore to the need for services of general interest, and on the other hand, interest in europe. the commission recognises that competition cannot meet all the needs of citizens and that member states are justified in creating and implementing services of general interest. but amendments. it is seeking to strike a balance between liberalisation and public services, and stresses that services of general interest must guarantee equal access, security of supply and continuity. in writing. - the risk of the manufacture and circulation of counterfeit euro notes is a serious risk for the period of the launch of the single currency, during the few years following the physical exchange of coins and banknotes on 1 january next. in this pivotal period, the confidence of the citizens will be paramount. but it seems that the danger was underestimated and then dealt with too late. it was only on 22 july 1998 that the commission produced its main communication on the subject, and it was in 1999 and 2000 that the first provisions, still partial, were adopted on the extension of europol's missions and the criminal sanctions against counterfeiting of euro coins. the draft decision we have just examined today complements this by providing for a community programme of training and assistance for the principal agents in the field of counterfeiting. the draft itself does not raise any major objections, but its delay and certain ambiguities reveal flaws in the design of the single currency. firstly, the text presented is constantly oscillating between the organization of 'training' and that of 'assistance', failing to state clearly that 48 days after the physical exchange of coins and banknotes, cooperation in this essential field is still not finalized. secondly, one of the objectives of this 'training and assistance' is the 'protection of the euro outside the union', which is not the subject of any community competence. this is an opportunity to discover, from a particular angle, how crippled the single currency system is, divided between community powers and others that remain national, with poorly organized coordination between the two. but could it be otherwise, since the aim at maastricht was to seduce the electorate into believing that the single currency was possible without a complete superstate?

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank mr jarzembowski for all the work he has done throughout this debate in a speech which is certainly difficult and in a discussion in which we all have to be aware of what we are playing for. i would therefore ask parliament, on the whole, to try to get as wide a support as possible for the report, with some nuances on what mr jarzembowski is proposing, with whom, for once, i do not agree on some of the points. i would remind you that 70% of trade with third countries depends on the efficiency of our ports. and it is clear that seaports play a fundamental role in the european union's trade. but if we want to tackle in a credible way the future of transport within the european union, not with the european union and third countries - where we will continue to be largely dependent on maritime transport - but within the european union, we must once and for all move from declaration, words and deeds to making what is called cabotage, or short sea shipping, a reality, and that requires that we have the most competitive, the most efficient ports, the best possible interconnected with the adjacent territory. in this respect, as the honourable members know, ports were first incorporated into the transeuropean networks a few months ago, precisely to integrate them fully into the internal transport chain of the union, thus playing a crucial role in making our transport system sustainable and competitive. the commission proposal is part of a package which deals with various port policy issues: the transparency of public funds flows to ports; the criteria for what constitutes state aid and what does not. these are aspects of competition between ports. the proposal for a directive which the honourable members are to vote on deals with the issue of competition between service providers within ports, covering in fact all services which are normally provided to port users and which have a commercial value. i shall refer in a moment to what has been pointed out by several honourable members, namely competition between ports. but now we are going to talk about the proposal for a directive on competition within ports. the proposal is based on two pillars: one relating to content and the other to procedures. in terms of content, we intend to match what parliament and the council have already legislated in similar areas, where rules have been set to open up the markets. i am talking about telecommunications, gas, electricity, but especially in the transport sector, ground-handling services at airports. although the treaty does not in principle allow restrictions on market access, ports have their own specificities, such as the possible space constraints and the fundamental importance of safety and environmental issues. our proposal ensures a fair balance between these needs. i am pleased to note that the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism welcomed this approach in its vote. we must allow self-help in ports where operators feel they can get the most out of their own equipment and we must ensure that, as in all other sectors, the number of service providers can only be limited where there are justifiable reasons, such as space constraints or the safety of maritime traffic in this case. every competent service provider must be on an equal footing to operate in the port he wishes. and this brings me to the second pillar of our proposal: procedures. the procedural rules must be transparent, non-discriminatory, objective and proportionate. nowadays, they're not always. i am convinced that what was possible in ground-handling services at airports must be possible in ports. and i think that although this will create some difficulties, as always happens when there is a change in factual situations which often drag on for a long time, even for centuries, it is true that this change will be to the benefit of the whole system, to the benefit of the economy, to the quality of life of the citizens of the european union in general. of course, local specificities must be taken into account, particularly in matters relating to safety, the environment and social aspects. our proposal will therefore allow for a great deal of flexibility at national, regional and, above all, local levels, so that ports can manage their own affairs in an open and fair manner. i would like to say that the commission, after examining the amendments in detail, accepts most of them. many amendments substantially improve our proposal as regards the clarification of the definitions of port services and self-service and include not only implicit but also explicit compensation rules, as is the case with amendments nos 18, 20, 32 and, in part, amendment no 46, which we fully accept. i would also like to mention amendment no 15, which allows the member states to extend the scope of the directive to the approaches to ports. we also accept some of the amendments nos 25 and 44, which allow for the number of service providers to be limited for reasons of maritime safety, rather than just the number of technical services. it is a reasonable measure and in line with the general interests of the commission in the field of maritime safety. we also agree that the period finally agreed for the maximum concession periods should allow for normal depreciation and return on investment, and we therefore accept an extension of the period and also, if necessary, compensation or compensation, if full depreciation had not occurred, as is suggested in some other amendments. other amendments, while not introducing changes, provide useful clarifications, particularly as regards the continued application of the existing safety, environmental and social standards. all these amendments can be accepted, albeit with a modified wording. however, there are some points which we cannot accept and you must understand that, for various reasons. in the case of some amendments to the recitals of the directive, there is no real correspondence with the legislative text itself, for example: 2, 3, 12. the commission cannot accept amendments which substantially change, alter or reduce the scope of the directive. at this point, let me point out two issues that have been at the heart of the debates in the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism in parliament: should groundhandling services be included in the scope of the directive, yes or no? the vast majority of the parties accept that this is necessary, and we could not accept any amendment, for example, amendment no 52, which would lead to the exclusion of this sector. if we want to have quality modern ports, what is possible and necessary in the ground services of airports must be possible and necessary in ports. this position has also received the majority support within the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism. the same applies to amendments aimed at excluding self-help and the right of service providers to employ the staff they wish, such as amendments nos 69, 70, 71, 72 and 73, which are also rejected. the latter is already covered by legislation. but as you can see by reading our proposal correctly, service providers cannot hire so-called 'pirate workers'. if that misunderstanding can be cleared up by clarification of our text, the commission is prepared to look for a suitable wording. another problem is the question of practice. again, the question is whether or not the practice should be included in the directive. many believe that certain safety considerations make it difficult to include this particular sector, but there are ways of ensuring safety other than those currently applied. the same applies to other technical services in the waterway sector, which is why the commission cannot accept amendments which exclude the practice from the scope of the directive. the committee responsible for this matter also supported our proposal. other amendments are also unacceptable for various reasons; in particular, economic considerations about the service provider should not be a criterion, as mentioned in the second part of amendment no 25. in fact, the service providers have to bear the commercial risks and the public authorities should not carry out economic assessments. that said, our proposal leaves an open door: when there are exceptional circumstances relating to the volume of cargo, the number of service providers may be restricted. i would also like to say that, without going into detail, we cannot accept certain amendments for technical reasons, and the list is at your disposal. finally, i would like to refer to amendment no 26. our proposal states that normally - and i repeat: normally - at least two service providers should be authorized for each category of cargo. if this article were to be deleted, the rule laid down in another paragraph would have to be applied, which would have to authorize as many service providers as possible, a result which i do not think was foreseen when the amendment was tabled. some amendments express the wish to place more emphasis on competition between ports than is done in the commission's port package. and let me get into this by saying that i am in favour of considering competition between ports too, but i think we have to find the most appropriate way of doing that. for example, increased transparency, amendments nos 9 and 48. the commission accepts this principle and i count on its support to find together the best way of applying this principle. another example would be the state aid provided for in amendment no 49. everyone agrees that there should be no such state aid, but we must first define clearly where the line is drawn between what is state aid and what is not. the treaty provides that the commission alone applies the rules of the treaty in the field of state aid. the legislative process under way will focus on this issue and i hope that we can sit down together to find a viable solution within the framework of the treaty that will clarify such a thorny issue. and if it is necessary to go further - and i have the impression from what the honourable members have said, and i share much of their concern that this is so - i have to say that i am prepared to go further than what the present proposal envisages in terms of state aid to ports and competition between ports. finally, a few words on amendment no 79, which proposes an exclusion of private ports, many of which do not apply access restrictions. the way in which this issue can be properly addressed should be considered during the legislative process. this is of course only the beginning president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, from the very first days of its existence, this commission has always considered enlargement as a top priority. enlargement is the right measure, the concrete test and the historical responsibility of europe, of its powers and its duties, of its potential and its ambitions. with enlargement, which is the unification of the continent, a chapter in europe's history is effectively closed and the foundations of the future are laid. through this process, the union is preparing to assume continental responsibilities which call for a new reflection on our means, our policies and the objectives of our action at global level. our commitment and courage must match the commitment and courage with which the candidate countries are preparing to join the union. of all the experiences i have had in the first part of my term as president of the commission, none has impressed me as much as the trips to the candidate countries, the meetings with the citizens of those countries and with the representatives of their governments, the contact with their parliaments, courageously engaged day and night in the difficult task of bringing about the transition of their societies, in which preparation for enlargement is the fundamental chapter. it is to them that i would like to address a message of fraternity, friendship and appreciation for their efforts from this seat in strasbourg. there are countries which, just ten years ago, were still quite literally detached from our europe and which have now joined the common values. even before they are formally admitted as new member states, these countries are beginning to reap the benefits of their integration and are already participating in this new area of stability and development, as evidenced by the increasing presence of member states' enterprises in the candidate countries. the progress made on the road to accession is extraordinary. the reports we are presenting today - and i really thank commissioner verheugen and his colleagues for making an effort which is unprecedented in terms of both quantity and quality, because they have initiated and tested a methodology which is truly extraordinary, and if we have sometimes failed, it is because we have really gone down an unknown road - analyse the preparation efforts as precisely as possible. in short, our reports show that this historic event of enlargement is indeed possible and imminent, provided that this pace is maintained. without going into details, which will be explained to you shortly by commissioner verheugen, i can tell you that progress is being made in virtually all the chapters of the accession process. i believe i can say that this incredible progress is largely inspired by nice, where we defined in concrete terms the milestones and the roadmap - we called it the roadmap - for the final stage of this complex enlargement process. in exactly one year's time, we will assess, together with you, the capacity of each candidate country to assume the rights and obligations associated with its participation in the union. we realize that by then we must have concluded the negotiations with the countries which have complied with the criteria laid down, or at least we must be extremely close to concluding the negotiations. in line with the objectives set by the european parliament and the european council, these countries will be able to complete the ratification procedures join the european union before the elections in june 2004, and thus sit here in the next parliament. next year will therefore be the decisive year for enlargement, as well as for the future of europe. in the negotiations we will deal with the most sensitive areas, such as agriculture, the structural funds and the budget. we shall do so with the same determination to find constructive solutions. the commission will present proposals from the beginning of the year, on the basis of the current acquis and the principles adopted at the berlin european council. much will depend on the continuity of efforts to adopt and apply the acquis in the candidate countries. as the commission underlines in its periodic reports this year, the candidate countries will also need to build up the administrative capacity needed to apply the union's rules and policies properly. the continuing efforts of the applicant countries, however, are only one side of the coin. for enlargement to be successful, it will be important to support the community method and the necessary cooperation between the council, parliament and the commission. 2002 will be a year of intense audit and monitoring activities, and i know that parliament will follow this work closely. i would also urge the member states to continue to respect the agreements already concluded on enlargement, in particular in the context of agenda 2000 and the financial perspective up to 2006, as agreed by the berlin european council in 1999. we cannot make enlargement conditional on further reforms, even if the responsibilities we assume with enlargement must serve us to prepare with political impetus and vision the new institutional process which will be launched by the laeken european council. similarly, the ongoing negotiations should not be linked to the question of the union's finances after 2006, as these are separate issues. any attempt to link them would mean changing the rules and would inevitably end up up upsetting the delicate balances in our negotiating process. the reports we are presenting to you also examine the impact of enlargement on the neighbouring countries, that is, other european countries, and on the mediterranean. the terrorist attacks of 11 september 2001 on the united states have profoundly changed the international context, making it less stable, less predictable and more distressing. the world needs a strong europe, confident in its values, spreading stability, predictability and security around itself and finally taking the lead on the world stage. enlargement will confirm europe's status as the world's leading economy and trading power, with a single internal market of 500 million consumers. from this reality, we have the capacity to extend beyond the union and the candidate countries the area of prosperity and stability that we need. this is why we need to develop a new 'neighbourhood policy', which is one of the strategic objectives of this commission. i have long been a supporter - and i confirmed this yesterday at the college of europe in bruges - of the need to go further and strengthen the range of instruments at the service of the euro-mediterranean partnership, the partnerships with russia, with ukraine and our stabilisation action in the balkans. the basic idea is to extend to all our neighbours the trade liberalisation, technical standards and legislation governing our single market. the form of these agreements will have to be negotiated free trade agreements or agreements of the type of the european economic area but the important thing will be to consolidate economic interpenetration. the central objective is to build the closest possible partnership with our neighbours, which will become the main factor of stability and security. we must, in essence, export stability, lay the foundations for a balanced development of the whole area close to the union, exploiting the main strengths of european integration. this will also facilitate, in due course, the integration of our nearest neighbours, namely those in the western balkans region. in this endeavour, we must not forget the importance of the cultural dimension of our partnership. that is why we are working on a new initiative to facilitate dialogue and mutual understanding between the two shores of the mediterranean. i am grateful to parliament for its support and for the constructive attitude with which it has followed and is following the enlargement process, and i hope that this support can continue in this delicate final phase of the negotiations. the work of meps will be crucial not only for ratification as such, but also for the broader view of support for enlargement by european citizens. indeed, surveys show that in many parts of the union, a large proportion of citizens still need to be convinced of the overall benefits of enlargement. the commission will of course continue and intensify its information strategy, but it is parliament and its members who can help develop the necessary democratic support for enlargement more effectively than anyone else. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, parliament's continued involvement in the enlargement process is essential, as it is essential for the debate on the future of europe, a debate in which substantial contributions are expected from the candidate countries and the future member states. the report presented by the commission today shows that the dawn of a new era for europe is just around the corner. let us achieve them together, let us continue and intensify our cooperation in the months ahead and thus lay the foundations for a wider, stronger and fully democratic union! strategy. the main focus will be on a closer review of turkish legislation and its approximation to the acquis. but we are not yet ready to suggest that we start screening for turkey. next year we will enter the most politically sensitive phase of the accession negotiations. for the negotiations on the financial chapters, we will present an overall framework which ensures that these chapters say that the negotiations are now about issues whose solutions have a direct impact on the living conditions of the citizens of the applicant countries. depending on the nature of these solutions, this will have a positive or negative impact on the acceptance of accession in the candidate countries. we must therefore make every effort to inform citizens in the present and future member states fully about enlargement. no partner should be overwhelmed in the accession process. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. the commission will therefore, on the basis countries are successfully concluded. it will also present a revised pre-accession strategy for those countries which are unable or unwilling to reach the target of concluding the negotiations by the mr president, allow me to congratulate our rapporteur, mr chichester, on his excellent work of analysis and proposal, and to say that i fully agree with his realistic and pragmatic approach, which maintains a balance between the various sources of energy, which is essential in the establishment of a european energy supply strategy. this strategy is based on three complementary objectives, which i support: reducing the european union's energy consumption by increasing the efficiency of certain sectors, particularly the building and automotive sectors; strengthening cooperation and investment with the supplier countries; diversifying energy resources with an objective which i consider essential; reducing dependence on oil. i am also pleased that this report sets out the means of achieving these objectives, in particular through the liberalisation of the energy sector, and i would like to stress the need not to give in to demagogic talk, particularly with regard to renewable energy and nuclear energy. we must remain realistic and understand that without the contribution of nuclear energy, the european union will not be able to achieve the objectives it has set itself on the reduction of greenhouse gases. i believe that the european union must make it a priority objective to meet the kyoto criteria. this is within our reach if we are clear-sighted in our choices, and i also note that the open tax avenues can be powerful incentives, provided they do not hinder the industrial development of the european union. several amendments tabled by the green group are counterproductive. instead of encouraging debate, they exclude several possible energy choices from the outset and i think they must be rejected for the sake of the coherence of this report. i hope we will do so in accordance with the recommendations of our rapporteur.
mr president, the successive oil shocks and the political and social fragility of the main oil-producing countries underline the importance of the notion of energy independence for our economies. but if we do not have the political will to achieve this independence, we are on the road to energy dependence. if we let things go on as they are, within 25 years the external energy dependence of the countries of the european union will reach 70%, instead of 50% today. this awareness is what gave rise to the green paper. if we want to remain in control of our destiny, we must focus on two lines of action. we must, on the one hand, promote energy saving everywhere. secondly, we must value our assets, our know-how and our resources. in this context, as the green paper and our rapporteur suggest, the question of the development of nuclear energy must be approached in a realistic and not ideological way. this implies recognition of the fact that the waste is unimpeachable in terms of greenhouse gases, but also that intensive research efforts are absolutely essential to achieve complete safety of the final waste, even if the latter represents only small volumes. it is certainly not by tackling reprocessing processes - as has just been done again by the wise study commissioned by stoa and whose scientific character is seriously questioned - that progress will be made in the right direction. instead of sterilizing their technological advances, european countries should make the most of them by directing their research towards the improvement of reprocessing/recycling techniques. the same research effort must be pursued in the field of biofuels, which have the merit of representing for us an important, non-polluting indigenous source of energy and offering promising outlets for our agricultural production. i regret that the green paper has not given sufficient attention to this.
