- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we welcome the proposal to sign an association agreement between the european union and egypt, which will help to strengthen the euro-mediterranean partnership. the union attaches particular importance to fundamental freedoms and rights. the strict respect of these rights must be the sine qua non of our signing this agreement. since 1981 egypt has been under an emergency law which grants broad prerogatives to the authorities, in violation of human rights and democratic freedoms. today, these are locked and under the strictest control of the authorities. the valuable work of ngos is a wake-up call to this question. we therefore call on the egyptian government to end this emergency law, so that men and women can fully enjoy all their rights, that sexual orientation, freedom of religion, freedom of opinion can be expressed without criminalization. we will not ignore the decision to condemn homosexuals, which is a violation of human rights and violates the values we stand for. no interference, no superiority of values, no lecturers, but the duty to denounce and condemn. human rights are universal and transcend all borders.
- mr president, we have been calling for an increase in aids funding for a long time in view of the tragic situation. the european parliament, in voting on the khanbhai report, confirmed this choice. the decision to release an additional 120 million was, of course, unanimously approved. however, the proposal we have today, with a number of delays, is only 60 million, and more to be taken from the existing budget. it is no longer a question of supplementary funds, and this without the permanent nature of these funds being available. we are also concerned about the allocation of this sum to the international fund alone. because what is the purpose of this fund? is it just prevention ? or will the need for access to the treatments of the southern countries also have to be taken into account? by equipping care facilities, by providing medication? i think these are questions to be asked. how will this fund be managed? how can those who need the funds, the countries of the south, be involved in decision-making, and not just the donor countries? i think all of these questions are questions we have to ask ourselves because people are dying every day, and we have the money, and it's up to us to help them.
- mr president, commissioner, we are facing an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe. forty million people are now infected with hiv and three million will die before the end of this year, according to the who report, which is being published today. the victims, of course, are mostly from sub-saharan africa. this is not just a health catastrophe, but an ecological and economic one. the who predicts that the least developed countries, because of this disease, will lose a fifth of their gdp by the year 2010, and for a country like zambia, that's a million children who will die. the sums announced may seem substantial, but as my colleague was saying just now, who is going to manage these funds, and are these funds really going to reach the recipients, the people who need them most? the fight against these diseases must be accompanied, as you know and i do, by infrastructure, such as clinics, and social structures, doctors, and this is not compatible with the fact that there are dictates from the imf and the world bank that prevent us from hiring civil servants and doctors. once again, mr president, i would like to say that cancelling the debt of the third world countries and allocating this money to education, prevention and health is a good way of fighting this disease in a lasting way. i would like to conclude by saying that it is no longer acceptable that we have seen what we saw last year, with the pharmaceutical industry allowing itself an arrogant attitude towards certain countries, it is unbearable. we now know that when pregnant women are given azt, they give birth to healthy babies. i wish this arrogance would end once and for all.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the meeting of politics and research is not always easy. research itself cannot be conceived without risks. today, research is beginning on stem cells, and we do not have time to wait for the results in 10 or 15 years. that is the purpose of the committee we set up last year. last week we voted, with the sixth research framework programme, to prioritise and fund genetic research. i agree with this measured vote, which is in line with the opinion of the european ethics committee. the risk that today's report raises is that medical research will lead to the desire for human cloning. the report proposes that such attempts should be banned and, above all, penalized. i am particularly pleased that we are going beyond the simple declaration of prohibition, and i have fought for the criminalisation of reproductive cloning. but does this mean that the therapeutic purpose of stem cell research, both adult and embryonic, must be denounced and rejected? who lends today's scientists and researchers necessarily evil projects? are they the researchers themselves, or are they other people than the researchers? we must avoid confusion between different cloning - i do not agree with the previous speaker - and perhaps think of humanity as capable of producing safeguards and controls. i will remind you, if you will, of the story of frankenstein, which is nevertheless a founding myth of our modernity. the creator of the monster is summoned by the monster to give him a companion, remember. the professor starts by creating the companion for frankenstein. he starts, then he gives up on making him a fiancée. he thus forfeits the chance to give the monster offspring, condemning him to loneliness and death. that's it, the end of the frankenstein story. in this founding myth of our time, humanity is shown in its ability to exercise self-control. so, in the hypothesis of therapeutic cloning, which deals with, let us remember, stem cells, two human realities come into play, and i would like to conclude on this, the question of the status of the embryo and that of the use of women's bodies. some, and this is complicated, confuse cells with embryos and do not want any research, not even research on surplus embryos, assisted reproduction, or embryos from abortion. let it be clear that in this way they are putting abortion back on the map. this is politics, not research. others, myself included, point out that the production of stem cells requires the use of eggs produced by women. we must be wary, and i join several speakers, of the exploitation of women in research. and i very much regret that in a recent meeting of coordinators, where unfortunately i was not present, it was decided to delete recital aj - it was one of my amendments - without any collective consultation. we've re-proposed it. this leads me, finally, to stress that there is a double concern, a concern on the part of those who want to advance the fight against abortion rights again, and on the part of those who would be there to market women's bodies. it's complicated and it's difficult. however, there are things about this report that i hold dear: the need for free, informed consent, and non-discrimination with genetic testing in employment and insurance.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, for once the european parliament is not behind in history. just as a u.s. firm has successfully cloned a human embryo, the temporary commission on human genetics publishes its report, which is excellent. it protects the human embryo by prohibiting cloning, both reproductive and therapeutic. it prohibits european public funding for research on human embryos by recommending the use of surplus embryos for infertile couples and, finally, by making maximum use of work on adult stem cells. man is not the owner of life, but merely the user of it. it cannot therefore appropriate even part of this inheritance, which by its nature is inalienable. those who, by playing the apprentice sorcerers, would thus enrich themselves would eventually have to pay royalties to the creator. under no circumstances should the human embryo be reduced to a mere laboratory material, an instrument for commercial purposes. the legislator must therefore define a status for the embryo which fills the current legal vacuum by prohibiting in particular the patenting of living embryos. in the face of such a fragile and complex genetic mechanism, which also touches on the mysterious and the sacred, it is to ignore the evolution of mankind, its past and its future, and to reap, under the pretext of research, ephemeral benefits. my colleagues from the national front and i stand for the integrity and dignity of human life from conception to natural death. those who oppose it have already, without knowing it, entered the realm of barbarism. to manipulate the mystery of life is to lead mankind to catastrophes far more terrible than those of mad cow disease and creutzfeldt-jakob disease.
mr president, we are unanimously against reproductive cloning, which shows how dangerous it is. but then why make a semantic difference with therapeutic cloning, when it's the same thing? does the addition of the word "therapeutic" change the act? have we been able to separate civilian and military nuclear? the new techniques will require the production of eggs at an accelerated rate, with the known consequences for the exploitation of women's bodies, the side effects for women and the trafficking of eggs. furthermore, research using adult stem cells opens up the same prospects without ethical problems. a word about the purpose of gene therapy: most often, the genetic character is a predisposition to the disease, and external factors will lead to the onset of the disease. are we going to change a gene for a single predisposition, when we now know after the discovery of the human genome that a gene changes other functions that we did not know before? my dear colleagues, it is not out of religious conviction but as an atheist that i call for the precautionary principle.
- mr president, bioethics or the ethics of living things confront us with essential questions, and it is an honour for our parliament to address them today. what is our conception of the human being? a utilitarian or scientist conception in which the human being, and more particularly the weaker, is placed at the service of science, or a humanist conception which places science at the service of the human being. what constitutes the dignity of the human being? will we accept that dignity can vary according to age, ability, health or the way the embryo is created? no, i want parliament to insist that, as laboratories provoke the world's conscience by cloning human beings, we all have the same dignity and the same humanity. what is the point of scientific research? will we let research be the mirage of a new financial eldorado? no, research must remain great, it must serve humanity and, in particular, it must alleviate suffering, help and care for the handicapped, improve the living conditions of all, including those in developing countries. there must be no contradiction between the dignity of the embryo and that of the patient. our position must be consistent and well founded. we must not be subject to the vagaries of the moment but must base our position on respect for the dignity of the human being, the only guarantee of scientific progress.
mr president, at a time when our fellow citizens are asking us, after having built the europe of goods, to build the europe of men, the embryo is now inviting itself to the heart of europe. and i would like to thank the president of parliament who, after the british debate last august on the authorization of cloning for therapeutic purposes, heard the voice of a number of us calling for the creation of an ad hoc committee which, after much hearing, resulted in the report by mr fiori, whom i commend for his remarkable commitment to this matter. unlike other parliaments, such as the french parliament, for example, we are therefore meeting at the right time when a private company announces to us, under the guise of a therapeutic objective, that it has carried out human cloning. i understand the objective, but we must realise that under this objective there is in fact a genuine alibi, if we remember that another objective is underlying it, the lure of profit and a potential market without measures. because what is it really about? in defiance of the principle of the unavailability and non-patrimonial nature of the human body from conception, defined in all international declarations, we are being offered to become what we are fighting against, genetically modified organisms by the creation of embryoes as spare parts for human beings, to repair the sick. we who always know that there is a moment in the decision-making process when we have to raise our nose to the wheel and ask ourselves: "do i continue or do i stop?" think that the time has come to draw the line, because the line is very thin between reproductive cloning and therapeutic cloning, since therapeutic cloning is really just interrupted reproductive cloning. i do not know whether i am in the ethical camp, but i am well aware, in any case, of not being in the modern camp. i don't care about these archaic classifications, because i believe that the real clash of civilizations is between those, neo-scientists, who consider man as a material, and those who consider him as a heritage that is not available for technical purposes. it is in this spirit that i tabled amendment no 213 on the non-patentability of living things, as amendment no 212 shows that there is no difference between therapeutic and non-therapeutic cloning. it is in this spirit that i also appeal to the president of parliament to make our committee permanent, to the president of the commission to engage the european bioethics states so that they do not confiscate this debate from the citizens, and finally to the heads of state and government to initiate an international bioethics convention.

in writing. - the text we have just examined aims to revise a 1980 directive which guarantees protection for employees in the event of the employer's insolvency, and in particular the payment of unpaid wages for a minimum period of three months. an update was needed, and we approved it, for example to clarify the treatment of cases of companies with establishments in several european countries, or to better protect parttime and homeworkers. however, we cannot accept the european parliament's over-supply of amendments, which, with the best of intentions, leads to a multiplicity of detailed requirements for all member states. it is certainly not uninteresting to imagine all the cases of employment relationships which may link a person to an undertaking, to list all forms of wages, allowances or subsidiary bonuses, or to inventory all cases of formal or informal insolvency, but it seems to us that these provisions should be referred to the legislation of the member states. similarly, it may be useful to extend the period of time during which wages are guaranteed, but it is for the member states to assess, in the context of their social relations and their own budgets, whether such an extension is useful and feasible. this is a concrete example of how a directive which should in theory be limited to setting general objectives can be perverted by various pressures to produce a binding and overly detailed text which may be unsuitable for the situation of certain member states.
in writing. - that we increase security at airports and on board planes, no one is against it. but the problem is, as the justification for an amendment worries, that the events of "september 11 in the united states have shown that the liberalization of airport services . . . made the strict enforcement of security measures much more complex". the privatisation of these services and the resulting race for profit, profitability and the over-exploitation of a precarious workforce, all of this does not go hand in hand with security. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of passengers is not compromised by the lack of safety standards. the rapporteur concludes instead that it is up to the member states to bear these costs. in his view, private interests may be irresponsible, unable to provide security worthy of the name, but they would still retain the right to make profits and, as a bonus, to be subsidized by the states, and therefore by the community! it's making fun of the world. that is why, while voting for a strengthening of security measures in the air transport sector, we denounce this new pretext for subsidizing private interests with public funds. we therefore voted against this report.
in writing. - we are obviously in favour of improving the quality of petrol and diesel fuels in order to protect the environment. but, once again, under this pretext, subsidies are offered not to consumers but to manufacturers. we are against any subsidy to big business and, in particular, to the very rich car and oil trusts, so we did not vote for this report.
in writing. - to improve air quality, especially in urban areas, three different but convergent means can be used: air quality legislation, vehicle emission standards and fuel standards. this is the third area where successive directives have been issued, providing for the phasing out of leaded petrol and the possibility for member states to use tax incentives for cleaner fuels. however, one point was left out, namely the specifications of sulphur-free fuels; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented. we are opposed to uniform european air quality regulations, which are a local problem, but we also believe that it is useful to harmonize fuel specifications, since the markets for refiners are far beyond national borders. this fuel standard issue should be an opportunity to introduce specifications favourable to biofuels much more vigorously; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not distorted by the fact that the fuels produced by our agricultural production are unimpeachable in terms of the greenhouse effect, make an important contribution to europe's energy independence and provide a very important outlet for some of our agricultural products. we must move much more aggressively towards legislation to encourage the substitution of increasing amounts of fossil hydrocarbons in engine fuels.
in writing. - the discussion on the ec-egypt euro-mediterranean agreement is a tragic illustration of the european union's foreign policy approach. in this type of agreement, the priority is the establishment of a free trade area in the mediterranean, the priority given to liberalization and the dismantling of public services. the member states have no reason to continue trading with the egyptian state, which is violating human rights, freedom of expression and conscience, which applies the death penalty and which does not respect political pluralism. today's imprisonment of 52 egyptians for homosexuality should be the moment to radically reorient our relations with egypt but also with other countries with totalitarian tendencies. the urgent thing for us today is to demand from president mubarak and his government the immediate and unconditional release of these 52 detainees. it is a matter of sanctioning the egyptian state and its policies by not contributing to the financial enrichment of a minority that disregards human rights. i voted for this report because it emphasizes this requirement.
in writing. - the commission's proposals to unify the definition of terrorism, to define a minimum base of sanctions, and to implement a european arrest warrant replacing the old system of extradition, leave us very dissatisfied. these are old federalist projects which are being put on the cards in the wake of the attacks of 11 september, but which in reality do not provide any concrete, decisive element in the fight against terrorism. the first proposal, on the definition of terrorism and its sanctions, was announced with great fanfare as if the absence of a harmonised definition in the countries of the european union today constituted a formidable gap into which terrorists would slip. it's not. definitions and penalties may vary from state to state, but none of them leave terrorists free. everyone agrees on the thing, even if the names vary. the proposed text thus satisfies the federalists' obsession with uniformity, but will not change much on the ground. the same applies to the second proposal, concerning the european arrest warrant. extradition is nowadays, without doubt, a rather lengthy procedure, but it protects individual rights. the european arrest warrant could be faster, but it is not even safe, because precautions must be taken. we ask in particular that the judicial authority in the executing country not be confined to a formal registration of the transfer request, but that safeguards be provided to ensure the protection of freedoms. this clause is all the more necessary because we no longer know, at the rate of accession, which countries will be members of the european union in ten or twenty years' time. the procedure should be even more restrictive when the executing country is asked to surrender one of its own nationals to another country. in this case, we believe that extradition in its traditional form, and not the european arrest warrant, should be the normal procedure.
in writing. - today's vote asks us to call acts of terrorism what we consider acts of solidarity, acts of justice. for example, "the disruption or interruption of the supply of water, electricity or any other basic resource". these actions are generally those of employees who organise themselves to defend their working conditions, their jobs, or even their tools of work, against the privatisations that threaten them. we're working people, not bin ladens! the substance of the proposal is to punish as a terrorist act all that is aimed at 'threatening and damaging or destroying the political, economic or social structures of a country', that is to say any challenge to the injustice and established order: the occupation of assedics or employment agencies by the unemployed for example, or that of empty houses by the homeless, or european demonstrations against structures such as the imf, the wto, the world bank. this system essentially aims to criminalize the social movement by calling into question basic rights. that is why i did not vote for this report which makes us terrorists.
in writing. - we voted against these reports which are nothing but the financial expression of the policy of the great imperialist powers in this part of the world. this so-called 'aid' to the balkans is in fact intended to 'support the balance of payments and to alleviate external financial constraints' of these countries, as stated in one of the färm (macedonia) reports. the major powers bear a major responsibility for the break-up of the former yugoslavia. they are responsible for the bombings which have affected not only the targeted areas but also the neighbouring areas, if only by driving part of the population of kosovo into exile. their diplomacy of varying geometry, sometimes supporting one another, sometimes playing on ethnic differences and thus fuelling them, does not bring peace to the region, but sows war. our vote against these reports expresses our opposition to the whole policy of the imperialist powers in the balkans and their interventions.
in writing. - to give its opinion on the preparations for the next intergovernmental conference, the european parliament has just adopted a very curious resolution. it does not even bother to mention the four themes which, according to the nice council, should form the basis for future discussion (distribution of powers, simplification, charter of fundamental rights, role of national parliaments), but goes on to list the traditional demands of the federalists in all areas. he capped it all with the demand for a "constitution for the union", a word which does not appear in the nice conclusions, but which, nevertheless, should constitute, according to him, the "objective" of the igc. the european parliament would have done better to give serious consideration to the analysis of declaration no 23 of the nice council, which mentions, not the objective of a european constitution, but that of improving 'the democratic legitimacy and transparency of the union', which seems to us to be quite different, even opposite. the constitution would imply the installation of a supranational power, even in fundamental matters, which would further distance europe from its peoples and weaken its democratic legitimacy. the council of nice was not, rather, aiming at another objective when it mentioned, among the four priority topics on the agenda of the future igc, 'the role of national parliaments in the european architecture'? this 'dance' shows that the time is ripe to bring national parliaments back 'inside' the european decision-making mechanisms, in order to re-establish links with the people. but the european parliament is far from this crucial debate, since its resolution does not say a word about it. the laeken council can still fly away into the federalist clouds if it wishes, but we would advise it to follow the reorientation initiated by the nice council if it wishes to respond to the real problems of europe.
in writing. - the summit is supposed to "take stock of the past months and prepare for the future", we are told. for workers in the european union, the result is tens of thousands of redundancies at moulinex, sabena, aom, danone, in companies linked to it and your so-called new economy, where people are being laid off faster than they are being hired. the result for the lower classes is an unbearable level of unemployment, an increase in precariousness and poverty, illiteracy and lack of health care. when the rapporteurs want 'political, economic and social progress, the security and well-being of the citizens' to be taken into account by 'establishing a balanced economic and monetary system by means of consolidating the policy of economic and social cohesion, ... strengthening the employment policy', they are merely repeating the empty words used by all those who do not know what fear of unemployment and the uncertainty of the future means. the creation of a convention to prepare the future of europe and the revision of the treaties, the name of the man who is expected to preside over it in france, giscard d'estaing, indicates how far it will be from the interests of the workers and the working population in europe. we voted against it.
in writing. - on 4 september last i had the opportunity to give a first reaction to the commission's white paper on european governance in this house, before president prodi. i explained that the concern for the deepening of democracy, within the orderly framework of representative democracy, seemed to me to be absent from the text. the debate that followed gave every possible confirmation to this criticism. the title of the report, european 'governance', a word which has no clear meaning in almost any language of the european union, has only added to the misunderstanding. but maybe it was done on purpose, to cover the tracks. because the more you think about it, the less innocent this white paper seems. i see in it an inconsistency, an omission and a contradiction. the inconsistency is to be found in the principle which, according to the white paper (title iv, page 37), inspired its authors: 'to integrate the peoples of europe with scrupulous respect for national identities'. it is as contradictory as jacques delors' "federation of nation states", of which the principal author of the white paper is a close associate. in the resulting confusion, the central pivot of european decision-making is lost: the nation state. the proposals in the report are aimed at (page 38), 'structuring the relationship between the european union and civil society', developing interactions with 'regional and local actors', increasing public confidence in the use of experts, etc... all these actions have the effect of bypassing the national states, which disappear from the report's field of vision, whereas they should be a mandatory point of entry. finally, as i said on 4 september, the white paper seems to believe that 'governance' can work without representative democracy. the kaufmann report voted by our assembly vigorously corrects this contradiction, and we welcome it, but it fails to point out that representative democracy is itself distorted, even distorted, when national democracy is not the most important factor.
in writing. - the fiori report on the ethical, legal, economic and social implications of human genetics was a good report, on which our colleague elizabeth montfort had worked a lot. unfortunately, it has been distorted by amendments, mainly from the left, with the aim of removing all moral barriers to genetic research. we therefore opposed this distorted text and finally, by a last-minute reversal of fortune, the european parliament rejected it to our great satisfaction. it is interesting to ask what conclusions can be drawn from this, particularly with regard to the vote at our previous part-session on article 3 of the framework programme for research 2002-06 presented by the caudron report, which was to decide on the conditions under which the european union would subsidize genetic research. a rather obscure and unsatisfactory amendment was then voted on, in anticipation of the fiori report, which seemed to authorize the financing of research into therapeutic cloning and embryonic stem cell research. the same amendment, which was introduced today in the fiori report to distort it, was also rejected by this house as a whole. the same text was adopted at the last part-session and then rejected at the present one, so the situation is not clear at all. in our view, we must stick to the traditional position of the european parliament, which rejects therapeutic cloning and research on embryos in the name of a just conception of human dignity.
in writing. - we voted against this report, which, even amended, is not acceptable. the fact that it contains gross scientific errors is not the worst. it is, above all, characterized, from one end to the other, by an obscurantist spirit towards science and its applications. some research can lead to deviations ? this is especially true in a society where the enforcement of the law is done by private companies for profit. but why would we want to ban some of them linked to genetic research, why would we want to deny public funding to certain researchers whose work - the future will tell - can be decisive for the improvement of the lives of countless human beings? we voted for the few good intentions in the text when they were not merely platonic, particularly as regards the protection of workers, the disabled and people with rare diseases. but we reject his whole approach, which is clerical, reactionary and misogynistic. we reject anything that violates the right of women to control their own bodies and to choose whether or not to terminate a pregnancy. as for patents, not only are we absolutely against the idea of patenting living things, but we are against equally vile patents on medical products that exclude the care of millions of human beings who are too poor to pay. more generally, we are against any form of patent on inventions which are not intended to protect the inventor but to ensure monopoly profits for the capitalist groups who market them. it is not research that must be curbed, but the profit-driven economy that must be put to an end. confident that humanity will one day be able to take control of its economy and social life, freeing itself from the shackles of private property, we affirm our confidence in the work of researchers and in what science can bring to a society free from exploitation, capitalist rule and obscurantism.
in writing. - the examination of the fiori report and its resolution was characterized by a brutal confrontation between those who advocate the exploitation of life and the embryo and those who defend its humanity and, therefore, its integrity. this heated debate took place largely against a background of confusion of values, confirming the historical fragility of the foundations of our humanist and christian civilization in the face of the combined attacks of scientism and materialism. this confusion of values in europe and in the member states has so far prevented any possibility of defining the status of the embryo, and i regret that. even though science has shown that the use of adult stem cells makes the use of embryonic cells pointless, the scientific mind persists in violating the "sanctuary of life" by promoting the exploitation of the human embryo. this is proof that the defenders of humanity in all its stages of development are faced with a real ideology, not only dehumanizing, but cloaked in a false humanism and realism.
in writing. - i voted for this report. i very much regret the rejection in plenary of the fiori report on the 'ethical, legal, economic and social implications of human genetics'. the problems related to human genetics should not be approached in emotional and reductive terms. this is what seems to have guided the majority of meps who voted against this balanced text. this vote marks an unprecedented breakthrough in european research. the union will thus lag considerably behind its international partners and leave many questions unanswered. in view of the great fundamental principles and universal values we stand for, the european parliament had the possibility of completely excluding the risks of eugenics and reproductive cloning, while putting in place strong legal safeguards to regulate what is possible and acceptable in genetic research. the european parliament, in failing to take a stand on this very topical matter, has lacked courage. this situation is all the more regrettable when we consider that many patients are waiting for the development of new therapies that represent a chance for many of them.
in writing. - the fiori report was a historic attempt in the european union to impose a common position on what is the foundation of civilisations: the definition of the human person and his dignity. we have seen a vicious struggle between those who defend the integral and non-negotiable dignity of the human person, including myself, and those who promote a scientific ideology mixed with materialism. by rejecting the report by 400 votes to 37, parliament has itself demonstrated clearly and irrefutably the limits of european parliamentarism. the members of this house have unanimously rejected any compromise solution, which is a victory for philosophy over political logic, and i welcome that. this is proof that the european parliament, supposed to be the "democratic organ" of the eu, has neither the institutional legitimacy nor the political capacity to impose a common position on what is based on the "nature of the human person" and his dignity. the european parliament has demonstrated by its vote that only the states can provide the appropriate framework for dealing with these essential questions, while respecting the cultural and spiritual tradition on which our civilization is based.
in writing. - i voted against the resolution as amended, as did my colleagues from the french socialist delegation and the group of the party of european socialists, because i found that the european parliament had failed to reach a reasonable and consensual position on the fundamental ethical and legal questions of human genetics, which i regret. i also think that the text thus obtained is inconsistent and contradictory on several points, for example on the funding of research on embryonic stem cells or on the use of surplus embryos. this negative vote shows the incapacity of the rapporteur and the temporary committee to conduct this difficult debate to a successful conclusion. the absence of an opinion from the european parliament is all the more damaging as it comes at a time when some member states will have to transpose the directive on the patentability of living things into their national legislation and thus amend their legislation in this field. i wanted to support freedom of research, particularly in the field of genetic research and surplus embryonic stem cells, and although this type of research involves uncertainties and risks, it would be very important to have community regulation and funding so that private research is not monopolized in this field.
in writing. - there are fundamental issues on which the very notion of compromise is no longer relevant and which place us before radical choices. the same is true of human genetics, which puts at stake the non-negotiable dignity of the human person. the divisions which cross this parliament were made clear in the vote on the fiori report. there is a liberal-libertarian line which uses the banner of freedom of research and invokes the so-called need not to be alienated by the united states to demand funding from the european union for research on embryonic stem cells and surplus embryos, thus opening the floodgates to the reification and commodification of human life in its nascent, extremely fragile embryonic stage, to the development of real embryo farms, where human embryos would be created for the sole purpose of killing them and growing their cells. a so-called compromise line seems particularly hypocritical and is only a subtle way of authorizing therapeutic cloning. the commission has already proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. the third position, which we support and which was defended with conviction and competence by elizabeth montfort, is to reject any exception to respect for the dignity of the human being, whatever his stage of development. we are calling for the ban on cloning to be maintained and we reject the false distinction between reproductive cloning and therapeutic cloning, when they are one and the same process. we call for a ban on research on embryonic stem cells and surplus embryos and for support for research on adult stem cells, which has particularly promising therapeutic applications.
in writing. - the fiori report was an attempt by some members to reintroduce into european political thought a so-called hierarchy of the dignity of persons. in my view, and i share the european cultural and spiritual tradition, no hierarchy is acceptable when it comes to the dignity of persons. whether sick or disabled, whether in the beginning of life or at the end, every human being enjoys the same dignity. i am therefore firmly opposed to any attempt to subject one part of humanity to the alleged benefit of the other. it is the greatness of man to seek his own integral good, and scientific research contributes to this as much as it must adapt to it. philosophy and history teach us that any compromise on respect for the human person inevitably leads to its denial. finally, it is through political courage and a clear vision of what constitutes the dignity and greatness of the human person that the maintenance of a truly human civilization and progress is made possible.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0416/2001), on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a regulation of the european parliament and of the council laying down the general principles and requirements of food law, establishing the european food authority and laying down procedures in matters of food safety (1088/1/2001 - c5-0414/2001 - 2000/0286 (cod)) (rapporteur: mr whitehead).
- madam president, faced with the multiplication of food crises: dioxin, salmonella, listeriosis, foot-and-mouth disease and bse, many member states have set up health surveillance structures. at the beginning of 2002, europe will set up its own food authority. this new body is intended to meet the expectations of citizens who place food security at the top of their daily priorities, on a par with unemployment, and to provide the european union with an institution capable of defending and promoting the european agricultural model on the international stage. agricultural products are now an integral part of the world trade organisation's trading cycle. the cairn group is opposed to agriculture including food security in the wto. however, in order to be operational, the authority will have to solve the following problems: firstly, the composition of the board of directors, to involve all the actors in the food chain, the authority will have to provide representatives of the agricultural world with a seat, as well as consumers, the agri-food industry and distributors. we therefore remain in favour of a board of directors of 16 members, not 12 as proposed in the report. finally, the definition of the tasks: who will be responsible for alerting, managing and controlling? the problem of the reorganization of the early warning system is a thorny one. the french agency's mission is limited to risk assessment, while the minister of agriculture is responsible for risk management. the european agency will have to limit itself to a monitoring mission. finally, potential conflicts with national agencies: france, great britain, ireland, belgium and greece have their own national agencies. germany, the netherlands, portugal and spain are about to set up their own. the european agency will have to stick to a coordination role while respecting the autonomy of the national agencies.
- madam, commissioner, colleagues, i have to say that i am not in favour of this. at a time when the eurofederalists are calling for a political europe, which they say would make it possible to steer the construction of europe towards more democracy, that is to say, to give less powers to the european commission, what do you think is going to happen? a new body is created, the european food safety authority, and it is clear that this authority, through the appointment of the representatives forming its future board of directors, will de facto depend on the european commission, despite its legal status. we must remember the unforgivable mistakes made by the european commission during the mad cow crisis, when the priority was to achieve the single market at all costs, not the food security of european consumers. in order to enhance the credibility of the european food safety authority in the eyes of the citizens of the member states, it is not sufficient that its seat is independent and physically distant from the european commission; it is necessary that the members of the future board of the new body be subject to scrutiny by the same citizens, through their representation in the european parliament. the authority does not appear to offer sufficient guarantees of independence. it will be subject to the power of the lobbies and the wishes of the european commission, and will therefore be independent only of universal suffrage. and who can guarantee that it will respect the principle of subsidiarity and food-specific principles? will it stifle food smes with ever more stringent regulations, which citizens are increasingly unable to tolerate? why call it "the authority" when it will have no legislative power? and finally, why give it so much money - €67 million, 339 civil servants - when by working in a network with the existing national agencies, it could be just as efficient and less costly. - thank you. - thank you.
- for years we have been trying to restore consumer confidence and i believe that the creation of this food safety authority is in that direction. we must recognize that the consultation was good in the management of this matter, and today we must not be late. there is no such thing as zero risk and the consequences of a bacteriological problem - whether related to terrorism or not - can be of considerable importance to all citizens. it is well known that foodborne illness can affect the greatest number of people. so safety must be at the heart of this device. we must not be dismayed, however, because the european food chain, after the many decisions we have taken here, is probably one of the safest in the world, but the shortcomings that have been identified in previous crises force us to take stronger food security measures. to be effective and credible, the authority must bring together the best scientific experts; the commission must, in the context of early warning, simply assess the risk, and the management of this risk must remain in the political domain. it must also work in a network with national agencies. the interventions should be proportionate to the level of risk involved: if there is simply rumour, then communication should be strengthened; if there is a risk, however, the necessary precautionary measures must be taken and, if the danger is confirmed, preventive measures. finally, this authority must be independent and fully transparent. at the same time, controls must be strengthened and the penalties for serious misconduct must be not only severe but effective.
- madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the greens will indeed vote for the whitehead report. the european food authority, an indispensable food safety tool for consumers and for european political bodies, is indispensable in the tasks that will be entrusted to it. the first is to trace all the dysfunctions that have led to the recent food security crises, whether it be the crisis in animal feed - dioxin chicken, foot and mouth disease, trafficking in veterinary products, over-consumption of vaccines and tranquilizers for animals - and above all the underlying bse crisis. i would remind you that even finland today has its first case of mad cow disease. so that's a first point. secondly, it must also stop the uncontrolled spread of contaminating gm products, which are even infesting traditional cereal crops, while consumers reject these gm plants, whose only virtues are commercial. so this agency also has to, in addition to fixing all of this, ensure safety from fork to fork. to do this, the food authority must apply the principles of transparency and monitoring that my colleagues have already mentioned from the beginning of next year. the failure of hygiene as the only criterion, highlighted by the many crises we have mentioned, in particular the crisis of animal meal, shows that such an agency must be able to give lists of good practice, labels, products with local specificities, agricultural qualities, instead of being limited to industrial standards alone, which do not prevent salmonella, listeria or even more dramatic epidemics. its main task is therefore to coordinate the national agencies, and this requires that it operate independently and transparently. i wonder, however, about amendment no 34, which deals with the appointment of the board of directors, an appointment which seems to be at least opaque, since we are talking about the meritocracy of the board of directors. what is the "meritocracy" of an agency that is supposed to be made up of relevant scientists? the board of directors, on the other hand, has a political and managerial role. i am very much afraid that this "meritocracy" is simply putting pressure on the big agro-food groups. i hope the commissioner can reassure me on this. as for the site of the future agency, this is a secondary issue for us...
- mr president, i take this opportunity to refute the report by the rules of procedure and the previous speakers who, by claiming that the committee on employment and social affairs voted unanimously on the bushill-matthews report, attribute to me a vote which is the opposite of my convictions. this report is a plea for greater financial assistance to small and mediumsized enterprises. i am all the more opposed to the idea of giving public money to private companies because behind the catchword smes there are often large financial and industrial groups. the rapporteur, who is known to be a fervent supporter of the so-called free market, would never have the idea of proposing financial assistance for workers made redundant by the same or similar industrial and financial groups. on the contrary, it is quite clearly aiming to ensure that public money goes, through guarantee mechanisms or seed funding, into the coffers of the large groups, and eventually adds to the private wealth of the shareholders. and with the hypocrisy that is so common to national governments and the european institutions, this increased financial assistance is being offered in the name of job creation. i shall of course vote against this report. public money should go to public services, health, education, public transport, which could and should create many more jobs that are useful to all than these young people who swallow money without their usefulness to society being obvious. health is reduced to a public quest to cope with certain diseases. let the bosses make public demands ! it is not for parliament to dispose of taxpayers' money in their favour.
- the agenda calls for the presentation by the commission of its work programme for 2002 and the communication on the future of the union 'renewing the community method'. i now give the floor to mr prodi, president of the commission.
president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the annual state of the union debate is one of our most important events, and this year it is being held at a key moment for the european union. in these days, in these months, the great europe is taking shape. the negotiations with the applicant countries which have met the criteria for enlargement can be concluded in less than 12 months, so that the union can welcome up to 10 new members before the next european elections. in less than three weeks the euro, the strongest and most visible sign of european union, not only economic but also political, will become a concrete reality. before the end of this week, the european council in laeken will take the decision to set up a convention to prepare the reform of the treaties, bringing together for the first time the representatives of national governments and parliaments, the european commission and this house. the great europe that is taking shape is a united, democratic europe, projected towards the future. it is with this view that the commission has been working in the year which is ending and intends to work in the year which is about to begin. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, before we go on to the commission's work in 2001 and the work planned for 2002, i would like to reiterate once again that i consider full and transparent cooperation between the institutions to be an essential condition for the proper functioning of the union. in the same spirit, i already announced to you in january this year the commission's intention to renew our common working method, so as to make cooperation between our institutions even more effective and transparent. before i explain these proposals, however, i would like to recall the basic principles which should guide our cooperation. first of all: the commission's right of initiative, which is one of the pillars of the community's construction and a guarantee of its integrity, must be safeguarded. a strong commission makes the european parliament stronger. secondly, the tripartite nature of interinstitutional cooperation must be defended. it will only be effective if the two legislatures, the parliament and the council, can dialogue with the commission on a common basis of transparency. i now wish to explain my proposals for renewal, which i am confident will help to improve the dialogue between our institutions decisively. firstly, as of this year, the work programme is no longer a catalogue of legislative intentions but becomes, as you have asked, a genuine political programme. in this programme, which the commission undertakes to respect, the priorities for the year in question are set out as well as the measures needed to achieve them. i know that some of you were surprised that we did not receive the annual catalogue of legislative intentions as an annex to the 2002 work programme, as we had done in previous years. i would like to stress, however, that we listened very carefully to the statements made by many of you in this house on 13 february. you were quite clear in asking the commission to abandon the list of legislative proposals method which had been followed up to that time and to use a new one. that's what we diligently did. these same reasons, which were explained to president fontaine in writing on 10 september, have led us to replace the catalogue with a much more reliable quarterly planning tool, which the college itself uses to plan its work and which you will have at your disposal on a regular basis. in any event, in the interests of full transparency, i have asked the secretary-general of the commission to forward to the secretary-general of parliament immediately the general list of proposals from the commission services, on the basis of which the work programme for 2002 was adopted. if this experiment proves successful, we are prepared to continue it in the years to come. secondly, it is equally important to stress that the preparation of such a programme must be based, in the years to come, on a more structured dialogue between our institutions. that is why we have planned a multi-stage approach for next year, starting at the beginning of the year with the preparation of the 2003 work programme. the two highlights of this political dialogue will be in february, when i will present the political priorities approved by the commission for 2003, and in november, when i will present the work programme adopted by the commission on the basis of these priorities. i am pleased to note that the debate we had at the conference of presidents has resulted in agreement between us on the broad guidelines i have just outlined. we shall begin to define the details of this and to put it into practice as soon as possible. mrs de palacio, who has begun a dialogue with you on this subject at my request, will continue her work and will continue to pursue the dialogue with the aim of concluding our agreements next january. finally, i think it is important to stress that the stages of the journey should not be too burdensome for our respective workloads, so that we can continue to assume our respective responsibilities. the 2001 budget: the list of things done in the course of a year is too long for me to be able to give a detailed account of them here and now. i would simply like to mention the areas in which the union, with the decisive contribution of the commission, achieved its greatest successes in 2001: preparation for the changeover to the euro; progress in the enlargement negotiations; relations with the balkans; the dialogue with russia; the opening of a new round of trade negotiations in doha; the adoption of a sustainable development strategy, which goes far beyond the mere adoption of a series of specific measures and will gradually lead us to a review of all our internal policies; finally, the reinvigoration, particularly visible since 11 september, of the work to create a common european area of justice and security. in each of these areas, and throughout the year, the commission's action has found decisive support in this house. turning now to 2002, in order to give you a clearer outline of our commitment for the coming year, i am equally confident that you will allow me, in presenting it to you, to group the seven priorities which the commission has indicated for its programme for 2002 into four fundamental chapters. these four major chapters are: the commission's communication on the future of the european union is based on the following three themes: internal security, the euro and economic and social issues, enlargement and, finally, the debate on the future of europe and the process of reform of the institutions. the annual strategy, which we drew up last february, had six priorities. the events of 11 september - you will all understand that such flexibility is an indispensable component of any programme to deal with unforeseen situations - have prompted us to adopt a seventh. the commission will therefore present in 2002 a series of measures to combat terrorism and organised crime and to ensure the safety of citizens. these include the launch of an integrated system of external border control, the development of civil protection, public health measures and the strengthening of transport safety. as i said in my speech in bruges on 12 november, the strengthening of judicial and police cooperation will lay the foundations for the creation, in the longer term, of an integrated police force to combat organised crime and terrorism. from the outset, this commission has indicated, as one of the four main lines of its action, the ambition to reorient the union's action, which up to that point had been essentially economic, in a broader sense, to economic, social and environmental action. the 2002 programme is no exception to this inspiration. the introduction of the euro will be the most significant and at the same time the most concrete stage in european integration. i am particularly pleased that all political differences have been overcome on the question of crossborder payments, and that president fontaine will shortly be able to announce the adoption of a common position. thanks to the efforts made on the way to the euro, our economy, although the most open in the world, is today a strong and stable one. what would have been the impact of 9/11 if we had not had the euro? stability is the basis of our future policies and we must protect it. of course, the economic situation is not easy today, but i am confident that we will be able to overcome the difficulties that arise in the short term. we have the means to do this, and i am referring in particular to the stability pact and the broad economic policy guidelines. but we must reflect on the need to improve the coordination of the budgetary policies of the euro area countries. our economies have never been so interdependent as they are now, as a result of the single currency. in this context, i recently mentioned the opportunity to work towards developing a code of conduct which, by explicitly taking into account the interdependencies between the budgetary policies of the euro area countries, would strengthen the overall coherence and credibility of our economic policy. it's rather the long term that i'm worried about. europe needs structural reforms. they are the necessary condition for long-term growth and job creation. we already have the right recipe for that. in two key stages, both in the first part of this commission's mandate - in lisbon in march 2000 and in gothenburg in june 2001 - the member states committed themselves to sustainable development, combining competitiveness, social justice and respect for the environment. the commission's work programme for 2002 confirms this approach. the implementation of the göteborg commitments is one of the seven priorities for the coming year. the same is true of the efforts to prepare for and make a success of the johannesburg meeting on sustainable development. so where does my concern come from? it is the delay in translating decisions which have already been formally adopted into concrete acts. the rock that is blocking the way for the development of galileo, an initiative and technology essential to the growth and competitiveness of the european economy, is only the latest in a series of setbacks that have gone on for too long. i do not need to mention all of them, just one example is enough: the european patent. the failure to follow up on the commitments solemnly made and announced and the lack of will to move forward on the road to the final completion of the single market are imposing very high prices on europe: the cost of non-europe, we might say the cost of non-lisbon, is rapidly becoming unbearable. the annual economic report which the commission will present in just over a month's time, in preparation for the spring council, will contain precise indications in this respect, and a decisive step will finally have to be taken in barcelona. as i said in bruges, however, the commission cannot do anything on its own: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. parliament too has a role to play: i am convinced, for example, that the lack of agreement on the new legislation on public procurement tenders has prevented a positive development of our financial markets. the weakness of the european economy in this area compared with that of the united states is still evident. the commission is aware of the many factors contributing to the well-being of the economy and will present legislative proposals of particular importance in the field of financial services and banking during 2002. we will also present a consumer protection policy strategy and measures to support private investment in research and development. one currency, one financial market, one economic policy: these are our goals. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. this will be the case in 2002 and for many years to come. we will therefore be presenting a communication in barcelona on the social aspects of company restructuring, addressed to the social partners, convinced that there is a positive correlation between social protection and competitiveness. complete enlargement and make it a success for the union as a whole: this has been the commission's number one priority since the beginning of its mandate. it was on 13 october 1999 that i asked the european council to complete the reforms necessary for enlargement by the end of 2002 and i stressed that the commission considered it possible to conclude negotiations with those countries which had fulfilled the accession criteria by that date. today, that date, 2002, has been formally adopted by the union. the progress made in two years has been impressive. we still have - and i know this - other extremely delicate negotiating stages ahead of us - think of the chapters on the structural funds or agriculture - but over the next twelve months, for those countries which, thanks to their efforts, have shown themselves to be ready, the door to accession will finally be able to open before the renewal of this assembly. 2002 will therefore be a decisive year and the commission's programme is a true reflection of the importance of this event. this is not only because, as i have just said, the negotiations must continue and then be concluded, but because the objectives and instruments corresponding to the new situation of an enlarged union with new member states must be progressively initiated and determined for each community policy. in 2002, but even more so in 2003 and 2004 - and the same will be true of our successors in the years to come - we will have to make a real intellectual revolution. the great europe will become the measure of our thinking, our planning, our action. adapting to this new european measure is essential for the commission, but it is also essential for the other institutions and for the member states of the union. we need to explain this new reality to our citizens to help them overcome their fears and appreciate the human, cultural and economic opportunities of enlargement. from an economic point of view, enlargement is one of those rare situations in which all parties involved can benefit. it will bring more growth, both for the new member states and for the fifteen. of course, the impact of enlargement will be, within the union, more or less strong from country to country, from region to region. but thanks to the single market, its benefits will be felt everywhere. this great europe cannot, however, be limited to eastward and southward expansion. it will have to continue on the path of gradual rapprochement with the balkans and promote an arc of stability at its doorstep, towards russia and ukraine and the mediterranean. in preparation for the valencia meeting in april, the commission will put forward proposals to improve the functioning and the euro-mediterranean partnership, especially in the field of education and culture. the commission will also propose in 2002 measures to stimulate investment and improve cooperation on immigration and to strengthen the union's role in the middle east peace process. enlargement is a historic achievement. it must not, however, lead to the union's paralysis. this is the background to the debate on european governance, which this commission helped to launch with its white paper. it is important that the dialogue between our two institutions on the issues raised in the white paper and the actions to be taken in the light of it should continue, and the work programme for 2002 gives precise indications in this regard. the debate on europe and the future has, however, gradually broadened far beyond the boundaries set out in the white paper to take on a more clearly constitutional nature. from the very beginning, this commission has been fighting for the union to give new impetus to the institutional debate. since september 1999, speaking before you in this very chamber, i have been strongly calling for a broader agenda to be adopted for the intergovernmental conference in 2000, beyond the 'remains of amsterdam'. i told you then that i feared a reform in the short term and, as such, incapable of giving us decisionmaking capacity. after the agreement in nice - which was essential, yes, but unquestionably minimal - the commission, together with parliament, immediately supported the idea of a convention, on which there is now general agreement. i am glad of this, because i am firmly convinced that this is the right way to build the new europe, which is more democratic and more transparent. in the meantime, a wide-ranging debate on the future of the union is already under way in all european countries. this debate must continue and help to feed the work of the convention. the time has come when we could continue to postpone the necessary reforms until tomorrow, as if events were to wait for our decisions. an important contribution to this reflection has already been made by the report by mr méndez de vigo and mr kaufmann and by the debate on it in the plenary of this parliament. in preparation for the laeken council, the commission itself presented a communication on 5 december. as we have explained in this document, which is simply intended to provide some guidance for the debate, the key to the problem is to renew and strengthen the community method. our aim must not be to alter the balances built up over the last 50 years. it is a question of modernising our system and making it feel like it belongs to the people of europe. i believe that the fruit of the work of the convention must be a coherent text, supported by a logic of its own and not by a list of expenditure; the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the text adopted by consensus, i.e. avoiding unanimity at all costs, and which, without sacrificing the necessary ambition, makes minority views visible. the commission is therefore proposing to amend the text of the charter of fundamental rights to make it simpler and easier to read, and to clarify both the principles underlying our action - and the charter of fundamental rights must be at the heart of this - and the objectives we are pursuing. a text that makes the organisation of european public authorities transparent, i.e. that clearly describes both the institutions and the instruments needed to achieve the objectives assigned to them; the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a new text which is capable of evolving and which, for this purpose, is divided into a set of basic rules and provisions of a more technical nature. before the convention's work begins, the commission will take a position on a number of issues, such as the competences of the union and the member states, the strengthening of the legislative role of parliament, the distinction between the executive and legislative functions of the council, and the executive tasks of the commission. the extension of majority voting, the procedures for revising the treaties and the union's own resources are other issues which are also the subject of political debate and which will have to be addressed in the near future. in concluding these reflections on the theme of the next convention, i would like to focus on an argument which is normally summed up in one word: the constitution. the essential thing for me is not the name given to the text which will be produced by the work of the convention and the intergovernmental conference. my aim is that this text, by its content, by the open and democratic nature of the process that has produced it, may eventually be considered by all as a constitution. i am confident that the 2002 work programme will provide the framework on which our two institutions can build an intensive, consistent and fruitful relationship of cooperation over the next 12 months. commission. – i would like to reiterate the commission's gratitude to the rapporteur and the shadow rapporteurs for the effective and constructive way in which they have participated in the discussions between the institutions over recent weeks. we are close to finding an overall compromise that will enable the regulation to be adopted without a requirement for conciliation, which will enable the european food safety authority to be established early next year. as regards the commission's position on the amendments, it is as follows. the commission can accept amendments nos 1, 7, 10, 13, 14, 16, 19, 21 to 24, 26 and 29 to 44. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 2 to 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15, 17, 18, 20, 25, 27 and 28. on the issue that has been raised by mr whitehead, as i indicated in the debate yesterday evening, i believe strongly that the seat of the authority should be chosen on rational and operational criteria that will facilitate the smooth functioning of the european food safety authority. as such, i can support the principles expressed in the resolution referred to by mr whitehead. (applause)
in writing. - present on 30 000 farms in the european union, the cultivation of grass and legume seeds, the main species covered by this common market organization, is of great importance for employment, the income of producers, the socioeconomic balance of many regions, biodiversity and security of supply. but on the one hand, market prices received by producers have fluctuated considerably in recent years and on the other hand, the european union is still running a deficit of some 15 000 tonnes. the maintenance of the seed aid at the current level is therefore to be welcomed, as it is necessary to maintain the balance between production and the market; in these circumstances, i do not think it is necessary to introduce a budgetary stabiliser, since the market has shown its capacity for self-regulation, especially since the commission's proposal for this stabilisation mechanism is general and vague. finally, i do not think it would be appropriate to use the model for rice seeds, which can be used as a bargaining chip on the food market. finally, and most importantly, it would be unwise to allocate a maximum guaranteed quantity between member states, since seed firms are often located in more than one country. that is the meaning of the amendments which i tabled in committee and which were adopted unanimously. i am glad to see that parliament has shared this wisdom in the plenary.
in writing. - we abstained on all reports on the fisheries agreements with guinea-bissau and cape verde because, while they provide a certain income to these states, they only formalize the plundering of the natural resources of guinea-bissau and cape verde by the large-scale fishing of european countries. the only reason we voted for amendments nos 7 to the lage report and 5 to the cunha report is that they at least have the merit of formalising a specific amount for financial compensation, without however prejudging the question of whether this amount actually compensates for the loss of this natural resource.
in writing. - the establishment of a 'european food authority' to monitor food safety at eu level could be a useful thing for consumers. we agree with the principle. but we would point out that, unlike similar administrations in other countries, notably the united states, the european food authority will have only an advisory role and no powers. what will his recommendations be worth in these circumstances? especially as many recent food scandals, from mad cow to chicken to dioxin, have shown that food security and the pursuit of profit are contradictory. the european food authority may, in these circumstances, be a purely decorative body.
in writing. - i voted for this report. we have been trying for years to restore consumer confidence, and the european food safety authority is one of the elements that fits into this context. there is no such thing as zero risk, and we know the consequences that a bacteriological problem (not just terrorism) would have on the greatest number of citizens. safety must therefore be at the heart of the planned system. we must not be alarmed, however, because we must not forget that the european food chain is one of the safest in the world, but in order to be effective and credible, the authority will have to surround itself with the best scientific experts, while relying on the network of existing national agencies. another important aspect to be emphasized is the necessary separation between risk assessment, which is a scientific matter, and risk management (decided measures), which is a matter for policy. i would remind you that the measures decided upon must be proportionate to the level of risk involved. in the case of a perceived risk, but without any basis - in the case of a rumor for example - a response should be provided by a communication to consumers. in the event of a potential risk, a precautionary measure must be taken; finally, in the event of a real risk, preventive measures are necessary. if we want maximum efficiency, the european food safety authority must be completely independent - the composition of its bodies will be decisive - and must be very transparent in its decisions. finally, the penalties for serious misconduct or fraud must not only be substantial but also be strictly enforced.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this recommendation because i believe that the common position as amended makes important improvements compared with the commission's original proposal. i fully agree with the wish expressed by the european institutions: the future european food safety authority must be set up very quickly and start its activities at the beginning of 2002. in this respect, i supported the rapporteur in his desire to see a text adopted which could be agreed by the council in order to avoid a conciliation procedure, which is always too long. the european food safety authority will be strong and will, i hope, help to control food-related risks better throughout the european union. monitoring and control will remain the responsibility of the member states, while risk management and the early warning system will remain the responsibility of the european commission. finally, i approve of the adoption of criteria for selecting, in the general interest, the best site for the european food safety authority: the city of lille seems to me to fully meet the conditions required by this recommendation.
